$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and

derivations.claim: The matrix commutators are antisymmetric and the odd-odd brackets are symmetric under interchange of the full generator labels: for the same-chirality bracket, $\epsilon_{\beta\alpha}Z^{JI}=(-\epsilon_{\alpha\beta})(-Z^{IJ})=\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ}$, and the dotted case is identical. The mixed bracket is symmetric by its Kronecker delta and the graded-skew rule. Each listed bracket has parity equal to the sum of its input parities, so the bracket is degree-preserving and graded-skew.

For matrices $X,Y,Z$, both $X(YZ-ZY)-(YZ-ZY)X$ and $(XY-YX)Z-Z(XY-YX)+Y(XZ-ZX)-(XZ-ZX)Y$ expand to $XYZ-XZY-YZX+ZYX$, so the commutator on $\mathfrak l$ satisfies Jacobi. Write $\rho_V(A,B)=A\otimes I+I\otimes B$. Operators acting on different tensor factors commute, hence $[\rho_V(A,B),\rho_V(A',B')]=[A,A']\otimes I+I\otimes[B,B']=\rho_V([(A,B),(A',B')])$. The two fundamental odd actions are representations by the same matrix-commutator identity, and the actions on $C_N$ and by $V$ are zero. Thus $\mathfrak l$ acts by representations on the abelian space $V\oplus C_N$ and on $\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$; expanding the even Jacobi identity leaves precisely these representation identities, while brackets internal to $V\oplus C_N$ vanish.

For two even inputs and one odd input, the Jacobi expression is $[\rho(L),\rho(L')]q-\rho([L,L'])q$, which is zero by the fundamental-action identities in [F1]; if either even input lies in $V\oplus C_N$, its odd action is zero and the same expression vanishes. This checks all orderings of the two-even/one-odd case by graded skew-symmetry.

For one even input $L=(A,B)$ and two odd inputs, Jacobi is equivariance of their odd bracket. On a mixed pair, the two fundamental actions on $Q$ and $\bar Q$ give exactly $A\otimes I+I\otimes B$ on $T$, so the mixed bracket is equivariant. On an equal-chirality pair, writing $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{pmatrix}$ gives $A^{\mathsf T}\epsilon+\epsilon A=0$ by direct multiplication; the identical calculation for $B$ preserves the dotted alternating form. The flavor tensors $Z^{IJ}$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ are Lorentz scalars, so both central brackets are equivariant. Even inputs from $V\oplus C_N$ act trivially on each side.

The given star squares to the identity on each generator. On the matrix-commutator bracket, entrywise conjugation preserves matrix multiplication and the minus signs in $(A,B)^*$ reverse the bracket; on the fundamental and tensor actions, star exchanges the two spinor factors and the corresponding minus sign gives $[x,y]^*=-[x^*,y^*]$. On odd-odd brackets, star exchanges $Q$ with $\bar Q$, transposes the bispinor indices of $T$, and exchanges $Z$ with $\bar Z$; the real alternating-form coefficients and antisymmetric flavor labels give $[x,y]^*=[x^*,y^*]$, as required for two odd inputs. Zero brackets remain zero. For homogeneous even-even, even-odd and odd-odd inputs, substituting these identities into $\tau=-*$, $i*$ and $-*$ respectively gives $\tau([x,y])=[\tau x,\tau y]$; conjugate-linearity gives $\tau^2=I$. Therefore the fixed space is closed under the bracket. Every $x$ decomposes as $x_+ + i x_-$ with $x_+=(x+\tau x)/2$ and $x_-=(x-\tau x)/(2i)$ fixed by $\tau$, so this fixed real algebra complexifies to the displayed graded algebra.

For three odd inputs, each inner bracket lies in $V\oplus C_N$. Both summands act trivially on the odd space, so each of the three terms in the odd-odd-odd super-Jacobi identity is zero. The four parity patterns checked in the preceding cases exhaust homogeneous triples, and multilinearity gives the identity for arbitrary triples.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following

derivations.claim: The function $s(p)=-\eta^{\mu\nu}p_\mu p_\nu=(p^0)^2-|\vec p|^2$ is continuous and nonnegative on the closed future cone in [F1]. For each Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$, $\{p\in\mathcal C_+^*:s(p)\in A\}$ is Borel in the full covector space because $\mathcal C_+^*$ is closed and $s$ is continuous there. Inverse images preserve disjoint unions, and the preimage of $[0,\infty)$ is $\mathcal C_+^*$, whose projection is $I$ by [F1]; therefore the pushforward $F(A):=E(\{p\in\mathcal C_+^*:s(p)\in A\})$ is a normalized PVM on $[0,\infty)$ by strong countable additivity of $E$.

For each Borel $A$, $F(A)$ is the projection $E(\{p\in\mathcal C_+^*:s(p)\in A\})$. The charge-domain reduction in [F1] therefore gives $F(A)D(Q)\subseteq D(Q)$ and $QF(A)\psi=F(A)Q\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q)$; the same argument applies to $Q^*$. This proves the spectral-subspace assertion.

Since $s(\Lambda_g^\vee p)=s(p)$, Lorentz covariance of $E$ implies $U(g,0)F(A)U(g,0)^*=F(A)$. Translation unitaries are bounded Borel functions of $E$, so they commute with every $F(A)$; $\Gamma$ commutes with $E$ by [F1]. Hence $\operatorname{ran}F(A)$ is closed and graded, invariant under the integrated even group, and invariant under every charge and adjoint with dense restricted domains: density follows by applying the bounded projection $F(A)$ to a dense operator domain. Irreducibility as defined in [F1] forces $F(A)=0$ or $F(A)=I$.

Choose any nonzero vector and normalize it to a unit vector $\psi\in\mathcal H$; set $\mu(A)=\langle F(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$. By [F3] this is a countably additive probability measure, and by step 2.2 every value is $0$ or $1$. The set $R=\{r\ge0:\mu([0,r])=1\}$ is nonempty: otherwise the countable union $[0,\infty)=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[0,n]$ would have measure zero. Put $m^2=\inf R$, which is a finite nonnegative real.

For every $\varepsilon>0$, the infimum property gives $r\in R$ with $r<m^2+\varepsilon$, so $\mu([0,m^2+\varepsilon])=1$. If $m^2>\varepsilon$, then $m^2-\varepsilon<m^2$ is not in $R$, and the zero-or-one property gives $\mu([0,m^2-\varepsilon])=0$. Thus for all sufficiently large $n$, the nested intervals $I_n=(\max(0,m^2-1/n),m^2+1/n]$ have measure one; when $m^2=0$, use $I_n=[0,1/n]$. Countable additivity of the finite measure gives continuity from above, hence $\mu(\{m^2\})=\lim_n\mu(I_n)=1$. Therefore $F(\{m^2\})\ne0$, and step 2.2 forces $F(\{m^2\})=I$. If $A$ contains $m^2$, monotonicity gives $F(A)=I$; if not, then $\mu(A)=0$ because $A$ is disjoint from $\{m^2\}$, so the zero-or-one property gives $F(A)=0$. This rule also proves uniqueness: any second value with projection $I$ would have to equal $m^2$, since the singleton projections for distinct values are orthogonal.

By [F4], $m^2$ has a unique nonnegative square root $m$. Step 2.1 shows that each charge maps vectors in a fixed mass-squared subspace into that same subspace; step 4.1 shows there is only one such spectral value in the irreducible representation. The argument uses the pushforward PVM rather than a normalizable sharp-momentum vector, and it includes $m=0$ without introducing a rest frame.

If an additional unitary group $V(g)$ preserves $D(Q)$ and satisfies $V(g)Q\psi=QV(g)\psi$ there, then for every $\psi\in D(Q)$ one has $V(g)(Q\psi)=Q(V(g)\psi)$; this is exactly the intertwining relation. Without that additional commutation hypothesis no gauge representation equality follows.

derivations.claim: At rest $P_0=-M I$ and $P_j=0$, so [F1] gives $\{Q^I_1,(Q^J_1)^*\}=2M\delta_{IJ}I$ and $\{Q^I_2,(Q^J_2)^*\}=2M\delta_{IJ}I$. Put $q_I=Q^I_1$ and $r_I=(Q^I_2)^*$; then $\{q_I,r_J^*\}=2z^{IJ}I$ and $\{r_J,q_I^*\}=2\bar z_{IJ}I$, with all these products defined on $\mathcal D$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb C^N$, define on $\mathcal D$ the charge combination $B_{u,v}=\sum_I\bar u_Iq_I+\sum_I\bar v_Ir_I$ and the combination of its summand adjoints $B^\sharp_{u,v}=\sum_Iu_Iq_I^*+\sum_Iv_Ir_I^*$. Expanding the algebraic anticommutator on $\mathcal D$ gives $B_{u,v}B^\sharp_{u,v}+B^\sharp_{u,v}B_{u,v}=\left(2M(\|u\|_2^2+\|v\|_2^2)+4\operatorname{Re}(u^*Zv)\right)I$. The diagonal blocks use the two mixed rest anticommutators in step 1.1, and the off-diagonal terms are $2u^*Zv$ and its complex conjugate. For every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, expanding the quadratic form term by term and using the adjoint identity for each individual charge gives $\langle(B_{u,v}B^\sharp_{u,v}+B^\sharp_{u,v}B_{u,v})\psi,\psi\rangle=\|B_{u,v}\psi\|^2+\|B^\sharp_{u,v}\psi\|^2\ge0$.

Fix a unit vector $v\in\mathbb C^N$. If $Zv\ne0$, choose $u=-Zv/\|Zv\|_2$, so $\|u\|_2=1$ and $u^*Zv=-\|Zv\|_2$. Applying step 2.1 to any nonzero $\psi\in\mathcal D$ yields $0\le4(M-\|Zv\|_2)\|\psi\|^2$, hence $M\ge\|Zv\|_2$. If $Zv=0$, the same inequality follows from $M>0$. Taking the supremum over all unit $v$ proves $M\ge\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

When $N=2$, $Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&z\\-z&0\end{pmatrix}$, so direct multiplication gives $Z^*Z=|z|^2I_2$ and therefore $\|Zv\|_2=|z|\|v\|_2$ for every $v$; thus $\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|z|$. With $q=Q^1_1$ and $r=Q^2_2$, expanding $A=q-e^{i\phi}r^*$ and $A^\sharp=q^*-e^{-i\phi}r$ gives $AA^\sharp+A^\sharp A=\{q,q^*\}+\{r^*,r\}-e^{-i\phi}\{q,r\}-e^{i\phi}\{r^*,q^*\}=2M+2M-2e^{-i\phi}z-2e^{i\phi}\bar z=4(M-|z|)I$ on $\mathcal D$. If $M=|z|$, step 4.1 gives $AA^\sharp+A^\sharp A=0$ on $\mathcal D$. The result is confined to the fixed rest fiber and asserts no state existence or stability.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

A **(possibly unbounded) linear operator on $H$** is a linear map
$T:D(T)\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]) whose **domain** $D(T)\subseteq H$ is a linear
subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

Therefore $Q$ maps $E_\lambda$ into itself.

The domain of $H$ is invariant under $\Gamma$: if $\psi\in D(H)$, then $\Gamma\psi\in D(Q)$ by hypothesis and $Q\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q\psi\in D(Q)$ because $Q\psi\in D(Q)$ and $D(Q)$ is $\Gamma$-invariant. Applying the anticommutation relation twice gives $H\Gamma\psi=\Gamma H\psi$. Hence $\Gamma E_\lambda=E_\lambda$, and $Q\Gamma=-\Gamma Q$ shows that $Q$ maps $E_\lambda^+$ to $E_\lambda^-$ and $E_\lambda^-$ to $E_\lambda^+$.

For $\psi,\varphi\in E_\lambda$, both vectors lie in $D(Q)$ and $Q\psi\in D(Q)$, by [F2], the adjoint is taken in the complete Hilbert space; self-adjointness in [F5] and the identity in [F4] give $\langle Q\psi,Q\varphi\rangle=\langle Q^2\psi,\varphi\rangle=\lambda\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle$. By [F6], and since $\sqrt\lambda$ is nonzero in the complex field by [F7], division by $\sqrt\lambda$ therefore makes $Q$ an isometry on $E_\lambda$. Also $(Q/\sqrt\lambda)^2\psi=Q^2\psi/\lambda=\psi$ there. Together with the parity exchange in step 2.1, this proves that the restriction $U_\lambda:E_\lambda^+\to E_\lambda^-$ is an isometry with inverse the restriction from $E_\lambda^-$ to $E_\lambda^+$; it is consequently unitary and the finite dimensions agree.

If $\psi\in\ker H$, then $\psi\in D(Q^2)$, so $Q\psi\in D(Q)$. By [F2], [F5] and the adjoint identity [F4], $\|Q\psi\|^2=\langle Q\psi,Q\psi\rangle=\langle Q^2\psi,\psi\rangle=0$. Positive definiteness in [F1] forces $Q\psi=0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Choose an embedded smooth submanifold $S\subset X$ of codimension $k$, a smooth positive density $\mu_S$, and an open neighborhood $U\subset X$ of a point $s\in S$. Embedded means that near each point of $S$, a smooth chart on $X$ identifies $S$ with $\mathbb R^{n-k}\times\{0\}$. A **gauge condition** on $U$ is a smooth map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R^k$ such that $U\cap S=\chi^{-1}(0)$ and, for every $s'\in U\cap S$, $d\chi_{s'}$ is surjective with kernel $T_{s'}S$. For every $x\in U$, the **infinitesimal orbit map** is $R_x:=d(\alpha_x)_e:\mathfrak k\to T_xX$, where $\alpha_x(g)=x\cdot g$; call its kernel the infinitesimal stabilizer at $x$. The **Faddeev–Popov operator** at $x$ is the ordinary linear map $M_x:=d\chi_x\circ R_x:\mathfrak k\to\mathbb R^k$. At a slice point $s'\in U\cap S$, call the condition **transverse** when $M_{s'}$ is an isomorphism. Choose a positive density $\nu$ on $\mathfrak k$ equal to $(\mu_K)_e$, and the standard positive density $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For every $x\in U$, the finite-dimensional Faddeev–Popov Jacobian $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)$ is the nonnegative density ratio defined by $M_x^*\lambda=\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)\nu$; in chosen bases it is $|\det M_x|$, and it is zero when $M_x$ is singular.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

citations.quote: A **finite-dimensional regulated gauge-slice datum** consists of integers $1\le k\le n$; a finite-dimensional Lie group $K$ of dimension $k$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak k:=T_eK$ and bracket transported from left-invariant vector fields; a chosen smooth positive left-invariant density $\mu_K$, meaning $(L_h^K)^*\mu_K=\mu_K$ for $L_h^K(g)=hg$; a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ with a chosen smooth positive density $\mu_X$; and a smooth right action $\alpha:X\times K\to X$, written $x\cdot g$, with $x\cdot e=x$ and $(x\cdot g)\cdot h=x\cdot(gh)$. A smooth positive density on an $m$-manifold has coordinate form $\rho(x)|dx^1\cdots dx^m|$ with smooth $\rho>0$, and transforms by the absolute coordinate Jacobian. The group $K$ and its action on $X$ are separate regulator data. They are not identified with the full gauge group or the full space of connections unless a particular finite model explicitly constructs such an action and verifies that it preserves $X$.

Choose an embedded smooth submanifold $S\subset X$ of codimension $k$, a smooth positive density $\mu_S$, and an open neighborhood $U\subset X$ of a point $s\in S$. Embedded means that near each point of $S$, a smooth chart on $X$ identifies $S$ with $\mathbb R^{n-k}\times\{0\}$. A **gauge condition** on $U$ is a smooth map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R^k$ such that $U\cap S=\chi^{-1}(0)$ and, for every $s'\in U\cap S$, $d\chi_{s'}$ is surjective with kernel $T_{s'}S$. For every $x\in U$, the **infinitesimal orbit map** is $R_x:=d(\alpha_x)_e:\mathfrak k\to T_xX$, where $\alpha_x(g)=x\cdot g$; call its kernel the infinitesimal stabilizer at $x$. The **Faddeev–Popov operator** at $x$ is the ordinary linear map $M_x:=d\chi_x\circ R_x:\mathfrak k\to\mathbb R^k$. At a slice point $s'\in U\cap S$, call the condition **transverse** when $M_{s'}$ is an isomorphism. Choose a positive density $\nu$ on $\mathfrak k$ equal to $(\mu_K)_e$, and the standard positive density $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For every $x\in U$, the finite-dimensional Faddeev–Popov Jacobian $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)$ is the nonnegative density ratio defined by $M_x^*\lambda=\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)\nu$; in chosen bases it is $|\det M_x|$, and it is zero when $M_x$ is singular.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $(X,K,\alpha,S,\chi,\mu_X,\mu_K,\mu_S)$ be finite-dimensional regulated gauge-slice data as defined above, with $\dim X=n$, $\dim K=k$, $1\le k\le n$, and $s_0\in S\cap U$. Thus $K$ acts smoothly on the right, $S$ is an embedded codimension-$k$ submanifold, $\chi:U\to\mathbb R^k$ is a smooth defining submersion with $\ker d\chi_s=T_sS$, and the Faddeev–Popov operator is $M_s=d\chi_s\circ R_s$. Suppose $M_{s_0}$ is an isomorphism. For $\Psi(g,s)=s\cdot g$, there are neighborhoods $V$ of the identity in $K$, $W$ of $s_0$ in $S$, and $O$ of $s_0$ in $X$ such that $\Psi:V\times W\to O$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. Consequently, each orbit has exactly one representative in $W$ among the representatives reached using $V$.

Fix group coordinates $\xi$ near the identity, slice coordinates $z$ near $s_0$, and adapted target coordinates $(y,z)=(\chi,z)$ near $s_0$. Write the densities there as $\mu_K=\rho_K(\xi)|d\xi|$, $\mu_S=\rho_S(z)|dz|$, and $\mu_X=\rho_X(y,z)|dy\,dz|$. The positive Jacobian $J_\Psi$ defined by $\Psi^*\mu_X=J_\Psi(\mu_K\otimes\mu_S)$ satisfies

$$
J_\Psi(e,s_0)=\frac{\rho_X(0,z_0)}{\rho_S(z_0)}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(s_0),
$$

where $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}$ uses the density $(\mu_K)_e$ and the standard density on $\mathbb R^k$. Thus, when the target and slice densities are normalized so that $\rho_X(0,z_0)=\rho_S(z_0)$, the ordinary finite-dimensional orbit-to-slice Jacobian is exactly $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(s_0)$. For every compactly supported Riemann-integrable function $f:O\to\mathbb R$, the local change-of-variables identity is
$$
\int_O f\,d\mu_X=\int_{V\times W}(f\circ\Psi)J_\Psi\,d\mu_K\,d\mu_S.
$$

For the exact multiplicity statement, fix $x\in X$ and a relatively compact open set $\Gamma\subset K$ such that $x\cdot\overline{\Gamma}\subset U$. Let $F_x(g)=\chi(x\cdot g)$. Let $r\ge 0$ be finite, and suppose $F_x$ has exactly $r$ zeros $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ in the support of a smooth function $\varphi$ compactly supported in $\Gamma$, each $M_{x\cdot g_i}$ is invertible, and the slice points $s_i=x\cdot g_i$ are distinct. Choose a nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$, supported in a ball $B_C(0)$ of finite radius $C>0$, with integral $1$, and set $\eta_\epsilon(y)=\epsilon^{-k}\eta(y/\epsilon)$. Then

$$
\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_\Gamma \varphi(g)\,\eta_\epsilon(F_x(g))\,\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x\cdot g)\,d\mu_K(g)=\sum_{i=1}^r\varphi(g_i).
$$

In particular, if $\varphi=1$ near the zeros, this finite-regulator expression counts the $r$ distinct transverse intersections exactly. The theorem asserts only a local chart and this finite-dimensional multiplicity formula; it gives no global gauge section, functional determinant, or continuum path-integral measure.

derivations.claim: Choose a positively oriented orthonormal coframe $e^1,e^2,e^3,e^4$ of $V^*$. The defining wedge identity gives $*_g e^{12}=e^{34}$, $*_g e^{13}=-e^{24}$, $*_g e^{14}=e^{23}$, $*_g e^{23}=e^{14}$, $*_g e^{24}=-e^{13}$, and $*_g e^{34}=e^{12}$. Thus $*_g$ permutes the orthonormal basis of $\Lambda^2V^*$ with signs, so it is an isometry; applying it twice to each of the six basis vectors gives $*_g^2=I$. The same conclusions hold after tensoring each basis vector with any member of an orthonormal basis of $W$.

For $\Phi^+=\tfrac12(\Phi+*_g\Phi)$ and $\Phi^-=\tfrac12(\Phi-*_g\Phi)$, the identity $*_g^2=I$ from step 1.1 gives $*_g\Phi^+=\Phi^+$, $*_g\Phi^-=-\Phi^-$, and $\Phi=\Phi^++\Phi^-$. If $*_g\alpha=\alpha$ and $*_g\beta=-\beta$, the isometry property from step 1.1 gives $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\langle *_g\alpha,*_g\beta\rangle=-\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$, hence $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=0$. The decomposition is unique because the intersection of the two eigenspaces is zero.

Under $\widehat g=\lambda^2g$, the induced inner product on $\Lambda^2V^*$ scales by $\lambda^{-4}$ because each covector factor scales by $\lambda^{-2}$, while the oriented volume form scales by $\lambda^4$. Hence for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^2V^*$, $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\widehat g}\,\mathrm{vol}_{\widehat g}=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$. The defining wedge identity therefore gives $\alpha\wedge *_{\widehat g}\beta=\alpha\wedge *_g\beta$ for every $\alpha$; nondegeneracy of the wedge pairing between two-forms in dimension four implies $*_{\widehat g}\beta=*_g\beta$. The identity extends $W$-linearly.

citations.quote:
Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

A **finite-dimensional real Lie group** is a group $G$, in the sense of
[[def-group]], together with the structure of a finite-dimensional real smooth
manifold such that the maps

$$m:G\times G\longrightarrow G,\qquad m(g,h)=gh,$$

and

$$\operatorname{inv}:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad \operatorname{inv}(g)=g^{-1},$$

are smooth in the sense of
[[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]. Its identity element is
denoted by $e$ (or occasionally $1$).

Unless an item explicitly says otherwise, every Lie group on this page is real,
finite-dimensional, and has no manifold boundary. Dimension zero is allowed;
for example, any countable discrete group with its discrete zero-dimensional
smooth structure is a Lie group. A Lie group cannot be empty because a group
contains its identity. The definition applies unchanged in dimension one,
uses no metric or nondegeneracy hypothesis, and makes no choice from a family
of sets.

derivations.claim: The generated equivalence classes contain one representative from each chart copy exactly when the base point is in $U\cap V$: the transition $(x,h)_V\mapsto(x,\tau(x)h)_U$ is bijective there, with inverse $(x,k)_U\mapsto(x,\tau(x)^{-1}k)_V$ by [F2]. Thus the canonical maps $j_U:U\times G\to P$ and $j_V:V\times G\to P$ are injective. For every open $W\subseteq U\times G$, the preimage of $j_U(W)$ in $Q$ is the open subset $W_U$ together with the inverse transition image of $W|_{(U\cap V)\times G}$ in the $V$ copy; hence $j_U(W)$ is open in the quotient. The same argument applies to $j_V$, so these maps are open embeddings and their images give product charts covering $P$. On their overlap $j_U^{-1}j_V(x,h)=(x,\tau(x)h)$, a diffeomorphism with inverse $(x,k)\mapsto(x,\tau(x)^{-1}k)$ by [F2]. Therefore these product charts define a smooth atlas on $P$.

The induced projection is continuous because the two product projections agree on the equivalence relation. If two points of $P$ project to distinct points of $X$, disjoint base neighborhoods separate them since $X$ is Hausdorff. If they project to the same $x$, choose $U$ or $V$ containing $x$; both points lie in that product chart, where distinct group coordinates have disjoint neighborhoods because the chart is Hausdorff. Hence $P$ is Hausdorff. Each product chart is second-countable, and the union of countable bases from the two charts is a countable base for $P$. The coordinate changes are smooth by step 1.1, so the resulting smooth manifold structure has the required separation and countability properties.

The formula $[x,h]_i\cdot k=[x,hk]_i$ is well-defined because $(x,\tau(x)h)_U\cdot k=(x,\tau(x)hk)_U\sim(x,hk)_V$; associativity and the identity law follow from the group law. In each chart it is the smooth product action by [F2], and it is free and transitive on each fibre because right multiplication on the $G$ coordinate has those properties. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, the charts are smooth product charts and $P$ is Hausdorff and second-countable. The map $\pi$ is smooth and locally the product projection, so [F1] applies and $P\to X$ is a smooth right principal $G$-bundle. The sections $s_U,s_V$ are smooth in these charts, and $[x,e]_V=[x,\tau(x)]_U$ gives $s_V=s_U\tau$.
