citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $G$ be a Lie group and $M$ a smooth manifold. A **smooth left action** of
$G$ on $M$ is a jointly smooth map

$$a:G\times M\longrightarrow M,\qquad (g,x)\longmapsto g\mathbin{\cdot}x,$$

such that, for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in M$,

$$e\mathbin{\cdot}x=x,\qquad (gh)\mathbin{\cdot}x=g\mathbin{\cdot}(h\mathbin{\cdot}x).$$

For each $g$, the map $a_g(x)=g\cdot x$ is then a diffeomorphism with inverse
$a_{g^{-1}}$. Joint smoothness is part of the definition; separate
smoothness of individual orbit maps is not substituted for it.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).
Under countable choice, every smooth manifold, also with boundary, admits a Riemannian metric.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every $(p,v)\in TM$ there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with $\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma'_{p,v}(0)=v$. Each $I_{p,v}$ is an open interval containing zero, the domain
$$\mathcal G=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$$
is open, and $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

Let $F:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ be a local Riemannian isometry between smooth Riemannian manifolds without boundary. For every $p\in M$, there are open neighborhoods $U\ni p$ and $V\ni F(p)$ such that $f=F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism and
$$df\bigl(\nabla^M_XY\bigr)=\nabla^N_{f_*X}(f_*Y)\circ f$$
for all smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $U$, where $\nabla^M$ and $\nabla^N$ are the Levi-Civita connections.

Consequently, if $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior, $\gamma:I\to M$ is smooth, and $W$ is a smooth vector field along $\gamma$, then
$$D_t^N\bigl(dF_{\gamma(t)}W(t)\bigr)=dF_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_t^M W(t)\bigr).$$
In particular, $F\circ\gamma$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic whenever $\gamma$ is. No completeness, connectedness, surjectivity, or length-minimizing hypothesis is required.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Choose a smooth Riemannian metric \(g_0\) by [F3], let \(\mu\) be the normalized Haar probability measure from [F2], and define
\[
g_p(v,w):=\int_T (g_0)_{t^{-1}p}\bigl((d a_{t^{-1}})_p v,(d a_{t^{-1}})_p w\bigr)\,d\mu(t)
\]
for \(p\in M\) and \(v,w\in T_pM\). [A1, F2, F3, construct]

In every pair of local tangent-bundle frames the integrand in step 1.1 is smooth in \(p\) and the torus coordinates; repeated application of [F4] on \([0,1]^r\) shows that the coefficients of \(g\) are smooth. Each integrand is a symmetric bilinear form, and for \(v\ne0\) its value on \((v,v)\) is strictly positive because \(d a_{t^{-1}}\) is invertible. Its continuous positive value has a positive minimum on compact \(T\) by [F5], so the integral is positive and \(g\) is a Riemannian metric. For \(s\in T\), translation invariance of \(\mu\), with the change of variable \(t=su\), gives \(g_{sp}(d a_s v,d a_s w)=g_p(v,w)\). Thus \(g\) is \(T\)-invariant. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

For each \(t\in T\), the equalizer \(\{p:a(t,p)=p\}\) is closed: if \(a(t,p)\ne p\), Hausdorffness gives disjoint neighborhoods of \(p\) and \(a(t,p)\), and continuity gives a neighborhood of \(p\) disjoint from the equalizer. Hence \(F\), their intersection, is closed in compact \(M\), and is compact. [F1, given, step 2.1]

Fix \(p\in F\). Each \(a_t\) is a \(g\)-isometry fixing \(p\); its differential \(\rho_p(t)=(d a_t)_p\) is an orthogonal linear action on \(T_pM\). The geodesic exponential \(\exp_p\) is defined and smooth near zero by [F6], has differential the identity at zero by the initial-velocity definition of a geodesic, and is a local diffeomorphism there by [F8]. Isometries preserve geodesics by [F7], so uniqueness in [F6] gives \(a_t(\exp_p v)=\exp_p(\rho_p(t)v)\) wherever both sides are defined. Choose a sufficiently small \(\rho_p(T)\)-invariant ball about zero on which \(\exp_p\) is injective; in its image the fixed set is exactly the image of the linear fixed subspace \((T_pM)^T\). These charts show that \(F\) is an embedded submanifold near every \(p\in F\) and \(T_pF=(T_pM)^T\). Since \(F\) is compact, its connected components are finite in number: its components are open in the manifold \(F\), so compactness gives a finite subcover by component neighborhoods. [F1, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1]

The orthogonal complement \(
u_{F,p}=(T_pF)^\perp\) has no fixed vector, since the fixed subspace is precisely \(T_pF\) by step 4.1. Complexify \(
u_{F,p}\); the commuting orthogonal transformations \(ho_p(t)\) become commuting unitary transformations, so simultaneous diagonalization decomposes the complexified fiber into character eigenspaces. Every character is nontrivial because the fixed eigenspace has been removed. A self-inverse character of the connected group \(T\) has image in \(\{1,-1\}\) and is therefore trivial; hence complex conjugation pairs the remaining \(\chi\) and \(\chi^{-1}\) eigenspaces. Using the fixed lattice identification, retain the character whose first nonzero integer coordinate is positive from each pair; this equips the real normal fiber with a \(T\)-invariant complex structure and orientation. For a character \(\chi\), the operator \(P_\chi=\int_T\overline{\chi(t)}ho_p(t)\,d\mu(t)\) is the orthogonal projection onto its \(\chi\)-eigenspace: on a \(\psi\)-eigenvector it acts by the scalar \(\int_T\overline{\chi(t)}\psi(t)\,d\mu(t)\). If \(\psi=\chi\), this integral is \(1\). If \(\psi
e\chi\), then \(	heta=\overline\chi\psi\) is a nontrivial character; choose \(t_0\in T\) with \(	heta(t_0)
e1\). Translation invariance gives \(I=\int_T	heta(t)\,d\mu(t)=\int_T	heta(t_0t)\,d\mu(t)=	heta(t_0)I\), so \(I=0\). The character averages are therefore exactly the eigenspace projections. Their coefficients vary smoothly with \(p\) by [F4]. Their ranks are integer-valued and continuous, hence locally constant, so they form smooth subbundles. At each \(p\), finitely many weight projections have ranks summing to the full fiber dimension; their ranks remain constant on a neighborhood, leaving no dimension for any other weight there. Thus the finite weight list is locally constant, and compactness of \(F\) gives a finite cover by such neighborhoods, so only finitely many weights occur globally. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

If \(r=0\), the action is trivial, \(F=M\), and \(\nu_F=0\), so the weight assertion is vacuous. If \(M\) is empty, all asserted submanifolds and bundles are empty. Otherwise the construction applies componentwise and uses no assumption on connectedness of \(M\). [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 3.1, step 5.1] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $r\geq 0$, let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$ with its product Lie-group structure, and let $M$ be a compact, finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. Let $a:T\times M\to M$ be a jointly smooth left action. Then $M$ admits a smooth Riemannian metric invariant under $a$. Its fixed set
$$
F=M^T:=\{p\in M:a(t,p)=p\text{ for every }t\in T\}
$$
is a compact embedded smooth submanifold with finitely many connected components, and $T_pF=(T_pM)^T$ for each $p\in F$. The orthogonal normal bundle $\nu_F=(TF)^\perp\subset TM|_F$ has no nonzero $T$-fixed vectors in any fiber. On each connected component of $F$, its normal representation has a finite weight decomposition into nontrivial characters of $T$, with constant multiplicities; equivalently, $\nu_F$ admits a smooth $T$-invariant complex structure and orientation on each component.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a smooth action of $G$ on $M$ and $x\in M$,
the map

$$\overline\Phi_x:G/G_x\longrightarrow M,\qquad gG_x\longmapsto g\cdot x,$$

is a $G$-equivariant injective immersion with image $G\cdot x$. Transporting
the quotient structure through this map gives the orbit its canonical
immersed homogeneous-space structure. The immersion need not be an embedding.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every $(p,v)\in TM$ there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with $\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma'_{p,v}(0)=v$. Each $I_{p,v}$ is an open interval containing zero, the domain
$$\mathcal G=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$$
is open, and $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

Let $F:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ be a local Riemannian isometry between smooth Riemannian manifolds without boundary. For every $p\in M$, there are open neighborhoods $U\ni p$ and $V\ni F(p)$ such that $f=F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism and
$$df\bigl(\nabla^M_XY\bigr)=\nabla^N_{f_*X}(f_*Y)\circ f$$
for all smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $U$, where $\nabla^M$ and $\nabla^N$ are the Levi-Civita connections.

Consequently, if $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior, $\gamma:I\to M$ is smooth, and $W$ is a smooth vector field along $\gamma$, then
$$D_t^N\bigl(dF_{\gamma(t)}W(t)\bigr)=dF_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_t^M W(t)\bigr).$$
In particular, $F\circ\gamma$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic whenever $\gamma$ is. No completeness, connectedness, surjectivity, or length-minimizing hypothesis is required.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: For a point \(x\in M\), let \(H=T_x\). By [F2], \(O=T\cdot x\) has the intrinsic manifold \(T/H\) and its orbit map into \(M\) is a continuous injective immersion. The domain \(T/H\) is compact as a continuous image of compact \(T\), and \(M\) is Hausdorff, so [F5] makes the orbit map a homeomorphism onto \(O\); together with immersion this makes \(O\) an embedded submanifold. [A1, F2, F5]

Now let \(S\subseteq M\) be any compact invariant embedded submanifold and write \(E(p,v)=\exp_p(v)\) on the open set where the geodesic exists up to time \(1\). The geodesic theorem in [F3] makes this a smooth map on an open neighborhood of the zero section. At \((p,0)\), its differential on \(T_pS\oplus\nu_p(S)\) is \((u,w)\mapsto u+w\): on the zero section \(E(p,0)=p\), while \(\frac{d}{ds}|_{s=0}E(p,sw)=w\) by the initial-velocity definition and time rescaling of the geodesic. This is an isomorphism because \(T_pM=T_pS\oplus\nu_p(S)\), so [F4] makes \(E\) a local diffeomorphism at every point of the zero section. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

The zero section of \(
u(S)\) is compact. A finite cover by the local diffeomorphism neighborhoods in step 1.2, followed by shrinking in local bundle charts, gives \(\epsilon_0>0\) such that \(E\) is defined and a local diffeomorphism on \(D_{\epsilon_0}(
u(S))\). Suppose no smaller uniform disk is injective. For each sufficiently large \(n\), choose distinct \((p_n,v_n),(q_n,w_n)\) with \(\|v_n\|,\|w_n\|<1/n\) and \(E(p_n,v_n)=E(q_n,w_n)\). Compactness and first countability of \(S\) give a subsequence with \(p_n	o p\) and then one with \(q_n	o q\): compactness gives a cluster point and a countable neighborhood basis gives the subsequence. Continuity and the vanishing fiber norms imply \(E(p_n,v_n)	o p\), \(E(q_n,w_n)	o q\), hence \(p=q\) by Hausdorffness of \(M\). Both bundle points then converge to \((p,0)\), contradicting local injectivity near \((p,0)\). Thus \(E\) is injective on some \(D_\epsilon(
u(S))\), and since it is a local diffeomorphism there, it is a diffeomorphism onto its open image. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.2]

Each \(t\in T\) is an isometry of \(g\), so [F3] and uniqueness of geodesics give \(E(t\cdot p,(d t)_p v)=t\cdot E(p,v)\). The norm of the normal vector is preserved, so the disk \(D_\epsilon(\nu(S))\) and its image are \(T\)-invariant, proving the equivariant tubular assertion. [F1, F3, step 2.1]

Apply the tube construction to \(S=O\) from step 1.1. The normal bundle of \(O\) is \(T\)-equivariantly isomorphic to \(T\times_H V\) by \([t,v]\mapsto (t\cdot x,(d t)_xv)\); this is well defined because replacing \((t,v)\) by \((th,h^{-1}v)\) leaves the vector unchanged. The isomorphism is smooth in the homogeneous charts of [F2], and it identifies the normal disk bundle with \(T\times_HD_\epsilon(V)\). If \(g_0\) fixes a point \([t,v]\), then \(g_0tH=tH\), hence \(t^{-1}g_0t\in H\); because \(T\) is abelian this means \(g_0\in H\). Thus every stabilizer in the slice neighborhood is contained in \(H\). [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1]

If \(S=\varnothing\) the zero bundle and neighborhood are empty. If \(S=M\), the normal bundle has rank zero and \(E\) is the identity. For the orbit of a fixed point, \(H=T\) and the displayed slice is the ordinary invariant normal disk. [step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

boundaries.evidence: step 5.1 sets both zero bundle and neighborhood empty when S is empty; the orbit assertion is only for an existing x in M.
step 5.1 handles S=M with zero normal rank and identity exponential; zero vectors map to their base points in step 1.2.
step 5.1 covers a singleton fixed orbit: H=T and its associated slice is an ordinary invariant disk.
step 5.1 treats the full-dimensional submanifold S=M and the maximal stabilizer H=T; step 4.1 still gives the claimed stabilizer containment.

boundaries.reason: The tube uses open disks of positive radius, not a closed radial interval; the Statement asserts no extension at the disk-radius boundary.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 uses compactness for a finite local cover and A1 for the sequence of colliding pairs in the contradiction argument; if S is empty step 5.1 bypasses those selections.

boundaries.reason: The Statement asserts existence of equivariant tubular and slice diffeomorphisms and stabilizer containment; it does not assert an if-and-only-if characterization.
No converse from stabilizer containment to existence of a prescribed tube is claimed; step 4.1 derives containment from the constructed slice only.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $H$ is a closed subgroup of a
finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, then the left-coset space $G/H$, with
its quotient topology, has a unique smooth manifold structure for which

$$q:G\longrightarrow G/H,\qquad q(g)=gH,$$

is a surjective submersion and the left $G$-action is smooth. Moreover,
$\dim(G/H)=\dim G-\dim H$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$,
the exponential map

$$\exp_G:\mathfrak g=T_eG\longrightarrow G$$

is smooth, satisfies $\exp_G(0)=e$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0\mathfrak g\simeq\mathfrak g$, has differential

$$d(\exp_G)_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}.$$

The countable-choice assumption is used exactly through the supplied smooth
tangent-bundle trivialization and one-parameter-subgroup results.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group
with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG$.

If $\gamma:\mathbb R\to G$ is a one-parameter subgroup and
$X=\gamma'(0)$, then

$$\gamma'(t)=d(L_{\gamma(t)})_eX=X^L_{\gamma(t)}$$

for every $t\in\mathbb R$; thus $\gamma$ is the integral curve through $e$ of
the left-invariant field $X^L$. Conversely, the global integral curve through
$e$ of $X^L$ is a one-parameter subgroup. Consequently every
$X\in\mathfrak g$ determines a unique one-parameter subgroup with initial
velocity $X$.

The countable-choice assumption is used exactly through the supplied smooth
invariant-field construction and completeness theorem.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group,
let $\mathfrak g=T_eG$, and let $\gamma_X$ denote the unique one-parameter
subgroup with initial velocity $X\in\mathfrak g$. Then, for every
$a\in\mathbb R$,

$$\gamma_X(a)=\exp_G(aX).$$

Consequently, for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$,

$$\exp_G((s+t)X)=\exp_G(sX)\exp_G(tX).$$

The countable-choice assumption is used exactly through the supplied
existence-and-uniqueness theorem for one-parameter subgroups.

The standard coordinate on $\mathbb R$ makes addition
$(s,t)\mapsto s+t$ and inversion $t\mapsto-t$ smooth, so
$(\mathbb R,+)$ is a one-dimensional Lie group in the sense of
[[def-lie-group]]. A **one-parameter subgroup** of a Lie group $G$ is a
Lie-group homomorphism

$$\gamma:(\mathbb R,+)\longrightarrow G$$

in the sense of
[[def-lie-group-homomorphism-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]. Thus $\gamma$ is
smooth, is defined for every real parameter, and satisfies

$$\gamma(s+t)=\gamma(s)\gamma(t),\qquad \gamma(0)=e,\qquad \gamma(-t)=\gamma(t)^{-1}.$$

The last two identities are consequences of the group-homomorphism law, not
extra data. A smooth curve defined only on an interval around $0$ is therefore
not yet a one-parameter subgroup, even if it satisfies the product law
whenever all displayed parameters remain in that interval. The term also
does not assert that the image is embedded or closed.

Both the domain and every Lie-group codomain are nonempty and boundaryless.
For a zero-dimensional codomain the definition still permits, for example,
the constant homomorphism; for a one-dimensional codomain it is unchanged.
No metric, nondegeneracy, or finite endpoint occurs, and all maps and group
operations are supplied explicitly, so no choice axiom is used. This is a
definition, not a biconditional characterization.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: Since \(T\) is compact and connected, \(Q=T/H\) is compact and connected. By [F1], it is a Lie group. It is abelian because \(T\) is abelian. It is not a point because \(H\subsetneq T\); a connected zero-dimensional Lie group is discrete and hence a point, so \(Q\) has dimension \(d\geq1\). [A1, F1, F4, given, algebra]

Let \(\mathfrak q=T_eQ\). The exponential map \(\exp_Q:\mathfrak q\to Q\) has differential the identity at zero by [F2], so [F3] makes it a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of zero onto a neighborhood of the identity. Since \(Q\) is abelian, \(\exp_Q(X+Y)=\exp_Q(X)\exp_Q(Y)\): the product of the one-parameter subgroups with velocities \(X,Y\) is a one-parameter subgroup with velocity \(X+Y\), and uniqueness of integral curves gives the identity. Thus \(\exp_Q(\mathfrak q)\) is a subgroup containing an open identity neighborhood, hence is open. Its other cosets are open, so its complement is open; connectedness of \(Q\) gives \(\exp_Q(\mathfrak q)=Q\). The kernel \(\Lambda=\ker(\exp_Q)\) is discrete because the exponential is injective near zero. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

The linear span of \(\Lambda\) is all of \(\mathfrak q\). Otherwise the quotient linear map \(\mathfrak q\to\mathfrak q/\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Lambda\) factors through the compact space \(Q=\mathfrak q/\Lambda\) and is onto a nonzero real vector space; that is impossible by [F4]. A discrete additive subgroup of a finite-dimensional real vector space that spans it is a lattice. To see this, a discrete subgroup has a neighborhood of zero containing no other subgroup point, so distinct subgroup points are uniformly separated and every bounded subset of it is finite. Choose a shortest nonzero vector \(\lambda_1\); the intersection with \(\mathbb R\lambda_1\) is \(\mathbb Z\lambda_1\), since any smaller positive step would contradict shortestness. If projections of subgroup points to \(\lambda_1^\perp\) approach zero, subtract nearest integer multiples of \(\lambda_1\); the resulting points lie in a bounded set, hence in a finite set, so zero is isolated in the projected subgroup. The projection remains discrete and spans \(\lambda_1^\perp\). Induction on \(d\) gives a lattice basis for the projection; lifting that finite basis and adjoining \(\lambda_1\) gives a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d\) of \(\Lambda\) that is also a real basis of \(\mathfrak q\). [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

Define the nonzero real linear functional \(\ell:\mathfrak q\to\mathbb R\) by \(\ell(\lambda_1)=1\) and \(\ell(\lambda_j)=0\) for \(2\leq j\leq d\). Then \(\ell(\Lambda)\subseteq\mathbb Z\). Define \(\chi_Q(\exp_Q X):=\exp(2\pi i\,\ell(X))\). This is well defined because two logarithms differ by an element of \(\Lambda\). It is a homomorphism by additivity of both the exponential map on the abelian Lie algebra and \(\ell\); it is smooth because the exponential map is a local diffeomorphism near zero and its translates are local diffeomorphisms everywhere. It is nontrivial: \(\exp_Q(\lambda_1/2)\ne e\), while \(\chi_Q(\exp_Q(\lambda_1/2))=-1\). [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Let \(\pi:T\to Q\) be the quotient homomorphism and set \(\chi=\chi_Q\circ\pi\). Surjectivity of \(\pi\) makes \(\chi\) nontrivial, while \(\pi(H)=e\) makes \(\chi|_H=1\). This proves the assertion. [F1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

boundaries.reason: A subgroup H contains the identity and therefore cannot be empty; T is nonempty as well. The Statement does not quantify over empty subgroups.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 excludes a zero-dimensional quotient: connected Q of dimension zero is a point, contradicting H proper. The Statement assumes r>=1.
step 3.1 starts its lattice induction with the shortest nonzero vector; in quotient dimension one it alone is a lattice basis, and step 4.1 defines its dual character.
step 1.1 uses properness to exclude H=T. For H={identity}, Q=T and steps 3.1–5.1 still construct a nontrivial character.

boundaries.reason: The annihilating-character existence statement has no interval or manifold-boundary parameter; evaluating a character at a half-lattice vector in step 4.1 is a witness, not an endpoint claim.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 establishes d>=1, so the spanning lattice in step 3.1 contains a nonzero vector; discreteness makes a shortest vector available and only finitely many basis lifts are selected, with A1 covering the Lie-quotient suppliers.

boundaries.reason: Only proper closed subgroup implies existence of a nontrivial character trivial on H is claimed; the Statement contains no biconditional.
The item does not formulate the converse characterization of proper closed subgroups by characters; step 5.1 concludes only the stated existence direction.

derivations.claim: The map \(S^{-1}f\) is injective. If \(f(m')/s=0\), the fraction relation gives \(t f(m')=0\) for some \(t\in S\). Then \(f(tm')=0\); injectivity of \(f\) gives \(tm'=0\), so \(m'/s=0\) in \(S^{-1}M'\). [given, construct]
The map \(S^{-1}g\) is surjective. For any \(m''/s\in S^{-1}M''\), surjectivity of \(g\) supplies \(m\in M\) with \(g(m)=m''\), and \(m/s\) maps to \(m''/s\). [given, choose]

Let \(m/s\in S^{-1}M\) lie in the kernel of \(S^{-1}g\). The zero-fraction criterion gives \(t\in S\) with \(t g(m)=0\), hence \(g(tm)=0\). Exactness of the original sequence gives \(m'\in M'\) with \(f(m')=tm\). Since \(t\in S\) is invertible in the localization, \(m/s=tm/(ts)=f(m')/(ts)\), which lies in the image of \(S^{-1}f\). [given, step 1.1, algebra]

Conversely \(g\circ f=0\), so every fraction in the image of \(S^{-1}f\) maps to zero under \(S^{-1}g\). Step 2.1 proves the reverse inclusion at the middle term, and steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove exactness at the two ends. If a module is zero, the same fraction criterion yields the unique zero map; no choice principle or flatness assumption is used beyond choosing one preimage for one element in step 1.2. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

boundaries.reason: The multiplicative set S is nonempty since it contains 1, and every module contains zero; empty denominator or empty module carriers are not permitted input data.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 explicitly includes a zero module; step 1.1 uses the zero-fraction criterion rather than assuming torsion-free modules.
Statement: if S={1}, fractions identify with the original modules and the localized sequence is the given exact sequence; denominator 1 is admitted throughout steps 1.1–2.1.
step 3.1 allows zero maps when a module vanishes; steps 1.1 and 2.1 retain the annihilating multiplier, so torsion does not invalidate the argument.
steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove respectively injectivity and surjectivity at the two nonzero ends of the short exact sequence; step 3.1 combines these with middle exactness.
step 1.2 chooses a preimage of one specified numerator using surjectivity of g. This is a single existential witness, not a simultaneous choice function, as step 3.1 states.
step 2.1 proves that a fraction killed by localized g belongs to the image of localized f, including the needed multiplier t.
step 3.1 proves the reverse inclusion: g composed with f is zero, so every fraction in the localized image belongs to the localized kernel.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

If $(X,A)$ is a relative CW complex, then $A\hookrightarrow X$ has the homotopy extension property; in particular it is a cofibration.

Explicitly, for every topological space $Y$, continuous $g:X\to Y$, and continuous $H:A\times I\to Y$ satisfying $H(a,0)=g(a)$, there is a continuous $\widetilde H:X\times I\to Y$ restricting to $H$ on $A\times I$ and to $g$ at time zero. Here $I=[0,1]$ and products have their ordinary product topologies. There is no finiteness or dimension bound on the CW complex, no separation hypothesis on $Y$, and no choice assumption. The CW structure, including its characteristic maps, is supplied as data.

On this page a **based space** is a compactly generated weak Hausdorff space
$X$ equipped with a chosen point $*_X\in X$. Products are the compactly
generated products from the published CGWH convention, and every quotient is
kified after taking the ordinary quotient.

A based space $X$ is **well-pointed** when the inclusion

$$ \{*_X\}\hookrightarrow X $$

is an unbased cofibration, in the sense of the published homotopy-extension
property. Thus well-pointedness is an additional hypothesis: it is not being
asserted for every based CGWH space. The structure spaces of every sequential
prespectrum on this page are required to be well-pointed. No choice principle
is used in these conventions.

Let $G$ be a topological group. All products, quotient spaces, and actions
below use the stated ordinary topologies.

For $N\geq0$, let $J_N^{\mathrm q}=G^{*(N+1)}$ denote the ordinary quotient of $\Delta^N\times G^{N+1}$ in which

$$ (t_0,\ldots,t_N;g_0,\ldots,g_N)\sim(t_0,\ldots,t_N;g'_0,\ldots,g'_N) $$

exactly when $g_i=g'_i$ for every $i$ with $t_i>0$. We write its points as finite formal sums $\sum_{i=0}^N t_i g_i$. Appending a zero coordinate gives the usual inclusions of these finite quotient joins.

As a **set**, Milnor's infinite join is the increasing union

$$ EG=G*G*\cdots=\bigcup_{N\geq0}J_N^{\mathrm q}. $$

Every point therefore has an expression

$$ x=\sum_{i\geq0}t_i g_i,\qquad t_i\geq0,\quad \sum_i t_i=1, $$

with only finitely many $t_i$ nonzero; a label $g_i$ is ignored when $t_i=0$. We choose one of two **ordinary topologies** on this set, according to $G$:

- If $G$ is compact Hausdorff, $EG$ has the ordinary weak direct-limit topology of the compact finite quotient joins $J_N^{\mathrm q}$: a set is open exactly when its intersection with every $J_N^{\mathrm q}$ is open. These are compact Hausdorff stages with closed inclusions. This branch makes the circle and two-point-group models the standard weak CW unions of their finite joins.
- Otherwise, $EG$ has Milnor's ordinary coordinate-label **strong topology**: the coarsest topology for which every barycentric function $t_i:EG\to[0,1]$ and every partial label function $g_i:\{t_i>0\}\to G$ is continuous. A map from any ordinary topological space into this strong join is continuous exactly when all its weights and all its labels on their positive-weight loci are continuous. This is not the weak direct-limit topology; the subspace topology on a finite-stage set need not equal the quotient topology of $J_N^{\mathrm q}$.

In both branches the weights $t_i$ and partial labels $g_i$ are continuous; in the weak branch this follows by checking their restrictions to the finite quotient stages. For compact Hausdorff $G$, each finite strong join and finite quotient join agree because the latter is compact and the former Hausdorff. Neither branch is additionally kified. The noncompact strong branch is an explicit ordinary-Top exception to the standing CGWH convention; all bundle charts and homotopies use ordinary products, as required by the library's ordinary bundle definition. We do not silently replace an ordinary product by a k-product.

The diagonal right action is

$$ \left(\sum_i t_i g_i\right)h=\sum_i t_i(g_i h). $$

Define $BG=EG/G$ with the ordinary orbit-quotient topology, and let $p:EG\to BG$ be the orbit map. Each $t_i$ is invariant and hence descends to a continuous function, again denoted $t_i$, on $BG$. We use the identity-labelled vertex in coordinate $1$ as $e_0\in EG$ and its orbit as $b_0\in BG$.

For a well-pointed topological group $G$ of CW type, the diagonal action on Milnor's $EG$ is free, $EG$ is contractible, and

$$ p:EG\longrightarrow BG $$

is a numerable principal $G$-bundle. The numeration satisfies the library's support-subordinate convention, not merely cozero containment.

The embeddings

$$e\left(\sum_i t_i g_i\right)=\sum_i t_i g_i\text{ in slot }2i,\qquad o\left(\sum_i t_i g_i\right)=\sum_i t_i g_i\text{ in slot }2i+1$$

are $G$-equivariantly homotopic to the identity. If $a,b:T\to EG$ are
continuous equivariant maps, then
$(1-t)e(a(-))+t\,o(b(-))$ is a continuous equivariant homotopy.

For $G=S^1$ or $G=\mathbb Z/2$, the selected compact-group topology identifies $BG$ with the standard weak CW colimit of the finite projective quotients $\mathbb{CP}^N$ or $\mathbb{RP}^N$, respectively.

Assume AC. Identify $\mathbb{CP}^\infty=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^\infty)$,
the space of complex lines in $\mathbb C^\infty$, and let
$u=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ be the class of
the tautological complex line. Then
$$H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\cdot u^k,\qquad H^{2k+1}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=0\qquad(k\geq0),$$
so $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[u]$ is a polynomial ring; and
$H_k(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank one for even $k$ and zero
for odd $k$, in particular finitely generated in every degree.

Assume AC. For every space $X$, abelian group $G$ and $n\ge0$ there is a natural short exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb Z),G)\xrightarrow{\iota}H^n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\beta}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_n(X;\mathbb Z),G)\longrightarrow0.$$
The same assertion holds with $(X,A)$ in every homology and cohomology term for any subspace $A\subseteq X$. Here $H_{-1}=0$ and Ext is computed from projective resolutions of the first variable, with the comparison identifications proved in the local extension lemma. The map $\beta$ is evaluation. Naturality is contravariant in continuous maps of spaces or pairs and covariant in coefficient homomorphisms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
right $R$-modules, and $G$ a left $R$-module. Then naturally in $C,G$,
$0\to H_n(C)\otimes_RG\to H_n(C\otimes_RG)\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(H_{n-1}(C),G)\to0$
is exact.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Give the graded tensor product the multiplication
$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=(-1)^{|b||a'|}(a\smile a')\otimes(b\smile b').$$
For arbitrary spaces $X,Y$, external product $a\times b=\operatorname{pr}_X^*a\smile\operatorname{pr}_Y^*b$ gives a unital graded-ring homomorphism to $H^*(X\times Y;R)$. This multiplicativity requires no AC.

Assume in addition AC, that $R$ is a PID, and that either every $H_q(Y;R)$ or every $H_p(X;R)$ is finite free over $R$. Then this homomorphism is an isomorphism.

For CW pairs $(X,A),(Y,B)$ with supplied characteristic maps, relative external product is likewise a graded-ring homomorphism
$$H^*(X,A;R)\mathbin{\widehat\otimes}_R H^*(Y,B;R)\longrightarrow H^*(X\times Y,(A\times Y)\cup(X\times B);R),$$
where the hat denotes the displayed graded multiplication on the ordinary graded direct-sum tensor product, not a completion. Relative rings need not have units. This relative multiplicativity is choice-free for every commutative unital $R$. Under AC and the PID hypothesis it is an isomorphism if either every $H_q(Y,B;R)$ or every $H_p(X,A;R)$ is finite free. Neither additive assertion requires bounded dimension or finite-rank singular chain groups. Products have their ordinary product topologies; AC enters only in additive bijectivity.

Assume AC. Let $L,M$ be numerable complex line bundles over a path-connected
CW complex with a vertex basepoint, or over a path-connected paracompact
Hausdorff CGWH space of CW homotopy type. Then
$$c_1(L\otimes M)=c_1(L)+c_1(M),\qquad c_1(L^*)=-c_1(L),\qquad c_1(\overline L)=-c_1(L),$$
where $L^*$ is the dual line and $\overline L$ the conjugate line.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle with $n\geq1$
over a path-connected CW complex $B$ (or over one of the CW-type bases of
[[thm-integral-complex-projective-bundle-theorem]]). By that theorem there are
unique classes $a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)$, $1\leq i\leq n$, such that
$$x_E^{\,n}-a_1x_E^{\,n-1}+a_2x_E^{\,n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^na_n=0\qquad\text{in }H^{2n}(P(E);\mathbb Z),$$
where $x_E\in H^2(P(E);\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of the underlying real
bundle of the tautological line
([[def-complex-projective-bundle-and-tautological-complex-line]]). The
**Chern classes** of $E$ are these coefficients:
$$c_i(E):=a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)\qquad(1\leq i\leq n),$$
completed by the conventions $c_0(E):=1\in H^0(B;\mathbb Z)$ and
$c_i(E):=0$ for $i>n$, and the **total Chern class** is the finite sum
$c(E):=\sum_{i\geq0}c_i(E)=1+c_1(E)+\cdots+c_n(E)\in H^*(B;\mathbb Z)$.

For the zero bundle of rank $0$ the conventions give $c(0_B)=1$. The definition
depends only on the isomorphism class of $E$, because an isomorphism of
bundles induces an isomorphism of projective bundles pulling $x$ back to $x$
and hence preserves the unique relation. For a complex line bundle $L\to B$ one
has $P(L)\cong B$ over $B$ with $\gamma_L$ corresponding to $L$ under that
identification, so the relation is $x_L-c_1(L)=0$; since $x_L=e(L_{\mathbb R})$
under the identification, this gives
$$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R}).$$
This is the normalization used throughout the page: the first Chern class of a
complex line is the Euler class of its underlying real bundle in the complex
orientation, not a separately chosen normalization.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, any spaces $X,Y$ and $n\ge0$, the singular cross product is a natural isomorphism
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(X;k)\otimes_kH_q(Y;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H_n(X\times Y;k).$$
The indices are nonnegative. No finite-dimensional restriction is imposed.

derivations.claim: The identity point is a zero-cell of the finite CW circle, so its inclusion is a relative CW subcomplex inclusion and is a cofibration by [F2]. Together with compact metrizability from [F1], this makes \(S^1\) a well-pointed group of CW type in the sense of [F2]. Hence [F3] applies. [F1, F2]

On one \(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}\) factor, apply [F5] with \(G=\mathbb Q\). By [F4], each integral homology group is free, so the Ext term is zero and evaluation identifies \(H^n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb Q)\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}(H_n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q)\). The natural coefficient map sends each integral generator \(u^k\) to the nonzero generator of the corresponding rational group. Thus the rational ring is \(\mathbb Q[u_{\mathbb Q}]\), with \(|u_{\mathbb Q}|=2\). [A1, F4, F5]

Apply [F6] to the integral singular chain complex with \(G=\mathbb Q\). Each integral homology group in [F4] is free, so the Tor term vanishes and \(H_n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb Q)\) is \(\mathbb Q\) for even \(n\) and zero for odd \(n\); it is finite free in every degree. [A1, F4, F6, given]

Let \(\chi:T\to S^1\) be a smooth character and restrict it to each coordinate one-parameter subgroup \(\gamma_i(s)=[0,\ldots,s,\ldots,0]\). Write \(f_i(s)=\chi(\gamma_i(s))\). The homomorphism law gives \(f_i(s+h)=f_i(s)f_i(h)\); differentiating in \(h\) at zero yields \(f_i'(s)=f_i(s)f_i'(0)\). Since \(|f_i(s)|=1\), differentiation of \(|f_i(s)|^2=1\) at zero shows \(f_i'(0)=2\pi i a_i\) for a real \(a_i\). By [F9], the derivative of \(e^{-2\pi i a_i s}f_i(s)\) is zero, so [F10] makes it constant \(1\); hence \(f_i(s)=e^{2\pi i a_i s}\). Since \(\gamma_i(1)\) is the identity, \(f_i(1)=1\) and [F9] gives \(a_i=n_i\in\mathbb Z\). The product decomposition of \(T\) now gives \(\chi([t])=e^{2\pi i\sum_i n_i t_i}\). Uniqueness follows by restricting again to each \(\gamma_i\). [F9, F10, given, construct]

The product \(E_T=(E_{S^1})^r\) is free for the coordinatewise right \(T\)-action, since a point fixed by \(t\) has every coordinate fixed and each factor action is free. It is contractible because it is a finite product of contractible spaces. Each Milnor quotient map is open: the saturation of an open set is the union of its translates. The finite product quotient map is therefore open and its fibers are exactly the \(T\)-orbits, so it induces \(BT\cong (BS^1)^r\cong(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r\) by [F3]. For \(r=0\) this is the one-point product. [F3, step 1.1, construct]

Iterating the ring cross product [F7] over the finite product \((\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r\) identifies its rational cohomology ring with the graded tensor product of \(r\) copies of \(\mathbb Q[u_{\mathbb Q}]\), using the finite-free homology in step 1.3. All generators have even degree, so the graded tensor multiplication has no sign changes and is \(\mathbb Q[u_1,\ldots,u_r]\). [A1, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3]

For \(k=\mathbb Q\) or \(\mathbb R\), [F6] applied to the same integral chain complex and \(G=k\) gives \(H_n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};k)=k\) for even \(n\) and zero for odd \(n\), since the integral groups in [F4] are free. Iterating [F11] over the finite product in step 2.1 identifies \(H_n(BT;k)\) with a direct sum over the finitely many \(r\)-tuples of nonnegative degrees summing to \(n\). Every summand is either zero or one-dimensional over \(k\), so \(H_n(BT;k)\) is finite-dimensional, and therefore finite-free, for every \(n\). For \(r=0\), only the degree-zero group \(k\) occurs. [A1, F4, F6, F11, step 2.1, algebra]

For the coordinate character \(\chi_i\), the associated line \(L_i\) restricts on each finite Milnor quotient stage to the tautological complex line: the map \([e,z]\mapsto z e\) is well defined under the right diagonal equivalence and identifies the fiber with the line spanned by \(e\). By [F4] and [F8], \(u_i=c_1(L_i)\) is a rational degree-two generator. For \(\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^r\), the associated line is the tensor product of \(L_i^{\otimes n_i}\), interpreting negative powers as dual lines; additivity and duality in [F8] give \(c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i\). This is nonzero exactly when \(\mathbf n\ne0\), by the polynomial basis in step 2.2. [F3, F4, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.4]

For \(r=0\), \(T\) and \(BT\) are points, the cohomology is \(\mathbb Q\) in degree zero, and there are no nontrivial characters. The finite product, universal-coefficient, and ring arguments above add no additional restriction beyond AC. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be any topological space and $G$ an abelian group. Its **singular cochains with coefficients in $G$** are
$$C^n(X;G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(C_n(X;\mathbb Z),G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad C^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0),$$
where the chains are those of [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. Addition and negatives of homomorphisms are pointwise. The **coboundary** is
$$\delta^n:C^n(X;G)\to C^{n+1}(X;G),\qquad \delta^n\varphi=\varphi\circ\partial_{n+1}$$
for $n\ge0$, and is zero for $n<0$. Composition with the homomorphism [[def-singular-boundary-operator|$\partial_{n+1}$]] is additive, so this is a homomorphism. The sign convention is positive: there is no extra degree sign on this composite. On a singular $(n+1)$-simplex it says
$$\delta^n\varphi(\sigma)=\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\circ\delta_i),$$
where $\delta_i$ denotes the affine face map, distinct from the superscripted coboundary. In particular $\delta^0\varphi$ on an oriented path is its endpoint value minus its initial value.

By [[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]], the integer chains are finite sums on the specified simplex set $S_n(X)$. Thus a cochain is equivalently an arbitrary function $S_n(X)\to G$: the extension sends $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ to $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$. The sum is finite and the formal coefficients are unique. The cochain need not have finite support.

For a commutative unital ring $R$ and an $R$-module $G$, there is a canonical identification
$$C^n(X;G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_n(X;R),G).$$
Indeed the given chain convention is $C_n(X;R)=C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$. A homomorphism $\varphi$ on integer chains defines an $R$-linear map by $c\otimes r\mapsto r\varphi(c)$; the defining additive and integer-balanced tensor relations are preserved. Conversely evaluate an $R$-linear map on $c\otimes1$. These operations are inverse since $c\otimes r=r(c\otimes1)$, and they intertwine the two coboundaries because the coefficient boundary is $\partial\otimes1$. The construction also covers the zero ring with its unital zero module.

The resulting graded group and coboundary are called the **singular cochain complex**. The square-zero identity follows by precomposition with $\partial^2=0$ in the chain complex and is spelled out in the next lemma. If $X$ is empty there are no singular simplices, so every cochain group is zero; if $G=0$ the same is true. The extension and tensor formulas are uniquely specified and require no AC.

For a space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, a degree-$n$ **singular cocycle** is a cochain in $Z^n(X;G)=\ker\delta^n$ and a degree-$n$ **singular coboundary** belongs to $B^n(X;G)=\operatorname{im}\delta^{n-1}$, for the positive coboundary convention of [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. The square-zero lemma [[lem-the-singular-coboundary-squares-to-zero]] implies $B^n\subseteq Z^n$: if $\varphi=\delta^{n-1}\psi$, then $\delta^n\varphi=0$.

The **singular cohomology group with coefficients in $G$** is
$$H^n(X;G)=Z^n(X;G)/B^n(X;G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad H^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0).$$
This is the abelian quotient with addition $[\varphi]+[\psi]=[\varphi+\psi]$: changing either representative by a coboundary changes the sum by a coboundary. Thus two cocycles represent the same class exactly when their difference is $\delta^{n-1}\eta$ for some degree-$(n-1)$ cochain $\eta$. In degree zero, $B^0=0$ because $C^{-1}=0$; hence $H^0=\ker\delta^0$. The zero convention in negative degrees agrees with the same kernel/image construction on the zero cochain groups.

If coefficients are a module over a commutative ring, the same groups and maps are modules and linear maps, and this is their module quotient. Empty $X$ or zero coefficients give zero cohomology in every degree. The notation does not define cohomology as the dual of homology; such identifications require their own theorems. No choice of cocycle representatives and no AC is part of this definition.

Let $H:X\times I\to Y$ be a homotopy from $f$ to $g$. Then the prism operator
$P_H$ of [[def-prism-operator-for-a-homotopy]] satisfies
$$g_\#-f_\#=\partial P_H+P_H\partial$$
as homomorphisms $C_n(X;G)\to C_n(Y;G)$ for every $n\geq 1$ and every abelian
group $G$. In degree $0$, the same identity reduces to
$$g_{\#,0}-f_{\#,0}=\partial P_H:C_0(X;G)\to C_0(Y;G).$$

derivations.claim:
For \(n\geq1\), define \(K^n:C^n(Y;k)\to C^{n-1}(X;k)\) by \(K^n\varphi=\varphi\circ P_H\), and set \(K^0=0\). Evaluating the chain identity [F2] on an \(n\)-chain and using the positive coboundary convention in [F1] gives
\[
(g^*-f^*)\varphi=\delta(K^n\varphi)+K^{n+1}(\delta\varphi).
\]
For \(n=0\), the first summand is zero because \(C^{-1}=0\), and the degree-zero case of [F2] gives the same identity. [F1, F2, algebra]

If \(\varphi\) is a cocycle, then [F1] gives \(\delta\varphi=0\), so step 1.1 says \(g^*\varphi-f^*\varphi=\delta(K^n\varphi)\), a coboundary; hence the induced cohomology classes agree. Negative cohomology groups are zero by [F1]. If \(f\) has homotopy inverse \(h\), apply the equality to \(hf\simeq\mathrm{id}_X\) and \(fh\simeq\mathrm{id}_Y\); functoriality of pullback then makes \(h^*\) a two-sided inverse for \(f^*\). [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a boundaryless Riemannian manifold. An open set $W\subseteq M$ is called **strongly geodesically convex** here when, for every ordered pair $(x,y)\in W\times W$, there is a unique affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to M$ that globally minimizes length from $x$ to $y$, its image lies in $W$, and $(x,y,t)\mapsto\gamma_{x,y}(t)$ is smooth.

Every point of $M$ has a strongly geodesically convex neighbourhood. More precisely, the neighbourhood may be chosen inside any prescribed open neighbourhood of the point, and it may be chosen so that every piecewise smooth curve attaining the global minimum between two of its points is a monotone reparametrization of the displayed connector. Every nonempty intersection of a positive finite family of strongly geodesically convex open sets is again strongly geodesically convex.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

derivations.claim: The neighborhoods in [F1] cover \(F\); compactness gives a finite subcover \(U_1,\ldots,U_N\). Each nonempty finite intersection remains strongly geodesically convex by [F1]. The nerve \(K\) has finitely many vertices and faces, so it is a finite simplicial complex. If \(F=\varnothing\), the empty cover and empty realization give the stated boundary case. [A1, F1, given, construct]

Choose a smooth partition of unity \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N\) subordinate to the finite cover by [F2]. Define \(f:F\to |K|\) by \(f(x)=\sum_i\phi_i(x)v_i\), where \(v_i\) is the \(i\)th vertex. The active indices \(\{i:\phi_i(x)>0\}\) all satisfy \(x\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i\subseteq U_i\), so they form a simplex of \(K\); hence the formula lands in \(|K|\). Finite sums of continuous coordinates make \(f\) continuous. [A1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

Let \(\operatorname{sd}K\) be the barycentric subdivision and \(h:|\operatorname{sd}K|\to|K|\) its canonical homeomorphism, sending the vertex indexed by a face \(\sigma\) to the barycenter of \(\sigma\). For each nonempty face \(\sigma\), choose \(x_\sigma\in U_\sigma\); there are only finitely many such choices. Define \(g:|\operatorname{sd}K|\to F\) on vertices by \(g(\sigma)=x_\sigma\). Inductively, a simplex of \(\operatorname{sd}K\) is a chain \(\sigma_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\sigma_m\). Its face opposite \(\sigma_0\) has already been mapped into \(U_{\sigma_1}\subseteq U_{\sigma_0}\); cone that face to \(x_{\sigma_0}\) along the unique minimizing geodesics in \(U_{\sigma_0}\). This extension maps the entire chain simplex into \(U_{\sigma_0}\). Deleting \(\sigma_0\) gives the already assigned opposite face; deleting any other vertex restricts the same coning formula to the corresponding face. Thus all face definitions agree, and finite simplex-by-simplex pasting makes \(g\) continuous. [A1, F1, step 1.1, construct]

For each \(x\in F\), the support of \(f(x)\) is a face \(\sigma\) whose every \(U_i\) contains \(x\). Every chain simplex containing \(h^{-1}f(x)\) has a smallest face \(\sigma_0\subseteq\sigma\), so \(x\in U_{\sigma_0}\); step 2.2 also gives \(g h^{-1}f(x)\in U_{\sigma_0}\). The open set \(P=\bigcup_i(U_i\times U_i)\) contains every pair \((x,g h^{-1}f(x))\). On each \(U_i\times U_i\), the unique minimizing connector is continuous by [F1]; connectors from different members agree on overlaps because they are globally unique. They therefore define a continuous connector on \(P\). Applying it to \(x\) and \(g h^{-1}f(x)\) gives a homotopy \(g h^{-1}f\simeq\operatorname{id}_F\). [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct]

For a face \(\sigma_0\) of \(K\), let \(C_{\sigma_0}\) be the subcomplex of faces \(\eta\) such that \(\eta\cup\sigma_0\) is a face. It contracts to the barycenter of \(\sigma_0\): for any point in a simplex \(\eta\) of \(C_{\sigma_0}\), the straight segment to that barycenter lies in the simplex \(\eta\cup\sigma_0\). On a chain simplex with smallest face \(\sigma_0\), the subdivision homeomorphism \(h\) lands in \(C_{\sigma_0}\); step 2.2 puts \(g\) in \(U_{\sigma_0}\), so every active vertex of \(f g\) forms a face jointly with \(\sigma_0\), and \(f g\) also lands in \(C_{\sigma_0}\). A face of the chain simplex has either the same smallest face or a larger one, whose carrier is contained in \(C_{\sigma_0}\). Induct over the finite simplices of \(\operatorname{sd}K\): the two endpoint maps and the already constructed boundary homotopy define a map from the boundary of each prism into its contractible carrier \(C_{\sigma_0}\); coning that boundary map to the carrier's barycenter extends the homotopy over the prism, relative to its boundary. The finite extensions paste continuously and give \(f g\simeq h\). Thus \(g h^{-1}\) is a homotopy inverse for \(f\), by steps 3.1 and 4.1. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, induction, construct] ∎
