derivations.claim: The infinitesimal $GL(V)$ action and the derivative of the complex ADHM equation form the complex $$C^0=\operatorname{End}(V)\xrightarrow{d_0}C^1=\operatorname{End}(V)t_1\oplus\operatorname{End}(V)t_2\oplus\operatorname{Hom}(W,V)\oplus\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)t_1t_2\xrightarrow{d_1}C^2=\operatorname{End}(V)t_1t_2,$$ where $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$ and $d_1(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)=[\dot B_1,B_2]+[B_1,\dot B_2]+\dot I J+I\dot J$. Expanding gives $d_1d_0(\xi)=[\xi,[B_1,B_2]+IJ]=0$, so this is a complex.

If $d_0(\xi)=0$, then $\xi$ commutes with both $B_i$ and $\xi I=0$. Therefore $\xi B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)=B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}\xi I(w)=0$ for every word and $w$. Stability says those vectors span $V$, hence $\xi=0$ and $d_0$ is injective.

To show $d_1$ is onto, use the nondegenerate trace pairing on $\operatorname{End}(V)$. If $\Theta$ annihilates its image, variation of $\dot J$ gives $\Theta I=0$, and variations of $\dot B_1,\dot B_2$ give $[\Theta,B_1]=[\Theta,B_2]=0$. The same word calculation as in step 2.1 then gives $\Theta=0$. Thus the annihilator of $\operatorname{im}d_1$ is zero, so $d_1$ is surjective.

Apply [F3] to the displayed equation and stability condition. Its proof uses the declared holomorphic implicit-function supplier, proves properness by word-frame bounds on both the gauge transformation and its inverse, and constructs holomorphic quotient charts. Thus the quotient here is a Hausdorff second-countable complex manifold, with tangent $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$ and complex dimension $2kN$. For $k=0$ the quotient is a point. This is the stable complex quotient; no real moment-map or sheaf/ASD identification is inferred.

At a $T$-fixed quotient point represented by $x$, [F3] gives the unique gauge lift $g(t)=C(x)\operatorname{diag}(e_{\alpha_\ell}t_1^{a_\ell}t_2^{b_\ell})C(x)^{-1}$ from a standard-framing word basis. This is a smooth representation of the compact torus itself. The fixed-orbit equations give $g(t)I(w_\alpha)=e_\alpha I(w_\alpha)$ and $g(t)B_i=t_iB_i g(t)$, so all weights generated by stability have the form $e_\alpha t_1^it_2^j$ with $i,j\ge0$. Under $t_1t_2hJ=Jg(t)^{-1}$, a nonzero component from a $V$-weight $\chi$ to the $\beta$th framing line requires $\chi=e_\beta t_1^{-1}t_2^{-1}$. Distinct integer characters on the compact torus cannot satisfy this equality with any generated weight, so $J=0$. The moment equation then gives $[B_1,B_2]=0$. No Zariski-density or algebraic lifting assertion is used.

For each framing line, the commuting pair $B_1,B_2$ makes its cyclic span a quotient of $\mathbb C[x,y]$, with $x,y$ acting by $B_1,B_2$. The torus weights $e_\alpha t_1^i t_2^j$ are distinct between colors and between monomials, so the kernel is a monomial ideal. Its standard monomials form a finite downward-closed subset of $\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^2$, hence a Young diagram $Y_\alpha$. Stability says the cyclic spans together exhaust $V$, so $\sum_\alpha|Y_\alpha|=\dim V=k$. Conversely, for any such tuple, take one basis vector per box, let each $B_i$ move a box one unit in direction $i$ and send it to zero when the next box is absent, let $I$ send the $\alpha$th framing vector to the origin box of $Y_\alpha$ when nonempty, and set $J=0$. Downward closure makes the shifts commute, the moment equation holds, and every box is generated from its origin. These data are stable and recover the given diagrams. The construction and recovery are inverse on gauge orbits, proving the fixed-point bijection.

Bring each torus-transformed representative back to the fixed representative by the inverse unique gauge lift from step 5.1. The variations then transform as $t_i\operatorname{End}(V)$ for $\dot B_i$, as $V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee$ for $\dot I$, and as $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$ for $\dot J$; the complex-equation target transforms as $t_1t_2\operatorname{End}(V)$. Thus the torus representations in the complex of step 1.1 are $C^0=\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf V_{\vec Y}$, $C^1=(t_1+t_2)\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf V_{\vec Y}+\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V_{\vec Y}$, and $C^2=t_1t_2\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf V_{\vec Y}$. Exactness at $C^0$ and $C^2$ follows from steps 2.1 and 3.1, so the tangent character is $[C^1]-[C^0]-[C^2]$, which is precisely the expression in the Statement.

The label set in step 6.1 is finite: for $k>0$ every box of a size-at-most-$k$ downward-closed diagram has both coordinates less than $k$, so the possible tuples lie in a finite collection of subsets; $k=0$ has only the empty tuple. Hence the fixed locus is a finite set in the Hausdorff quotient from [F3], and each point is isolated. By [F3] the quotient has a finite invariant affine atlas with algebraic action of $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^{N+2}$. In each slice its coordinate functions are eigenfunctions. A point fixed by the compact torus has every nonzero-weight coordinate equal to zero, since each nontrivial integer character is nontrivial on that compact torus; conversely these equations make the point fixed by $T_{\mathbb C}$. Thus the two fixed loci have the same point set. The fixed subscheme is smooth by [F4], because $T_{\mathbb C}$ is diagonalizable and hence linearly reductive. Its fixed ideal in these affine coordinates is generated by the nonzero-weight coordinates. Linearizing that ideal, using the tangent-kernel description in [F4], identifies its tangent with the invariant tangent subspace. A smooth fixed scheme with a finite point set has dimension zero at every point, so that subspace is zero. Therefore every complex tangent weight is a nonzero character. Its associated $u_\chi$ is a nonzero integer linear polynomial in the algebraically independent variables and is invertible in $K$. The tangent has complex dimension $2kN$, so the Euler product has exactly $2kN$ factors counted with multiplicity.

For each fixed $k$, there are finitely many partitions of $k$, hence finitely many $N$-tuples of total size $k$; every summand $E_{\vec Y}^{-1}$ is in $K$ by step 7.1. Therefore the coefficient is a finite sum and the sequence of coefficients defines the formal power series $Z_N^{\mathrm{fp}}(q)\in K\langle\!\langle q\rangle\!\rangle$. At $k=0$, $V=0$, the empty tuple is the unique fixed point, the Euler product is empty and equals $1$, so the constant coefficient is $1$.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and standard Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$ and $J:V\to W$. Define the complex and real polynomial expressions

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Work in $\mathrm{ZF}+\mathrm{AC}$. Let $T$ be a compact torus acting smoothly on a compact oriented smooth $n$-manifold $M$ without boundary; use the standard Hausdorff, second-countable manifold convention, and assume the action preserves the orientation. Write $F=M^T=\coprod_{j=1}^{s}F_j$ for its fixed locus, with $s<\infty$, and $i_j:F_j\hookrightarrow M$ for each connected component. Give each normal bundle $\nu_j$ a $T$-equivariant orientation and orient $F_j$ by $o(TM|_{F_j})=o(TF_j)\wedge o(\nu_j)$. Use real Borel equivariant cohomology, $\mathcal R=H^*(BT;\mathbb R)$, the multiplicative set $S$ generated by nonzero character classes, and the degree-shifting fiber-integration convention of the preceding definition. For every homogeneous $\alpha\in H_T^k(M;\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_M\alpha=\sum_j\int_{F_j}\frac{i_j^*\alpha}{e_T(\nu_j)}\quad\text{in }S^{-1}H^{k-n}(BT;\mathbb R).$$

If the fixed locus is nonempty and consists of isolated points, necessarily $n=2m$. Use the ambient orientation on each normal space $\nu_p=T_pM$ and the positive orientation on each point $p$. Choose a $T$-invariant complex structure on each $T_pM$ and let $\chi_{p,1},\ldots,\chi_{p,m}$ be its nonzero character weights. Let $\epsilon_p=+1$ when its complex orientation agrees with the orientation of $M$ at $p$ and $-1$ otherwise. Then the same formula specializes to

$$\int_M\alpha=\sum_{p\in M^T}\frac{\epsilon_p\,i_p^*\alpha}{\prod_{a=1}^{m}u_{\chi_{p,a}}}\quad\text{in }S^{-1}\mathcal R.$$

If the fixed locus is empty, the fixed-component formula is the empty sum $0$ for every $n$; no parity condition or integer $m$ is needed in that case.

This is a finite-dimensional formula for compact manifolds; it does not assert a formula for arbitrary noncompact instanton spaces or infinite-dimensional field spaces.

Assume full AC. Fix integers $N\geq1$ and $k\geq0$ and a positive real stability parameter $\zeta$. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ have their standard Hermitian structures. Define $\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N}$ to be the geometric quotient by $GL(V)$ of data $(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, $I\in\operatorname{Hom}(W,V)$, $J\in\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$, $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$, and $\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w):m\geq0,\ w\in W\}=V$. The positive parameter $\zeta$ specifies the positive-FI stability chamber. Let $T=(S^1)^2\times(S^1)^N$, with rotation characters $t_1,t_2$ and dual framing characters $e_1,\ldots,e_N$. Thus $W$ has character $\mathbf W=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and $W^\vee$ has character $\mathbf W^\vee=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$, where $h$ acts on $W$ with weights $e_\alpha^{-1}$. Work over the rational function field $K=\mathbb Q(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_1,\ldots,a_N)$ in algebraically independent variables. For $\chi=t_1^{m_1}t_2^{m_2}\prod_\alpha e_\alpha^{n_\alpha}$ set $u_\chi=m_1\epsilon_1+m_2\epsilon_2+\sum_\alpha n_\alpha a_\alpha$.

For a partition $Y$, a Young diagram means a finite downward-closed subset of $\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^2$; write $|Y|$ for its number of boxes. For an $N$-tuple $\vec Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N)$ set $|\vec Y|=\sum_\alpha|Y_\alpha|$, $\mathbf W=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$, $\mathbf W^\vee=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$, and
$$\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^N e_\alpha\sum_{(i,j)\in Y_\alpha}t_1^it_2^j.$$
Then $\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N}$ is smooth of complex dimension $2kN$, and its $T$-fixed points are isolated and in bijection with the $N$-tuples of partitions of total size $k$. At the fixed point $\vec Y$, the tangent character is
$$\operatorname{ch}_T(T_{\vec Y}\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N})=\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf V_{\vec Y}(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V_{\vec Y}.$$
Let $E_{\vec Y}$ be the product of $u_\chi$ over the tangent weights counted with multiplicity; the fixed points are isolated, so none of these weights is zero. Define the fixed-point series by
$$Z^{\mathrm{fp}}_N(q)=\sum_{k\geq0}q^k\sum_{|\vec Y|=k}E_{\vec Y}^{-1}\in K\langle\!\langle q\rangle\!\rangle.$$
Each coefficient is a finite sum, and the series is formal; no analytic convergence is asserted.

The quotient is a separated smooth finite-type complex algebraic variety with a finite invariant affine word-slice atlas for the algebraic complex torus $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^{N+2}$. This result concerns the stable matrix quotient and a formal series. It asserts no sheaf/ASD dictionary or integration identity.

Let $T$ be a compact torus acting smoothly on a compact oriented smooth $n$-manifold $M$ without boundary; use the standard Hausdorff, second-countable manifold convention, and assume the action preserves the orientation. Write $F=M^T=\coprod_{j=1}^{s}F_j$ for its fixed locus, with $s<\infty$, and $i_j:F_j\hookrightarrow M$ for each connected component. Give each normal bundle $\nu_j$ a $T$-equivariant orientation and orient $F_j$ by $o(TM|_{F_j})=o(TF_j)\wedge o(\nu_j)$. Use real Borel equivariant cohomology, $\mathcal R=H^*(BT;\mathbb R)$, the multiplicative set $S$ generated by nonzero character classes, and the degree-shifting fiber-integration convention of the preceding definition. For every homogeneous $\alpha\in H_T^k(M;\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_M\alpha=\sum_j\int_{F_j}\frac{i_j^*\alpha}{e_T(\nu_j)}\quad\text{in }S^{-1}H^{k-n}(BT;\mathbb R).$$

If the fixed locus is nonempty and consists of isolated points, necessarily $n=2m$. Use the ambient orientation on each normal space $\nu_p=T_pM$ and the positive orientation on each point $p$. Choose a $T$-invariant complex structure on each $T_pM$ and let $\chi_{p,1},\ldots,\chi_{p,m}$ be its nonzero character weights. Let $\epsilon_p=+1$ when its complex orientation agrees with the orientation of $M$ at $p$ and $-1$ otherwise. Then the same formula specializes to

$$\int_M\alpha=\sum_{p\in M^T}\frac{\epsilon_p\,i_p^*\alpha}{\prod_{a=1}^{m}u_{\chi_{p,a}}}\quad\text{in }S^{-1}\mathcal R.$$

If the fixed locus is empty, the fixed-component formula is the empty sum $0$ for every $n$; no parity condition or integer $m$ is needed in that case.

This is a finite-dimensional formula for compact manifolds; it does not assert a formula for arbitrary noncompact instanton spaces or infinite-dimensional field spaces.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\geq 2$ and let $S^4=\mathbb R^4\cup\{\infty\}$ be the one-point compactification, oriented so the coordinates $x^1,x^2,x^3,x^4$ on $\mathbb R^4$ have $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4>0$. Give $S^4$ a smooth round metric in the conformal class of the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^4$. A framed $U(N)$ connection is a smooth unitary connection $A$ on a Hermitian rank-$N$ vector bundle $E\to S^4$, together with a chosen unitary frame $\Phi:E_\infty\to\mathbb C^N$ of its fiber at $\infty$. Gauge transformations are smooth unitary bundle automorphisms that equal the identity in this frame at $\infty$. The curvature is $F_A$, and the Hodge operator is defined by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$ on two-forms. Set $F_A^+=(F_A+*_gF_A)/2$ and $F_A^-=(F_A-*_gF_A)/2$; the anti-self-dual condition is $F_A^+=0$, and the self-dual condition is $F_A^-=0$.

Let $\mathfrak u(N)$ be the anti-Hermitian matrices and put $B_N(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_N(XY)$. In the trace convention of the library, the charge of $A$ is $q_N(A)=(8\pi^2)^{-1}\int_{S^4}B_N(F_A\wedge F_A)$, and the positive anti-self-dual instanton number is $k(A)=-q_N(A)$. For $k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, the framed anti-self-dual charge-$k$ moduli set $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}$ consists of framed pairs $(E,A)$ with $F_A^+=0$ and $k(A)=k$, modulo the stated based gauge transformations. The integer-charge condition is part of the selected bundle sector; no analytic existence or uniqueness assertion is included in this definition. The trace and Hodge conventions agree with the supplied compact-four-manifold definition of $q_B$; its special $SU(2)$ integrality clause is not used to assert $U(N)$ integrality.

For $k\geq0$, take Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$. The ADHM data are
$$B_1,B_2\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),\qquad I\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V),\qquad J\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W).$$
Their data space is $\mathcal R_{k,N}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)^2\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V)\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W)$, and their complex and real moment-map expressions are
$$\mu_{\mathbb C}=[B_1,B_2]+IJ\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V).$$
Here $[X,Y]=XY-YX$, and $\dagger$ is the Hermitian adjoint. The two displayed formulas define maps $\mu_{\mathbb C}:\mathcal R_{k,N}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ and $\mu_{\mathbb R}:\mathcal R_{k,N}\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$, where $\mathcal R_{k,N}$ is the stated product of four Hom spaces and $\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ is the real vector space of Hermitian endomorphisms. They are the complex and real ADHM moment-map expressions, with these formulas fixing their normalization. A datum is stable when
$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w):m\geq0,\ i_j\in\{1,2\},\ w\in W\}=V,$$
where the word of length zero is the identity. Equivalently, no proper $B_1,B_2$-invariant subspace of $V$ contains $\operatorname{im}I$. The group $GL(V)$ consists of invertible complex-linear endomorphisms, and $U(V)$ is its subgroup preserving the chosen Hermitian inner product. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. For $\zeta>0$, the stable complex ADHM quotient $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{GIT},\zeta}_{k,N}$ is the geometric quotient of $\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \text{stable}\}$ by $GL(V)$ in the positive stability chamber; $\zeta$ labels that chamber and is not an additional coordinate on the complex equation set.

For a real parameter $\zeta\geq0$, the real moment-map presentation is the quotient of $\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta\,\mathrm{id}_V,\ \text{stable}\}$ by $U(V)$. At $\zeta>0$ this is called the resolved or positive-FI ADHM quotient; at $\zeta=0$ its affine completion includes the small-instanton locus. The equations and quotient are definitions; this item does not assert that the real moment-map quotient is isomorphic to the stable complex quotient or to an instanton moduli space.

Write $\mathbb{CP}^2$ for the complex projective plane, $\ell_\infty=\{[0:z_1:z_2]\}$ for its line at infinity, and $\mathcal O_{\ell_\infty}$ for the sheaf of holomorphic functions on that line. The affine chart $\mathbb{CP}^2\setminus\ell_\infty$ is $\mathbb C^2$; projective compactification adds the whole line $\ell_\infty$, unlike the one-point compactification $S^4$. Let $\mathcal O(1)$ be the hyperplane line bundle and $\mathcal O(m)=\mathcal O(1)^{\otimes m}$ for $m\geq0$. A coherent sheaf is a sheaf of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb{CP}^2}$-modules that is locally finitely presented; it is torsion-free when no nonzero local section is annihilated by a nonzero local function. Its rank is the dimension of its generic fiber over the function field. Define its Hilbert polynomial by $P_E(m)=\sum_{i=0}^2(-1)^i\dim_{\mathbb C}H^i(\mathbb{CP}^2,E\otimes\mathcal O(m))$ for all sufficiently large integers $m$. The framed Gieseker moduli space $\mathcal G_{k,N}$ is the moduli of pairs $(E,\Phi)$ with $E$ a rank-$N$ torsion-free coherent sheaf, $P_E(m)=N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$, and $\Phi:E|_{\ell_\infty}\cong\mathcal O_{\ell_\infty}^{\oplus N}$. Its locally-free locus is distinguished from the boundary of non-locally-free sheaves. The Uhlenbeck set-theoretic compactification is the disjoint union of strata $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k-\ell,N}\times\operatorname{Sym}^{\ell}(\mathbb R^4)$ for $0\leq\ell\leq k$, where $\operatorname{Sym}^{\ell}(\mathbb R^4)=(\mathbb R^4)^\ell/S_\ell$ records ideal point defects. The Gieseker space and the Uhlenbeck space are distinct: the former retains torsion-free sheaf data at the small-instanton boundary, while the latter records only ideal points. No compactness of either full space is asserted here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$, $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, and let $(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ satisfy $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$ and be stable, meaning that the vectors obtained by applying all words in $B_1,B_2$ to $I(W)$ span $V$. Costable means that no nonzero common $B_1,B_2$-invariant subspace lies in $\ker J$, and regular means stable and costable. On $\mathbb P^2$ with coordinates $[z_0:z_1:z_2]$, define

$$\alpha=\begin{pmatrix}z_0B_1-z_1\\z_0B_2-z_2\\z_0J\end{pmatrix}:V\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to(V\oplus V\oplus W)\otimes\mathcal O,\qquad \beta=\begin{pmatrix}-z_0B_2+z_2&z_0B_1-z_1&z_0I\end{pmatrix}:(V\oplus V\oplus W)\otimes\mathcal O\to V\otimes\mathcal O(1).$$

Fix integers $N\geq1$ and $k\geq0$ and a positive real stability parameter $\zeta$. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ have their standard Hermitian structures. Define $\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N}$ to be the geometric quotient by $GL(V)$ of data $(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, $I\in\operatorname{Hom}(W,V)$, $J\in\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$, $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$, and $\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w):m\geq0,\ w\in W\}=V$. The positive parameter $\zeta$ specifies the positive-FI stability chamber. Let $T=(S^1)^2\times(S^1)^N$, with rotation characters $t_1,t_2$ and dual framing characters $e_1,\ldots,e_N$. Thus $W$ has character $\mathbf W=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and $W^\vee$ has character $\mathbf W^\vee=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$, where $h$ acts on $W$ with weights $e_\alpha^{-1}$. Complexify the characters and work over the rational function field $K=\mathbb Q(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_1,\ldots,a_N)$, where $\epsilon_i=c_1^T(t_i)$ and $a_\alpha=c_1^T(e_\alpha)$.

For a partition $Y$, a Young diagram means a finite downward-closed subset of $\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^2$; write $|Y|$ for its number of boxes. For an $N$-tuple $\vec Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N)$ set $|\vec Y|=\sum_\alpha|Y_\alpha|$, $\mathbf W=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$, $\mathbf W^\vee=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$, and
$$\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^N e_\alpha\sum_{(i,j)\in Y_\alpha}t_1^it_2^j.$$
Then $\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N}$ is smooth of complex dimension $2kN$, and its $T$-fixed points are isolated and in bijection with the $N$-tuples of partitions of total size $k$. At the fixed point $\vec Y$, the tangent character is
$$\operatorname{ch}_T(T_{\vec Y}\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N})=\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf V_{\vec Y}(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V_{\vec Y}^{\vee}\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V_{\vec Y}.$$
For each character $\chi$, let $u_\chi=c_1^T(\chi)$. Let $E_{\vec Y}$ be the product of $u_\chi$ over the tangent weights counted with multiplicity; the fixed points are isolated, so none of these weights is zero. Define the fixed-point series by
$$Z^{\mathrm{fp}}_N(q)=\sum_{k\geq0}q^k\sum_{|\vec Y|=k}E_{\vec Y}^{-1}\in K\langle\!\langle q\rangle\!\rangle.$$
Each coefficient is a finite sum, and the series is formal; no analytic convergence is asserted.

Assume full AC as inherited from the supplied instanton-charge convention. If a $T$-equivariant isomorphism from the positive-FI quotient to the moduli of framed rank-$N$ torsion-free coherent sheaves on $\mathbb{CP}^2$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$ is supplied, it transfers the fixed-point classification and tangent characters to that Gieseker space. The ordinary framed anti-self-dual moduli space is a separate zero-FI regular locus: identifying that locus with the regular ADHM quotient uses the separate ordinary dictionary below, and no fixed-point count or equality of series is asserted for it. If a separately proved noncompact equivariant pushforward for $\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N}$ has a localization identity with these isolated fixed points and tangent Euler classes, then its value on the unit is the coefficient displayed above. The compact ABBV formula alone does not establish such an identity: $\mathcal M^\zeta_{k,N}$ is noncompact for $k>0$. This theorem makes no identification with an ordinary continuum gauge-theory path integral.

Let $G$ be a finite group with identity $e$, let $A$ be a finite abelian group written additively, and let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{Aut}(A)$ be a left action, so $\rho_{gh}=\rho_g\rho_h$ and $\rho_e=\operatorname{id}_A$. A group $2$-cochain is a function $c:G^2\to A$; it is normalized when it vanishes if either input is $e$. Its coboundary is

$$
(\delta_\rho c)(g,h,k)=\rho_g c(h,k)-c(gh,k)+c(g,hk)-c(g,h).
$$

A normalized group $3$-cocycle is a function $\beta:G^3\to A$ that vanishes whenever any argument is $e$ and satisfies

$$
\rho_g\beta(h,k,l)-\beta(gh,k,l)+\beta(g,hk,l)-\beta(g,h,kl)+\beta(g,h,k)=0
$$

for all $g,h,k,l\in G$. Two normalized $3$-cocycles represent the same class when their difference is $\delta_\rho c$ for a normalized $2$-cochain $c$; this is an equivalence relation by additivity of $\delta_\rho$. The class $[\beta]$ is the Postnikov class in this skeletal model.

The corresponding skeletal categorical $2$-group has objects $g\in G$ and, for each $g$, one automorphism labelled by each $u\in A$; there are no morphisms between distinct objects. Composition of automorphisms adds their labels, tensor product is

$$
(g,u)\otimes(h,v)=(gh,u+\rho_gv),
$$

and the associator from $(gh)k$ to $g(hk)$ has label $\beta(g,h,k)$. The two pentagon path labels are $\beta(gh,k,l)+\beta(g,h,kl)$ and $\rho_g\beta(h,k,l)+\beta(g,hk,l)+\beta(g,h,k)$; equality of these labels is exactly the displayed $3$-cocycle equation.

A finite ordered simplicial complex $K$ is a finite vertex set with a total order and a collection of nonempty finite vertex subsets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. Write each simplex in increasing order. A $q$-cochain with values in a local coefficient system assigns an element to each ordered $q$-simplex at its first vertex. A flat $G$-valued edge cochain is a family $a_{ij}\in G$ for each edge $i<j$ such that $a_{ij}a_{jk}=a_{ik}$ on every triangle. It defines the local coefficient system with fiber $A$ at each vertex and transport $\rho_{a_{ij}}$ from vertex $j$ to vertex $i$.

For each integer $q\geq0$ and local-coefficient $q$-cochain $c$, define the twisted coboundary on each ordered $(q+1)$-simplex by

$$
(\delta_a c)_{i_0\ldots i_{q+1}}=\rho_{a_{i_0i_1}}c_{i_1\ldots i_{q+1}}+\sum_{r=1}^{q+1}(-1)^r c_{i_0\ldots\widehat{i_r}\ldots i_{q+1}}.
$$

In particular, for an $A$-valued $2$-cochain $B$,

$$
(\delta_aB)_{ijkl}=\rho_{a_{ij}}B_{jkl}-B_{ikl}+B_{ijl}-B_{ijk},\qquad (a^*\beta)_{ijkl}=\beta(a_{ij},a_{jk},a_{kl}).
$$

A finite $2$-group background on $K$ is a flat edge cochain $a$ and an $A$-valued $2$-cochain $B$ satisfying $\delta_aB=a^*\beta$ on every ordered tetrahedron. This fixes the cochain representative, local coefficient action, and sign convention.

A $1$-gauge transformation consists of vertex labels $g_i\in G$ and edge labels $\lambda_{ij}\in A$ at vertex $i$. Define

$$
a^g_{ij}=g_i a_{ij}g_j^{-1},
$$

$$
\zeta^g_{ijk}=-\beta(g_i,a_{ij},a_{jk})+\beta(a^g_{ij},g_j,a_{jk})-\beta(a^g_{ij},a^g_{jk},g_k),
$$

$$
B^{g,\lambda}_{ijk}=\rho_{g_i}B_{ijk}+\zeta^g_{ijk}+(\delta_{a^g}\lambda)_{ijk},\qquad (\delta_{a^g}\lambda)_{ijk}=\rho_{a^g_{ij}}\lambda_{jk}-\lambda_{ik}+\lambda_{ij}.
$$

Fix a finite ordered simplicial complex $K$, a finite group $G$, a finite abelian group $A$ in additive notation, a left action $\rho:G\to\operatorname{Aut}(A)$, and a normalized inhomogeneous $3$-cocycle $\beta:G^3\to A$. A background $x=(a,B)$ has flat edge labels $a_{ij}a_{jk}=a_{ik}$ and satisfies $\delta_aB=a^*\beta$, with coefficients at the first vertex. Here $(\delta_a t)_{ij}=\rho_{a_{ij}}t_j-t_i$ for a vertex cochain, $(\delta_a\lambda)_{ijk}=\rho_{a_{ij}}\lambda_{jk}-\lambda_{ik}+\lambda_{ij}$ for an edge cochain, and $(\delta_aB)_{ijkl}=\rho_{a_{ij}}B_{jkl}-B_{ikl}+B_{ijl}-B_{ijk}$. The cocycle convention is

$$
D(s,t,r,q):=\rho_s\beta(t,r,q)-\beta(st,r,q)+\beta(s,tr,q)-\beta(s,t,rq)+\beta(s,t,r)=0.
$$

The **background gauge 2-groupoid** $\mathcal B(K)$ has these backgrounds as objects. A $1$-arrow $f:x\to y$ is a raw pair $(g,\lambda)$ of vertex $G$-labels and edge $A$-labels with target $y=(b,C)$ given by

$$
b_{ij}=g_i a_{ij}g_j^{-1},\qquad \zeta^g_{ijk}(a)=-\beta(g_i,a_{ij},a_{jk})+\beta(b_{ij},g_j,a_{jk})-\beta(b_{ij},b_{jk},g_k),\qquad C=\rho_gB+\zeta^g(a)+\delta_b\lambda.
$$

Raw pairs remain distinct even when their induced functions on backgrounds coincide. For fixed $g$ and target edge labels $b$, a $2$-arrow $t:(g,\lambda)\Rightarrow(g,\lambda')$ is a vertex $A$-cochain satisfying $\lambda'-\lambda=\delta_b t$. There are no $2$-arrows between different vertex labels $g$. Vertical composition adds vertex cochains; the identity $2$-arrow is zero.

For consecutive $1$-arrows $(g,\lambda):x\to y$ and $(h,\mu):y\to z$, write $a,b,c$ for the successive edge labels. Their composite is $(hg,\nu)$, where

$$
\nu_{ij}=\rho_{h_i}\lambda_{ij}+\mu_{ij}+\tau(h,g;a)_{ij},\qquad \tau(h,g;a)_{ij}=\beta(h_i,g_i,a_{ij})-\beta(h_i,b_{ij},g_j)+\beta(c_{ij},h_j,g_j).
$$

Horizontal composition of $t$ on the first arrow and $s$ on the second is $s+\rho_h t$. Identity $1$-arrows have all vertex labels $e$ and edge labels zero. For three consecutive arrows $g,h,k$, the associator from $((k\circ h)\circ g)$ to $k\circ(h\circ g)$ is the vertex cochain $\sigma_i=\beta(k_i,h_i,g_i)$. Unit constraints are identity $2$-arrows.

A $2$-groupoid here means these data form a bicategory: each pair of objects has a category of $1$-arrows and $2$-arrows; horizontal composition preserves identities and vertical composition; associators are natural and obey the pentagon; units obey the triangle identity; all $2$-arrows are invertible and every $1$-arrow has a reverse up to invertible $2$-arrows. Finiteness means all three sets of labels are finite. Coherence of the displayed data is a separate theorem.

Write $\pi_0\mathcal B(K)$ for the equivalence classes of objects under $1$-arrows. For an object $x$, let $\pi_1(\mathcal B(K),x)$ be the group of $2$-isomorphism classes of $1$-automorphisms of $x$, and let $\pi_2(\mathcal B(K),x)$ be the abelian group of $2$-automorphisms of its identity $1$-arrow. In particular, $\pi_2$ retains vertex cochains with $\delta_a t=0$ rather than discarding them. For a subcomplex $L\subseteq K$ and fixed background $s$ on $L$, the **relative background 2-groupoid** has objects restricting exactly to $s$, $1$-arrows with $g=e$ on vertices of $L$ and $\lambda=0$ on edges of $L$, and $2$-arrows with $t=0$ on vertices of $L$.

Let $a_{ij}\in G$ be flat on every ordered triangle, let $B_{ijk}\in A$ be an $A$-valued $2$-cochain at the first vertex, and assume on every ordered tetrahedron that

$$

$$

For arbitrary vertex labels $g_i\in G$ and edge labels $\lambda_{ij}\in A$, put $a'_{ij}=g_i a_{ij}g_j^{-1}$ and

$$
\zeta_{ijk}=-\beta(g_i,a_{ij},a_{jk})+\beta(a'_{ij},g_j,a_{jk})-\beta(a'_{ij},a'_{jk},g_k).
$$

$$
B'_{ijk}=\rho_{g_i}B_{ijk}+\zeta_{ijk}+\rho_{a'_{ij}}\lambda_{jk}-\lambda_{ik}+\lambda_{ij}.
$$

Then $a'$ is flat and $(a',B')$ satisfies the same twisted tetrahedron equation. If $(g,\lambda)$ is followed by $(h,\mu)$, with $a''_{ij}=h_i a'_{ij}h_j^{-1}$, their composite is $(hg,\nu)$ where

$$

Each transformation is invertible: for a fixed source background, put $h_i=g_i^{-1}$ and

$$

$$

Fix a finite ordered simplicial complex $K$, a finite group $G$, a finite abelian group $A$ in additive notation, a left action $\rho:G\to\operatorname{Aut}(A)$, and a normalized inhomogeneous $3$-cocycle $\beta:G^3\to A$. A background $x=(a,B)$ has flat edge labels $a_{ij}a_{jk}=a_{ik}$ and satisfies $\delta_aB=a^*\beta$, with coefficients at the first vertex. Here $(\delta_a t)_{ij}=\rho_{a_{ij}}t_j-t_i$ for a vertex cochain, $(\delta_a\lambda)_{ijk}=\rho_{a_{ij}}\lambda_{jk}-\lambda_{ik}+\lambda_{ij}$ for an edge cochain, and $(\delta_aB)_{ijkl}=\rho_{a_{ij}}B_{jkl}-B_{ikl}+B_{ijl}-B_{ijk}$. The cocycle convention is

$$
D(s,t,r,q):=\rho_s\beta(t,r,q)-\beta(st,r,q)+\beta(s,tr,q)-\beta(s,t,rq)+\beta(s,t,r)=0.
$$

The **background gauge 2-groupoid** $\mathcal B(K)$ has these backgrounds as objects. A $1$-arrow $f:x\to y$ is a raw pair $(g,\lambda)$ of vertex $G$-labels and edge $A$-labels with target $y=(b,C)$ given by

$$
b_{ij}=g_i a_{ij}g_j^{-1},\qquad \zeta^g_{ijk}(a)=-\beta(g_i,a_{ij},a_{jk})+\beta(b_{ij},g_j,a_{jk})-\beta(b_{ij},b_{jk},g_k),\qquad C=\rho_gB+\zeta^g(a)+\delta_b\lambda.
$$

Raw pairs remain distinct even when their induced functions on backgrounds coincide. For fixed $g$ and target edge labels $b$, a $2$-arrow $t:(g,\lambda)\Rightarrow(g,\lambda')$ is a vertex $A$-cochain satisfying $\lambda'-\lambda=\delta_b t$. There are no $2$-arrows between different vertex labels $g$. Vertical composition adds vertex cochains; the identity $2$-arrow is zero.

For consecutive $1$-arrows $(g,\lambda):x\to y$ and $(h,\mu):y\to z$, write $a,b,c$ for the successive edge labels. Their composite is $(hg,\nu)$, where

$$
\nu_{ij}=\rho_{h_i}\lambda_{ij}+\mu_{ij}+\tau(h,g;a)_{ij},\qquad \tau(h,g;a)_{ij}=\beta(h_i,g_i,a_{ij})-\beta(h_i,b_{ij},g_j)+\beta(c_{ij},h_j,g_j).
$$

Horizontal composition of $t$ on the first arrow and $s$ on the second is $s+\rho_h t$. Identity $1$-arrows have all vertex labels $e$ and edge labels zero. For three consecutive arrows $g,h,k$, the associator from $((k\circ h)\circ g)$ to $k\circ(h\circ g)$ is the vertex cochain $\sigma_i=\beta(k_i,h_i,g_i)$. Unit constraints are identity $2$-arrows.

A $2$-groupoid here means these data form a bicategory: each pair of objects has a category of $1$-arrows and $2$-arrows; horizontal composition preserves identities and vertical composition; associators are natural and obey the pentagon; units obey the triangle identity; all $2$-arrows are invertible and every $1$-arrow has a reverse up to invertible $2$-arrows. Finiteness means all three sets of labels are finite. Coherence of the displayed data is a separate theorem.

Write $\pi_0\mathcal B(K)$ for the equivalence classes of objects under $1$-arrows. For an object $x$, let $\pi_1(\mathcal B(K),x)$ be the group of $2$-isomorphism classes of $1$-automorphisms of $x$, and let $\pi_2(\mathcal B(K),x)$ be the abelian group of $2$-automorphisms of its identity $1$-arrow. In particular, $\pi_2$ retains vertex cochains with $\delta_a t=0$ rather than discarding them. For a subcomplex $L\subseteq K$ and fixed background $s$ on $L$, the **relative background 2-groupoid** has objects restricting exactly to $s$, $1$-arrows with $g=e$ on vertices of $L$ and $\lambda=0$ on edges of $L$, and $2$-arrows with $t=0$ on vertices of $L$.

$$

$$

$$
|\pi_1(\mathcal B(K),x)|=|S_x|/|\operatorname{im}\delta_a|.
$$

A **finite groupoid** is a small category in which every morphism is invertible, with finitely many isomorphism classes and a finite automorphism group at every object. Write $\pi_0(\mathcal C)$ for its set of isomorphism classes. Its **groupoid cardinality** is

$$|\mathcal C|:=\sum_{[c]\in\pi_0(\mathcal C)}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(c)|}.$$

For an isomorphism-invariant function $f:\pi_0(\mathcal C)\to\mathbb C$, define

$$\int_{c\in\mathcal C} f(c):=\sum_{[c]\in\pi_0(\mathcal C)}\frac{f(c)}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(c)|}.$$

For finite groupoids $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$, a functor $p:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, and an object $d$ of $\mathcal D$, its **homotopy fiber** $\mathcal C_d$ has objects $(c,\alpha)$ with $\alpha:p(c)\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}d$ and morphisms $u:(c,\alpha)\to(c',\alpha')$ satisfying $\alpha'\circ p(u)=\alpha$. Define pullback and pushforward of invariant functions by

$$(p^*g)([c])=g([p(c)]),\qquad (p_!f)([d])=\int_{(c,\alpha)\in\mathcal C_d} f([c]).$$

A span $\mathcal X\xleftarrow{a}\mathcal E\xrightarrow{b}\mathcal Y$ of finite groupoids therefore induces the linear map $b_!a^*$ on invariant functions.

$$

For any subcomplex $L$ and fixed field $s$ on $L$, the higher sum over the relative $2$-groupoid is

$$
Z_{K,L}^{(2)}(s)=\frac{c(K)}{c(L)}\sum_{x|_L=s}W_K(x).
$$

citations.quote: A **fusion category** is a finite semisimple tensor category. In particular the unit of a fusion category is simple, whereas a multifusion unit may split.
A **tensor-invertible object** $D$ is an object for which some object $E$ satisfies $D\otimes E\cong\mathbf 1$ and $E\otimes D\cong\mathbf 1$.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let $G$ be a group. A
**finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$** is a finite-dimensional
$k$-vector space $V$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-dimension]]) together with a
group homomorphism
$$\rho:G\longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}(V),$$
where $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ denotes the group of invertible $k$-linear maps
$V \to V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]], [[def-group-homomorphism]]).

The associated action is
$$g \cdot v:=\rho(g)(v).$$
This makes $V$ into a $G$-module over $k$ in the sense of
[[def-g-module-over-a-commutative-ring]].

The **degree** of the representation is the dimension of its underlying vector
space:
$$\deg(\rho):=\dim_k V.$$

Let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional representation of
$G$ over a field $k$ ([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).

A **subrepresentation** is a linear subspace $W \le V$
([[def-linear-subspace]]) such that $\rho(g)(W) \subseteq W$ for every
$g \in G$. Equivalently, $g \cdot w \in W$ for all $g \in G$ and $w \in W$.

If $\sigma:G \to \operatorname{GL}(W)$ is another representation, the
**direct sum representation** $\rho \oplus \sigma$ on $V \oplus W$ is defined by
$$g \cdot (v,w):=(\rho(g)v,\sigma(g)w).$$

The representation $\rho$ is **irreducible** when $V \ne 0$ and its only
subrepresentations are $0$ and $V$ itself.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that $$V=W\oplus U.$$
The set $\operatorname{Irr}_{\mathbb C}(H)$ is finite and $$\sum_{[\pi]\in\operatorname{Irr}_{\mathbb C}(H)}(\dim_{\mathbb C}\pi)^2=|H|.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group
([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]).

**Unipotent subgroups.** A closed subgroup $U\subseteq G$ is **unipotent** if
every non-zero finite-dimensional rational $U$-module has a non-zero $U$-fixed
vector. This fixed-vector condition is the characterization used in Brion's
Example 1.22 (printed p. 8), and it is
the only form of the notion used in this pair. Equivalently, by the Lie–Kolchin
theorem, $U$ is unipotent in the standard sense that it admits no non-trivial
rational characters and all its elements are unipotent; this equivalence is
recorded as a sourced parenthetical companion to the definition (Brion Example
1.22 cites Lie–Kolchin) and is not used as a supplier anywhere in this pair, so
no edge to the higher-order unipotent/solvable page is introduced.

**Reductive and linearly reductive groups.** The group $G$ is **reductive** if
it has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, and **linearly
reductive** if every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely
reducible, i.e. a direct sum of simple $G$-submodules
([[def-completely-reducible-representation]], [[def-semisimple-module]]).

Over $\mathbf C$ the two notions coincide: every complex
reductive affine algebraic group is linearly reductive, and conversely a
linearly reductive $G$ has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup.
Both implications, together with the identity-component reduction below, are
proved in
[[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]];
this definition only records them for consumers of that theorem.

Both notions depend only on the identity component, in the sense that $G$ is
reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is, and $G$ is linearly reductive if and
only if $G^\circ$ is; the passage from $G^\circ$ to the finite component group
for both notions is carried out in the same theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group
([[def-reductive-and-linearly-reductive-over-c]]).

(i) Every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely reducible, so
$G$ is linearly reductive.

(ii) Every rational $G$-module $V$ is a direct sum of simple submodules; the
invariant subspace $V^G$ therefore has a unique $G$-stable complement $V_G$,
the sum of all simple submodules on which $G$ acts non-trivially. The
projection $R_V:V\to V^G$ with kernel $V_G$ is the **Reynolds operator** of
$V$; it is $G$-equivariant, restricts to the identity of $V^G$, and is natural:
for every morphism $f:V\to W$ of rational $G$-modules one has
$R_W\circ f=f^G\circ R_V$, and if $f$ is surjective then so is
$f^G:V^G\to W^G$.

(iii) If $A$ is a commutative $G$-algebra on which $G$ acts by algebra
automorphisms and which is a rational $G$-module, then $R_A$ is $A^G$-linear:
$R_A(ab)=a\,R_A(b)$ for $a\in A^G$, $b\in A$.

(iv) When $K\subseteq G$ is a compact subgroup whose Zariski closure in $G$ is
all of $G$, the Reynolds operator of a finite-dimensional rational $G$-module
is the invariant average $R_V(v)=\int_K g\cdot v\,dg$ with respect to
normalized Haar measure; in particular $R_V(v)$ is the unique element of $V^G$
in the convex hull of the $K$-orbit of $v$.

Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ on four-dimensional Minkowski space $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Fix a complex affine algebraic group $G$ with no nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, where unipotent means that every nonzero finite-dimensional rational module has a nonzero fixed vector; this is the reductive hypothesis. Fix a finite set $I$ of field species. For each $i\in I$, fix a finite-dimensional complex $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space $\Phi_i=\Phi_i^{\bar 0}\oplus\Phi_i^{\bar 1}$, a field parity, and an algebraic representation $\rho_i:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\Phi_i)$. Include the declared spacetime-index action in $G$ or in its specified finite-dimensional representation data. A field configuration assigns smooth component functions on $M$ to the even generators and formal odd Grassmann generators with smooth coefficient functions to the odd generators.

Fix a derivative cutoff $r\geq0$, a maximum polynomial field degree $q\geq0$, and a rational engineering weight $\Delta_i$ for each field species. A derivative $\partial_\mu$ has engineering weight one, and an $s$-jet generator is a component of $\partial_{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{\mu_s}\phi_i(x)$ for $0\leq s\leq r$. If covariant derivatives are used, their finite jet generators and $G$-action are included explicitly in the same data. Let $J_r$ be the resulting finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space with its specified algebraic representation $\rho_r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(J_r)$. Its polynomial algebra is the supercommutative algebra $P_r=\operatorname{Sym}(J_{r,\bar 0}^{*})\otimes\Lambda(J_{r,\bar 1}^{*})$: even generators commute and odd generators anticommute. For a fixed weight $D\in\mathbb Q$, let $P_{r,q,D}$ be the complex span of monomials of total engineering weight $D$ and total polynomial degree at most $q$.

A scalar operator invariant under the declared symmetries is an element of $V_{r,q,D}=P_{r,q,D}^{G}$. Engineering dimension means this assigned mass weight; it is not a statement about an observed quantity. In four dimensions a term with operator $\mathcal O_D$ has the convention $C\mathcal O_D/\Lambda^{D-4}$, where $\Lambda$ has mass dimension one and $C$ is dimensionless. Reality conditions, when required for a real action, are additional conjugation data on $V_{r,q,D}$.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the polynomial algebra consists only of constants, so its degree-at-most-$q$ subspace has dimension at most one. The subspace $P_{q,D}$ is spanned by the subset of those finitely many monomials whose assigned weights sum to $D$, so it is finite-dimensional; if no monomial has weight $D$, it is the zero space. The invariant vectors $P_{q,D}^{G}$ form a linear subspace of $P_{q,D}$ because the action preserves parity and weight, and every subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space is finite-dimensional.

Any action, boundary, or observable interpretation of the selected identities is extra mathematical data and must be stated with the result that verifies it.

The finite-order invariant operator-basis quotient is

$$
\mathcal Q_D:=V_D/R_D.
$$

Two invariant operators represent the same class exactly when their difference lies in $R_D$. Assume full AC. Use four-dimensional natural units $c=\hbar=1$ and a finite jet-polynomial field model with its declared finite rational action of a complex reductive affine algebraic group $G$. Let $S_0[\phi]$ and each $S_j[\phi]$ be $G$-invariant local polynomial functionals of these field configurations, so their formal Taylor expansions through order $N$ are defined. Let the variational derivative $\mathcal E_a^{(0)}[\phi]$ of $S_0$ be defined by

$$
D S_0[\phi](h)=\mathcal I\!\left(\sum_a h^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}[\phi]\right)
$$

for every admitted compactly supported parity-compatible variation $h$. A leading-equation relation is a density $F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}$ with local, compact-support-preserving, parity-compatible $G$-equivariant $F^a[\phi]$ for which this density lies in $W_D$; an integration-by-parts relation is a density $\partial_\mu J^\mu$ satisfying the stated boundary convention. For every $1\leq k\leq N$, the local identity-leading change of variables $\Psi_k(\phi)=\phi-\epsilon^kF[\phi]$ is invertible as a formal map through order $N$ and satisfies

$$
S_\epsilon[\Psi_k(\phi)]=S_\epsilon[\phi]-\epsilon^k\mathcal I\!\left(F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)}[\phi]\right)+O(\epsilon^{k+1}).
$$

Thus a coefficient $+\epsilon^k\mathcal I(F^a\mathcal E_a^{(0)})$ can be removed at order $k$ without changing lower-order coefficients, provided all induced terms through the retained order are kept. The quotient $\mathcal Q_D$ identifies exactly the declared polynomial, boundary, and leading-equation relation span; it asserts no equivalence of arbitrary off-shell Green functions and does not by itself assert a quantum measure or amplitude equivalence.

Fix the field data and Minkowski convention from the earlier finite-jet definition and a truncation order $N\geq0$. A regulated perturbative generating datum consists, for each regulator label $\rho$, of a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded complex space $X_\rho$ of field-mode coordinates, a specified integration functional $d\mu_\rho$ on its even/odd coordinates, a local action $S_{\rho,\epsilon}:X_\rho\to\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{N+1})$, and a generating functional

$$
Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]=\int_{X_\rho}\exp\!\bigl(iS_{\rho,\epsilon}(\varphi)+i\langle J,\varphi\rangle\bigr)\,d\mu_\rho(\varphi),\qquad Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]\text{ is a unit},
$$

where $J\in X_\rho^*$ is a linear source and the integral is either an actual convergent finite-dimensional integral or a specified formal perturbative integral. “A unit” means that the constant coefficient of $Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]$ is nonzero, so the normalized functional $Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]/Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]$ is defined in the truncated ring. An admissible field-coordinate change is a local, parity-preserving formal map $F_{\rho,\epsilon}:X_\rho\to X_\rho$ with $F_{\rho,0}=\operatorname{id}$ and an inverse modulo $\epsilon^{N+1}$; local means each output field at $x$ depends on a finite jet at $x$. Its regulated Jacobian factor $\mathcal J_{F,\rho}$ is the factor specified by the exact change-of-variables identity

$$
\int h(\varphi)\,d\mu_\rho(\varphi)=\int h(F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi))\,\mathcal J_{F,\rho}(\psi)\,d\mu_\rho(\psi)
$$

for every admissible integrand $h$; no assertion that this factor is $1$ is part of the definition. In the transformed coordinates the source is $J\cdot F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi)$, so the field insertion remains the same named original coordinate.

An LSZ amplitude datum is an additional limit of connected momentum-space Green functions as regulators are removed, when that limit exists. The connected $n$-point function is $i^{-n}$ times the $n$th source derivative of $\log(Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]/Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0])$ at $J=0$, Fourier transformed with convention $\widetilde f(p)=\int e^{ip\cdot x}f(x)\,d^4x$; the overall momentum-conservation delta function is removed. For each external one-particle channel $a$ (with a fixed polarization component when the field has spin), the datum specifies a mass $m_a>0$ and nonzero simple-pole residue $Z_a$ at $s_a=m_a^2$, where $s_a=-\eta^{\mu\nu}p_{a,\mu}p_{a,\nu}$. Here “stable external channel” means precisely that this isolated pole exists with nonzero residue and zero width. The transformed interpolating fields must have an invertible one-particle overlap matrix; this is part of the datum. For every $n$-point function it requires pole factorization

$$
G_n(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{Z_{a_j}^{1/2}}{s_j-m_{a_j}^2}\right)\mathcal A_n(p_1,\ldots,p_n)+\text{terms missing at least one external pole}.
$$

The normalized LSZ amplitude is the joint residue

$$
\mathcal A_n=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n Z_{a_j}^{-1/2}\right)\lim_{s_j\to m_{a_j}^2}\left(\prod_{j=1}^n(s_j-m_{a_j}^2)\right)G_n.
$$

This definition supplies only the regulator and pole data needed for a conditional amplitude statement. It does not assert that a continuum limit, stable particles, or LSZ poles exist for a given quantum field theory.

Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group
([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]).

**Unipotent subgroups.** A closed subgroup $U\subseteq G$ is **unipotent** if
every non-zero finite-dimensional rational $U$-module has a non-zero $U$-fixed
vector. This fixed-vector condition is the characterization used in Brion's
Example 1.22 (printed p. 8), and it is
the only form of the notion used in this pair. Equivalently, by the Lie–Kolchin
theorem, $U$ is unipotent in the standard sense that it admits no non-trivial
rational characters and all its elements are unipotent; this equivalence is
recorded as a sourced parenthetical companion to the definition (Brion Example
1.22 cites Lie–Kolchin) and is not used as a supplier anywhere in this pair, so
no edge to the higher-order unipotent/solvable page is introduced.

**Reductive and linearly reductive groups.** The group $G$ is **reductive** if
it has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, and **linearly
reductive** if every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely
reducible, i.e. a direct sum of simple $G$-submodules
([[def-completely-reducible-representation]], [[def-semisimple-module]]).

Over $\mathbf C$ the two notions coincide: every complex
reductive affine algebraic group is linearly reductive, and conversely a
linearly reductive $G$ has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup.
Both implications, together with the identity-component reduction below, are
proved in
[[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]];
this definition only records them for consumers of that theorem.

Both notions depend only on the identity component, in the sense that $G$ is
reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is, and $G$ is linearly reductive if and
only if $G^\circ$ is; the passage from $G^\circ$ to the finite component group
for both notions is carried out in the same theorem.

Fix a regulator $\rho$ and make the substitution $\varphi=F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi)$ in the original integral. By A2 and F3, its density becomes $\mathcal J_{F,\rho}(\psi)d\mu_\rho(\psi)$, the action becomes $S_{\rho,\epsilon}(F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi))$, and the source becomes $J\cdot F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi)$. Thus the unnormalized source functionals are equal coefficientwise through order $N$. Their zero-source values are the same unit, so their normalized functionals are equal as well.

The functions and all external pole residues are equal by step 2.1, so the residue-normalized amplitudes are equal coefficientwise through order $N$. This conclusion is conditional on the common stable-pole limit; if it does not exist, no amplitude claim is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite set $I$ of field species. For each $i\in I$, fix a finite-dimensional complex $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space $\Phi_i=\Phi_i^{\bar 0}\oplus\Phi_i^{\bar 1}$, a field parity, and an algebraic representation $\rho_i:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\Phi_i)$. Include the declared spacetime-index action in $G$ or in its specified finite-dimensional representation data. A field configuration assigns smooth component functions on $M$ to the even generators and formal odd Grassmann generators with smooth coefficient functions to the odd generators.

Fix a derivative cutoff $r\geq0$, a maximum polynomial field degree $q\geq0$, and a rational engineering weight $\Delta_i$ for each field species. A derivative $\partial_\mu$ has engineering weight one, and an $s$-jet generator is a component of $\partial_{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{\mu_s}\phi_i(x)$ for $0\leq s\leq r$. If covariant derivatives are used, their finite jet generators and $G$-action are included explicitly in the same data. Let $J_r$ be the resulting finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded vector space with its specified algebraic representation $\rho_r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(J_r)$. Its polynomial algebra is the supercommutative algebra $P_r=\operatorname{Sym}(J_{r,\bar 0}^{*})\otimes\Lambda(J_{r,\bar 1}^{*})$: even generators commute and odd generators anticommute. For a fixed weight $D\in\mathbb Q$, let $P_{r,q,D}$ be the complex span of monomials of total engineering weight $D$ and total polynomial degree at most $q$.

A local operator in this finite-order data is an element of $P_{r,q,D}$ evaluated at $x$ on the $r$-jet of the fields. Engineering dimension means this assigned mass weight; it is not a statement about an observed quantity. Reality conditions, when required for a real action, are additional conjugation data on $V_{r,q,D}$.

derivations.claim: For a compactly supported variation $h$, the kinetic variation is $-\mathcal I(\partial_\mu h\,\partial^\mu\phi)=\mathcal I(h\Box\phi)$, since $\partial_\mu(h\partial^\mu\phi)$ integrates to zero. The potential variation is $\mathcal I(h(-m^2\phi-g\phi^3/6))$. Thus $DS_0[\phi](h)=\mathcal I(h\mathcal E_0)$ with the displayed $\mathcal E_0$.

The field has weight one and each derivative has weight one, so $\mathcal O_6$ has weight six; $M_s^2\phi^4$ and $g\phi^6$ also have weight six. Their derivative orders and field degrees lie within the stated cutoffs, so the displayed identity concerns elements of the declared finite operator space.

The product rule gives $\partial_\mu(\phi^3\partial^\mu\phi)=3\phi^2\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi+\phi^3\Box\phi$. The boundary convention therefore yields $\mathcal I(\phi^3\Box\phi)=-3\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)$.

Before specialization, substituting $\widehat{\mathcal E}_0=\Box\phi-M_s^2\phi-g\phi^3/6$ into step 1.3 gives $\mathcal I(\phi^3\widehat{\mathcal E}_0)=-3\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)-\mathcal I(M_s^2\phi^4)-(g/6)\mathcal I(\phi^6)$. Each density has weight six, and the relation subspace contains this leading-equation density and the divergence from step 1.3. The quotient definition [F2] therefore gives the displayed class identity.

Put $a=C/(3\Lambda^2)$ and use [F3] with $k=1$ and $F[\phi]=-a\phi^3$, so its map $\phi-\epsilon F[\phi]$ is $\phi+\epsilon a\phi^3$. Its units are those of $\phi$, and its first-order action change is $-\epsilon\mathcal I(F\mathcal E_0)=\epsilon a\mathcal I(\phi^3\mathcal E_0)$, as also follows from step 1.1. Since $\epsilon^2=0$, substituting the shifted field into the order-$\epsilon$ term changes that term only by zero in the truncated ring.

Specialize $M_s=m$ in step 2.1, insert that identity into step 2.2, and add the original $+\epsilon(C/\Lambda^2)\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)$ term. Its coefficient cancels because $3a=C/\Lambda^2$, leaving exactly the quartic and sextic shifts displayed in the Example.

citations.quote: With the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2N}$, $\rho_N$ is a real-linear isometry. A supplied finite-dimensional truncated RG datum for this scheme is an open set $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^{2N}$ and a supplied continuous map $\beta:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{2N}$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Use the oriented Volterra form and shared state-Lipschitz constant to bound the trajectory distance by the initial distance plus its time integral, and bound that distance uniformly.
Iterate the integral inequality and bound its final remainder by 4r times (Ld)^m/m!.
Let m tend to infinity to obtain the exponential continuous-dependence estimate, including equality at the base time.

Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. An external scalar datum consists of a spin-zero species assigned a mass $m>0$ and elastic two-particle threshold $s=4m^2$. This is a mathematical input package; it does not construct a one-particle scattering state or a scattering matrix. For real on-shell momenta $p_1,p_2$ incoming and $p_3,p_4$ outgoing, with $p_j^2=-m^2$ and $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$, define

$$s=-(p_1+p_2)^2,\qquad t=-(p_1-p_3)^2,\qquad u=-(p_1-p_4)^2.$$

Then $s+t+u=4m^2$. The forward slice is the complex-valued function $A(s)=\mathcal A(s,0,4m^2-s)$ obtained by analytically continuing the identical-scalar $2\to2$ amplitude to $t=0$. The crossing action on this slice is $s\mapsto4m^2-s$, which exchanges $s$ and $u$. Assume $A(s)=A(4m^2-s)$ wherever both sides are defined.

For context, when a full $t$-dependent amplitude is supplied, use the partial-wave normalization

$$\mathcal A(s,t,u)=16\pi\sqrt{\frac{s}{s-4m^2}}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)P_\ell\!\left(1+\frac{2t}{s-4m^2}\right)a_\ell(s),\qquad P_\ell(1)=1,$$

where $\ell$ is a nonnegative integer and $P_\ell$ is the Legendre polynomial. The forward result below uses only the optical-theorem sign $\operatorname{Im}A(s+i0)\ge0$ for $s>4m^2$; a full partial-wave realization is not inferred from this definition. In the displayed normalization, this sign follows when the forward partial-wave sum converges and the supplied partial waves obey $\operatorname{Im}a_\ell(s)\ge|a_\ell(s)|^2\ge0$.

Put $\nu_0=2m^2$ and $v=s-2m^2$, so $u-2m^2=-v$. Choose finitely many real numbers $p_j\in(0,4m^2)\setminus\{2m^2\}$ and real residues $r_j$, and set

$$P(s)=\sum_j\left(\frac{r_j}{s-p_j}+\frac{r_j}{4m^2-p_j-s}\right).$$

Each summand pair is the real simple-pole principal part at $s=p_j$ and its $s\leftrightarrow u$ crossing partner; hence $P(4m^2-s)=P(s)$. These poles lie off the two-particle cuts. Define the pole-subtracted forward function $B(v)=A(2m^2+v)-P(2m^2+v)$. Assume $B$ is holomorphic on

$$\Omega_{\nu_0}=\mathbb C\setminus\bigl((-\infty,-\nu_0]\cup[\nu_0,\infty)\bigr),$$

real analytic there, meaning $B(\overline v)=\overline{B(v)}$, and has finite upper and lower boundary values on both cuts except at their endpoints. Here the two-particle gap is the open interval $(-\nu_0,\nu_0)$ in the $v$ variable; no massless pole or cut reaches the forward point $t=0$.

Require additionally that $B$ extends continuously from each open half-plane onto every compact segment of either real cut bank avoiding $\pm\nu_0$. Assume the exact high-energy condition $B(w)=o(|w|^2)$ uniformly as $|w|\to\infty$ in the closed upper half-plane, including upper cut-bank limits. In particular this holds on the large upper semicircles after any fixed bounded horizontal translation. For $\nu\ge\nu_0$, define the absorptive density $\rho(\nu)=\operatorname{Im}B(\nu+i0)$. Require $\rho$ to be nonnegative and Riemann integrable on every compact subinterval of $[\nu_0,\infty)$, and require $\int_{\nu_0}^{\infty}\rho(\nu)\nu^{-3}\,d\nu$ to converge as a finite improper Riemann integral. For every real $v$ with $|v|<\nu_0$, require the integrals along both sides of the two cuts of $[B(x)-B(0)]/[x^2(x-v)]$, with boundary values taken from the upper and lower half-planes, to exist as finite improper Riemann limits. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: The entries of $U^*U-I_2$ and $\det U-1$ are continuous real polynomial functions of the eight real coordinates of $U$. Their common zero set $SU(2)$ is therefore closed. Since $U^*U=I_2$, each column of $U$ has Euclidean norm one, so every matrix entry has modulus at most one; hence $SU(2)$ is bounded in $\mathbb R^8$. By [F2], $SU(2)$ is compact. Its real Lie-group structure is supplied by [F1].

The matrices $g=\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$ and
$h=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfy $g^*g=h^*h=I_2$ and
$\det g=\det h=1$, so both lie in $SU(2)$. Direct multiplication gives
$gh=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$hg=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}$; therefore $gh\ne hg$ and the group is noncommutative.

By [F1], every element of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has the form
$\begin{pmatrix}i\alpha&z\\-\overline z&-i\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ with
$\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $z\in\mathbb C$. Thus $T_1,T_2,T_3$ form a real
basis. Multiplying the displayed matrices gives
$[T_1,T_2]=T_3$, $[T_2,T_3]=T_1$, and $[T_3,T_1]=T_2$; antisymmetry and
bilinearity give the stated $\epsilon_{abc}$ formula.

The same finite matrix products give
$-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(T_aT_b)=\delta_{ab}$. Since each $X\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$
has real coordinates in this basis, $\kappa(X,X)$ is the sum of their squares,
and $\kappa$ is positive definite; trace cyclicity gives symmetry. For every
$g\in SU(2)$,
$\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_gX,\operatorname{Ad}_gY)
=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(gXYg^{-1})
=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)=\kappa(X,Y)$, so the form is
$\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant.

\mathcal L_{\mathrm{YM}}(A_i)\,d^4x=-\frac{1}{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2}\,\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i),\qquad [A_i]=\mathrm m^{-1},\quad [F_i]=\mathrm m^{-2}.
$$

For any relatively compact region on which the density is integrable, the
action is its integral. On all of $M$, the action is defined when that
integral converges. Local stationarity is tested through relative action
differences under smooth compactly supported adjoint-bundle-valued
one-form variations; these differences have compact support and are finite.
No boundary values are imposed at infinity. On a finite region, admissible
variations vanish near its boundary. This is an adopted classical model and
normalization, not a theorem, measured law, or claim that a quantum
continuum theory exists.

Each instance of the adopted classical pure Yang–Mills model has spacetime $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$,
coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$ of length, orientation
$dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, time orientation of increasing
$x^0$, and Lorentz metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Use

$\mathrm m$, and the natural action $S/\hbar$ is dimensionless.

Fix the global structure group $G=SU(2)$, not its quotient $SO(3)$. Each
instance selects a smooth right principal $SU(2)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and
admits only its bundle sector $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. The matter-representation label set
is empty, so there are no matter fields or current source. The Lie algebra is
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with basis $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2$ and positive
$\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant form
$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$, normalized by
$\kappa(T_a,T_b)=\delta_{ab}$. The positive coupling $g_{\mathrm{YM}}$ is a
fixed dimensionless model parameter.

description unless a global trivialization has been specified.

$\omega(Z_P)=Z$ and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$, where

$Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_{SU(2)}(tZ)$. In a local
section $s_i:U_i\to P$, let $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and let
$F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$ be its curvature. Here the bracket is the
alternating-form extension of the Lie bracket, and the local forms on
overlaps satisfy the right-action transition convention
$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+g_{ij}^{-1}dg_{ij}$ and
$F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i$ when $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$. Thus

associated adjoint bundle; the invariant form $\kappa$ makes
$\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i)$ a global scalar four-form.

$\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and put
$T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ for $a\in\{1,2,3\}$. Then $G$ is compact and

$\kappa(X,Y)=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is positive
definite, symmetric, and invariant under

Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle as in
[[def-smooth-principal-g-bundle]]. A **smooth gauge transformation** of $P$ is
a smooth diffeomorphism $\Phi:P\to P$ satisfying
$$\pi\circ\Phi=\pi,\qquad \Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g\quad(p\in P,\ g\in G).$$
Here diffeomorphism has the meaning of
[[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]. The **gauge
group** $\mathcal G(P)$ is the set of these transformations under composition.
The identity is a smooth diffeomorphism and composites of smooth maps are
smooth by
[[prop-identity-maps-and-composites-of-smooth-maps-are-smooth]]; composites of
diffeomorphisms are diffeomorphisms because their inverses are composites of
the smooth inverses. The identity covers $M$ and commutes with the right
action. If $\Phi,\Psi\in\mathcal G(P)$, then $\Phi\circ\Psi$ covers $M$ and
$(\Phi\circ\Psi)(pg)=\Phi(\Psi(p)g)=\Phi(\Psi(p))g$, so the conditions are
closed under composition. The inverse of such a $\Phi$ also covers $M$: if
$q=\Phi(p)$ then $\pi(\Phi^{-1}(q))=\pi(p)=\pi(q)$. Equivariance gives
$$\Phi^{-1}(qg)=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(p)g)=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(pg))=pg.$$

group under the composition law of [[def-group]].

on the total bundle by automorphisms over the identity map of $M$. They are

curvatures from

$X,Y\in T_pP$,
$$K_{\Phi_*H}(d\Phi_pX,d\Phi_pY)=d\Phi_p(K_H(X,Y)).$$

principal connections.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle for a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, with $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$. A supplied principal connection is a smooth, right-invariant complement $TP=VP\oplus H$, where $VP=\ker d\pi$; write $v:TP\to VP$ for the projection along $H$, and let $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$ be its vertical-valued curvature. The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$$\omega_p(X):=\zeta_p^{-1}(v_pX),\qquad X\in T_pP.$$

Then $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$ for every fixed $g\in G$. Conversely, a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form with the reproduction and equivariance properties determines the principal connection $H=\ker\omega$. $$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. $$
(\nabla^\omega\sigma)_i=d\psi_i+\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i,
$$

where $(\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i)(X)=\rho_*(A_i(X))\psi_i$ for $X\in TU_i$. These expressions patch to a smooth $E$-valued 1-form on $M$, independently of the chosen local sections, and satisfy $\nabla^\omega(f\sigma)=df\otimes\sigma+f\nabla^\omega\sigma$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ on $M$.

derivations.claim:
Put $H^\Phi=d\Phi(H)$ and let $\omega^\Phi$ be its connection form. Equivariance of $\Phi$ gives $d\Phi_p(Z_P(p))=Z_P(\Phi(p))$ for every $Z\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Since $d\Phi$ transports both the vertical and horizontal summands, their projections commute with $d\Phi$; the defining formula $\omega=\zeta^{-1}v$ therefore gives
$\omega^\Phi_{\Phi(p)}(d\Phi_pX)=\omega_p(X)$ for every $X\in T_pP$.

By [F3] and [F5],
$\Omega_{H^\Phi,\Phi(p)}(d\Phi_pX,d\Phi_pY)
=\omega^\Phi_{\Phi(p)}(K_{H^\Phi}(d\Phi_pX,d\Phi_pY))
=\omega_p(K_H(X,Y))
=\Omega_{H,p}(X,Y)$.
Thus $\Omega_{H^\Phi}=(\Phi^{-1})^*\Omega_H$.

On a local trivializing set, $\Phi^{-1}\circ s_i$ is another smooth section, so there is a unique smooth $v_i:U_i\to SU(2)$ with $\Phi^{-1}\circ s_i=s_i v_i$. Pulling the curvature identity of step 2.1 back along $s_i$ gives
$F_i^\Phi=(\Phi^{-1}\circ s_i)^*\Omega_H$. Apply the section-transition formula in [F5] to the two sections $s_i$ and $s_i v_i$; it yields
$F_i^\Phi=\operatorname{Ad}_{v_i^{-1}}F_i$. This uses only the local transition function and does not construct a global map $M\to SU(2)$.

The Hodge operator acts on the spacetime-form factors and commutes pointwise with the adjoint action. By [F1],
$\kappa(F_i^\Phi\wedge *_\eta F_i^\Phi)
=\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_{v_i^{-1}}F_i\wedge *_\eta\operatorname{Ad}_{v_i^{-1}}F_i)
=\kappa(F_i\wedge *_\eta F_i)$
on every trivializing set. These equal local scalar four-forms define the same global action density by the adjoint-bundle pairing, so their integrals over every region where the action is defined agree. No boundary term is introduced because the density is unchanged pointwise.

In one local section, expand the Cartan formula at $A_i+\varepsilon a$:
$F_{A_i+\varepsilon a}
=F_i+\varepsilon(da+[A_i\wedge a])
+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}[a\wedge a]
=F_i+\varepsilon D_{A_i}a+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}[a\wedge a]$.
Here $[A_i\wedge a]=[a\wedge A_i]$ because both inputs have degree one and the graded bracket is symmetric in that degree.

In a Lie-algebra basis, differentiate the scalar-valued form
$\kappa(a\wedge *_\eta F_i)$. The ordinary graded product rule gives
$\kappa(da\wedge *_\eta F_i)-\kappa(a\wedge d *_\eta F_i)$. Invariance of
$\kappa$, together with moving the degree-one factors $A_i$ and $a$ past
one another, gives
$\kappa([A_i\wedge a]\wedge *_\eta F_i)
=\kappa(a\wedge[A_i\wedge *_\eta F_i])$. Therefore
$d\kappa(a\wedge *_\eta F_i)
=\kappa(D_{A_i}a\wedge *_\eta F_i)
-\kappa(a\wedge D_{A_i} *_\eta F_i)$.

The difference of the two action densities vanishes outside the compact support of $a$ and its derivatives. Apply the parameter-differentiation clause of [F5] to its smooth coordinate coefficients. Symmetry of $\kappa$ and the even degree of $F_i$ then give
$\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_0\Delta(S/\hbar)_i(\varepsilon;a)
=-\frac{1}{g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2}\int
\kappa(D_{A_i}a\wedge *_\eta F_i)$.

Write the compactly supported scalar three-form as
$\kappa(a\wedge *_\eta F_i)=\sum_{\mu=0}^3h_\mu\widehat{dx^\mu}$ with
$h_\mu\in C_c^1(U_i)$. Its exterior derivative is
$\sum_\mu(\partial_\mu h_\mu)d^4x$. Apply the integration-by-parts clause
of [F5] with the constant function $1$ to each coefficient $h_\mu$; each
integral is zero, so $\int d\kappa(a\wedge *_\eta F_i)=0$. Substitution in
step 2.1 yields
$\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_0\Delta(S/\hbar)_i(\varepsilon;a)
=-\frac{1}{g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2}\int
\kappa(a\wedge D_{A_i} *_\eta F_i)$.

Conversely, assume stationarity. In a local coordinate chart and the orthonormal basis from [F1], write
$J_i=D_{A_i} *_\eta F_i
=\sum_{\mu=0}^3\sum_{b=1}^3J_{\mu b}T_b\,\widehat{dx^\mu}$,

$dx^\mu\wedge\widehat{dx^\mu}=d^4x$. For fixed $\mu,b$, choose
$a=\psi T_b dx^\mu$ with arbitrary smooth compactly supported real $\psi$.

throughout the chart. All coefficients vanish, so the local equation holds.
