$s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, then [F2] gives
$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij})$ and
$(*_\eta F_j)=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}(*_\eta F_i)$. For
$X\in T_x(U_i\cap U_j)$, put $Z=\theta_L(g_{ij})(X)$ and use the path

The section-transition law in [F3], applied to $s^u=su$ and $A=0$, gives
$A^u=u^{-1}du$. Since $u=\exp(T_3\sin(x^0/\ell))$ and $T_3$ commutes with itself, differentiation yields
$u^{-1}du=T_3\ell^{-1}\cos(x^0/\ell)\,dx^0$. If the phase were constant,
the same formula would give the zero potential; the chosen sine has
nonzero derivative, so $A^u$ is nonzero.

The coefficient of $A^u$ depends only on $x^0$ and its one-form factor is $dx^0$, so $dA^u=0$. Every value of $A^u$ is proportional to $T_3$, hence $[A^u\wedge A^u]=0$ by [F2]. factor $(dx^0-dx^3)$ already present in the wedge product; the covariant
bracket term also vanishes because both Lie-algebra factors are $T_3$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For a spatial wave vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, with each component in
$\mathrm m^{-1}$ and the Euclidean norm, define
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, with
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here $\omega_\mu$ is the temporal wave number, not the
SI angular frequency; the corresponding SI angular frequency is
$c\omega_\mu$. Energy and momentum are $E=\hbar c\omega_\mu$ in joules and
$\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With
$p=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$, the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

For a selected local action represented on a chart region
$\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by
$$\frac{S}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathcal U}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\,d^4x,\quad d^4x:=dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3,$$
the natural Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. Since $x^0=ct$, the corresponding SI Lagrangian density is
$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}:=\hbar c\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ and has unit
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. This unit conversion alone does not identify a
Lagrangian density with the model's Hamiltonian energy density.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
use the formal field symbols $\phi_{\rm n}$ and $\psi_{\rm n}$ in the selected
scalar and Dirac kinetic terms, assigning them length degrees $-1$ and
$-3/2$, respectively. These are the dimensions fixed by those free kinetic
terms, not exact scaling dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous
dimensions, when present, are separate quantities. These symbols do not
assert pointwise field maps or operator fields; a model supplies its field
space and regularity. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

In a supplied four-component spinor representation, let
$\gamma^a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^4)$, $a=0,1,2,3$, be
dimensionless linear maps satisfying
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}:=\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a
=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$, where $I_4$ is the identity map. Set $\beta:=\gamma^0$
and $\alpha^i:=\beta\gamma^i$; then $\beta^2=I_4$ and
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$. For a supplied four-component spinor $\psi$ write
$\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta$. The effective Clifford metric is $-\eta$.
A supplied free Dirac model may use
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ for its model-supplied spinor field
$\psi$; that model supplies its field domain and regularity. The phase and
Clifford choices are conventions; this item proves no representation or field
equation.

For the autonomous evolution convention, assume Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice
function. Let a selected model supply a complex Hilbert space $\mathscr H$
as in [[def-hilbert-space]] and a time-independent complex-linear Hamiltonian
$H:D(H)\to\mathscr H$ with a specified dense linear domain
$D(H)\subseteq\mathscr H$ and SI energy
unit joules. Require self-adjointness as in
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]: $H=H^*$,
including equality of domains and values. Here $y\in D(H^*)$ precisely when
there is a $z\in\mathscr H$ such that
$\langle Hx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in D(H)$, and
$H^*y=z$; density makes $z$ unique.

The published mathematical supplier
[[lem-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cc-arbitrary-hilbert-spectral-calculus]]
then supplies the spectral measure $E_H$ on the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R$. This is a normalized projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]: its values are bounded orthogonal
projections, $E_H(\mathbb R)=I$, $E_H(B\cap C)=E_H(B)E_H(C)$, and it is
countably additive in norm on every vector. For $\xi\in\mathscr H$ put
$\nu_\xi(B):=\langle E_H(B)\xi,\xi\rangle$, a finite positive measure.
The spectral integral of $\lambda$ represents $H$, on exactly the domain
$D(H)=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,d\nu_\xi(\lambda)<\infty\}$.
For real $t$ in seconds define the autonomous evolution by bounded Borel
functional calculus,
$$U(t):=\exp(-itH/\hbar):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda).$$
The spectral variable $\lambda$ carries unit joule. This exponential is a
bounded operator on all of $\mathscr H$, even when $H$ is unbounded; it
does not mean an operator power series on arbitrary vectors. The supplier
gives a strongly continuous unitary group: $U(0)=I$,
$U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$ and $\|U(t)\xi-U(t_0)\xi\|\to0$ as $t\to t_0$ for
each $\xi\in\mathscr H$. A model may restrict it to a declared
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$. Each $U(t)$ is a surjective complex-linear map
satisfying $\langle U(t)\xi,U(t)\zeta\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in\mathscr H$; write $U(t)^*:=U(t)^{-1}$. The exponent
is dimensionless because $\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For any
model-supplied complex-linear operator $O:D(O)\to\mathscr H$, with specified
linear domain $D(O)\subseteq\mathscr H$, define its Heisenberg conjugate by
$$O_H(t):=U(t)^*O\,U(t),\quad D(O_H(t)):=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:U(t)\xi\in D(O)\}.$$
The model supplies the Hamiltonian and operator domains; the spectral supplier
justifies this evolution only for those data and hypotheses. This dictionary
constructs no model-specific Hamiltonian or field representation and does not
adopt a physical dynamics law. Where a free-field
module uses an inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the
repository's first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction. It
asserts only matrix-element continuity and the stated linear maps; all further
operator properties, locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior must be supplied by a constructed
model. Test-function units can be chosen so a specified smeared observable is
dimensionless; there is no universal test-function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

supplier_excerpts.excerpt:
Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. A **non-Abelian gauge datum on $M$** consists of the following specified objects.

First choose a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ that is compact in its manifold topology (every open cover has a finite subcover) and noncommutative (there are $g,h\in G$ with $gh\ne hg$). The actual group $G$, including its global form, is part of the datum. Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$ with the bracket transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields.

Choose a smooth right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$: the projection and right action are smooth, the action is free and transitive on each fibre, and there are local trivializations $\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$ that are equivariant diffeomorphisms over each open $U\subseteq M$.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

Two smooth right principal $G$-bundles over $M$ are isomorphic over $M$ when a smooth diffeomorphism between their total spaces covers $\operatorname{id}_M$ and commutes with the right $G$-actions. A **bundle sector** is one equivalence class under this relation. The datum specifies a set $\Sigma$ of admitted bundle sectors and requires $[P]\in\Sigma$; a model may take $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. The Lie algebra alone does not replace the chosen group or sector. This definition does not choose a connection, an action functional, or a quantum theory.

Use natural units c=ℏ=1, with physical dimensions assigned using the QFT unit convention of the selected model. A finite-regulator effective-field-theory model-data record consists of a finite undirected graph Γ=(X,EΓ) with nonempty vertex set X, the graph distance dΓ, retained real coordinates ℓ∈ℝ^X, integrated real coordinates χ∈ℝ^X, a Borel ultraviolet action SUV(ℓ,χ)∈ℝ, and a specified Borel probability measure νH on ℝ^X for the integrated coordinates. The full ultraviolet data are these objects before any integration. This definition does not assert that the integral of exp(−SUV) exists; finiteness and positivity are checked when the Wilsonian action is defined.

For the positive heavy-scalar Gaussian submodel, include a real symmetric matrix A on ℝ^X satisfying uᵀAu≥0 for every u and Axy=0 when dΓ(x,y)>1. Its entries have mass-squared units and its operator norm satisfies √‖A‖≤Λ. Choose M>0 and put K=M²I+A. The heavy coordinate χ has mass-inverse units, so χᵀKχ is dimensionless. A source J(ℓ)∈ℝ^X has mass units, so J(ℓ)ᵀχ is dimensionless. When the source is restricted to external energy E, require J(ℓ)=PEJ(ℓ), where PE is the orthogonal spectral projection of A onto eigenvalues in [0,E²].

The scale data are a positive Wilsonian matching scale $\mu_W$, a heavy mass $M>0$, an external energy bound $E\ge0$, and a regulator cutoff $\Lambda>0$, with $\sqrt{\|A\|}\le\Lambda$ in the Gaussian submodel. The Wilsonian scale $\mu_W$ records where the retained low-coordinate action is specified; $M$ is the heavy quadratic mass; $E$ bounds the admitted source spectrum; and $\Lambda$ bounds the finite regulator. These are separately named parameters, and this definition imposes no relation among their numerical values. A small-remainder theorem may require an additional hierarchy such as $E<M$.

Light and heavy name the roles in the declared split: ℓ is retained at μW and χ is integrated in the finite measure νH. They do not assert that every retained field is massless or that every integrated field is heavy in an unrestricted continuum theory. If the model includes non-Abelian gauge data, record the actual global group, Lie algebra, principal bundle, representations, and admitted bundle sectors as one supplied gauge-data object. That object selects no connection, action, or quantum measure by itself. The Gaussian submodel below keeps any such gauge data as fixed context and makes no gauge-field integration claim.

This is a finite-dimensional regulator description. It makes no assertion that a general interacting functional measure exists, that a cutoff can be removed, or that any selected model describes nature.

Take a finite-regulator model datum with retained coordinates $\ell$, integrated coordinates $h$, a normalized Borel probability measure $\nu_H$ on the finite-dimensional $h$-space, and a real Borel ultraviolet action $S_{\rm UV}(\ell,h)$. For each retained configuration $\ell$ define

$$
Z_H(\ell):=\int e^{-S_{\rm UV}(\ell,h)}\,d\nu_H(h).
$$

On the domain of $\ell$ for which $0<Z_H(\ell)<\infty$, the finite-regulator Wilsonian action at scale $\mu_W$ is

$$
S_W(\ell;\mu_W):=-\log Z_H(\ell).
$$

Thus “integrating out” the high sector means this specified finite integral over $h$ while $\ell$ is held fixed. The measure, action, regulator, and low/high split are inputs; the definition does not assert that every interacting model has a finite or well-defined integral. Replacing $\nu_H$ by a positive constant multiple changes $S_W$ only by an additive constant independent of $\ell$, which is fixed by the chosen normalization convention.

A one-particle-irreducible effective action, when it exists, is the Legendre transform of a connected source-generating functional for the retained fields. It is a different construction from the high-coordinate integral above. No 1PI functional is needed or asserted here.

derivations.claim: The identity $A^0=I$ has range zero. If $A^r$ has range at most $r$, then $(A^{r+1})_{xy}=\sum_{z\in X}(A^r)_{xz}A_{zy}$. A nonzero summand requires $d_\Gamma(x,z)\le r$ and $d_\Gamma(z,y)\le1$, so the triangle inequality gives $d_\Gamma(x,y)\le r+1$. Induction yields range at most $r$ for every $A^r$.

Each term of $S_N$ is a scalar multiple of $A^r$ with $r\le N$. Therefore every matrix entry of $S_N$ vanishes when $d_\Gamma(x,y)>N$. It is a finite-range approximation to the finite-regulator Wilsonian kernel; no convergence or generic remainder follows from this range calculation.

finite_checks: For N=0, S0=M^-2 I has range zero; step 1.1 proves range at most r for each finite power A^r.
The range assertion is proved exactly in steps 1.1–2.1; no convergence test is used.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Use natural units c=ℏ=1, with physical dimensions assigned using the QFT unit convention of the selected model. A finite-regulator effective-field-theory model-data record consists of a finite undirected graph Γ=(X,EΓ) with nonempty vertex set X, the graph distance dΓ, retained real coordinates ℓ∈ℝ^X, integrated real coordinates χ∈ℝ^X, a Borel ultraviolet action SUV(ℓ,χ)∈ℝ, and a specified Borel probability measure νH on ℝ^X for the integrated coordinates. The full ultraviolet data are these objects before any integration. This definition does not assert that the integral of exp(−SUV) exists; finiteness and positivity are checked when the Wilsonian action is defined.

For the positive heavy-scalar Gaussian submodel, include a real symmetric matrix A on ℝ^X satisfying uᵀAu≥0 for every u and Axy=0 when dΓ(x,y)>1. Its entries have mass-squared units and its operator norm satisfies √‖A‖≤Λ. Choose M>0 and put K=M²I+A. The heavy coordinate χ has mass-inverse units, so χᵀKχ is dimensionless. A source J(ℓ)∈ℝ^X has mass units, so J(ℓ)ᵀχ is dimensionless. When the source is restricted to external energy E, require J(ℓ)=PEJ(ℓ), where PE is the orthogonal spectral projection of A onto eigenvalues in [0,E²].

The scale data are a positive Wilsonian matching scale $\mu_W$, a heavy mass $M>0$, an external energy bound $E\ge0$, and a regulator cutoff $\Lambda>0$, with $\sqrt{\|A\|}\le\Lambda$ in the Gaussian submodel. The Wilsonian scale $\mu_W$ records where the retained low-coordinate action is specified; $M$ is the heavy quadratic mass; $E$ bounds the admitted source spectrum; and $\Lambda$ bounds the finite regulator. These are separately named parameters, and this definition imposes no relation among their numerical values. A small-remainder theorem may require an additional hierarchy such as $E<M$.

Light and heavy name the roles in the declared split: ℓ is retained at μW and χ is integrated in the finite measure νH. They do not assert that every retained field is massless or that every integrated field is heavy in an unrestricted continuum theory. If the model includes non-Abelian gauge data, record the actual global group, Lie algebra, principal bundle, representations, and admitted bundle sectors as one supplied gauge-data object. That object selects no connection, action, or quantum measure by itself. The Gaussian submodel below keeps any such gauge data as fixed context and makes no gauge-field integration claim.

This is a finite-dimensional regulator description. It makes no assertion that a general interacting functional measure exists, that a cutoff can be removed, or that any selected model describes nature.

Take a finite-regulator model datum with retained coordinates $\ell$, integrated coordinates $h$, a normalized Borel probability measure $\nu_H$ on the finite-dimensional $h$-space, and a real Borel ultraviolet action $S_{\rm UV}(\ell,h)$. For each retained configuration $\ell$ define

$$
Z_H(\ell):=\int e^{-S_{\rm UV}(\ell,h)}\,d\nu_H(h).
$$

On the domain of $\ell$ for which $0<Z_H(\ell)<\infty$, the finite-regulator Wilsonian action at scale $\mu_W$ is

$$
S_W(\ell;\mu_W):=-\log Z_H(\ell).
$$

Thus “integrating out” the high sector means this specified finite integral over $h$ while $\ell$ is held fixed. The measure, action, regulator, and low/high split are inputs; the definition does not assert that every interacting model has a finite or well-defined integral. Replacing $\nu_H$ by a positive constant multiple changes $S_W$ only by an additive constant independent of $\ell$, which is fixed by the chosen normalization convention.

A one-particle-irreducible effective action, when it exists, is the Legendre transform of a connected source-generating functional for the retained fields. It is a different construction from the high-coordinate integral above. No 1PI functional is needed or asserted here.

In the finite graph model, a matrix $B$ on $\mathbb R^X$ has range at most $r$ when $B_{xy}=0$ whenever $d_\Gamma(x,y)>r$. The positive heavy-sector matrix $A$ from the model data has range at most one. A derivative expansion of its inverse kernel is the formal operator series

$$
(M^2I+A)^{-1}\sim M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(-A/M^2)^r.
$$

Its order-$N$ truncation, for an integer $N\ge0$, is the finite operator

$$
S_N:=M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-A/M^2)^r.
$$

It has range at most $N$ in this regulator. For a source $J$ supported in the spectral interval $[0,E^2]$ of $A$, the dimensionless power-counting parameter is $E/M$. This definition is an organized finite-order approximation; it does not assert convergence for unrestricted sources, a generic error bound, or a continuum local-operator expansion. The positive Gaussian theorem supplies a remainder bound only under its exact hypotheses.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $A:D(A)\subseteq H\to H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint and nonnegative, and let $M>0$. Set $K=M^2I+A$ on $D(A)$ and let $E_A$ be the spectral measure of $A$. Define $f_M(a)=(M^2+a)^{-1}$ for $a\ge0$. The bounded spectral operator $f_M(A)$ is the inverse $K^{-1}$ and satisfies $\|K^{-1}\|\le M^{-2}$. For $J\in H$ define the matched quadratic effective-action contribution
$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{eff}}(J):=-\tfrac12\langle J,K^{-1}J\rangle.$$
The inner product is the complex Hilbert pairing, linear in its first variable; the displayed quadratic form is real and nonpositive. In natural units $\hbar=c=1$, $A$ and $K$ have mass-squared units; normalize the source/pairing so $\langle J,K^{-1}J\rangle$ is dimensionless, hence $\|J\|^2$ has mass-squared units. In a finite real regulator, integration of $\exp[-\tfrac12\chi^TK\chi+j^T\chi]$ divided by the zero-source Gaussian integral yields $\exp[\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j]$, so the corresponding effective action changes by $-\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j$. Since $\log$ is the inverse of $\exp$ on positive reals, taking $-\log$ of that normalized integral gives this effective-action contribution. Determinants and Lebesgue integration are finite-regulator quantities only; this definition supplies no infinite-dimensional Gaussian measure or determinant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite, and let $j\in\mathbb R^d$. Let $\gamma_{K^{-1}}=N_d(0,K^{-1})$, where covariance is the matrix $\mathbb E[XX^T]$. Then
$$\frac{\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp(-\tfrac12x^TKx+j^Tx)\,dx} {\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp(-\tfrac12x^TKx)\,dx} =\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{j^Tx}\,d\gamma_{K^{-1}}(x) =\exp\!\left(\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j\right).$$
Equivalently, in the finite real Gaussian regulator with normalized weight $e^{-S}$ and $\hbar=1$, completing the source shift $\chi=K^{-1}j+\eta$ gives
$$\tfrac12\chi^TK\chi-j^T\chi=\tfrac12\eta^TK\eta-\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j.$$
Use $\hbar=1$ and coordinate/source units for which $x^TKx$ and $j^Tx$ are dimensionless. Both integrals are finite; their common Gaussian normalization cancels in the ratio. No infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure or determinant is asserted.

Assume the hypotheses and notation of the positive heavy-mode Gaussian matching data. Let $E\ge0$ be an energy and let $P_E:=E_A([0,E^2])$ be the spectral projection of $A$. For $J=P_EJ\in H$ and an integer $N\ge0$, define
$$S_NJ:=M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-A/M^2)^rJ,$$
which is well-defined since $J$ has bounded spectral support. Put $R_NJ:=K^{-1}J-S_NJ$. Then
$$\|R_NJ\|\le M^{-2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}\|J\|,$$
and
$$\left|\Delta S_{\mathrm{eff}}(J)+\tfrac12\langle J,S_NJ\rangle\right| =\tfrac12|\langle J,R_NJ\rangle| \le \frac{\|J\|^2}{2M^2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}.$$
Use natural units $\hbar=c=1$: $A$ has units of mass squared, $E,M$ have mass units, and $E^2/M^2$ is dimensionless. Under the source normalization of the positive heavy-mode Gaussian matching data, $\|J\|^2/M^2$ and the action remainder are dimensionless. These are exact conditional bounds for every $E\ge0$; the truncation is small/useful when $E<M$. No claim is made for unrestricted sources or arbitrary interacting matching.

derivations.claim: For every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $x^TKx=M^2\|x\|^2+x^TAx>0$, so $K$ is symmetric positive definite and the finite Gaussian supplier applies. On the complexification, real symmetry makes $A$ self-adjoint; for $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, the cross terms in $\langle x+iy,A(x+iy)\rangle$ cancel because $x^TAy=y^TAx$, leaving $x^TAx+y^TAy\ge0$. Thus the positive-operator hypotheses of [F4] also hold.

By [F5], $Z_H(J)=\exp(\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J)$; the normalized reference measure makes $Z_H(0)=1$, so no determinant factor remains in this ratio. By the definition of the Wilsonian action in [F2], taking $-\log$ gives $\Delta S_W(J)=-\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J$.

By [F4] and step 2.1, the heavy Gaussian effective-action contribution equals $\Delta S_W(J)$. Apply [F6] to the band-limited source $J=P_EJ$ and the positive operator verified in step 1.1; its vector and action inequalities are the two displayed remainder bounds. When the additional condition $E<M$ holds, the factor $E^2/M^2$ is less than one and the bound decreases geometrically with $N$. This conclusion is conditional and remains within the finite Gaussian sector.

finite_checks: At J=0 the normalized source integral is 1 and both remainders vanish. At N=0, S0J=M^-2J; the source theorem gives the stated bound for all E≥0.
texp-aqft-finite-heavy-scalar-matching.finite_checks_disposition: Exact conditional formulas; geometric decrease is asserted only for E<M. No fit or empirical inference is used.

Statement permits E=0 and J=0; the normalized source integral and both bounds give the zero-source case.
Statement includes d=1 and step 1.1 proves K positive definite there.
Statement permits A=0; M>0 keeps K positive definite by step 1.1.
Statement allows E=0 and N=0; bounds hold for every E≥0 and step 3.1 makes geometric decrease conditional on E<M.
Statement assumes AC; A1 and A2 record the Gaussian and countable-choice inputs.

Assume the hypotheses and notation of the positive heavy-mode Gaussian matching data. Let $E\ge0$ be an energy and let $P_E:=E_A([0,E^2])$ be the spectral projection of $A$. For $J=P_EJ\in H$ and an integer $N\ge0$, define
$$S_NJ:=M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-A/M^2)^rJ,$$
which is well-defined since $J$ has bounded spectral support. Put $R_NJ:=K^{-1}J-S_NJ$. Then
$$\|R_NJ\|\le M^{-2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}\|J\|,$$
and
$$\left|\Delta S_{\mathrm{eff}}(J)+\tfrac12\langle J,S_NJ\rangle\right| =\tfrac12|\langle J,R_NJ\rangle| \le \frac{\|J\|^2}{2M^2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}.$$
Use natural units $\hbar=c=1$: $A$ has units of mass squared, $E,M$ have mass units, and $E^2/M^2$ is dimensionless. Under the source normalization of the positive heavy-mode Gaussian matching data, $\|J\|^2/M^2$ and the action remainder are dimensionless. These are exact conditional bounds for every $E\ge0$; the truncation is small/useful when $E<M$. No claim is made for unrestricted sources or arbitrary interacting matching.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the finite-regulator model data in the definitions below. Let $d\ge1$, let $A$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, let $M>0$, and put $K=M^2I+A$. Use natural units with $\chi$ in mass-inverse units, $A$ and $K$ in mass-squared units, and a source $J\in\mathbb R^d$ in mass units. Let $E\ge0$, let $P_E$ be the spectral projection of the complexification of $A$ onto $[0,E^2]$, and assume $J=P_EJ$. In the finite Gaussian sector, let $\gamma_{K^{-1}}=N_d(0,K^{-1})$ and define

$$ Z_H(J):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{J^T\chi}\,d\gamma_{K^{-1}}(\chi) $$

$$ \Delta S_W(J):=-\log Z_H(J) $$

For each integer $N\ge0$, put

$$
S_NJ:=M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-A/M^2)^rJ.
$$

Then both finite Gaussian integrals are finite and

$$ Z_H(J)=\exp\!\left(\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J\right) $$

$$ \Delta S_W(J)=-\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J $$

The inverse-kernel and action remainders satisfy

$$
\|K^{-1}J-S_NJ\|\le M^{-2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}\|J\|,
$$

$$ \left|\Delta S_W(J)+\tfrac12J^TS_NJ\right| \le \frac{\|J\|^2}{2M^2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1} $$

These are exact conditional statements for a finite positive quadratic heavy sector. The remainder is small in the stated band when $E<M$; no claim is made for unrestricted sources, arbitrary interactions, a continuum measure, or a differentiated Wilsonian flow.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $C_1,C_2$ be real symmetric positive-semidefinite $d\times d$ covariance matrices, and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty]$ be Borel. For a covariance matrix $C$, let $\gamma_C$ denote the centered Gaussian probability with covariance $C$, including when $C$ is singular, and define

$$
T_Cf(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x+z)\,d\gamma_C(z).
$$

For a finite nonnegative Borel potential $V$, $0<T_C(e^{-V})(x)\le1$; define the finite nonnegative potential $V_C(x):=-\log T_C(e^{-V})(x)$. Then

$$
T_{C_2}(T_{C_1}f)(x)=T_{C_1+C_2}f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d)
$$

as an equality in $[0,\infty]$, and

$$
e^{-(V_{C_1})_{C_2}(x)}=e^{-V_{C_1+C_2}(x)}.
$$

The Gaussian measures are normalized probabilities, so no determinant or vacuum constant appears. This is a finite-regulator composition identity; it asserts no derivative equation along a covariance path and no continuum limit.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$. For a real symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix $C$, write $\gamma_C=N_d(0,C)$, allowing singular $C$. For a nonnegative Borel function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty]$, define the normalized shell transform
$$T_Cf(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x+z)\,d\gamma_C(z)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is a Borel function of $x$. If $V:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ is finite-valued and Borel, define
$$V_C(x):=-\log\bigl(T_C(e^{-V})(x)\bigr).$$
Then $V_C$ is a finite nonnegative Borel function, and $0<T_C(e^{-V})(x)\le1$ for every $x$. The covariance convention is $\mathbb E[ZZ^T]=C$. The coordinates $x,z$ use the same finite-regulator field-coordinate convention, so $C$ has the square units of those coordinates. The scalar $V(x)$ is dimensionless in $e^{-V(x)}$; if a physical interpretation identifies $V$ with an action, it is normalized as $S/\hbar$. The measures $\gamma_C$ are normalized probabilities, with no determinant/vacuum factor in $T_C$. The transform is defined at finite regulator only.

derivations.claim: Here $K=5m_0^2$ is positive, $J$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $E^2=m_0^2$, and $E<M$. Thus $K^{-1}J=1/(5m_0)$ and $S_0J=M^{-2}J=1/(4m_0)$. By [F1], $Z_H(J)=e^{1/10}$ and $\Delta S_W=-1/10$, while the order-zero action is $-\tfrac12J^TS_0J=-1/8$.

The vector remainder is $|1/(5m_0)-1/(4m_0)|=1/(20m_0)\le1/(16m_0)$, the bound in [F1] for $N=0$. The action remainder is $|-1/10+1/8|=1/40$, while [F1] bounds it by $\tfrac12(m_0^2/(4m_0^2))(m_0^2/(4m_0^2))=1/32$. Both inequalities are exact rational comparisons.

For $Z_C\sim N_1(0,C)$, [F3] gives $\mathbb E Z_C=0$ and $\mathbb E Z_C^2=C$. Hence [F4] gives $T_Cf(x)=\mathbb E[(x+Z_C)^2]=x^2+C$. Therefore $T_3(T_1f)(0)=T_3(x^2+1)(0)=4=T_4f(0)$, in agreement with [F2]. The shell measures are normalized, so no determinant factor is introduced.

Use natural units c=ℏ=1, with physical dimensions assigned using the QFT unit convention of the selected model. A finite-regulator effective-field-theory model-data record consists of a finite undirected graph Γ=(X,EΓ) with nonempty vertex set X, the graph distance dΓ, retained real coordinates ℓ∈ℝ^X, integrated real coordinates χ∈ℝ^X, a Borel ultraviolet action SUV(ℓ,χ)∈ℝ, and a specified Borel probability measure νH on ℝ^X for the integrated coordinates. The full ultraviolet data are these objects before any integration. This definition does not assert that the integral of exp(−SUV) exists; finiteness and positivity are checked when the Wilsonian action is defined.

For the positive heavy-scalar Gaussian submodel, include a real symmetric matrix A on ℝ^X satisfying uᵀAu≥0 for every u and Axy=0 when dΓ(x,y)>1. Its entries have mass-squared units and its operator norm satisfies √‖A‖≤Λ. Choose M>0 and put K=M²I+A. The heavy coordinate χ has mass-inverse units, so χᵀKχ is dimensionless. A source J(ℓ)∈ℝ^X has mass units, so J(ℓ)ᵀχ is dimensionless. When the source is restricted to external energy E, require J(ℓ)=PEJ(ℓ), where PE is the orthogonal spectral projection of A onto eigenvalues in [0,E²].

The scale data are a positive Wilsonian matching scale $\mu_W$, a heavy mass $M>0$, an external energy bound $E\ge0$, and a regulator cutoff $\Lambda>0$, with $\sqrt{\|A\|}\le\Lambda$ in the Gaussian submodel. The Wilsonian scale $\mu_W$ records where the retained low-coordinate action is specified; $M$ is the heavy quadratic mass; $E$ bounds the admitted source spectrum; and $\Lambda$ bounds the finite regulator. These are separately named parameters, and this definition imposes no relation among their numerical values. A small-remainder theorem may require an additional hierarchy such as $E<M$.

Light and heavy name the roles in the declared split: ℓ is retained at μW and χ is integrated in the finite measure νH. They do not assert that every retained field is massless or that every integrated field is heavy in an unrestricted continuum theory. If the model includes non-Abelian gauge data, record the actual global group, Lie algebra, principal bundle, representations, and admitted bundle sectors as one supplied gauge-data object. That object selects no connection, action, or quantum measure by itself. The Gaussian submodel below keeps any such gauge data as fixed context and makes no gauge-field integration claim.

This is a finite-dimensional regulator description. It makes no assertion that a general interacting functional measure exists, that a cutoff can be removed, or that any selected model describes nature.

supplier_excerpts.excerpt:
Take a finite-regulator model datum with retained coordinates $\ell$, integrated coordinates $h$, a normalized Borel probability measure $\nu_H$ on the finite-dimensional $h$-space, and a real Borel ultraviolet action $S_{\rm UV}(\ell,h)$. For each retained configuration $\ell$ define

$$
Z_H(\ell):=\int e^{-S_{\rm UV}(\ell,h)}\,d\nu_H(h).
$$

On the domain of $\ell$ for which $0<Z_H(\ell)<\infty$, the finite-regulator Wilsonian action at scale $\mu_W$ is

$$
S_W(\ell;\mu_W):=-\log Z_H(\ell).
$$

Thus “integrating out” the high sector means this specified finite integral over $h$ while $\ell$ is held fixed. The measure, action, regulator, and low/high split are inputs; the definition does not assert that every interacting model has a finite or well-defined integral. Replacing $\nu_H$ by a positive constant multiple changes $S_W$ only by an additive constant independent of $\ell$, which is fixed by the chosen normalization convention.

A one-particle-irreducible effective action, when it exists, is the Legendre transform of a connected source-generating functional for the retained fields. It is a different construction from the high-coordinate integral above. No 1PI functional is needed or asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.excerpt:
In the finite graph model, a matrix $B$ on $\mathbb R^X$ has range at most $r$ when $B_{xy}=0$ whenever $d_\Gamma(x,y)>r$. The positive heavy-sector matrix $A$ from the model data has range at most one. A derivative expansion of its inverse kernel is the formal operator series

$$
(M^2I+A)^{-1}\sim M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(-A/M^2)^r.
$$

Its order-$N$ truncation, for an integer $N\ge0$, is the finite operator

$$
S_N:=M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-A/M^2)^r.
$$

It has range at most $N$ in this regulator. For a source $J$ supported in the spectral interval $[0,E^2]$ of $A$, the dimensionless power-counting parameter is $E/M$. This definition is an organized finite-order approximation; it does not assert convergence for unrestricted sources, a generic error bound, or a continuum local-operator expansion. The positive Gaussian theorem supplies a remainder bound only under its exact hypotheses.

supplier_excerpts.excerpt:
A supplied finite-dimensional truncated RG datum for this scheme
is an open set $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^{2N}$ and a supplied
continuous map $\beta:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{2N}$. A truncated RG trajectory is
a continuously differentiable curve $C:I'\to\mathbb C^N$, on an interval
$I'\subset I$ for which $(t,\rho_N(C(t)))\in\Omega$, satisfying
$$\frac{d}{dt}\rho_N(C(t))=\beta(t,\rho_N(C(t))).$$
The components of $\beta$ are the beta functions under this logarithmic-scale
convention. If the supplied flow is complex-linear, with a supplied matrix
function $\Gamma:I'\to\mathbb C^{N\times N}$, its equation can be written
$C'=\Gamma(t)C$, where the real-coordinate vector field is
$\beta(t,\rho_N(C))=\rho_N(\Gamma(t)C)$. In this column-vector convention,
$\Gamma$ is called the anomalous-dimension matrix. A scheme record does not
assert that its coefficient-coordinate maps solve a supplied RG equation; that
relation, the entries of $\beta$, and any matching map are separate inputs.
This definition calculates no QFT beta function and supplies no bound on
omitted perturbative or higher-dimension terms.

$I'\subset I$ for which $(t,\rho_N(C(t)))\in\Omega$, satisfying

The components of $\beta$ are the beta functions under this logarithmic-scale
convention. If the supplied flow is complex-linear, with a supplied matrix
function $\Gamma:I'\to\mathbb C^{N\times N}$, its equation can be written
$C'=\Gamma(t)C$, where the real-coordinate vector field is
$\beta(t,\rho_N(C))=\rho_N(\Gamma(t)C)$. In this column-vector convention,
$\Gamma$ is called the anomalous-dimension matrix. A scheme record does not
assert that its coefficient-coordinate maps solve a supplied RG equation; that
relation, the entries of $\beta$, and any matching map are separate inputs.
This definition calculates no QFT beta function and supplies no bound on
omitted perturbative or higher-dimension terms.

A declared matching calculation supplies a finite list of renormalized amplitudes or Green-function values $A_{\sigma,j}(t,c;\lambda_{\mathrm{IR}})$, where $j$ indexes the selected external states and kinematics, $c$ is a coefficient vector, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{IR}}$ denotes the common infrared regulator used in both descriptions. Let $U_\sigma\subset\mathbb C^{N_\sigma}$ be open coefficient domains for $\sigma\in\{+,-\}$. The supplied matching family is a jointly continuously differentiable real map $\widehat{\mathcal M}:\mathcal V\to\rho_{N_-}(U_-)$ on an open domain $\mathcal V\subset J\times\rho_{N_+}(U_+)$. Its admissible domain is the open subset $\mathcal U=\{(t,x)\in\mathcal V:(t,x)\in\Omega_+,\ (t,\widehat{\mathcal M}(t,x))\in\Omega_-\}$. It defines $M_t(c):=\rho_{N_-}^{-1}(\widehat{\mathcal M}(t,\rho_{N_+}(c)))$ for each admitted $(t,c)$, and $\widehat M_t(x):=\widehat{\mathcal M}(t,x)$ on the corresponding slice. Thus the scale derivative and coefficient derivative in the compatibility condition below both exist and are continuous. It is a matching map through the declared loop order, operator dimension, and mass-expansion order when, for every selected $j$ and every admitted pair $(t,c)$ with $c\in U_+$, the prescribed truncations of $A_{+,j}(t,c;\lambda_{\mathrm{IR}})$ and $A_{-,j}(t,M_t(c);\lambda_{\mathrm{IR}})$ agree. The truncation projection and its retained orders are part of the datum. This equality records only the selected amplitudes and orders; it neither estimates discarded terms nor asserts that a matching calculation exists for every model.

A matching map is RG-compatible on these domains when, in realified coefficient coordinates,
$$\partial_t\widehat M_t(x)+D_x\widehat M_t(x)\,\beta_+(t,x)=\beta_-\!\left(t,\widehat M_t(x)\right)$$
for every admitted $(t,x)$. Here $D_x$ is the ordinary real derivative with respect to the coefficient coordinates. RG-compatibility is an additional condition to be checked from the supplied beta functions and matching calculation; it does not follow merely from defining $M_t$ by amplitude equality.

Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common interval
containing $t_0$. Here local well-posedness means local existence, uniqueness,
and this uniform continuous dependence on initial coefficient data. Under
$C=\rho_N^{-1}(x)$, realified solutions give complex coefficient trajectories.
The theorem asserts no global solution, no bound on omitted terms, and no
calculation of a QFT beta function.

Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. An external scalar datum consists of a spin-zero species assigned a mass $m>0$ and elastic two-particle threshold $s=4m^2$. This is a mathematical input package; it does not construct a one-particle scattering state or a scattering matrix. For real on-shell momenta $p_1,p_2$ incoming and $p_3,p_4$ outgoing, with $p_j^2=-m^2$ and $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$, define

$$s=-(p_1+p_2)^2,\qquad t=-(p_1-p_3)^2,\qquad u=-(p_1-p_4)^2.$$

Then $s+t+u=4m^2$. The forward slice is the complex-valued function $A(s)=\mathcal A(s,0,4m^2-s)$ obtained by analytically continuing the identical-scalar $2\to2$ amplitude to $t=0$. The crossing action on this slice is $s\mapsto4m^2-s$, which exchanges $s$ and $u$. Assume $A(s)=A(4m^2-s)$ wherever both sides are defined.

For context, when a full $t$-dependent amplitude is supplied, use the partial-wave normalization

$$\mathcal A(s,t,u)=16\pi\sqrt{\frac{s}{s-4m^2}}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)P_\ell\!\left(1+\frac{2t}{s-4m^2}\right)a_\ell(s),\qquad P_\ell(1)=1,$$

where $\ell$ is a nonnegative integer and $P_\ell$ is the Legendre polynomial. The forward result below uses only the optical-theorem sign $\operatorname{Im}A(s+i0)\ge0$ for $s>4m^2$; a full partial-wave realization is not inferred from this definition. In the displayed normalization, this sign follows when the forward partial-wave sum converges and the supplied partial waves obey $\operatorname{Im}a_\ell(s)\ge|a_\ell(s)|^2\ge0$.

Put $\nu_0=2m^2$ and $v=s-2m^2$, so $u-2m^2=-v$. Choose finitely many real numbers $p_j\in(0,4m^2)\setminus\{2m^2\}$ and real residues $r_j$, and set

$$P(s)=\sum_j\left(\frac{r_j}{s-p_j}+\frac{r_j}{4m^2-p_j-s}\right).$$

Each summand pair is the real simple-pole principal part at $s=p_j$ and its $s\leftrightarrow u$ crossing partner; hence $P(4m^2-s)=P(s)$. These poles lie off the two-particle cuts. Define the pole-subtracted forward function $B(v)=A(2m^2+v)-P(2m^2+v)$. Assume $B$ is holomorphic on

$$\Omega_{\nu_0}=\mathbb C\setminus\bigl((-\infty,-\nu_0]\cup[\nu_0,\infty)\bigr),$$

real analytic there, meaning $B(\overline v)=\overline{B(v)}$, and has finite upper and lower boundary values on both cuts except at their endpoints. Here the two-particle gap is the open interval $(-\nu_0,\nu_0)$ in the $v$ variable; no massless pole or cut reaches the forward point $t=0$.

Require additionally that $B$ extends continuously from each open half-plane onto every compact segment of either real cut bank avoiding $\pm\nu_0$. This is an extra admissibility assumption on the supplied data, not a consequence of finite pointwise boundary values or a claim about every quantum field theory. 

Assume the exact high-energy condition $B(w)=o(|w|^2)$ uniformly as $|w|\to\infty$ in the closed upper half-plane, including upper cut-bank limits. In particular this holds on the large upper semicircles after any fixed bounded horizontal translation. For $\nu\ge\nu_0$, define the absorptive density $\rho(\nu)=\operatorname{Im}B(\nu+i0)$. Require $\rho$ to be nonnegative and Riemann integrable on every compact subinterval of $[\nu_0,\infty)$, and require $\int_{\nu_0}^{\infty}\rho(\nu)\nu^{-3}\,d\nu$ to converge as a finite improper Riemann integral. For every real $v$ with $|v|<\nu_0$, require the integrals along both sides of the two cuts of $[B(x)-B(0)]/[x^2(x-v)]$, with boundary values taken from the upper and lower half-planes, to exist as finite improper Riemann limits. Require also that the small endpoint arcs at $\pm\nu_0$ for this integrand vanish in the contour limit. Since $P$ is real off its poles, $\rho(\nu)=\operatorname{Im}A(2m^2+\nu+i0)$ for $\nu>\nu_0$ on the right cut.

The normalized forward Taylor coefficients are $c_n=B^{(2n)}(0)/(2n)!$ for integers $n\ge1$. They have units $(\text{mass})^{-4n}$; $\nu_0$ has units $(\text{mass})^2$. No sign is assigned here to a generic off-shell Lagrangian coefficient.

A local operator in this finite-order data is an element of $P_{r,q,D}$ evaluated at $x$ on the $r$-jet of the fields. A scalar operator invariant under the declared symmetries is an element of $V_{r,q,D}=P_{r,q,D}^{G}$. Engineering dimension means this assigned mass weight; it is not a statement about an observed quantity. In four dimensions a term with operator $\mathcal O_D$ has the convention $C\mathcal O_D/\Lambda^{D-4}$, where $\Lambda$ has mass dimension one and $C$ is dimensionless.

Thus $\int d\xi_i\,1=0$ and $\int d\xi_i\,\xi_i=1$. Fix the ordered measures
$$ \int d^2\theta:=\int d\theta^2\,d\theta^1,\qquad \int d^2\bar\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1},\qquad \int d^4\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1}\,d\theta^2\,d\theta^1. $$
With this order, $\int d^4\theta$ extracts the coefficient of $\theta^1\theta^2\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}$. For superspace coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^{1,3}$ in natural units $\hbar=c=1$, assign mass dimensions $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta^\alpha]=[\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, $[d\theta^\alpha]=[d\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=\tfrac12$, and hence $[d^2\theta]=[d^2\bar\theta]=1$ and $[d^4\theta]=2$. derivations.claim: For any even smooth superspace function $X$, substitute the operators from [F1] into $\delta X$. Since the odd parameters are constant, the odd Leibniz rule gives $\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)$ and $-\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}X=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)$. The remaining terms are ordinary spacetime derivatives, so $\delta X=-\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}(\epsilon^\alpha X)+\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}(\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}X)+\partial_\mu(-i\epsilon^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}X+i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$.

For a chiral superfield $X(y,\theta)$, use $y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta$ and the left-derivative rules in [F1]–[F3]. The chain rule gives $Q_\alpha=\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}|_y$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}|_y+2i\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_{y^\mu}$. Since $X$ is independent of $\bar\theta$, $\delta X=\epsilon^\alpha\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}X+2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu X$.

Expand the supercharge anticommutators from [F1]. The only nonzero terms in $\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}$ are $\{\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha},i\theta^\gamma\sigma^\mu_{\gamma\dot\beta}\partial_\mu\}=i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and $\{-i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\gamma}\bar\theta^{\dot\gamma}\partial_\mu,-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\beta}}\}=i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$. Terms with two odd coordinates cancel under symmetrization, and derivatives in distinct generators anticommute by [F3]. Hence $\{Q_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta}\}=2i\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}\partial_\mu$ and both same-chirality anticommutators are zero.

Apply step 1.1 to the even D-term integrand $X=K(\bar\Phi,\Phi)$, whose finite nilpotent Taylor expansion is smooth. Each odd-coordinate derivative has zero top coefficient in the ordered Grassmann basis from [F3], so its Berezin integral vanishes. The spacetime-divergence term integrates to zero because the field-dependent part of $K$ is compactly supported and its constant exterior value has zero supersymmetry variation. The fixed physical factor $-1/4$ multiplies zero, so the D-term action is invariant.

The first term in step 1.2 integrates to zero under $d^2\theta$ by the same coefficient-extraction calculation as step 2.1. The second is the spacetime divergence $\partial_\mu(2i\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\theta^\beta\sigma^\mu_{\beta\dot\alpha}X)$; compact support removes its boundary term. Holomorphicity and chirality make $W(\Phi)$ chiral, and complex conjugation gives the same conclusion for its antichiral conjugate. The fixed physical factor $1/2$ and its conjugate preserve this zero variation, so the F-term action is invariant.

By [F2], the transformations preserve the chiral constraint, so the transformed field has the unique component expansion in [F1]. Coefficient extraction is linear; therefore the operator identities in step 1.3 induce the same translation algebra on every component, including the independent auxiliary field $F^i$. No Euler–Lagrange equation was used, proving off-shell closure.

For each matter representation, let $V_R$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hermitian space and $R:SU(2)\to U(V_R)$ a smooth unitary representation; write $\rho_{R*}$ for its Lie-algebra differential. In the fundamental representation set $T_a=-i\sigma_a/2\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $t_a=iT_a=\sigma_a/2$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_2(t_at_b)=\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$. In representation $R$, set $t_{a,R}=i\rho_{R*}(T_a)$. In a local trivialization write $V=V^at_a$ and $V_R=V^at_{a,R}$, and set $A_\mu=-i g_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu$ when $B_\mu=B_\mu^at_a$ is its vector component. Thus the matter covariant derivative is $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+\rho_{R*}(A_\mu)=\partial_\mu-i g_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu^at_{a,R}$.

A **vector superfield prepotential** is a dimensionless smooth even real matrix-valued superfield $V$ in the finite Grassmann-valued superspace of the N=1 chiral-superfield convention. Under a global rigid supersymmetry variation it transforms as $\delta V=(\epsilon^\alpha Q_\alpha+\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\alpha})V$, with the supercharges defined in the chiral-superfield convention. Its local gauge transformations are $\Phi_R\mapsto e^{i\Lambda_R}\Phi_R$ and $e^{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}\mapsto e^{i\Lambda_R^\dagger}e^{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}e^{-i\Lambda_R}$, where $\Phi_R$ is chiral, $V_R=V^at_{a,R}$, and $\Lambda_R=\Lambda^at_{a,R}$ is a dimensionless chiral gauge-parameter superfield in the represented complexified Lie algebra $\mathfrak{su}(2)_{\mathbb C}=\mathfrak{su}(2)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$. The associated represented matrix curvature is defined by

$$\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}=-\tfrac14\bar D^{\dot\beta}\bar D_{\dot\beta}\!\left(e^{-2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}D_\alpha e^{2g_{\mathrm{YM}}V_R}\right),$$

Distinguish this represented curvature from the abstract connection-normalized Lie-algebra-valued curvature $\mathcal W_\alpha$. With canonical adjoint component field strength $W^a_{\mathrm{can},\alpha}$, the matrix convention is $\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}=2g_{\mathrm{YM}}t_{a,R}W^a_{\mathrm{can},\alpha}$, whereas $\mathcal W_\alpha=g_{\mathrm{YM}}T_aW^a_{\mathrm{can},\alpha}$. Since $t_{a,R}=i\rho_{R*}(T_a)$, their precise dictionary is

$$\rho_{R*}(\mathcal W_\alpha)=\frac{\mathscr C_{\alpha,R}}{2i}.$$

In the fundamental representation this gives $\kappa_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal W^\alpha,\mathcal W_\alpha)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2(\mathscr C^\alpha\mathscr C_\alpha)$, where $\kappa_{\mathbb C}=-2\operatorname{Tr}_2$ is evaluated on the Lie-algebra matrices $\mathcal W$, not on the raw $\mathscr C$. Thus the chiral action coefficient $\kappa_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal W^\alpha,\mathcal W_\alpha)/(4g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2)$ equals $\operatorname{Tr}_2(\mathscr C^\alpha\mathscr C_\alpha)/(8g_{\mathrm{YM}}^2)$, before adding its Hermitian conjugate. This is a fixed real-coupling classical normalization identity; it is not a quantum-field rescaling or measure identity. Both curvatures are chiral and have the corresponding conjugation/transition law. The abstract $\mathcal W$ has the connection-normalized gaugino and auxiliary components specified below.

Here $\theta^2=\theta^\alpha\theta_\alpha$ and $\bar\theta^2=\bar\theta_{\dot\alpha}\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$ use the fixed antisymmetric spinor tensors. Their dimensions are $[B_\mu]=1$, $[\lambda_B]=3/2$, and $[D_B]=2$. The connection-normalized fields are $A_\mu=-ig_{\mathrm{YM}}B_\mu$, $\lambda=g_{\mathrm{YM}}\lambda_B$, and $D=g_{\mathrm{YM}}D_B$; hence $[A_\mu]=1$, $[\lambda]=3/2$, and $[D]=2$. $$ \int d^2\theta:=\int d\theta^2\,d\theta^1,\qquad \int d^2\bar\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1},\qquad \int d^4\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1}\,d\theta^2\,d\theta^1. $$
With this order, $\int d^4\theta$ extracts the coefficient of $\theta^1\theta^2\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}$. For superspace coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^{1,3}$ in natural units $\hbar=c=1$, assign mass dimensions $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta^\alpha]=[\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, $[d\theta^\alpha]=[d\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=\tfrac12$, and hence $[d^2\theta]=[d^2\bar\theta]=1$ and $[d^4\theta]=2$. Let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_{\bar0}\oplus\mathcal A_{\bar1}$ be the finite-dimensional supercommutative complex coefficient algebra, and let $\Lambda_4$ have ordered generators $\theta^1,\theta^2,\bar\theta^{\dot1},\bar\theta^{\dot2}$ and the product, parity, derivatives and conjugation specified in the four-dimensional superspace Grassmann algebra. Use the mostly-plus metric and the matrices $\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}$ specified by the four-dimensional super-Poincare algebra. A **chiral superfield** is an even element $\Phi\in\mathscr S$ satisfying the two equations

$$\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\Phi=0,\qquad \bar D_{\dot\alpha}:=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}-i\sum_{\alpha,\mu}\theta^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu,\quad \dot\alpha\in\{\dot1,\dot2\}.$$

Define the nilpotent coordinate shift $\Delta y^\mu=i\sum_{\alpha,\dot\alpha}\theta^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$ and $y^\mu=x^\mu+\Delta y^\mu$. For a smooth coefficient function $f$, $f(y)$ means the finite Taylor substitution $\sum_{k=0}^{2}(\Delta y^{\mu_1}\cdots\Delta y^{\mu_k}/k!)\,\partial_{\mu_1}\cdots\partial_{\mu_k}f(x)$, with the $k=0$ term equal to $f(x)$ and repeated spacetime indices summed; higher terms vanish in $\Lambda_4$. The chiral components are the unique smooth coefficient functions $A,F\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^{1,3},\mathcal A_{\bar0})$ and $\psi_1,\psi_2\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^{1,3},\mathcal A_{\bar1})$ in

$$\Phi(y,\theta)=A(y)+\theta^1\psi_1(y)+\theta^2\psi_2(y)+\theta^1\theta^2F(y).$$

The total parity of every term is even. Define the supersymmetry generators on $\mathscr S$ by

$$Q_\alpha=\partial^L_{\theta^\alpha}-i\sum_{\mu,\dot\alpha}\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu,\qquad \bar Q_{\dot\alpha}=-\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}}+i\sum_{\mu,\alpha}\theta^\alpha\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\alpha}\partial_\mu.$$

For external odd constant parameters $\epsilon^\alpha,\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}$ that anticommute with the odd generators and coefficient algebra, set $\delta_{\epsilon,\bar\epsilon}\Phi=\sum_\alpha\epsilon^\alpha Q_\alpha\Phi+\sum_{\dot\alpha}\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}\Phi$. The component transformation is, by definition, the unique ordered-basis coefficient tuple of this transformed superfield in the displayed $y,\theta$ expansion. The space of fields is classical and smooth, so these differential operations have common domain $\mathscr S$; no quantum-field operator domain or field equation is assumed. In natural units $[x^\mu]=-1$ and $[\theta]=[\bar\theta]=-\tfrac12$. If $[\Phi]=d$ is assigned, the formal component dimensions are $[A]=d$, $[\psi_\alpha]=d+\tfrac12$, and $[F]=d+1$; no value of $d$ is fixed. In the same natural-unit convention, $D_\alpha$, $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$, $Q_\alpha$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha}$ have mass dimension $+\tfrac12$, while $[\epsilon^\alpha]=[\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, so $\delta_{\epsilon,\bar\epsilon}$ is dimensionless.

Let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_{\bar0}\oplus\mathcal A_{\bar1}$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z_2$-graded complex algebra whose homogeneous elements satisfy $ab=(-1)^{|a||b|}ba$, equipped with a conjugate-linear parity-preserving involutive anti-automorphism $a\mapsto a^*$ extending complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$. For the ordered index set $J=\{1,2,3,4\}$, let $\Lambda_4$ be the complex vector space with specified basis $(e_S)_{S\subseteq J}$, including $e_\varnothing=1$. Define
$$ \nu(S,T)=|\{(s,t)\in S\times T:s>t\}|,\qquad e_Se_T=\begin{cases}0,&S\cap T\ne\varnothing,\\(-1)^{\nu(S,T)}e_{S\cup T},&S\cap T=\varnothing.\end{cases} $$
Put $\xi_1=\theta^1=e_{\{1\}}$, $\xi_2=\theta^2=e_{\{2\}}$, $\xi_3=\bar\theta^{\dot1}=e_{\{3\}}$, and $\xi_4=\bar\theta^{\dot2}=e_{\{4\}}$. Then each $\xi_i$ is odd, $\xi_i^2=0$, and $\xi_i\xi_j=-\xi_j\xi_i$ for $i\ne j$. Give $\Lambda_4$ the grading $|e_S|=|S|\bmod2$. The superspace coefficient vector space is $\mathcal A\otimes_\mathbb C\Lambda_4$ with total parity and graded-tensor multiplication
$$ (a\otimes e_S)(b\otimes e_T)=(-1)^{|S||b|}(ab)\otimes(e_Se_T) $$
for homogeneous $a,b$. On the basis, the left derivative removes $i$ with sign $(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<i\}|}$ and the right derivative removes $i$ with sign $(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s>i\}|}$ when $i\in S$, and both give zero when $i\notin S$. On a coefficient-left homogeneous tensor $a\otimes e_S$, define $\partial^L_{\xi_i}(a\otimes e_S)=(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes\partial^L_{\xi_i}e_S$ and $\partial^R_{\xi_i}(a\otimes e_S)=a\otimes\partial^R_{\xi_i}e_S$; in particular both vanish on $a\otimes1$. The algebra axioms and derivative rules below are verified in the local well-definedness result. Complex conjugation on this coefficient algebra extends the given operation on $\mathcal A$ by $i^*=-i$, $(\theta^\alpha)^*=\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}$, $(\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha})^*=\theta^\alpha$, and $(uv)^*=v^*u^*$. In the coefficient-left tensor notation this means $(a\otimes e_S)^*=(-1)^{|a||S|}a^*\otimes e_S^*$, where $e_S^*$ is obtained by reversing the ordered generator word for $e_S$ and applying the stated generator conjugation.

For each $i\in J$, the left derivative $\partial^L_{\xi_i}$ is the unique odd derivation of the graded tensor algebra that vanishes on $\mathcal A$ and has $\partial^L_{\xi_i}\xi_j=\delta_{ij}$; on homogeneous $u,v$ it obeys
$$ \partial^L_{\xi_i}(uv)=(\partial^L_{\xi_i}u)v+(-1)^{|u|}u(\partial^L_{\xi_i}v). $$
The right derivative $\partial^R_{\xi_i}$ is the unique right odd derivation vanishing on $\mathcal A$ with $\partial^R_{\xi_i}\xi_j=\delta_{ij}$ and
$$ \partial^R_{\xi_i}(uv)=(-1)^{|v|}(\partial^R_{\xi_i}u)v+u(\partial^R_{\xi_i}v). $$
For one generator, write a polynomial uniquely with that generator on the left as $f=f_0+\xi_i f_1$, with $f_0,f_1$ independent of $\xi_i$, and define its Berezin integral by the complex-linear coefficient-extraction rule $\int d\xi_i\,f=f_1$. Thus $\int d\xi_i\,1=0$ and $\int d\xi_i\,\xi_i=1$. Fix the ordered measures
$$ \int d^2\theta:=\int d\theta^2\,d\theta^1,\qquad \int d^2\bar\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1},\qquad \int d^4\theta:=\int d\bar\theta^{\dot2}\,d\bar\theta^{\dot1}\,d\theta^2\,d\theta^1. $$
With this order, $\int d^4\theta$ extracts the coefficient of $\theta^1\theta^2\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}$. For superspace coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^{1,3}$ in natural units $\hbar=c=1$, assign mass dimensions $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta^\alpha]=[\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=-\tfrac12$, $[d\theta^\alpha]=[d\bar\theta^{\dot\alpha}]=\tfrac12$, and hence $[d^2\theta]=[d^2\bar\theta]=1$ and $[d^4\theta]=2$. These are formal engineering dimensions; no physical model or empirical unit convention is asserted.

Thus the substitutions and all polynomial products are defined in the commutative even chiral ring. For matrices $A,B$ over that ring, index expansion gives $\operatorname{Tr}_2(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\sum_{j,i}B_{ji}A_{ij}=\operatorname{Tr}_2(BA)$. In particular $\operatorname{Tr}_2(UAU^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_2(A)$, so tracelessness is preserved.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge2$. A fixed massive rest representation fiber consists here of a nonzero complex Hilbert space $\mathcal K$, a number $M>0$ with $P^0=MI$ and $P^j=0$, and scalar central charges $Z^{IJ}=z^{IJ}I$, where $Z=(z^{IJ})$ is the complex antisymmetric $N\times N$ matrix in the four-dimensional algebra with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\epsilon_{12}=1$. Suppose the charge operators and their actual Hilbert adjoints have a common dense invariant domain $\mathcal D$ on the fiber and every product in the expanded anticommutators is defined there. Use natural units $\hbar=c=1$, so $M$ and each $z^{IJ}$ have mass dimension one. For $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)\in\mathbb C^N$ define $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_I|v_I|^2$ and for $u,v\in\mathbb C^N$ put $u^*Zv=\sum_{I,J}\bar u_Iz^{IJ}v_J$. Define

$$\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Zv\|_2.$$

Then $M\ge\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. For $N=2$, write $z=z^{12}$, so $Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&z\\-z&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|z|$. If $z=e^{i\phi}|z|$ (with any $\phi$ when $z=0$), define on $\mathcal D$

$$A:=Q^1_1-e^{i\phi}(Q^2_2)^*,\qquad A^\sharp:=(Q^1_1)^*-e^{-i\phi}Q^2_2.$$

The algebraic anticommutator $AA^\sharp+A^\sharp A$ equals $4(M-|z|)I$ on $\mathcal D$. Here $A^\sharp$ is the displayed combination of the individual actual adjoints; it is not asserted to be the adjoint of an unbounded sum on its maximal domain. If $\mathcal K$ is finite-dimensional, all charge domains equal $\mathcal K$ and $A^\sharp=A^*$, so the formula is the ordinary operator anticommutator. At saturation $M=|z|$, for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$ one has $A\psi=A^\sharp\psi=0$. This is a representation-theoretic fiber statement: it does not assert that the fixed-momentum fiber is a normalizable subspace of the full Hilbert space, or that a state with specified charge exists or is stable.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the complex Hilbert-space convention that the inner product is linear in its first variable and conjugate-linear in its second. Let $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\sigma^0=I_2$, $\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Define $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)=\{H\in M_2(\mathbb C):H^\dagger=H\}$ and $\Phi:\mathbb R^{1,3}\to\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$ by $\Phi(x)=-\sigma^\mu x_\mu$. For $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)=\{g\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det g=1\}$, define $\Lambda_g$ by $\Phi(\Lambda_gx)=g\Phi(x)g^\dagger$; the real-linear map $\Phi$ is an isomorphism because $I_2,\sigma^1,\sigma^2,\sigma^3$ form a basis of $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$, and $\det\Phi(x)=-\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu$ is preserved. Congruence by $g$ preserves positive-semidefinite Hermitian matrices, so $\Lambda_g$ preserves the chosen future cone. Let $\Lambda_g^\vee$ be the dual action on covectors, $(\Lambda_g^\vee p)(x)=p(\Lambda_g^{-1}x)$. The spin-cover Poincare group is $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with product $(g,a)(h,b)=(gh,a+\Lambda_gb)$.

A **positive unitary super-Poincare representation** in this item is the following data. It includes a nonzero complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, a bounded self-adjoint grading $\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^2=I$, and a strongly continuous unitary representation $U$ of $\mathcal P$ commuting with $\Gamma$. It also includes a regular projection-valued measure $E$ on the Borel subsets of the covector space $(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ such that

$$U(1,a)=\Phi_E(p\mapsto e^{i p(a)}),\qquad U(g,0)E(B)U(g,0)^*=E(\Lambda_g^\vee B),\qquad E(\mathcal C_+^*)=I,$$

where $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral, $\mathcal C_+^*=\{p:p^0=-p_0\ge |\vec p|\}$ is the closed future cone in covector coordinates, and $p(a)=p_\mu a^\mu$. The PVM functional calculus makes every translation unitary commute with every $E(B)$. For each coordinate define the self-adjoint translation generator

$$P_\mu=p_\mu(E),\qquad D(P_\mu)=\left\{\psi\in\mathcal H:\int |p_\mu|^2\,dE_\psi(p)<\infty\right\},\qquad E_\psi(B)=\langle E(B)\psi,\psi\rangle.$$

Here $p_\mu(E)$ is the unbounded PVM integral with its truncation domain; the real-valued integral is self-adjoint under Countable Choice. Thus $P^0=\eta^{0\nu}P_\nu$ is nonnegative. The joint PVM is part of the representation data; no joint spectral measure is inferred from formal commutators on a dense domain.

For each $I,\alpha$, the supercharge $Q^I_\alpha$ is a closed densely defined operator on $\mathcal H$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ is its actual Hilbert adjoint, with exactly the adjoint domain. The central generators $Z^{IJ}$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ are represented by closed densely defined operators with $\bar Z_{IJ}=(Z^{IJ})^*$ as an actual Hilbert adjoint. On a common dense graded linear domain $\mathcal D$, contained in the domains of every generator product in the bracket table, the operator supercommutator is the displayed algebra bracket. In particular,

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J,\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

The domain $\mathcal D$ is invariant under those generators and under $U(\mathcal P)$. The even group acts on the charge domains exactly: for every $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)$, conjugation by $U(g,0)$ sends each closed charge to the corresponding fundamental or dotted spinor transform as an equality of operators, including equality of domains. The central generators transform as Lorentz scalars, commute with translations, and commute on $\mathcal D$ with all supercharges; these relations also include their domain invariance.

For every Borel set $B\subseteq(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ and every charge $Q$ or $Q^*$, require the reducing-projection/domain conditions

$$E(B)D(Q)\subseteq D(Q),\qquad Q E(B)\psi=E(B)Q\psi\quad(\psi\in D(Q)),$$

and the same conditions with $Q^*$ in place of $Q$. Require also $\Gamma E(B)=E(B)\Gamma$ for every Borel $B$. In particular this supplies integrated translation covariance with domain invariance; a relation $[P_\mu,Q]=0$ on a common core alone is not substituted for it. A closed graded subspace $K$ is invariant when $U(g,a)K=K$ for all $(g,a)\in\mathcal P$ and each charge and adjoint maps $D(Q)\cap K$ into $K$, with those intersections dense in $K$. The representation is irreducible when its only such invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$.

$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and a selected pure four-dimensional

The microscopic matter-hypermultiplet index set is empty, as explicitly adopted in the independent pure-model postulate. In $\mathcal N=1$ language the gauge sector is one vector superfield and one adjoint chiral superfield with scalar $\phi\in\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$, connection normalization $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=\phi/g$, positive dimensionless gauge coupling $g$, zero chiral superpotential and no ultraviolet matter mass. A **classical Coulomb-branch configuration** is a constant adjoint scalar
configuration satisfying the model's zero auxiliary-field conditions, taken
modulo the compact $SU(2)$ gauge action. This uses the compact-group orbit
quotient in the preceding vacuum-moduli definition; it does not replace that
quotient by a complexified-group stability construction. In the
weak-coupling semiclassical frame, let $a$ be the eigenvalue coordinate fixed
by $\phi=\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(a,-a)$, of mass dimension one. When a quantum
theory with a vacuum-moduli set has actually been constructed, the **quantum
Coulomb-branch coordinate** $u$ denotes the chosen gauge-invariant chiral
quadratic-operator expectation value in the source trace normalization for

On an open patch $U$ of the $u$-plane where the period functions are
holomorphic and the local gauge-coupling matrix has positive imaginary part,
an **electric/magnetic frame** means a chosen ordered basis of the formal
charge lattice that fixes local cycle representatives. Their period

two-derivative abelian gauge action is encoded by a holomorphic
**prepotential** $\mathcal F_U(a)$ of mass dimension two, defined on that

$$a_D=\frac{\partial\mathcal F_U}{\partial a},\qquad \tau=\frac{\partial a_D}{\partial a}=\frac{\partial^2\mathcal F_U}{\partial a^2},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau>0.$$

The dimensionless $\tau$ is the local complexified gauge coupling; changing

For this source-normalized data, define the **formal electric/magnetic charge
label lattice** to be $\Gamma_{\mathrm{SW}}=\mathbb Z^2$, with a label
$(n_e,n_m)$ and period pairing
$\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{SW}}(u;n_e,n_m)=n_ea(u)+n_ma_D(u)$. The pair labels
the central-charge formula; the lattice definition does not assert that every

The word **exact** in this page refers only to the adopted source-proposed

path integral, a global single-valued prepotential, or an exact statement

$c=\hbar=1$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and a positive

derivations.claim:
By [F3], the formal period pairing for the chosen label is
$\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{SW}}=n_ea(u)+n_ma_D(u)$. By [A2], the scalar
central-charge entry is therefore
$z=\sqrt2\bigl(n_ea(u)+n_ma_D(u)\bigr)$.

For the antisymmetric $N=2$ matrix
$Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&z\\-z&0\end{pmatrix}$, direct multiplication gives
$Z^*Z=|z|^2I_2$, hence $\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|z|$. Apply [F1] to obtain
$M\ge\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|z|
=\sqrt2\,|n_ea(u)+n_ma_D(u)|$.

If equality holds, then $M=|z|$. The N=2 saturation conclusion in [F1],
with $e^{-i\varphi}z=|z|$, gives $A\psi=A^\sharp\psi=0$ for every
$\psi\in\mathcal D$. The conclusion remains confined to this represented
