For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, the **unreduced mapping cylinder** is
$$M_f=(Y\amalg(X\times I))/((x,0)\sim f(x)).$$
Write $j:X\to M_f$, $j(x)=[x,1]$, and $r:M_f\to Y$, $r(y)=y$, $r([x,s])=f(x)$. The formula for r descends continuously by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The **unreduced mapping cone** is $C_f=M_f/j(X)$, collapsing the entire free end to a point when it is nonempty. If X is empty this quotient is Y, with no extra cone point adjoined. These constructions do not collapse a basepoint track. Reduced cones and suspensions are defined separately below. Deformations always use the homotopy convention in [[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]].

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

For a well-pointed CGWH based space $(X,x_0)$ set
$$CX=(X\times I)/(X\times\{1\}\cup\{x_0\}\times I),\qquad \Sigma X=CX/(X\times\{0\}).$$
The common collapsed set is the basepoint; the copy of X at height zero is the cone base. All products and mapping conventions are those of [[def-compactly-generated-conventions-for-based-homotopy]], and well-pointedness means [[def-cofibration-and-homotopy-extension-property]].

For a based $f:X\to Y$ put $C_f=Y\cup_f CX$, the **reduced homotopy cofiber**, with $i:Y\to C_f$ the inclusion and $q:C_f\to\Sigma X$ collapsing Y. This reduced notation is used in this item and its based consumers; it differs from the unreduced cone of [[def-mapping-cylinder-and-mapping-cone]]. A reduced cylinder also collapses the basepoint track. Maps on all these quotients are defined by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]].

Write $\rho_X([x,t])=[x,1-t]$ and $-\Sigma f=\rho_Y\Sigma f$. The cofiber sequence convention is
$$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{i}C_f\xrightarrow{q}\Sigma X\xrightarrow{-\Sigma f}\Sigma Y\xrightarrow{-\Sigma i}\Sigma C_f\xrightarrow{-\Sigma q}\Sigma^2X\xrightarrow{\Sigma^2 f}\Sigma^2Y\longrightarrow\cdots.$$
The homotopy equivalences and mapping-set exactness behind this notation are proved below; this definition does not assert a covariant exact sequence of homotopy groups.

For a space $X$ and commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, put
$$H^*(X;R)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^n(X;R),\qquad [\varphi]\smile[\psi]=[\varphi\smile\psi].$$
The groups and equality of representatives are those of [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]]. The multiplication descends through both quotient maps by [[thm-cup-product-leibniz-identity]], including simultaneous changes. Extend to finite sums of homogeneous classes by distributivity; only finitely many summands occur, so each product belongs to the displayed direct sum.

This is the **singular cohomology ring**. To check the ring assertion before using it, let $\varphi,\psi,\eta$ have degrees $p,q,r$. On an arbitrary $(p+q+r)$-simplex both parenthesizations of their cochain cup product evaluate to
$$\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\,\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\,\eta(\sigma[p+q,\ldots,p+q+r]).$$
Restriction to a face and then a face of that face is restriction to the listed vertex block, and multiplication in $R$ is associative. Thus cochain associativity holds exactly and descends to classes. Bilinearity gives the two distributive laws. Addition, additive inverses and zero come from the abelian quotient groups. Products of degrees $p,q$ have degree $p+q$.

Its multiplicative unit is the class of the cochain $\mathbf1\in C^0(X;R)$ assigning $1_R$ to every singular vertex. On any edge, $\delta\mathbf1=1_R-1_R=0$. The front/back formula gives $\mathbf1\smile\varphi=\varphi=\varphi\smile\mathbf1$ on every simplex. This includes all components at once: degree-zero cochains need not have finite support on the set of vertices or components.

If $X$ is empty or $R=0$, the ring is the zero ring and its unit equals zero, as allowed by our unital-ring convention. The formula for three factors works also when any degree is zero and for degenerate simplices; for one-point $X$ it has the same unit. Nothing here chooses a representative for every class: the quotient operation is defined by representative independence. No AC is used.

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients:
$$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

Let $q : X \to Y$ be a quotient map ([[def-quotient-topology]]). Then:

1. **Characteristic property.** For every space $W$ and every function
   $k : Y \to W$,
   $$k \text{ is continuous } \iff k \circ q \text{ is continuous} .$$
2. **Factorisation.** Let $f : X \to W$ be continuous and **constant on the
   fibres of $q$**, that is $q(x) = q(x')$ implies $f(x) = f(x')$. Then there is
   exactly one function $\bar f : Y \to W$ with $\bar f \circ q = f$, and it is
   continuous.
3. **Composites.** If $q : X \to Y$ and $p : Y \to Z$ are quotient maps then
   $p \circ q : X \to Z$ is a quotient map.

The quotient projection

$$p:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,\qquad t\longmapsto[t],$$

is a universal covering space of the quotient circle, pointed by $0\mapsto[0]$.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

For every r≥1, degree is an isomorphism $\pi_r(S^r,b)\to\mathbb Z$, sending the identity to +1 and cubical concatenation, equivalently oriented pinch sum, to addition. Two based sphere self-maps are homotopic through based maps if and only if their degrees agree. No infinite choice principle is needed.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Let $f:S^3\to S^2$ be a based continuous map. Give $S^2$ an orientation and give the attached $4$-cell its chosen orientation. Its mapping cone is the CW complex $C_f=S^2\cup_fD^4$, with the basepoint as its $0$-cell. Let $x\in H^2(C_f;\mathbb Z)$ be the unique class restricting to the positive generator of $H^2(S^2;\mathbb Z)$, and let $y\in H^4(C_f;\mathbb Z)$ be the generator determined by the oriented $4$-cell. Define the integral mapping-cone Hopf invariant $H(f)\in\mathbb Z$ by the equation
$$x\smile x=H(f)y.$$

Assume AC. Every numerable fiber bundle, with its supplied ordinary local product charts and support-subordinate locally finite partition of unity, is a Hurewicz fibration in all ordinary spaces. In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

For integers $0\le k<r$, $r\ge1$, every continuous based map $(S^k,a)\to(S^r,b)$ is nullhomotopic through maps fixing a. For k=0 this says every point of $S^r$ can be joined to b. No arbitrary choice principle is required.

Let

$$C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$$

with the Euclidean subspace topology. The function

$$h:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\longrightarrow C,\qquad h([t])=(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),$$

is a homeomorphism. Thus $[t]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle and sends $[0]$ to $(1,0)$.

Let $G$ be an abelian group. For a based well-pointed space $X$—meaning that the basepoint inclusion
$\{x_0\}\hookrightarrow X$ is a cofibration—reduced singular homology has
natural isomorphisms
$\widetilde H_{n+1}(\Sigma X;G)\cong\widetilde H_n(X;G)$ for all integers $n$. Here $\Sigma X$ is the suspension with two distinct
apices, as in [[def-adjunction-cone-suspension]].

derivations.claim: The Hopf map is a locally trivial circle bundle: in the chart $z_0\ne0$ with $w=z_1/z_0$, the section is $(1,w)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}$ and the fiber coordinate is $z_0/|z_0|$; use $(w,1)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}$ and $z_1/|z_1|$ in the other chart. These formulas give continuous inverse bundle charts. Put $a_i([z])=|z_i|^2/(|z_0|^2+|z_1|^2)$, $b_i=\max(0,a_i-1/4)$ and $\rho_i=b_i/(b_0+b_1)$. At least one $a_i\ge1/2$, so the denominator is positive, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\subseteq\{a_i\ge1/4\}\subseteq\{z_i\ne0\}$. This is a finite numeration with closed supports subordinate to the charts. By [F6] the Hopf bundle is Hurewicz and hence Serre. By [F1], $\pi_2(S^1)=\pi_3(S^1)=0$; the LES [F2] therefore makes $h_*:\pi_3(S^3)\to\pi_3(S^2)$ an isomorphism. By [F3] its source is generated by the identity, so $[h]$ generates $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$.

Write $\mathbb{CP}^2=\{[z_0:z_1:z_2]\}$ and use the open cell $z_2\ne0$ with representative $(w_0,w_1,1)$, $w\in\mathbb C^2$. Its characteristic disk can be taken as the unit ball in $\mathbb C^2$ via $w\mapsto[w_0:w_1:\sqrt{1-|w|^2}]$; the interior parametrizes the complement of $\mathbb{CP}^1$, and on $|w|=1$ the boundary map is $[w_0:w_1]=h(w)$. Thus $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is the mapping cone $C_h$. By [F4], the degree-two generator squares to the degree-four generator, so [F5] gives $H(h)=1$.

Let $d_m:S^3\to S^3$ have degree $m$. The radial cone extension $D^4\to D^4$, $ru\mapsto r d_m(u)$, has relative degree $m$ and boundary $d_m$: on collapsing the disk boundary its map is $\Sigma d_m$, whose degree is $m$ by the natural homology suspension in [F6]. Together with the identity on $S^2$, it defines a map $C_{h\circ d_m}\to C_h$, since the boundary attaching maps agree. It pulls the degree-two generator of $C_h$ back to that of $C_{h\circ d_m}$ and the degree-four generator back to $m$ times the latter. Pulling back $x_h^2=y_h$ therefore gives $x_{h\circ d_m}^2=m y_{h\circ d_m}$, which is exactly $H(h\circ d_m)=m$ by [F5].

The coefficient $H(f)$ is invariant under a based homotopy $H_t$ of attaching maps. A comparison $C_{f_0}\to C_{f_1}$ is the identity on $S^2$; on a cone point $[x,t]$ it equals $H_{2t}(x)$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ and the target cone point $[x,2t-1]$ for $1/2\le t\le1$. The formulas agree at the seam, respect the tip, and are continuous by quotient descent. Reversing the homotopy gives its homotopy inverse: the composites insert a path followed by its reverse, which contracts by shrinking its traversed homotopy parameter, and then a linear cone reparametrization removes the constant collar. Both maps restrict to the identity on the bottom sphere and have relative top-cell degree $+1$, so cup-product naturality preserves $H$. Since step 1.1 identifies every homotopy class with $[h\circ d_m]$ for a unique integer $m$, step 2.1 implies that any attachment with $H(f)=m$ has class $m[h]$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Give the graded tensor product the multiplication
$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=(-1)^{|b||a'|}(a\smile a')\otimes(b\smile b').$$
For arbitrary spaces $X,Y$, external product $a\times b=\operatorname{pr}_X^*a\smile\operatorname{pr}_Y^*b$ gives a unital graded-ring homomorphism to $H^*(X\times Y;R)$. This multiplicativity requires no AC.

Assume in addition AC, that $R$ is a PID, and that either every $H_q(Y;R)$ or every $H_p(X;R)$ is finite free over $R$. Then this homomorphism is an isomorphism.

For CW pairs $(X,A),(Y,B)$ with supplied characteristic maps, relative external product is likewise a graded-ring homomorphism
$$H^*(X,A;R)\mathbin{\widehat\otimes}_R H^*(Y,B;R)\longrightarrow H^*(X\times Y,(A\times Y)\cup(X\times B);R),$$
where the hat denotes the displayed graded multiplication on the ordinary graded direct-sum tensor product, not a completion. Relative rings need not have units. This relative multiplicativity is choice-free for every commutative unital $R$. Under AC and the PID hypothesis it is an isomorphism if either every $H_q(Y,B;R)$ or every $H_p(X,A;R)$ is finite free. Neither additive assertion requires bounded dimension or finite-rank singular chain groups. Products have their ordinary product topologies; AC enters only in additive bijectivity.

Let $(Z,z_0)$ be a based topological space. Define its reduced suspension as $\Sigma Z=(Z\times[0,1])/(Z\times\{0,1\}\cup\{z_0\}\times[0,1])$, with the collapsed subset as basepoint. Let $\iota_1,\iota_2:\Sigma Z\to\Sigma Z\vee\Sigma Z$ be the wedge inclusions. The reduced suspension pinch map $p_Z:\Sigma Z\to\Sigma Z\vee\Sigma Z$ is induced by
$$p_Z([z,t])=\begin{cases}\iota_1([z,2t]),&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\\iota_2([z,2t-1]),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$
At $t=\tfrac12$ both values are the wedge basepoint.

On $W$, $q$ is the fold into the bottom $S^2$ of $C_\beta$, so $q^*x=a+b$. On the open $4$-cell, the extension is the characteristic disk of $C_\beta$ with degree $+1$ by [A1], so $q^*y=ab$.

In the cone $C_\beta$, $x^2=H(\beta)y$ by [F1]. Pulling back with step 1.1 yields $(a+b)^2=H(\beta)ab$. Since $a^2=b^2=0$ and degree-two classes commute, the left side is $2ab$. The class $ab$ is a generator, so $H(\beta)=2$.

Let $i:W\hookrightarrow S^2\times S^2$ be the $2$-skeleton inclusion. The characteristic disk extends $i\alpha$ over $D^4$, so $\Sigma i\circ\Sigma\alpha$ is null. Define
$$r=(\Sigma p_1\vee\Sigma p_2)\circ\operatorname{pinch}:\Sigma(S^2\times S^2)\longrightarrow\Sigma S^2\vee\Sigma S^2,$$
where $p_1,p_2$ are the projections and the pinch is [F3]. On the first suspended wedge summand, the first projection branch is the identity up to linear rescaling of the suspension coordinate and the second branch is constant; on the second summand the roles reverse. Composing with $\Sigma\nabla$ gives $\Sigma\beta\simeq *$. By the definition of the suspension homomorphism, this is $2[\Sigma h]=0$ because $[\beta]=2[h]$ from step 2.1 and [F1] identifies $[h]$ as the generator.

Assume AC. For every integer $n\geq0$,
$$H^*(\mathbb {CP}^n;\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[c_n]/(c_n^{n+1}),\qquad |c_n|=2,$$
where $c_n$ is reduction modulo two of the normalized integral generator. Also
$$H^*(\mathbb {CP}^{\infty};\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[c],\qquad |c|=2.$$
All odd cohomology groups vanish. Standard skeletal restrictions preserve the
named generators and are isomorphisms in every degree at most twice the
complex dimension of the finite target.

For every integer $k$, $Sq^k$ is independent of the cocycle representative and
of the chosen coherently carried higher-diagonal system. It is additive and
natural for maps of spaces and pairs. Thus

$$
Sq^k\colon H^n(X,A;\mathbb F_2)\longrightarrow H^{n+k}(X,A;\mathbb F_2)
$$

is a natural homomorphism, with the outside-range values fixed to zero by the
definition.

For $x\in H^n(X;\mathbb F_2)$,

$$
Sq^0x=x,\qquad Sq^k x=0\ \text{if }k>n,\qquad Sq^n x=x\smile x.
$$

The same assertions hold relatively. On reduced cohomology of based CW
complexes, every square commutes with the standard cohomology suspension:

$$
Sq^k(\sigma x)=\sigma(Sq^k x).
$$

Assume AC. Let $a,b$ be positive integers with $0<a<2b$. For every space
$X$, every $q\geq0$, and every $x\in H^q(X;\mathbb F_2)$,

$$Sq^aSq^b(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor a/2\rfloor}\binom{b-j-1}{a-2j}Sq^{a+b-j}Sq^j(x).$$

The binomial coefficients are reduced modulo two. A binomial coefficient is
zero when its lower index is negative or exceeds its nonnegative upper index,
and a Steenrod square with an index outside its defining nonnegative range is
zero.

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients:
$$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

For a well-pointed CGWH based space $(X,x_0)$ set
$$CX=(X\times I)/(X\times\{1\}\cup\{x_0\}\times I),\qquad \Sigma X=CX/(X\times\{0\}).$$
The common collapsed set is the basepoint; the copy of X at height zero is the cone base. All products and mapping conventions are those of [[def-compactly-generated-conventions-for-based-homotopy]], and well-pointedness means [[def-cofibration-and-homotopy-extension-property]].

For a based $f:X\to Y$ put $C_f=Y\cup_f CX$, the **reduced homotopy cofiber**, with $i:Y\to C_f$ the inclusion and $q:C_f\to\Sigma X$ collapsing Y. This reduced notation is used in this item and its based consumers; it differs from the unreduced cone of [[def-mapping-cylinder-and-mapping-cone]]. A reduced cylinder also collapses the basepoint track. Maps on all these quotients are defined by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]].

Write $\rho_X([x,t])=[x,1-t]$ and $-\Sigma f=\rho_Y\Sigma f$. The cofiber sequence convention is
$$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{i}C_f\xrightarrow{q}\Sigma X\xrightarrow{-\Sigma f}\Sigma Y\xrightarrow{-\Sigma i}\Sigma C_f\xrightarrow{-\Sigma q}\Sigma^2X\xrightarrow{\Sigma^2 f}\Sigma^2Y\longrightarrow\cdots.$$
The homotopy equivalences and mapping-set exactness behind this notation are proved below; this definition does not assert a covariant exact sequence of homotopy groups.

For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, the **unreduced mapping cylinder** is
$$M_f=(Y\amalg(X\times I))/((x,0)\sim f(x)).$$
Write $j:X\to M_f$, $j(x)=[x,1]$, and $r:M_f\to Y$, $r(y)=y$, $r([x,s])=f(x)$. The formula for r descends continuously by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The **unreduced mapping cone** is $C_f=M_f/j(X)$, collapsing the entire free end to a point when it is nonempty. If X is empty this quotient is Y, with no extra cone point adjoined. These constructions do not collapse a basepoint track. Reduced cones and suspensions are defined separately below. Deformations always use the homotopy convention in [[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]].

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $C_{\eta_2}=\mathbb{CP}^2$ and $Sq^2$ sends its bottom degree-two generator to the nonzero degree-four class by [F2]. For reduced cones, suspension commutes with this cell cofiber: both $\Sigma C_f$ and $C_{\Sigma f}$ are the quotient of $I\times S^n\sqcup I\times S^{n+1}\times I$ by the same relations, collapsing suspension ends, cone tips and based tracks and identifying $(s,x,0)$ with $(s,f(x))$. Quotient descent therefore gives inverse continuous comparison maps. By [F5], ordinary cones are based homotopy equivalent to these reduced cones. Thus for every $n\ge2$ there is a based equivalence $C_{\eta_n}\simeq\Sigma^{n-2}C_h$, preserving the bottom and top cohomology classes. Suspension compatibility in [F2] therefore gives a nonzero $Sq^2:H^n(C_{\eta_n};\mathbb F_2)\to H^{n+2}(C_{\eta_n};\mathbb F_2)$.

Suppose for contradiction that $\eta_n\eta_{n+1}$ is null. Put $f=\eta_n:S^{n+1}\to S^n$ and $g=\eta_{n+1}:S^{n+2}\to S^{n+1}$. Let $K:CS^{n+2}\to S^n$ be a based cone extension of $f\circ g$, and let $\chi:CS^{n+1}\to C_f$ be the characteristic map of the cell attached by $f$. Decompose $S^{n+3}$ into two cones on $S^{n+2}$. On the first define $k:S^{n+3}\to C_f$ by $\chi\circ Cg$; on the second define it by $K$ followed by $S^n\hookrightarrow C_f$. On the common equator both formulas equal $f\circ g$, and on the chosen basepoint both equal the target basepoint, so they paste to a based continuous map. Attach an $(n+4)$-cell along $k$, obtaining $X=C_f\cup_kD^{n+4}$. Its cells have dimensions $0,n,n+2,n+4$. Collapsing the bottom $S^n$ gives an attaching map $\bar k=(\Sigma g)\circ c$, where $c:S^{n+3}\to S^{n+3}$ collapses the hemisphere carrying $K$ and expands the other hemisphere. In suspension coordinates $[x,s]$, $-1\le s\le1$, take $c[x,s]=[x,\varphi(s)]$, where $\varphi(s)=-1$ for $s\le0$ and $\varphi(s)=2s-1$ for $s\ge0$. The coordinate maps $\varphi_t(s)=(1-t)s+t\varphi(s)$ preserve the endpoints and give a based homotopy from the identity to $c$. Hence $\bar k$ is based homotopic to $\Sigma g=\eta_{n+2}$. An attaching homotopy $H$ induces a cone comparison equal to the identity on the bottom sphere, equal to $H(x,2t)$ on the first half of the cone, and equal to the target cone point $[x,2t-1]$ on the second half. The reverse homotopy gives an inverse up to homotopy by cancelling the traversed homotopy and its reverse. This comparison has degree $+1$ on the relative top cell. Consequently $X/S^n\simeq C_{\eta_{n+2}}$ by a based homotopy equivalence preserving both upper cellular generators. No covariant homotopy exact sequence for cofibers is assumed.

The cells of $X$ have dimensions $0,n,n+2,n+4$, so its cellular cochain differential is zero and $H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb F_2)=0$. Let $x,y,z$ denote the nonzero classes in degrees $n,n+2,n+4$, respectively. Inclusion $C_{\eta_n}\hookrightarrow X$ induces isomorphisms in degrees $n$ and $n+2$, since these cellular cochain groups and their differentials are unchanged by the single top cell. By step 1.1 and naturality [F2], $Sq^2x=y$. The based equivalence $X/S^n\simeq C_{\eta_{n+2}}$ from step 1.2 preserves the upper generators, so the quotient has nonzero $Sq^2$ between degrees $n+2$ and $n+4$ by step 1.1 at index $n+2$. Collapsing the bottom subcomplex removes precisely its $0$- and $n$-cells from the cellular cochains; the quotient map preserves the upper cellular generators and their differentials. Naturality [F2] therefore gives $Sq^2y=z$. Thus $Sq^2Sq^2x=z\ne0$. But $H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb F_2)=0$, so $Sq^1x=0$.
On the other hand, [F3] gives $Sq^2Sq^2x=Sq^3Sq^1x=0$ by step 2.1. This contradicts $Sq^2Sq^2x=z\ne0$, so the assumed null composite is impossible. Hence $\eta_n\eta_{n+1}\ne0$ for every $n\ge2$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1 and 1.2: n>=2 fixes nonempty based spheres and a CW cone with a bottom and a top positive-dimensional cell. The contradiction complex adds an actual top cell; its vanishing degree-(n+1) group is a missing cochain degree, not an empty ambient space.
The null-composite case is assumed and contradicted. (step 3.1).

Steps 2.1 and 3.1: Sq^1 x lies in H^(n+1)(X;F_2)=0, so it is zero. Thus the Adem expression Sq^3 Sq^1 x vanishes, contradicting the nonzero Sq^2 Sq^2 x=z; the degree-one operation is explicitly essential.
The degenerate null composite is the contradiction hypothesis, not an omitted case. (step 1.2).

Step 1.2: the two cone formulas for k agree on their common equator with f composed with g and preserve the based track. The collapse interpolation phi_t preserves both suspension endpoints, while the later cone comparison pastes at t=1/2 and respects the tip.

Facts and step 1.2: AC is retained for the imported cohomology and Steenrod suppliers. The cone extension K is obtained from the single assumed nullhomotopy in the contradiction argument; this is not a choice of extensions over an unspecified family.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts nonnullity of every specified eta_n composed with eta_(n+1). Assuming nullity to construct a contradiction complex is a proof by contradiction, not the forward half of an equivalence claim.
There is no converse characterizing maps by a Steenrod obstruction; the argument uses the obstruction only to disprove nullity of the named Hopf composites.

lem-qftx-suspended-hopf-composite-adem-o.finite_checks_disposition: No programmatic finite check proves these general topological statements; the applicable finite boundary cases are recorded explicitly and discharged by the cited numbered steps.

citations.quote:
A **locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $F$** is a continuous map $p:E\to B$, an open cover $(U_i)_{i\in S}$ of $B$, and homeomorphisms
$$\theta_i:p^{-1}(U_i)\longrightarrow U_i\times F,\qquad \operatorname{pr}_1\theta_i=p|_{p^{-1}(U_i)}.$$
Here bundle charts, including those used later for principal and associated bundles, are charts in ordinary topological spaces with ordinary product and subspace topologies. A bundle whose spaces are CGWH in addition can be considered in the CGWH fibration convention; we do not silently replace an ordinary product chart by a weaker k-product-chart assumption. Products and homeomorphisms have the meanings of [[thm-product-universal-property]] and [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]].

On $U_i\cap U_j$, the coordinate change has the form $(b,x)\mapsto(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$, with continuous inverse $(b,y)\mapsto(b,g_{ij}(b,y))$. In particular each $g_{ji}(b,-)$ is a homeomorphism of $F$. The identities $g_{ii}(b,x)=x$ and $g_{ki}(b,x)=g_{kj}(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$ hold because the corresponding chart composites cancel. No topology on a homeomorphism group of $F$ is assumed.

The bundle is **numerable** when the data include a partition $(\rho_i:B\to[0,1])_{i\in S}$ with locally finite cozero sets, sum one, and
$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho_i)=\overline{\{b:\rho_i(b)>0\}}\subseteq U_i.$$
This is the support-subordinate convention of [[def-partition-of-unity-subordinate-to-a-cover]]. Repeating a chart with multiple indices is allowed, so a partition subordinate to a refinement can be accompanied by an explicitly assigned original chart. Merely having pointwise finite sums or cozero containment is not this specified numerating data.

An empty base forces $E$ empty and allows the empty cover and partition. The fiber $F$ may be empty: then every chart domain, hence $E$, is empty even when $B$ is nonempty. When $F$ is nonempty the charts imply surjectivity by taking one point in the chart fiber for each particular base point; this assertion does not require choosing a simultaneous section. Over a point a chart identifies $E$ with $F$. No AC is assumed in the definition.

Assume AC. Every numerable fiber bundle, with its supplied ordinary local product charts and support-subordinate locally finite partition of unity, is a Hurewicz fibration in all ordinary spaces. In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $M$. A family of smooth functions $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ with $\phi_i:M\to [0,1]$ is a **smooth partition of unity subordinate to** $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ when:

1. the family $(\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i))_{i\in I}$ is locally finite;
2. $\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$; and
3. $\sum_i \phi_i(p)=1$ for every $p\in M$.

derivations.claim: Fix $v_0\in S^{2N-1}$. Choose an orthonormal basis $w_1,\ldots,w_{N-1}$ of $v_0^\perp$ so the matrix $(w_1,\ldots,w_{N-1},v_0)$ has determinant $1$. For $v$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood $U$ of $v_0$, project each $w_i$ onto $v^\perp$ and apply Gram–Schmidt in that fixed order. The projected vectors remain linearly independent after shrinking $U$, because their Gram determinant is continuous and equals $1$ at $v_0$. The resulting orthonormal frame depends smoothly on $v$. Multiply its first vector by the inverse of the determinant of the frame if necessary; this scalar has modulus one and the adjustment is smooth, preserves orthonormality, and makes the determinant exactly one. Thus $s(v)\in SU(N)$ is a smooth local section of $p$ on $U$.

For $g\in p^{-1}(U)$ with last column $v$, the matrix $s(v)^{-1}g$ fixes the last basis vector. Unitarity makes its orthogonal complement invariant, so it is block diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(A,1)$; determinant one gives $A\in SU(N-1)$. The maps
$$(A,v)\longmapsto s(v)\operatorname{diag}(A,1),\qquad g\longmapsto(\operatorname{upperBlock}(s(p(g))^{-1}g),p(g))$$
are smooth inverses between $SU(N-1)\times U$ and $p^{-1}(U)$. This proves local triviality with the asserted fiber.

The sphere is compact, so finitely many such neighborhoods cover it; [F2] gives a smooth partition of unity and hence a numeration. Applying [F1] proves the bundle is a Hurewicz fibration. For $N=2$, the stabilizer of the last column in $SU(2)$ has its upper block in $SU(1)=\{1\}$, so the fiber is a point.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 1.1: for N>=2 each unit column v_0 has an (N-1)-dimensional orthogonal complement with a finite orthonormal frame. The base sphere and every fiber are nonempty; the identity belongs to SU(N-1).

Step 1.1: a zero Gram determinant is excluded by choosing a neighborhood where projected vectors remain independent; it equals 1 at v_0. A unitary frame has nonzero determinant of modulus one, making its inverse phase correction defined.

Statement and step 3.1: at the minimal N=2 the fiber is SU(1)={1}, so the local product has a one-point fiber. The construction still has one perpendicular frame vector on which to perform the determinant correction.
At N=2 the fiber SU(1) is the one-point group. (step 3.1).

boundaries.reason: N ranges over integers N>=2 without an upper endpoint, and p is a last-column bundle map, not an interval-parametrized path. The N=2 fiber is handled explicitly rather than by a limiting endpoint argument.

boundaries.evidence: Facts and steps 1.1 and 3.1: AC is declared for the numerable-bundle supplier. A finite orthonormal frame is selected at each chart center; compactness gives a finite trivializing cover and the partition-of-unity supplier gives its numeration.

boundaries.reason: The claim constructs local bundle charts for the specified last-column map. It does not assert that every smooth SU(N-1) bundle arises from such a column map.
No converse reconstructing a special-unitary matrix from an arbitrary sphere fibration is claimed; reconstruction occurs only inside the explicit local chart with a supplied local section.

lem-qftx-special-unitary-column-fibratio.finite_checks_disposition: No programmatic finite check proves these general topological statements; the applicable finite boundary cases are recorded explicitly and discharged by the cited numbered steps.

citations.quote: For each integer $N\ge2$, let $SU(N)=\{U\in M_N(\mathbb C):U^*U=I,\det U=1\}$ and let $p:SU(N)\to S^{2N-1}\subset\mathbb C^N$ send a matrix to its last column. Then $p$ is a smooth, locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $SU(N-1)$ over the last standard basis vector; for $N=2$, the fiber is the one-point group $SU(1)$.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

For integers $0\le k<r$, $r\ge1$, every continuous based map $(S^k,a)\to(S^r,b)$ is nullhomotopic through maps fixing a. For k=0 this says every point of $S^r$ can be joined to b. No arbitrary choice principle is required.

For every r≥1, degree is an isomorphism $\pi_r(S^r,b)\to\mathbb Z$, sending the identity to +1 and cubical concatenation, equivalently oriented pinch sum, to addition. Two based sphere self-maps are homotopic through based maps if and only if their degrees agree. No infinite choice principle is needed.

Let $(X,x_0)$ be a based CW complex that is $(n-1)$-connected, where $n\ge1$. Let $\Sigma X=C_+X\cup_X C_-X$ be its unreduced two-cone suspension, based at the lower cone point $p_-$. The suspension homomorphism
$$E:\pi_i(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_{i+1}(\Sigma X,p_-),\qquad [h]\longmapsto[\Sigma h],$$
where the source sphere is also suspended by the two-cone construction and based at its lower cone point, is an isomorphism for $1\le i<2n-1$ and a surjection for $i=2n-1$. In degree zero both $\pi_0(X)$ and $\pi_1(\Sigma X)$ are singletons, so the corresponding pointed map is a bijection. The theorem and these precise basepoint conventions require no choice principle. No endpoint injectivity is asserted.

Let $h:S^3\to\mathbb{CP}^1\cong S^2$ be the Hopf map $h(z_0,z_1)=[z_0:z_1]$ on the unit sphere in $\mathbb C^2$. Then $h$ generates $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$. Use the integral mapping-cone Hopf invariant $H(f)$ defined for based maps $f:S^3\to S^2$ by $x^2=H(f)y$ in $C_f=S^2\cup_fD^4$, with the positive degree-two and oriented top-cell generators. With the complex orientations, $C_h\cong\mathbb{CP}^2$, $H(h)=1$, and for every integer $m$ and degree-$m$ map $d_m:S^3\to S^3$, $H(h\circ d_m)=m$.

Give $S^2\times S^2$ its product CW structure with $2$-skeleton $W=S^2\vee S^2$ and one oriented $4$-cell attached by $\alpha:S^3\to W$. Let $\nabla:W\to S^2$ fold the two oriented summands by the identity and put $\beta=\nabla\circ\alpha$. For a based map $f:S^3\to S^2$, its integral Hopf invariant $H(f)$ is defined by $x^2=H(f)y$ in the mapping cone $C_f=S^2\cup_fD^4$, where $x$ and $y$ are the positive generators of $H^2(C_f;\mathbb Z)$ and $H^4(C_f;\mathbb Z)$. With the product orientation, $H(\beta)=2$. Moreover the suspension $\Sigma\beta:S^4\to S^3$ is nullhomotopic. Consequently, if $\eta_3=\Sigma h$ is the suspension of the Hopf generator, then $2[\eta_3]=0$ in $\pi_4(S^3)$.
Set $\eta_2=h:S^3\to S^2$ and $\eta_j=\Sigma^{j-2}h:S^{j+1}\to S^j$ for $j\ge2$. For every $n\ge2$, the composite $\eta_n\circ\eta_{n+1}:S^{n+2}\to S^n$ is not nullhomotopic.

derivations.claim: The unit-quaternion parametrization $q=a+bi+cj+dk\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}a+bi&c+di\\-c+di&a-bi\end{pmatrix}$ is a continuous bijection from compact $S^3$ to Hausdorff $SU(2)$; direct multiplication shows it is unitary with determinant one, and every matrix in $SU(2)$ has this form. It is therefore a homeomorphism. By [F3], $\pi_1(S^3)=\pi_2(S^3)=0$ and $\pi_3(S^3)=\mathbb Z$.

By [F5], the generator of $\pi_3(S^2)$ suspends to an element $\eta_3$ generating the quotient $\pi_4(S^3)$ by [F4]. The second part of [F5] gives $2\eta_3=0$. The nonzero composite $\eta_3\circ\eta_4$ in [F5] implies $\eta_3\ne0$, since a composite with a null factor is null. Thus the cyclic quotient generated by $\eta_3$ has exactly two elements, proving $\pi_4(SU(2))\cong\mathbb Z/2$; the same nonzero composite lies in $\pi_5(S^3)$, so that group is nonzero.

Induct on $N\ge3$. The base sphere $S^{2N-1}$ has dimension at least five, so [F3] makes its homotopy groups in degrees $1,2,3,4$ zero. Exactness [F2] at degrees one and two therefore gives $\pi_1(SU(N-1))\cong\pi_1(SU(N))$ and $\pi_2(SU(N-1))\cong\pi_2(SU(N))$; at degree three it gives $\pi_3(SU(N-1))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))$. The component exact sequence and the connected fiber and base show $SU(N)$ is path connected: the map on components is onto, and its kernel is the image of the one-point component set of the fiber. Starting from [step 1.1], induction gives all three displayed low groups and connectedness for every $N$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 1.1: SU(2) is the nonempty unit-quaternion sphere, with its identity basepoint. Step 3.1 propagates connectedness through nonempty column fibrations, so no empty component set enters the homotopy sequence.
The zero classes in pi1 and pi2 are the stated low-degree vanishings. (step 3.1).

Steps 1.1 and 3.1: pi_1(SU(N)) vanishes from the S^3 base case and the LES induction. The point fiber SU(1) in the preceding column construction is not an extra N=1 case of this theorem, whose rank assumption is N>=2.
The base rank N=2 is handled separately before the induction. (step 3.1).
Steps 1.1 and 3.1: N=2 is the quaternion base case. For N=3 the sphere is S^5, and the required sphere degrees 1,2,3,4 are all strictly below 5, so the induction already works at its first rank.

Facts and step 3.1: ZF+AC is explicitly assumed because the numerable column-bundle supplier uses AC. The induction transfers the actual base-case groups through the LES; no additional family of homotopy representatives is selected.

boundaries.reason: The theorem lists connectedness and particular homotopy groups of SU(N), with extra SU(2) values. It does not give an equivalence recognizing spaces from this list of groups.
There is no converse inferring that a space is SU(N) from low homotopy data; the matrix groups and their column fibrations are fixed inputs.

lem-qftx-low-unitary-homotopy-inputs.finite_checks_disposition: No programmatic finite check proves these general topological statements; the applicable finite boundary cases are recorded explicitly and discharged by the cited numbered steps.

citations.quote: For every $N\ge2$, $SU(N)$ is path connected, $\pi_1(SU(N))=\pi_2(SU(N))=0$, and $\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. In addition, $\pi_4(SU(2))\cong\mathbb Z/2$ is finite and $\pi_5(SU(2))\ne0$. Here $SU(2)\cong S^3$ by the map sending a unit quaternion to its defining special-unitary matrix.

For each integer $N\ge2$, let $SU(N)=\{U\in M_N(\mathbb C):U^*U=I,\det U=1\}$ and let $p:SU(N)\to S^{2N-1}\subset\mathbb C^N$ send a matrix to its last column. Then $p$ is a smooth, locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $SU(N-1)$ over the last standard basis vector; for $N=2$, the fiber is the one-point group $SU(1)$.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, let $N\ge2$, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the standard unitary representation of $SU(N)$ on $\mathbb C^N$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas with relatively compact coordinate domains and a subordinate partition of unity. For each integer $k>d/2+1$, let $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ be the Sobolev completions of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms. Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. The next lemma proves that the pointwise product and inverse close on this set and make it a Hilbert Lie group. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology; the next lemma also verifies that the induced pointwise operation makes it a Hilbert Lie group.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty$ be the smooth gauge group, with the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. In a local section of $P$, write a connection as a matrix-valued one-form $A$ and a gauge section as a map $u$ into $SU(N)$; the right gauge action is $A^u:=u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$, equivalently pullback by the gauge automorphism associated with $u$. The calculus lemma proves that this formula defines a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Let $X$ be a compact finite-dimensional smooth manifold, $K\subseteq X$ a closed smooth submanifold with a chosen collar, $M$ a compact smooth manifold, and $E\to M$ a finite-rank smooth real vector bundle. Let $s:X\times M\to E$ be a continuous family of sections, meaning $s(x,m)\in E_m$ and $(x,m)\mapsto s(x,m)$ is continuous. Assume $x\mapsto s(x,\cdot)$ is continuous in the uniform topology, its restriction to $K$ is continuous in the $C^\infty$ section topology, and for distinct marked points $m_1,\ldots,m_q\in M$ the values $s(x,m_i)=v_i\in E_{m_i}$ are independent of $x$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a family $\widetilde s:X\to\Gamma^\infty(E)$ continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology, equal to $s$ on $K$, equal to $v_i$ at every $m_i$, and satisfying $\sup(\{0\}\cup\{\|\widetilde s(x,m)-s(x,m)\|:(x,m)\in X\times M\})<\varepsilon$ for any fixed bundle norm. The straight-line homotopy in each vector fiber from $s$ to $\widetilde s$ fixes $K$ and all marked values.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. Thus $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $M$.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed embedded smooth submanifold. After
shrinking the tubular neighbourhood from the Euclidean tubular neighbourhood
theorem, the tubular retraction agrees with the unique nearest-point
projection onto $S$.

derivations.claim: Realize $Ad(P)$ as the associated bundle with fiber $SU(N)$ under conjugation and embed that fiber in the real vector space of complex matrices with its Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The associated matrix bundle has linear conjugation transition functions. A continuous family of sections parametrized by a compact smooth pair $(X,K)$ is a continuous family of sections of this matrix bundle; on $K$ it is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology. Apply [F2], using the fixed basepoint value $I$ as a marked fiber value in the based case, to obtain a uniformly close matrix-valued smooth-section family, unchanged on $K$ and at that point.

The compact matrix submanifold $SU(N)$ has a positive-radius tubular neighborhood by [F3]. The Hilbert–Schmidt metric is invariant under conjugation by $SU(N)$; uniqueness of the nearest point therefore makes the retraction equivariant under every transition function of $Ad(P)$. Choose the approximation in step 1.1 closer than half the tubular radius and compose it fiberwise with this retraction. The result is a family of smooth $SU(N)$-sections, continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology; it still agrees with the original family on $K$ and at the fixed fiber value because the retraction fixes $SU(N)$.

For each parameter and each $t\in[0,1]$, the straight segment from the original matrix section to its close approximation stays in the tubular neighborhood: every point on the segment is within the approximation error of the original $SU(N)$ value. Applying the retraction to this segment gives a continuous homotopy through $SU(N)$-sections, relative to $K$ and the fixed fiber value.

For surjectivity on $\pi_j$ with $j\ge1$, take a continuous sphere family $f:S^j\to\mathcal G^0(P)$ based at the identity section and apply steps 1.1–3.1 with empty relative boundary, obtaining a homotopy $F_t$ to a family continuous into the smooth-section topology. If $x_0$ is the parameter basepoint, normalize this entire homotopy by $\widehat F_t(x)=F_t(x_0)^{-1}F_t(x)$. Its initial family is $f$, its value at $x_0$ is the identity for every $t$, and its endpoint is continuous in the smooth-section topology because multiplication and inversion there are continuous. In the based spatial subgroup this normalization also preserves the value $I$ at the marked fiber. Thus the smooth representative and its comparison homotopy are genuinely based in the parameter variable. For injectivity, a nullhomotopy in the continuous group is a family $H:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal G^0(P)$ whose restriction to $S^j$ is the given smooth-topology family; apply the relative construction with $K=S^j$ to make the extension smooth in the section variable while fixing its boundary. Choose the basepoint $x_0\in S^j$ on the boundary and identify the disk with the unit ball; the contraction $R_t(x)=(1-t)x+t x_0$ fixes $x_0$ and contracts the boundary into the disk's interior. Then $H(R_t(x))$ is a based nullhomotopy because its value at $x_0$ is the fixed boundary value $e$. Thus injectivity holds in based homotopy groups, not only free homotopy classes. For path components, approximate a single section for surjectivity; for injectivity, approximate a continuous path relative to its two smooth endpoints using $X=I$ and its collared boundary $K=\{0,1\}$. These constructions give the component bijection without imposing identity normalization on arbitrary components. In the based subgroup, mark the chosen fiber and preserve the value $I$ throughout. Pointwise multiplication and inversion on $\mathcal G_\infty$ are continuous in its $C^\infty$ topology: in each finite-atlas chart the product rule and chain rule bound each derivative seminorm by finitely many seminorms of the inputs. The compact-open section group is also a topological group because $SU(N)$ multiplication and inversion are continuous and $M$ is compact. Thus translations in both groups are homeomorphisms and transfer the identity-based conclusion to every basepoint.

The sphere/disk relative identifications follow from the same two constructions: absolute sphere families are approximated relative to no boundary, and any equality or nullhomotopy of their restrictions is approximated relative to its collared boundary. These prove the asserted weak homotopy equivalences for both section groups, conditional on [A1].

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 4.1: the frame over m makes the spatial base nonempty, and both gauge groups contain the identity section. Absolute sphere smoothing explicitly uses an empty relative parameter boundary; the collar correction is then omitted, while based normalization still fixes the parameter basepoint.
The identity section remains fixed at the marked fiber. (step 4.1).

Step 4.1: j=1 is a circle family for surjectivity and a disk D^2 with boundary S^1 for injectivity. Multiplication by the inverse of the value at the chosen parameter basepoint keeps the comparison homotopy based, including this first positive homotopy degree.
The j=0 case is stated separately as a path-component bijection. (step 4.1).
The projected straight homotopy agrees with the original and smoothed families at its endpoints. (step 3.1).

Facts and steps 1.1 and 2.1: the configuration context carries full AC, and the vector-bundle smoothing supplier uses it for partitions of unity. The tubular nearest-point retraction is unique and conjugation-equivariant, so chart retractions are not selected independently.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts the two inclusions induce component bijections and homotopy-group isomorphisms. Surjectivity and injectivity are separately proved properties of these maps, not a biconditional between unrelated conditions.
The injectivity argument smooths a given nullhomotopy relative to its boundary; it is not a converse saying every weak equivalence of section spaces comes from this smoothing construction.

A **locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $F$** is a continuous map $p:E\to B$, an open cover $(U_i)_{i\in S}$ of $B$, and homeomorphisms
$$\theta_i:p^{-1}(U_i)\longrightarrow U_i\times F,\qquad \operatorname{pr}_1\theta_i=p|_{p^{-1}(U_i)}.$$
Here bundle charts, including those used later for principal and associated bundles, are charts in ordinary topological spaces with ordinary product and subspace topologies. A bundle whose spaces are CGWH in addition can be considered in the CGWH fibration convention; we do not silently replace an ordinary product chart by a weaker k-product-chart assumption. Products and homeomorphisms have the meanings of [[thm-product-universal-property]] and [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]].

On $U_i\cap U_j$, the coordinate change has the form $(b,x)\mapsto(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$, with continuous inverse $(b,y)\mapsto(b,g_{ij}(b,y))$. In particular each $g_{ji}(b,-)$ is a homeomorphism of $F$. The bundle is **numerable** when the data include a partition $(\rho_i:B\to[0,1])_{i\in S}$ with locally finite cozero sets, sum one, and

Repeating a chart with multiple indices is allowed, so a partition subordinate to a refinement can be accompanied by an explicitly assigned original chart. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: In a trivializing ball around $m$, choose a smooth bump $b$ supported in that ball with $b(m)=1$. For $g$ near $I$, use a smooth logarithm $X=\log g\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and define a gauge section by $u_g(x)=\exp(b(x)X)$ in that chart and the identity outside. This gives a continuous local section of evaluation near $I$. To see that every value is attained, begin at $N=2$: [F4] gives a bundle $SU(1)\to SU(2)\to S^3$ with one-point fiber, and [F5] makes the base path connected; the component exactness [F3] therefore makes $SU(2)$ path connected. Inductively, [F4] is a surjective locally trivial bundle with path-connected fiber $SU(N-1)$ and path-connected base sphere [F5]; path lifting and [F3] imply $SU(N)$ is path connected. A path from $I$ to any $g_0$ is covered by finitely many logarithm neighborhoods; subdividing it writes $g_0$ as a finite product of elements in the identity chart. Multiplying the corresponding bump-supported sections gives a gauge section $v_0$ with $v_0(p_m)=g_0$. Translation of the identity-neighborhood section by $v_0$ yields a local section near every $g_0$.

The finite group $Z_N$ acts on the Hausdorff topological group $\mathcal G(P)$ by free translations. Choose an identity neighborhood $V$ with $V^{-1}V\cap Z_N=\{e\}$; this is possible because the finite set $Z_N\setminus\{e\}$ is closed and avoids the identity. The translates $Vz$ are pairwise disjoint. Since the quotient map is open and identifies each translate homeomorphically with the image of $V$, that image is evenly covered. Translation gives the same construction around every group element, so the quotient map is a covering with exactly $|Z_N|=N$ sheets. By [F1] and [A1], this is the finite-center quotient specified in the Statement.

In the finite-atlas $C^\infty$ topology, pointwise multiplication and inversion are continuous: each derivative seminorm of a product or inverse is bounded on compact chart supports by finitely many derivative seminorms of the inputs, by the finite-dimensional product and chain rules. If $s:U\to\mathcal G(P)$ is one of the local sections, the maps
$$(v,g)\longmapsto v\,s(g),\qquad u\longmapsto\bigl(u\,s(ev_m(u))^{-1},ev_m(u)\bigr)$$
are continuous inverses between $\mathcal G_m(P)\times U$ and $ev_m^{-1}(U)$. The first coordinate in the inverse evaluates to $e$, and the product reconstructs $u$. Thus evaluation is a locally trivial bundle with fiber exactly its kernel $\mathcal G_m(P)$. A finite cover of compact $SU(N)$ by such neighborhoods and a partition of unity make this bundle numerable. By [F2] it is a Hurewicz fibration; [F3] supplies its homotopy LES.

The base $SU(N)$ is compact, so the finite local trivializations of evaluation admit a subordinate partition of unity. By [F2, F3] the evaluation bundle is a Serre fibration with the homotopy LES. The finite quotient is a covering; [F6] gives its homotopy lifting property and hence its fibration property. This completes the claims.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, let $N\ge2$, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the standard unitary representation of $SU(N)$ on $\mathbb C^N$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas with relatively compact coordinate domains and a subordinate partition of unity. For each integer $k>d/2+1$, let $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ be the Sobolev completions of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms. Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. The next lemma proves that the pointwise product and inverse close on this set and make it a Hilbert Lie group. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology; the next lemma also verifies that the induced pointwise operation makes it a Hilbert Lie group.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty$ be the smooth gauge group, with the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. In a local section of $P$, write a connection as a matrix-valued one-form $A$ and a gauge section as a map $u$ into $SU(N)$; the right gauge action is $A^u:=u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$, equivalently pullback by the gauge automorphism associated with $u$. The calculus lemma proves that this formula defines a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Let $M$ be a compact connected oriented boundaryless smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$, let $N\ge2$, let $P\to M$ be a smooth principal $SU(N)$ bundle, and fix a frame $p_m$ over $m\in M$. Use the adjoint group bundle $Ad(P)=P\times_{Ad}SU(N)$. Write $\mathcal G_\infty(P)$ for the smooth gauge group with its $C^\infty$ section topology as defined from finite-atlas derivative seminorms, and set $\mathcal G_{\infty,m}(P)=\{u\in\mathcal G_\infty(P):u(p_m)=e\}$. Define $\mathcal G^0(P)$ as the group of continuous sections of $Ad(P)$ with the compact-open topology and $\mathcal G^0_m(P)=\{u\in\mathcal G^0(P):u(p_m)=e\}$. Then the inclusions $\mathcal G_\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal G^0(P)$ and $\mathcal G_{\infty,m}(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal G^0_m(P)$ induce bijections on path components and isomorphisms on all homotopy groups at every basepoint. More precisely, finite sphere/disk parameter families and their relative homotopies have the same classes in the smooth and continuous section topologies.

Let $P\to S^r$ be a smooth principal $SU(N)$ bundle with $r\in\{3,4\}$, $N\ge2$, a chosen point $m\in S^r$, and a chosen frame $p_m$ in its fiber. Write $\mathcal G(P):=\mathcal G_\infty(P)$ for the smooth gauge group defined by the finite-atlas $C^\infty$ section topology, let $\mathcal G_m(P):=\{u\in\mathcal G_\infty(P):u(p_m)=e\}$, and put $\overline{\mathcal G}(P):=\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty(P)=\mathcal G_\infty(P)/Z_N$, where $Z_N$ is the finite subgroup of constant central gauge sections. Evaluation $ev_m(u)=u(p_m)$ gives a locally trivial bundle
$$\mathcal G_m(P)\longrightarrow\mathcal G(P)\xrightarrow{ev_m}SU(N),$$
and the quotient map $\mathcal G(P)\to\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ is a finite covering. For a local section $s:U\to\mathcal G(P)$, the bundle chart has the commutative form
$$\begin{array}{ccc}\mathcal G_m(P)\times U&\xrightarrow{\Phi_s}&ev_m^{-1}(U)\\\downarrow{\operatorname{pr}_2}&&\downarrow{ev_m}\\U&\hookrightarrow&SU(N)\end{array}$$
where $\Phi_s(v,g)=v\,s(g)$; the square commutes because $ev_m(v)=e$ and $ev_m(s(g))=g$. The corresponding TikZ source is:
```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal G_m(P)\times U \arrow[r,"\Phi_s"] \arrow[d,"\operatorname{pr}_2"'] & ev_m^{-1}(U) \arrow[d,"ev_m"]\\
U \arrow[r,hook] & SU(N)
\end{tikzcd}
```
The evaluation bundle is numerable; both maps are Serre fibrations and have the homotopy long exact sequence.

Naturally for a well-pointed based CGWH space $X$ and a based CGWH space $Y$, there is a bijection $[\Sigma X,Y]_*\cong[X,\Omega Y]_*$, where $\Omega Y$ is the kified compact-open space of loops based at $y_0$.

For a based CGWH space X and n≥1, $\pi_n(X,x_0)\cong\pi_0(\Omega^nX)$ naturally. The operation on components on the right is induced by concatenating the first cube coordinate of the adjoint n-loop, and this bijection respects it.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], the gauge group under consideration consists of smooth sections with value $e$ at $p_m$, and [F3] identifies this subgroup with the evaluation fiber and its subspace topology. First calculate its continuous-section model, which is related by [F2]. Hemisphere trivializations exist directly from the supplied smooth reference connection: choose a frame at the center of each closed disk and transport it along its radial segments. The ODE statement [F6] gives a smooth section up to the equator, including the disk center, and the two sections give the smooth transition $\psi$ in [A1]. In that model a based section is a pair of maps $f_+:D_+^r\to SU(N)$ and $f_-:D_-^r\to SU(N)$ satisfying [A1] and $f_+(m)=e$. Let $J=\operatorname{Map}_*((D_+^r,m),(SU(N),e))$. For $f\in J$ define a map on the lower disk by
$$\sigma_f(\rho q)=\psi(q)^{-1}f(\rho q)\psi(q),\quad 0<\rho\le1,\qquad \sigma_f(0)=e,$$
where $q\in S^{r-1}$ is the radial direction and the upper-disk center $m$ is identified with $0$. At $\rho=1$ this has boundary value $\psi^{-1}f(q)\psi$, and as $\rho\to0$ it tends uniformly to $e$ because $f(0)=e$ and $S^{r-1}$ is compact; hence it is continuous on $D_-^r$.

For each compatible pair $(f_+,f_-)$, the product $v=\sigma_{f_+}^{-1}f_-$ is the identity on $\partial D_-^r$, so it descends continuously to a based map $D_-^r/\partial D_-^r\cong S^r\to SU(N)$. Conversely, given $f\in J$ and such a based map $v$, the pair $(f,\sigma_f v)$ satisfies the clutching condition. Both assignments are continuous for compact-open topologies (they are restrictions, finite pastings on closed hemispheres, and multiplication of continuous matrix-valued families), and are inverse. Thus the continuous based section space is homeomorphic to $J\times\operatorname{Map}_*(S^r,SU(N))$.

The space $J$ is contractible by $f_t(x)=f((1-t)x)$, which keeps the center value $e$. Hence projection of the product in step 2.1 onto $\operatorname{Map}_*(S^r,SU(N))$ induces a bijection on components and isomorphisms on all homotopy groups. Equivalently, the restriction to the upper disk is a trivial fibration with contractible base $J$; [F5] gives the same conclusion from its exact sequence.

By [F4], the homotopy groups of $\operatorname{Map}_*(S^r,SU(N))$ are $\pi_{j+r}(SU(N))$ for $j\ge1$, and its pointed components are based homotopy classes $[S^r,SU(N)]_*=\pi_r(SU(N))$. Finally [F2] transfers these continuous-section identifications to the smooth based gauge group.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1 and 2.1: each section space has its identity and J contains the constant map. The hemisphere compatibility problem has an explicit solution sigma_f, so the product-model fibers are nonempty even for a nontrivial clutching map.
The constant based map represents the distinguished component and group identity. (step 4.1).

Statement and step 4.1: at j=1 the adjunction gives pi_1(G_m)=pi_(r+1)(SU(N)). Components j=0 are treated separately as pointed sets, so the proof does not assume they are the same sort of group isomorphism.
The radial extension is continuous at its center because the family is based there. (step 1.1).
The contraction fixes the basepoint and contracts J to the constant map. (step 3.1).

Facts and steps 1.1 and 4.1: the actual configuration context includes AC and the parametric smoothing supplier retains it. A fixed reference connection and chosen hemisphere frames determine the trivializations; sigma_f is then an explicit formula from the fixed clutching function.

boundaries.reason: The claim gives homotopy-group identifications independent of clutching class, not an equivalence asserting that different bundles are isomorphic. It explicitly allows the unbased evaluation fibration to retain clutching dependence.
No reverse implication from equality of these homotopy groups to equality of clutching classes is claimed. The product description concerns the based section space of a fixed P.

lem-qftx-based-gauge-sphere-homotopy.finite_checks_disposition: No programmatic finite check proves these general topological statements; the applicable finite boundary cases are recorded explicitly and discharged by the cited numbered steps.

For every $j\ge1$ there is a group isomorphism
$$\pi_j(\mathcal G_m(P),e)\cong\pi_{j+r}(SU(N),e),$$
and there is a bijection of pointed component sets $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P),e)\cong\pi_r(SU(N),e)$. These identifications are independent of the clutching class of $P$; the unbased evaluation fibration may still depend on that class.

For every $N\ge2$, $SU(N)$ is path connected, $\pi_1(SU(N))=\pi_2(SU(N))=0$, and $\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. In addition, $\pi_4(SU(2))\cong\mathbb Z/2$ is finite and $\pi_5(SU(2))\ne0$. Here $SU(2)\cong S^3$ by the map sending a unit quaternion to its defining special-unitary matrix.
For every integer $N\ge2$, $\pi_5(SU(N))$ is nonzero. The claim is only nonvanishing; no full computation of these groups is asserted.

These assertions require no AC.
For a covering $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$, the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_1(E,e_0)\to\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is injective.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.

derivations.claim:
Suppose $r=3$. By [F3, F4], $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. The evaluation LES [F2, F6] has the component segment
$$\pi_1(SU(N))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(SU(N)).$$
The outer terms are one-point sets by [F4]. The induced map on components is surjective by exactness, and its fibers are the orbits of $\pi_1(SU(N))$ on $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))$ in the action clause of [F6]. That acting group is trivial, so each fiber is a singleton and the middle map is a bijection. Thus $\mathcal G(P)$ has infinitely many components. Since $\mathcal G(P)\to\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ is a covering with $N$ sheets, components downstairs correspond to orbits of the finite deck group on components upstairs: a path downstairs lifts by [F7] to a path whose endpoint differs from its starting lift by one deck transformation, and each deck orbit is therefore one quotient component. Each orbit has at most $N$ elements, so infinitely many components remain.

Suppose $r=4$. By [F3] and [F5], $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_5(SU(N))\ne0$. In the evaluation LES, the map $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\to\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))$ has preceding term $\pi_2(SU(N))=0$ by [F4]; exactness makes it injective. The finite covering in [F2] induces an injection $\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))\hookrightarrow\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ by [F6]. Hence $\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ contains a nonzero subgroup. The two cases establish the statement for every $r,N,P$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1 and 2.1: identity sections give basepoints upstairs and downstairs. For r=3 the component set upstairs is Z, not empty; finite deck orbits cannot turn it into a finite component set. For r=4 an injected nonzero subgroup witnesses nontriviality.
The pi1 conclusion rules out the zero fundamental group for r=4. (step 2.1).

Step 2.1 proves the first based homotopy group downstairs is nonzero when r=4 by two injections. In step 1.1 singleton outer component sets and the trivial pi_1(SU(N)) make the middle component map a bijection; singleton sets are not being treated as empty.
The r=3 case is handled by components, including every N and bundle sector. (step 1.1).
The only sphere dimensions are r=3 and r=4, and both are treated. (step 1.1).

Facts and steps 1.1 and 2.1: the configuration/fibration suppliers retain full AC. The proof uses finite deck orbits and injections on fundamental groups, without selecting representatives of all components or all nonzero homotopy classes.

boundaries.reason: The alternatives more than one component or some nonzero positive homotopy group form a disjunction, not a biconditional. The sharper r=3 and r=4 conclusions are separately established.
Neither infinite components nor nonzero pi_1 is claimed to characterize bundles over S^3 or S^4; the base sphere and rank are fixed hypotheses.

thm-qftx-reduced-gauge-group-sphere-nont.finite_checks_disposition: No programmatic finite check proves these general topological statements; the applicable finite boundary cases are recorded explicitly and discharged by the cited numbered steps.

citations.quote:
A **locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $F$** is a continuous map $p:E\to B$, an open cover $(U_i)_{i\in S}$ of $B$, and homeomorphisms
$$\theta_i:p^{-1}(U_i)\longrightarrow U_i\times F,\qquad \operatorname{pr}_1\theta_i=p|_{p^{-1}(U_i)}.$$
Here bundle charts, including those used later for principal and associated bundles, are charts in ordinary topological spaces with ordinary product and subspace topologies. A bundle whose spaces are CGWH in addition can be considered in the CGWH fibration convention; we do not silently replace an ordinary product chart by a weaker k-product-chart assumption. Products and homeomorphisms have the meanings of [[thm-product-universal-property]] and [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]].

On $U_i\cap U_j$, the coordinate change has the form $(b,x)\mapsto(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$, with continuous inverse $(b,y)\mapsto(b,g_{ij}(b,y))$. In particular each $g_{ji}(b,-)$ is a homeomorphism of $F$. The identities $g_{ii}(b,x)=x$ and $g_{ki}(b,x)=g_{kj}(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$ hold because the corresponding chart composites cancel. No topology on a homeomorphism group of $F$ is assumed.

The bundle is **numerable** when the data include a partition $(\rho_i:B\to[0,1])_{i\in S}$ with locally finite cozero sets, sum one, and
$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho_i)=\overline{\{b:\rho_i(b)>0\}}\subseteq U_i.$$
This is the support-subordinate convention of [[def-partition-of-unity-subordinate-to-a-cover]]. Repeating a chart with multiple indices is allowed, so a partition subordinate to a refinement can be accompanied by an explicitly assigned original chart. Merely having pointwise finite sums or cozero containment is not this specified numerating data.

An empty base forces $E$ empty and allows the empty cover and partition. The fiber $F$ may be empty: then every chart domain, hence $E$, is empty even when $B$ is nonempty. When $F$ is nonempty the charts imply surjectivity by taking one point in the chart fiber for each particular base point; this assertion does not require choosing a simultaneous section. Over a point a chart identifies $E$ with $F$. No AC is assumed in the definition.

A based map $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ induces $f_*[a]=[f\circ a]$ on all pointed component and cubical homotopy sets. For $n\ge1$ this is a homomorphism, identities and composition are preserved, and based homotopic maps induce equal maps. Based homotopy equivalences induce isomorphisms.

derivations.claim: Define $\Phi:B\times H\to E$ by $\Phi(b,h)=s(b)h$. Every $e\in E$ lies over a unique $b=p(e)$ and the principal action is free and transitive on $p^{-1}(b)$, so there is a unique $h$ with $e=s(b)h$. Thus $\Phi$ is bijective. In each local principal chart, $s$ is a continuous local section and the group coordinate $h$ is continuous; these charts cover $B$, so the inverse $e\mapsto(p(e),h(e))$ is continuous. The forward map is continuous by the action. Hence $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism.

Fix $b_0\in B$. Under $\Phi$, the inclusion $i:H\to E$, $h\mapsto s(b_0)h$, and the map $r:E\to H$, $r(e)=\operatorname{pr}_H(\Phi^{-1}(e))$, satisfy $r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_H$.
