Let $N\geq2$, $k\geq0$, and let $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ADHM,reg}}_{k,N}$ be the quotient by $U(k)$ of the raw data satisfying both zero moment equations and stable-and-costable regularity in the conventions stated in the following references section. Let $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}$ be the framed unitary ASD sector on the round oriented $S^4$ with $q_N=-k$ in those same conventions. Conditional on the real monad normalization and Ward inputs stated below, the construction gives a $T=(S^1)^2\times(S^1)^N$-equivariant bijection

$$\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ADHM,reg}}_{k,N}\;\longleftrightarrow\;\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}.$$

The zero-FI real quotient is also diffeomorphic to the stable-and-costable complex $GL(k)$ quotient. Under the stated projective GAGA and family base-change hypotheses, the corresponding framed sheaves on $\mathbb P^2$ are exactly the locally free locus among the framed torsion-free sheaves with rank $N$ and Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$. The positive-FI stable quotient includes non-locally-free sheaves and is not identified with the ordinary framed ASD moduli. Under the same family and normal-form hypotheses, the correspondence is compatible with first-order framed deformations and their tangent spaces.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and standard Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$ and $J:V\to W$. Define the complex and real polynomial expressions

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Assume AC. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$, $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, and let $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ satisfy the raw complex equation $\mu_{\mathbb C}=[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. Put $K=V\oplus V\oplus W$. For $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$ put

$$a_z=(B_1-z_1,B_2-z_2,J)^T,\qquad b_z=(-B_2^\dagger+\bar z_2,B_1^\dagger-\bar z_1,I^\dagger)^T,\qquad D_z=\begin{pmatrix}b_z^\dagger\\a_z^\dagger\end{pmatrix}.$$

Then

$$D_zD_z^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}b_z^\dagger b_z&\mu_{\mathbb C}\\\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger&a_z^\dagger a_z\end{pmatrix},\qquad b_z^\dagger b_z-a_z^\dagger a_z=\mu_{\mathbb R}.$$

The maps $b_z^\dagger$ are onto for every $z$ exactly when the datum is stable; the maps $a_z$ are injective for every $z$ exactly when it is costable. Consequently, when both moments vanish, regularity is equivalent to $D_z$ being onto for every $z$. On this locus $f_z=a_z^\dagger a_z=b_z^\dagger b_z$ is positive definite and

$$P_z=1-D_z^\dagger\operatorname{diag}(f_z^{-1},f_z^{-1})D_z$$

is the smooth orthogonal projection onto a rank-$N$ bundle over $\mathbb R^4$. The projection connection $\nabla=P\,d$ is unitary and satisfies $F^+=0$ for the positive stereographic orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, where $z_1=x^0+ix^1$, $z_2=x^2+ix^3$.

In homogeneous coordinates $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]$ on $\mathbb P^3$, put $A=B_1\lambda_1-B_2^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_1$, $C=B_2\lambda_1+B_1^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_2$ and

$$\alpha=(A,C,J\lambda_1+I^\dagger\lambda_2)^T,\qquad\beta=(-C,A,I\lambda_1-J^\dagger\lambda_2).$$

The polynomial identity is $\beta\alpha=\lambda_1^2\mu_{\mathbb C}+\lambda_1\lambda_2\mu_{\mathbb R}-\lambda_2^2\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger$. With $\sigma(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1)$, one has $\beta(v)=\alpha(\sigma v)^\dagger$. The real line over $z$ is $\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2$, $\mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2$; the line at infinity is $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0$. For regular zero-moment data these maps form a holomorphic bundle monad, trivial on each real line, with middle cohomology on the line over $z$ canonically $\ker D_z$. Its framing at infinity is $W$. The torus acts on the homogeneous coordinates by $(\lambda_1,t_1t_2\lambda_2,t_1\mu_1,t_2\mu_2)$ and on the raw data by $(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$; the monad isomorphism has source, middle and target factors $(t_1t_2)^{-1}$, $\operatorname{diag}(t_2^{-1},t_1^{-1},h)$ and $1$, respectively. It preserves the framing representation $W$ with weights $e_\alpha^{-1}$.

This proves a forward raw block construction. It does not assert that every real Ward monad has this normal form, that its inverse extraction is unique, or that the connection extends with charge $k$; those global correspondence and charge assertions require their separate proofs.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $E\to S^4$ be a smooth Hermitian rank-$N$ vector bundle with $N\geq2$, a smooth unitary connection $A$, and a unitary framing at $\infty$. Give $S^4$ the round metric and the orientation specified in the definition of the framed ASD sector, and assume $F_A^+=0$. Then the induced determinant-line connection on $\det E=\Lambda^N E$ is flat. Its framing at $\infty$ determines a unique global unit parallel section, so the framed unitary bundle reduces to a framed $SU(N)$ bundle. With $q_N=-(8\pi^2)^{-1}\int_{S^4}\operatorname{tr}_N(F_A\wedge F_A)$ and the determinant Chern-form convention $c(A)=\det(I-F_A/(2\pi i))$, one has

$$q_N(E,A)=-\langle c_2(E),[S^4]\rangle\in-\mathbb Z_{\geq0}.$$

Thus $k=-q_N=\langle c_2(E),[S^4]\rangle$ is a nonnegative integer, with the sign corresponding to the anti-self-dual equation $F_A^+=0$.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

A connection on a finite-rank smooth vector bundle $E\to M$ is flat if and
only if every point of $M$ has a neighborhood carrying a local frame
$(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ of parallel sections, meaning $\nabla_Xe_a=0$ for every
local vector field $X$ and every $a$.

Let $E\to M$ carry a flat connection, meaning $R^\nabla=0$. For every
$p\in M$ there is a coordinate ball $U$ about $p$ such that, whenever two
piecewise smooth paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to U$ have the same initial
and terminal points,

$$P_{\gamma_0}=P_{\gamma_1}.$$

This is a local assertion; it makes no claim about transport around loops in a
non-simply-connected larger domain.
Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^n)$ is $\mathbb R$ in degrees $0,n$ and zero otherwise. For $S^0$ it is $\mathbb R^2$ in degree zero and zero otherwise.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume AC. Fix $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, standard Hermitian $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$ and ADHM data $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with the complex equation $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. Stability means that the $B_1,B_2$ words applied to $I(W)$ span $V$; costability means no nonzero common invariant subspace of $V$ lies in $\ker J$; regular means both. Set

$$\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

For every $\zeta>0$, each stable $GL(V)$ orbit meets $\mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V$ in exactly one $U(V)$ orbit, and the inclusion induces a diffeomorphism of smooth real manifolds

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^s/GL(V).$$

At $\zeta=0$, every stable datum satisfying the real equation is automatically costable. Each regular complex orbit meets the zero real level in exactly one unitary orbit, giving instead

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=0,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V).$$

Both identifications are equivariant for the compact rotation/framing torus in the raw-data convention. For $k=0$ all spaces are points. This theorem identifies the stated finite-dimensional quotients; it asserts no correspondence with sheaves or ASD connections, and no identification of the entire positive-FI quotient with the zero-FI regular locus.

derivations.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Then $I'J'=IJ$, $I'I'^\dagger=II^\dagger$ and $J'^\dagger J'=J^\dagger J$. The word span is unchanged and $\ker J'=\ker J$, so both moments and regularity are unchanged. On the finite stereographic chart the raw kernel matrix annihilates the added framing line, and its orthogonal projection is $P_1\oplus1$. Thus [A1] produces a smooth rank-two ASD connection whose restriction to that chart is a line connection plus the flat added line and whose charge is $q_2=-k$. By [F2] its determinant curvature vanishes. On that chart this curvature is exactly the first line's curvature, so the whole rank-two curvature is zero there. Smoothness makes it zero also at infinity, hence $q_2=0$ and $k=0$. Thus no regular rank-one zero-FI datum exists for $k>0$, conditional on the exact retained rank-two input. By [F6], a regular complex rank-one orbit would have such a zero-real-moment representative, so the same emptiness conclusion applies to the complex regular quotient.

Independently, stabilize any framed unitary ASD line connection by the trivial framed flat line. The result is a smooth unitary ASD rank-two connection. Its determinant connection is the original line connection, since $\det(L\oplus\mathbb C)=L$ and the added connection is flat. By [F2] the original connection is flat, so $q_1=0$. Its sector is therefore empty if $k>0$. If $k=0$, transport the unit vector fixed by its framing from infinity. Any two paths differ by a null-homotopic loop by [F3]; subdivide a compact null-homotopy into finitely many cells lying in parallel-frame coordinate balls. Boundary transports in each cell are identity and internal edges cancel, so the loop transport is identity. The resulting global unit parallel section gives the unique framed isomorphism to the trivial flat line. A parallel automorphism fixing its value at infinity is identity. On the raw side at $k=0$ every map is the unique zero-dimensional map, both regularity conditions hold, and $U(0)$ is trivial. This proves the point classification and absence of framed stabilizers.

To type first-order bundle families without presuming a global trivialization, first use step 1.2 to identify the special fiber with its framed parallel line. Choose local lifts of this frame in a locally free Hermitian $D$-line family. If a lift has Hermitian Gram scalar $1+\varepsilon r$ with $r$ real, multiplication by $1-\varepsilon r/2$ makes it unitary, so unitary local lifts exist. Their transition functions have form $1+\varepsilon f_{ij}$, with imaginary-valued smooth $f_{ij}$ and additive cocycle identity. For a subordinate partition $(\rho_k)$, set $u_i=\sum_k\rho_k f_{ki}$ on chart $i$; terms extend by zero where needed. On an overlap, $u_j-u_i=\sum_k\rho_k(f_{kj}-f_{ki})=f_{ij}$. Changing local frames by $1-\varepsilon u_i$ kills the transitions. A constant unitary infinitesimal scalar then matches the given framing at infinity. Hence every such family can be written globally on the fixed framed line as $d+\varepsilon a$, with $a$ a smooth imaginary-valued one-form; the remaining gauge changes are $1+\varepsilon\phi$ with imaginary-valued $\phi$ and $\phi(\infty)=0$.

The coefficientwise ASD equation in this global frame is $(da)^+=0$. Write $a=i\alpha$ for a real one-form. Since $d\alpha$ is ASD, $\int|d\alpha|^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\alpha=-\int d(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)=0$ by [F4]. Continuity and nonnegativity imply $d\alpha=0$. Again [F4] gives $\alpha=df$; subtract the constant $f(\infty)$ and put $\phi=-if$. The based gauge $1+\varepsilon\phi$ removes $a$. This gauge is unique: a residual imaginary scalar with zero derivative is constant and its value at infinity is zero. Ordinary framed stabilizers were already trivial in step 1.2. The first-order connection groupoid is therefore the trivial point, not merely a set with one known reduced point.

A regular raw first-order family with $k>0$ would reduce to a prohibited datum from step 1.1, so none exists; the connection family for $k>0$ has no allowable special fiber by step 1.2. At $k=0$ the rank-zero internal $D$-module and all raw maps are uniquely zero, with trivial internal gauge group. Its forward monad is the constant framed line and its forward connection is $d$, also over $D$. Step 3.1 supplies a unique framed gauge from every first-order connection object to this one. Thus this explicit construction is an equivalence of the two first-order groupoids. Reduction and involution-preserving scalar maps commute with it, because the zero datum and the constant line pull back to themselves and the framed trivializing isomorphism is unique. The same argument after complexifying the real tangent spaces gives zero complexified tangent spaces; it does not assert a correspondence for arbitrary complex connections without the Hermitian real condition.

Stabilization intertwines $T$ with the rank-two compact action having framing weights $(h,1)$. In the zero-charge classification, inverse rotations and framing changes send a flat framed object to a flat framed object; the unique framed parallel trivialization identifies it with the same point. Its uniqueness also makes the first-order identifications equivariant. They hold for every first-order Hermitian family defined above, hence also for the subset satisfying the exact locally-free/cohomology-base-change hypotheses retained in [A1]; no extra family statement is obtained from an orbit-set bijection. Positive-FI rank-one stable data and their non-locally-free sheaves and formal fixed-point series were not used in any step.

boundaries.evidence: Statement; steps 1.1 and 1.2: Positive k raw rank-one data are excluded by exact rank-two stabilization, while ordinary unitary-line ASD emptiness follows independently from determinant flatness.
Statement; steps 1.2, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1: k=0 is the unique framed flat point, with its actual first-order unitary groupoid reduced to that point.
Statement; steps 1.1 and 1.2: Framing rank N=1 is the subject of the lemma; no positive-FI rank-one fixed point is identified with an ordinary positive-charge line connection.
Statement; step 4.1: A free rank-zero internal module and U(0) are unique; the based unitary first-order gauge action has no remaining stabilizer.
Statement; steps 1.1, 1.2 and 5.1: k=0 is separated from every k>0, and the smooth infinity framing and compact action are retained.
Statement; steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1: Inherited AC and exact rank-two analytic inputs remain explicit; the zero-charge datum is constructed and no selection from an empty positive-charge space is made.
Statement; steps 1.1 and 4.1: A regular rank-one datum can only be the k=0 datum, whose flat connection/family is explicit.
Statement; steps 1.2, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1: A framed ordinary unitary-line ASD connection/family is the unique flat k=0 object and recovers the unique raw rank-zero datum.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as inherited from the equivariant
constructible and Borel-stabilization suppliers. Let $G=\prod_v\mathrm{GL}_{n_v}(\mathbb C)$,
let $k$ be a characteristic-zero field, and use bounded algebraically constructible complexes of
$k$-sheaves in the analytic topology, in the equivariant derived category
$D^b_{G,c}(-;k)$ of [[def-equivariant-constructible-derived-category-for-complex-algebraic-varieties]].
All functors are derived.

**Dualizing normalization and Borel–Moore homology.** The equivariant dualizing object is
normalized by $\omega_X^G|_X=\omega_X$, rather than by the dimension of the quotient stack; here
$\omega_X=a_X^!k$ is the ordinary constructible dualizing object and
$\omega_X^G\simeq k_X[2d]$ for a smooth complex $d$-dimensional $X$
([[thm-constructible-six-functors-proper-base-change-and-verdier-duality]]). Define
$$H_j^{\mathrm{BM},G}(X;k)=H_G^{-j}(X,\omega_X^G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b_{G,c}(X;k)}(k_X,\omega_X^G[-j]).$$
Equivalently, use the general linear Stiefel approximations $U$ and their geometric quotients
supplied by [[lem-cartesian-simplicial-sheaves-model-equivariant-constructible-derived-hom]],
with $b=\dim_{\mathbb C}U-\dim_{\mathbb C}G$. In each fixed degree, once the supplied
bounded-Hom comparison applies, the group is the stable value
$H_{j+2b}^{\mathrm{BM}}(X\times_GU;k)$. Comparison on products of sufficiently acyclic
resolutions makes it independent of the chosen such stage. Other free smooth models require
the same bounded-Hom and quotient hypotheses; freeness alone does not assert stabilization. Ordinary
Borel–Moore homology is the case $G=1$ in the same formula, i.e.
$H_j^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;k)=\operatorname{Hom}(k_X,\omega_X[-j])$, and the smooth complex orientation
gives $\omega_X=k_X[2d]$ for $X$ smooth of pure complex dimension $d$.

**Correspondences.** Let $f_i:X_i\to E$ be finitely many proper $G$-equivariant algebraic maps
with $X_i$ smooth of pure complex dimension $d_i$. Put $Z_{ij}=X_i\times_EX_j$ (reduced
analytically), $T_{ijk}=X_i\times_EX_j\times_EX_k$, and let $h:T_{ijk}\to Z_{ik}$ forget the
middle point; it is proper, being the base change of $f_j$
([[lem-proper-stable-base-change]]). The first coordinate is the source.
For $a\in H_p^{\mathrm{BM},G}(Z_{ij})$, $b\in H_q^{\mathrm{BM},G}(Z_{jk})$, define
$$a*b=h_*\Delta_{X_j}^{!}(a\boxtimes b)\in H_{p+q-2d_j}^{\mathrm{BM},G}(Z_{ik}).$$
Here $\Delta_{X_j}^{!}$ is the refined oriented middle-diagonal operation on supports of
[[lem-complex-oriented-diagonal-thom-class-realizes-the-six-functor-exchange-on-supports]]: it
restricts the external class to $T_{ijk}$ by the Thom class of the complex normal bundle $TX_j$
of $X_j\hookrightarrow X_j\times X_j$. It is defined on arbitrary closed supports; no
transversality of $Z_{ij}$ and $Z_{jk}$ is assumed. Proper pushforward is the dualizing trace.
The ordered coordinates are $(i,j,j,k)$, and the two middle factors are contracted without a
permutation. If intermediate indices differ, the product is set to zero. Put degree $d_i+d_j-p$
on the $(i,j)$ corner. The normalized diagonal class $[\Delta_{X_i}]$ has corner degree zero.

**Sheaf model.** The sheaf model of the refined Thom operation uses the exchange morphism
$v'^*u^!\to u'^!v^*$ for the middle Cartesian square: with $u:Z_{ij}\to X_j$,
$v:Z_{jk}\to X_j$, $T=Z_{ij}\times_{X_j}Z_{jk}$ and projections $v':T\to Z_{ij}$,
$u':T\to Z_{jk}$, the morphism is obtained as the adjunction mate of proper base change
$v^*u_!\xrightarrow{\sim}u'_!v'^*$. Explicitly, its value at $C$ is adjoint to
$u'_!v'^*u^!C\to v^*u_!u^!C\to v^*C$, the first map being inverse base change and the
second the exceptional counit. It is a morphism, not an asserted isomorphism for arbitrary supports.
Its orientation is fixed by the Thom class restricting to $+1$ on every positively
complex-oriented normal fiber. Agreement of this model with the stated refined geometric
operation, and compatibility with composition, are proved in
[[thm-verdier-duality-identification-intertwines-yoneda-product-and-convolution]] after the
foundational six-functor inputs are available.

**Well-formedness.** The definition is independent of the chosen sufficiently acyclic Stiefel stage
because the stable Borel value exists and the product-resolution comparisons are coherent by
[[lem-cartesian-simplicial-sheaves-model-equivariant-constructible-derived-hom]]; the product is
defined because the refined middle-diagonal operation of
[[lem-complex-oriented-diagonal-thom-class-realizes-the-six-functor-exchange-on-supports]] is
defined on arbitrary closed supports and $h$ is proper, so its dualizing trace is available; the
degree bookkeeping is fixed by the pure complex dimension $d_j$ of the middle factor. The claim
that the sheaf model and the geometric operation agree, and that the product is compatible with
composition and units, is not assumed here: it is the content of
[[thm-verdier-duality-identification-intertwines-yoneda-product-and-convolution]], which is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps` because that theorem depends on this
definition. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the cited suppliers, including proper
base-change stability; their descent, injective, Thom and Borel constructions declare it;
the definition itself introduces no further choice principle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), that $k$ has
characteristic zero, and that a finite product
$G=\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$ of complex general linear groups
acts algebraically on separated finite-type complex varieties
([[def-equivariant-constructible-derived-category-for-complex-algebraic-varieties]]).
For equivariant algebraic maps between such varieties, the coherent ordinary
six-operation contract holds in the equivariant bounded constructible category
$D^b_{G,c}$:

1. the functors $f^*,Rf_*,Rf_!,f^!$ are defined on $D^b_{G,c}$, with
   $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, $Rf_!\dashv f^!$, and the tensor and internal-Hom
   adjunction $\otimes_k^L\dashv R\mathcal Hom$;
2. composition and identity comparisons, support localization, the projection
   formula and the trace hold, and for a Cartesian square with $f:X\to Y$,
   $u:Y'\to Y$, $v:X'\to X$ and $f':X'\to Y'$ the exchange
   $u^*Rf_!\simeq Rf'_!v^*$ and its dual mate $u^!Rf_*\simeq Rf'_*v^!$ obey
   Cartesian pasting; proper $f$ satisfies $Rf_!=Rf_*$;
3. the normalized dualizing object $\omega^G$ restricts to the ordinary
   $\omega_X$ of [[thm-verdier-duality-on-oriented-stratified-complex-varieties]],
   and for a smooth complex $d$-dimensional $X$ one has
   $\omega_X^G\simeq k_X[2d]$; this is not the unnormalized quotient-stack
   dualizing shift.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $r\geq0$, let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, and use $E_T=(E_{S^1})^r$, the product of the right Milnor join models, with $BT=E_T/T$. For the $i$th coordinate character $\chi_i([t_1,\ldots,t_r])=\exp(2\pi i t_i)$, let $L_i=E_T\times_T\mathbb C_{\chi_i}$ be the associated complex line bundle over $BT$, with the right diagonal equivalence $(e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi_i(t)^{-1}z)$, and put $u_i=c_1(L_i)\in H^2(BT;\mathbb Q)$. Then
$$
BT\cong(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r,\qquad H^*(BT;\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q[u_1,\ldots,u_r],\qquad |u_i|=2.
$$
Every smooth character $\chi:T\to S^1$ is uniquely $\chi_{\mathbf n}([t])=\exp(2\pi i\sum_i n_it_i)$ for $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb Z^r$, and its associated line satisfies $c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i$. In particular a nontrivial character has a nonzero degree-two class. For each $k\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}$, $H_q(BT;k)$ is finite-dimensional in every degree $q$. For $r=0$, $BT$ is a point and its rational cohomology is $\mathbb Q$.

derivations.claim: Since $T=(\mathrm{GL}_1)^r$, [F1] supplies the normalized equivariant Borel–Moore groups and the stable scalar-frame construction. For $U_m=(\mathbb C^{m+1}\setminus\{0\})^r$, the quotient is $B_m=(\mathbb{CP}^m)^r$ and $\dim_{\mathbb C}U_m-\dim_{\mathbb C}T=rm$, giving the stated degree shift. AC is inherited from [F1] and is the only choice assumption added here.

The polar decomposition $T\cong K\times(\mathbb R_{>0})^r$ makes $K\hookrightarrow T$ a homotopy equivalence. Choose one contractible free $T$-space $E$; it is also free for $K$, and $E/K\to E/T$ has contractible fiber $T/K$. The Borel fibrations $(E\times X)/K\to E/K$ and $(E\times X)/T\to E/T$ have common fiber $X$, with identity map on that fiber. Their homotopy exact sequences therefore make $(E\times X)/K\to(E\times X)/T$ a weak equivalence. Model independence of the universal free contractible space identifies this with the product right Milnor model and the algebraic-torus approximation in [F1].

By [F3], each nontrivial character has $u_\chi=\sum_i n_i u_i\neq0$ in the polynomial domain $R_T$. Therefore finite products of such classes remain nonzero, and concatenating two finite products shows that $S_T$ contains $1$, is multiplicatively closed, and excludes $0$. The localization by fractions is consequently defined.

The operations in the Definition are the proper pushforward, open restriction, and support maps of [F2]; the cap action is the action of Borel cohomology through $E_K\times_KX\to B_K$. For smooth pure complex dimension $d$, the normalized dualizing object restricts to $\mathbb Q_X[2d]$, so the complex orientation gives $[X]_T$ degree $2d$. These constructions respect the stable comparison of [F1].

boundaries.evidence: The Definition takes S_T to contain 1 as the empty character product and allows the empty variety. Its Borel-Moore groups are then zero; at r=0 the coordinate-character index set is empty, R_T=Q and S_T={1}.

Assume the Axiom of Choice exactly as in the general Thom theorem, and let
$\xi\to B$ be an $R$-oriented numerable real rank-$n$ vector bundle over a
base in the scope of that theorem. Let $u_\xi\in H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$ be its
normalized Thom class, let
$$j^*:H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)\longrightarrow H^n(D(\xi);R)$$ be the relative-to-absolute map of the pair sequence, and let $s:B\to D(\xi)$ be the zero section. The **Euler class** of $\xi$ is $$e(\xi)=e_{\rm Th}(\xi):=s^*j^*(u_\xi)\in H^n(B;R).$$
This is the class already introduced in
[[def-thom-euler-class-of-an-oriented-vector-bundle]]: on this page we write
$e(\xi)$ for it, and the shorthand $s^*u_\xi$ always means the composite
$s^*j^*(u_\xi)$, the relative-to-absolute map being understood. For rank zero
with supplied orientation $o\in H^0(B;R)$, normalization gives $u_\xi=o$ and
$j$ and $s$ are identities, so
$$e(0_B,o)=o\in H^0(B;R).$$
In particular, the standard unit orientation gives $e(0_B,1)=1$.
For $R=\mathbb F_2$ every real bundle is canonically $\mathbb F_2$-oriented by
[[def-r-oriented-vector-bundle-and-orientation-local-system]], so in that
case $e_2(\xi):=e(\xi)\in H^n(B;\mathbb F_2)$ is defined for every real
bundle in the Thom scope; for $R=\mathbb Z$ the class depends on the chosen
integral orientation, and reversing the orientation negates it.

derivations.claim: The set $D(f)$ is $T$-invariant because $f(t\cdot x)=\chi(t)f(x)$. On its Borel construction, define $s([e,x])=[e,f(x)]$ in the associated character line. This is well-defined: replacing $(e,x)$ by $(e\cdot t,t^{-1}\cdot x)$ replaces $f(x)$ by $f(t^{-1}\cdot x)=\chi(t)^{-1}f(x)$, exactly the right equivalence $(e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi(t)^{-1}z)$. Since $f$ never vanishes on $D(f)$, $s$ is a nowhere-zero section and trivializes that line bundle. The same formula trivializes its restriction to every $T$-invariant open $V\subseteq D(f)$.

On each finite Borel approximation, the first Chern class of the trivialized line is zero. By [F2] this is the Euler class of the line, and by [F3] its cap action on the approximating Borel–Moore groups is zero. The stable comparison in [F1] therefore gives $u_\chi\cap\beta=0$ for every $\beta\in H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(D(f);\mathbb Q)$, and the identical argument holds on $V$.

Since $\chi$ is nontrivial, $u_\chi\in S_T$ is invertible after localization. For any class $\beta$, its localized image satisfies $\beta/1=(u_\chi\cap\beta)/u_\chi=0$ by step 2.1. The localized groups on both $D(f)$ and $V$ consequently vanish. If the opposite character convention is used, the class is $-u_\chi$, which is also in $S_T$ up to the unit $-1$ and has the same annihilation consequence.

derivations.claim: Fix a member $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of the invariant affine cover. Choose finitely many algebra generators of $A$. The algebraic $T$-action makes $A$ a rational $T$-comodule, so the coaction of each generator is a finite Laurent sum and the generator is a finite sum of character eigenfunctions. Replacing the generators by these finitely many eigencomponents still generates $A$, since their sums recover the original generators. The fixed ideal in $A$ is generated by its nontrivial-weight subspace: the coaction sends a weight-$\chi$ element $f$ to $f\otimes\chi$, so the equalizer with the trivial coaction kills $f$ when $\chi\ne1$, and the quotient by all such elements has only weight-zero functions and hence trivial action. The ideal generated by the nontrivial-weight algebra generators contains every nonzero-weight polynomial in the generators, since each monomial of nonzero total weight has a nonzero-weight factor. Thus $U\setminus F$ is covered by the finitely many invariant principal opens $D(f)$ for those generators.

Taking these principal opens over the finitely many affine charts gives a finite invariant open cover $\{D_a\}$ of $X\setminus F$. Every nonempty finite intersection is a $T$-invariant open subset of at least one $D_a$; [F2] therefore makes its localized Borel–Moore groups zero in every degree.

For a finite invariant open cover of $X\setminus F$, the augmented Čech complex with terms $j_{I!}\mathbb Q_{D_I}$, where $D_I$ is an intersection and $j_I:D_I\hookrightarrow X\setminus F$ is open, resolves the constant equivariant sheaf. At a point the indices containing it form a nonempty simplex, whose augmented cochain complex is contracted by its least index. Applying derived Hom into the normalized dualizing object gives a finite Čech spectral sequence for Borel–Moore homology: open base change identifies each term with the Borel–Moore group of an intersection $D_I$. Those groups vanish after localization by [F2]. Since the Čech filtration is finite and localization is exact by [F4], the abutment $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F;\mathbb Q)$ is zero for every $j$.

The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. Both outside groups vanish by step 3.1, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism. If $F=\varnothing$, the same argument gives zero localized Borel–Moore homology for $X$; if $F=X$, $i_*$ is the identity. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness.

Assume the Axiom of Choice where the geometric suppliers of the named items use it. Let $G$ be a linearly reductive affine group variety over $k$ acting on a smooth variety $X$. Then the fixed-point subscheme $X^G$ is smooth (Milne, Ch. 13); if $S\subseteq G(k)$ is Zariski-dense then $X^S=X^G$ and both are smooth (13.5-13.7); if $k$ is algebraically closed and $g\in G(k)$ is semisimple, then the closure of the subgroup generated by $g$ is linearly reductive and $X^g=X^{G_0}$ is smooth (13.8). In particular, if a linearly reductive group $H$ acts on a smooth algebraic group $G$, then the fixed subgroup $G^H$ is smooth; when $H\subseteq G$ acts by conjugation this is $C_G(H)$ (13.9), and for a subgroup $H\subseteq G$ of multiplicative type the centralizer $C_G(H)$ and normalizer $N_G(H)$ are smooth, with no smoothness assumption on $H$. If $H$ is smooth, its geometric points are schematically dense, and these are also the unique smooth closed subgroup schemes whose geometric points are the centralizer and normalizer of $H(k^{\mathrm a})$ (13.10-13.11). The pointwise identification is not asserted for nonsmooth $H$: for $H=\mu_p$ embedded by $t\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(t,1)$ in $\mathrm{GL}_2$ in characteristic $p$, $H(k^{\mathrm a})=1$ but $C_G(H)$ is the diagonal torus.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Give the graded tensor product the multiplication
$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=(-1)^{|b||a'|}(a\smile a')\otimes(b\smile b').$$
For arbitrary spaces $X,Y$, external product $a\times b=\operatorname{pr}_X^*a\smile\operatorname{pr}_Y^*b$ gives a unital graded-ring homomorphism to $H^*(X\times Y;R)$. This multiplicativity requires no AC.

Assume in addition AC, that $R$ is a PID, and that either every $H_q(Y;R)$ or every $H_p(X;R)$ is finite free over $R$. Then this homomorphism is an isomorphism.

For CW pairs $(X,A),(Y,B)$ with supplied characteristic maps, relative external product is likewise a graded-ring homomorphism
$$H^*(X,A;R)\mathbin{\widehat\otimes}_R H^*(Y,B;R)\longrightarrow H^*(X\times Y,(A\times Y)\cup(X\times B);R),$$
where the hat denotes the displayed graded multiplication on the ordinary graded direct-sum tensor product, not a completion. Relative rings need not have units. This relative multiplicativity is choice-free for every commutative unital $R$. Under AC and the PID hypothesis it is an isomorphism if either every $H_q(Y,B;R)$ or every $H_p(X,A;R)$ is finite free. Neither additive assertion requires bounded dimension or finite-rank singular chain groups. Products have their ordinary product topologies; AC enters only in additive bijectivity.

Assume AC.  Every $R$-oriented rank-$n$ numerable vector bundle over a CW
complex, or over a paracompact Hausdorff base of CW type, has a unique
normalized Thom class $u_\xi$, and

for every $k$.  Without a supplied orientation, the canonical twisted form is
$$H^k(B;\mathcal O_R(\xi))\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R).$$
The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $r\geq 0$, let $T=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act algebraically on a separated finite-type complex variety $X$, and suppose $X$ has a finite cover by $T$-invariant affine open subvarieties. Use rational coefficients. Let $K=(S^1)^r$ be the maximal compact subgroup of $T$, and use the product right Milnor model $E_K=(E_{S^1})^r$, $B_K=E_K/K=(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r$. The inclusion $K\subset T$ gives the same topological Borel construction up to homotopy. For each algebraic character $\chi:T\to\mathbb C^\times$, let $L_\chi=E_K\times_K\mathbb C_{\chi|_K}\to B_K$, with right equivalence $(e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi(t)^{-1}z)$, and put $u_\chi=c_1(L_\chi)$. For the coordinate characters $\chi_i$ and $u_i=u_{\chi_i}$, the coefficient ring is $R_T=H^*(B_K;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q[u_1,\ldots,u_r]$, with $|u_i|=2$ and $u_\chi=\sum_i n_i u_i$ for $\chi(t_1,\ldots,t_r)=\prod_i t_i^{n_i}$. Let $S_T$ be the multiplicative set consisting of $1$ and finite products of $u_\chi$ for nontrivial $\chi$.

Let $H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b_{T,c}(X;\mathbb Q)}(\mathbb Q_X,\omega_X^T[-j])$, where $\omega_X^T$ is the normalized equivariant dualizing object whose restriction is the ordinary dualizing object $\omega_X$, without a quotient-stack dimension shift. Equivalently, this is the stable value in degree $j$ of $H^{\mathrm{BM}}_{j+2rm}(X_m;\mathbb Q)$, where $U_m=(\mathbb C^{m+1}\setminus\{0\})^r$ has the free right scalar $T$-action, $X_m=(U_m\times X)/T$ uses $(e,x)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,t^{-1}\cdot x)$, and the supplied bounded-Hom comparison is taken in its stable range. The ring $R_T$ acts by pullback from $B_K$ and cap product. For an $R_T$-module $M$, $S_T^{-1}M$ consists of fractions $m/s$ with $m\in M$, $s\in S_T$, and $m/s=m'/s'$ exactly when some $t\in S_T$ satisfies $t(s'm-sm')=0$; addition and scalar multiplication are the induced fraction operations. Proper equivariant maps induce degree-preserving pushforwards, invariant open inclusions induce Borel–Moore restrictions, and a smooth pure $d$-dimensional complex variety has its complex-oriented fundamental class $[X]_T$ in degree $2d$. Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as inherited from the analytic six-functor and equivariant constructible suppliers below. Assume the supplied duality construction has localization, tensor–Hom adjunction, coherent exchange maps, and the smooth orientation normalized by the positive compactly supported generator on a complex coordinate ball ([[thm-analytic-sheaf-six-operations-have-coherent-base-change-projection-and-trace]], [[thm-verdier-duality-on-oriented-stratified-complex-varieties]]), with its equivariant constructible form supplied by [[thm-constructible-six-functors-proper-base-change-and-verdier-duality]]. The refined pullback of dualizing classes on the support $A\times B$ by the ambient middle diagonal $M\to M\times M$ is the operation induced by the mate $\mathrm{ex}:a^*q^!\to b^!u^*$ of the base-change morphism $u^*q_!\to b_!a^*$ of this square, after tensor evaluation and dualizing transitivity. It equals cap product with the positive middle-diagonal Thom class and lowers Borel–Moore degree by $2d$, even for singular, nontransverse supports. Ordered iterated diagonals are compatible with composed refined operations. For a complex vector bundle, zero-section self-intersection is cap product with its oriented Euler class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice exactly as in the general Thom theorem, and let
$\xi\to B$ be an $R$-oriented numerable real rank-$n$ vector bundle over a
base in the scope of that theorem. Let $u_\xi\in H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$ be its
normalized Thom class, let
$$j^*:H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)\longrightarrow H^n(D(\xi);R)$$ be the relative-to-absolute map of the pair sequence, and let $s:B\to D(\xi)$ be the zero section. The **Euler class** of $\xi$ is $$e(\xi)=e_{\rm Th}(\xi):=s^*j^*(u_\xi)\in H^n(B;R).$$
This is the class already introduced in
[[def-thom-euler-class-of-an-oriented-vector-bundle]]: on this page we write
$e(\xi)$ for it, and the shorthand $s^*u_\xi$ always means the composite
$s^*j^*(u_\xi)$, the relative-to-absolute map being understood. For rank zero
with supplied orientation $o\in H^0(B;R)$, normalization gives $u_\xi=o$ and
$j$ and $s$ are identities, so
$$e(0_B,o)=o\in H^0(B;R).$$
In particular, the standard unit orientation gives $e(0_B,1)=1$.
For $R=\mathbb F_2$ every real bundle is canonically $\mathbb F_2$-oriented by
[[def-r-oriented-vector-bundle-and-orientation-local-system]], so in that
case $e_2(\xi):=e(\xi)\in H^n(B;\mathbb F_2)$ is defined for every real
bundle in the Thom scope; for $R=\mathbb Z$ the class depends on the chosen
integral orientation, and reversing the orientation negates it.

Assume AC.  For ordered oriented bundles $\xi\to B$ and $\eta\to C$ of ranks
$n,m$, the canonical product-pair identification gives
$$u_{\xi\times\eta}=u_\xi\times u_\eta.$$
For bundles over one base, diagonal pullback gives
$$u_{\xi\oplus\eta}=u_\xi\smile u_\eta.$$
Interchanging the ordered summands changes the orientation and the displayed
class by the Koszul sign $(-1)^{nm}$.

Assume AC. Let $F$ be a compact finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary, equipped with a Riemannian metric, and let $k$ be a field. There is a finite CW complex $K$ homotopy equivalent to $F$, and an integer $N\geq1$ such that $H^q(F;k)=0$ for every $q\geq N$. Consequently the ideal $J=\bigoplus_{q>0}H^q(F;k)$ in the graded cohomology ring satisfies $J^N=0$. If $F=\varnothing$, take $K=\varnothing$, $N=1$, and $J=0$.

Assume AC. Let $r\geq0$, let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$ use the product Milnor model $BT=(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r$ with its ordinary product topology, and let $F$ be a compact finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. Then $BT\times F$ is paracompact Hausdorff and has the homotopy type of a CW complex. In fact, there is a finite CW complex $K$ such that $BT\times F\simeq BT\times K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $r\geq0$, let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, and use $E_T=(E_{S^1})^r$, the product of the right Milnor join models, with $BT=E_T/T$. For the $i$th coordinate character $\chi_i([t_1,\ldots,t_r])=\exp(2\pi i t_i)$, let $L_i=E_T\times_T\mathbb C_{\chi_i}$ be the associated complex line bundle over $BT$, with the right diagonal equivalence $(e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi_i(t)^{-1}z)$, and put $u_i=c_1(L_i)\in H^2(BT;\mathbb Q)$. Then
$$
BT\cong(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r,\qquad H^*(BT;\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q[u_1,\ldots,u_r],\qquad |u_i|=2.
$$
Every smooth character $\chi:T\to S^1$ is uniquely $\chi_{\mathbf n}([t])=\exp(2\pi i\sum_i n_it_i)$ for $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb Z^r$, and its associated line satisfies $c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i$. In particular a nontrivial character has a nonzero degree-two class. For each $k\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}$, $H_q(BT;k)$ is finite-dimensional in every degree $q$. For $r=0$, $BT$ is a point and its rational cohomology is $\mathbb Q$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $F$ is smooth and $T_xF=(T_xX)^T$. The quotient $T_xX/T_xF$ therefore has no invariant vector. On an affine open of a connected fixed component the base ring has trivial $T$-action, so the coaction on the finite-rank normal bundle is linear over that ring. Each of finitely many local module generators has finite character support; the character-coefficient projections are orthogonal idempotents summing to the identity. Their images are locally free direct summands. These decompositions agree on overlaps because the projections are defined by the group coaction. The zero-weight image has zero fiber at every point by $T_xF=(T_xX)^T$, so $\nu_F$ is the finite direct sum of nontrivial character subbundles. Thus $i$ is a closed regular embedding with the stated complex normal bundle.

The complex normal orientation gives the refined Gysin map in the normalized Borel–Moore grading. The Thom class is normalized to restrict to the positive complex-oriented generator on every normal fiber, so $i^![X]_T=[F]_T$. A $K$-invariant tubular neighborhood of each fixed component identifies the embedding locally in the Borel construction with the zero section of its normal bundle. By [F3] and the Thom class in [F4], this zero-section operation satisfies $i^!i_*\beta=e_T(\nu_F)\cap\beta$; the degree is lowered by twice the complex codimension $c$. The result is independent of the chosen tubular neighborhood because the refined exchange and orientation comparisons are canonical.

Now let $F_0$ be a connected component of proper $F$. It is a compact smooth complex manifold, and $T$ acts trivially on it. The Borel normal bundle is a complex vector bundle over $BT	imes F_0$; [F5] puts its base in the Thom theorem's scope. By [F6], $H_T^*(F_0;\mathbb Q)=H^*(BT;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}H^*(F_0;\mathbb Q)$. The weight subbundles from step 1.1 have ranks $m_\chi$ constant on $F_0$. Restricting the Borel normal bundle to $BT	imes\{x\}$, for any $x\in F_0$, gives $ igoplus_{\chi
e1}L_\chi^{\oplus m_\chi}$. By [F4] and the zero-section definition of Euler class, the restriction of $e_T(
u_F)$ is $w_0=\prod_{\chi
e1}u_\chi^{m_\chi}$. Each $u_\chi$ is a generator of $S_T$, so $w_0$ is invertible after localization.

Under the Künneth decomposition of step 2.2, write $e_T(\nu_F)=w_0+\eta$, where $\eta\in J_0\otimes_{\mathbb Q}H^*(BT;\mathbb Q)$; restriction to a point detects the degree-zero $F_0$ component $w_0$. By [F5], $J_0^N=0$ for some finite $N$, so $z=w_0^{-1}\eta$ has $z^N=0$ in the localized ring. Therefore $e_T(\nu_F)^{-1}=w_0^{-1}\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}(-z)^a$ is a finite inverse. If the normal rank is zero, the empty product is $w_0=1$, $\eta=0$, and the same formula gives $e_T=1$. There are finitely many connected components because $F$ is finite type; the componentwise inverses give a unit on all of $F$. If $F=\varnothing$, the Euler-unit clause is vacuous.

boundaries.reason: The fixed-embedding self-intersection formula has discrete normal codimension c and homological degrees, without a real endpoint limit. The minimal codimension c=0 is expressly included through Euler class 1.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 gives canonical character projections, and Step 3.1 constructs the inverse by a finite sum.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $i_*$ is an isomorphism in each degree after localization, so its inverse is a unique $S_T^{-1}R_T$-linear map. The proper inclusion $i$ and the proper map $p_F$ give the stated Borel–Moore pushforwards by [F1].

Composition of the inverse with $p_{F*}$ is therefore a well-defined degree-preserving map on the localized Borel–Moore groups. The insertion convention is well-defined because [F1] supplies the cap action and the smooth complex orientation gives $[X]_T$ degree $2d$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ is proper, functoriality gives $p_{X*}=p_{F*}i_*$, so $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{F*}i_*(i_*)^{-1}=p_{X*}$. If $F=\varnothing$, then $F\to\mathrm{pt}$ is proper and [F2] forces the localized groups of $X$ to be zero, so the defined trace is the zero map. For $r=0$, $T$ is trivial, $F=X$, $i$ is the identity, and the properness hypothesis makes this the usual proper pushforward.

Let $T=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act on a smooth separated finite-type complex variety $X$ with a finite invariant affine open cover. Let $F=X^T$ be proper, $i:F\hookrightarrow X$, $p_F:F\to\mathrm{pt}$, and $S_T$ the character multiplicative set. By the finite-affine-atlas concentration isomorphism, $i_*:S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F;\mathbb Q)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)$ is invertible. Define the intrinsic localized pushforward
$$
p^{\mathrm{loc}}_*:=p_{F*}\circ(i_*)^{-1}:S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(\mathrm{pt};\mathbb Q),
$$
where $p_{F*}$ is the genuine proper Borel–Moore pushforward. For a homogeneous $\alpha\in H_T^q(X;\mathbb Q)$ and smooth complex dimension $d$, an allowed insertion is $\alpha\cap[X]_T\in H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{2d-q}(X;\mathbb Q)$; the fundamental class $[X]_T$ is the complex-oriented class, not the cohomological unit $1\in H_T^0(X;\mathbb Q)$. This construction does not define an ordinary pushforward along a nonproper map $X\to\mathrm{pt}$.

On each fiber the restriction of $e_T(\nu_F)$ to $BT$ is the product of the corresponding character classes with multiplicity. $$
i^!i_*\beta=e_T(\nu_F)\mathbin{\cap}\beta
$$
for every $\beta\in H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_*(F;\mathbb Q)$, using the normalized Borel–Moore grading and complex orientation. If $F$ is proper, then $e_T(\nu_F)$ is a unit in $S_T^{-1}H_T^*(F;\mathbb Q)$. Empty components contribute no class, and a rank-zero normal bundle has Euler class $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $r\geq 0$, let $T=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act algebraically on a separated finite-type complex variety $X$, and suppose $X$ has a finite cover by $T$-invariant affine open subvarieties. Use rational coefficients. Let $K=(S^1)^r$ be the maximal compact subgroup of $T$, and use the product right Milnor model $E_K=(E_{S^1})^r$, $B_K=E_K/K=(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r$. The inclusion $K\subset T$ gives the same topological Borel construction up to homotopy. For each algebraic character $\chi:T\to\mathbb C^\times$, let $L_\chi=E_K\times_K\mathbb C_{\chi|_K}\to B_K$, with right equivalence $(e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi(t)^{-1}z)$, and put $u_\chi=c_1(L_\chi)$. For the coordinate characters $\chi_i$ and $u_i=u_{\chi_i}$, the coefficient ring is $R_T=H^*(B_K;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q[u_1,\ldots,u_r]$, with $|u_i|=2$ and $u_\chi=\sum_i n_i u_i$ for $\chi(t_1,\ldots,t_r)=\prod_i t_i^{n_i}$. Let $S_T$ be the multiplicative set consisting of $1$ and finite products of $u_\chi$ for nontrivial $\chi$.

Let $H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b_{T,c}(X;\mathbb Q)}(\mathbb Q_X,\omega_X^T[-j])$, where $\omega_X^T$ is the normalized equivariant dualizing object whose restriction is the ordinary dualizing object $\omega_X$, without a quotient-stack dimension shift. For an $R_T$-module $M$, $S_T^{-1}M$ consists of fractions $m/s$ with $m\in M$, $s\in S_T$, and $m/s=m'/s'$ exactly when some $t\in S_T$ satisfies $t(s'm-sm')=0$; addition and scalar multiplication are the induced fraction operations. derivations.claim: The map $i:F\hookrightarrow X$, its components $i_a$, and the localized groups are intrinsic; the finite affine cover is only a hypothesis used to prove [F2]. Since $i_*$ is the same canonical proper pushforward for every such cover, its inverse is unique. Therefore the definition $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{F*}(i_*)^{-1}$ is independent of the cover.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

If $F=\varnothing$, [F2] makes the localized Borel–Moore groups of $X$ zero and the component sum is empty. If $F$ is finite, every $F_a$ is a point and $e_T(\nu_a)$ is the product of its nonzero tangent-character classes, so each summand is the stated reciprocal-Euler term. If $c_a=0$, the normal bundle is rank zero and its complex-oriented Euler class is $1$. These cases agree with the formula and the degree computation above.

derivations.claim: The affine plane itself is an affine $T$-invariant chart. A point is fixed exactly when both coordinates vanish, so $F=\{0\}$ is proper. Differentiating the action at $0$ gives the representation $\mathbb C_{\chi_1}\oplus\mathbb C_{\chi_2}$; hence $e_T(\nu_F)=u_1u_2$ by [F3].

The denominator has cohomological degree $4$, so its inverse has Borel–Moore degree $4$, matching the fundamental class.

$$
i^!i_*\beta=e_T(\nu_F)\mathbin{\cap}\beta
$$
for every $\beta\in H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_*(F;\mathbb Q)$, using the normalized Borel–Moore grading and complex orientation. If $F$ is proper, then $e_T(\nu_F)$ is a unit in $S_T^{-1}H_T^*(F;\mathbb Q)$. Empty components contribute no class, and a rank-zero normal bundle has Euler class $1$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice through the Poincare and Sobolev suppliers below. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, and let $L$, $a$ and the real coefficient functions $a^{ij},b^i,c$ be as in [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]], with ellipticity constant $\theta$ and bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$. Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $u\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be a real local weak subsolution of $Lu=f$. Suppose the weak sign condition
$$\int_\Omega\bigl(c\,\zeta+b^iD_i\zeta\bigr)dx\ge0\qquad\text{for every }\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega),\ \zeta\ge0,$$
holds, and assume $c\ge0$ a.e. on $\Omega$. Then:

1. **Homogeneous case.** If $f=0$ a.e., then
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^+,$$
with the boundary supremum of [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]]. If in addition $b\equiv0$, $c\equiv0$, and $u$ is a weak solution of $Lu=0$, then $\operatorname{ess\,sup}_\Omega u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u$.

2. **Forcing with signed lower order.** If $b\equiv0$, $c\ge0$ a.e. and $f\in L^q(\Omega)$ for some $q>n/2$ ($q>1$ when $n=2$), then the local inequality extends to all nonnegative $H^1_0(\Omega)$ tests and
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^++C\|f^+\|_{L^q(\Omega)},\qquad C=C(n,q,\theta,M_a,M_c,\Omega),$$
where $\Omega$ enters $C$ only through its Poincare constant and volume.

If $u$ is a weak supersolution of $Lu=f$ under either set of hypotheses, apply the corresponding bound to $-u$ for the **same** operator coefficients $(a,b,c)$ and source $-f$. This gives $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^-$ in the homogeneous case and $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^- -C\|f^-\|_{L^q(\Omega)}$ in the forcing case. The maximum-principle conclusions concern real-valued classes and real coefficients.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $n<p<\infty$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain for some $0<\alpha<1$. If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $-\Delta u=f$ with $f\in L^p(\Omega)$, then $u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\bigr),$$
where $C=C(n,p,\Omega)$. This is a weak-to-strong regularity theorem; the estimate applies to the weak solution only after its $W^{2,p}$ membership has been established, and the assumption $p>n$ is the range in which the bootstrap of Sobolev exponents terminates at $p$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice together with Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$,
$0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, let
$f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$. Then
the weak Dirichlet problem $-\Delta u=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=g$ on
$\partial\Omega$ (understood as $u-g\in H^1_0(\Omega)$) has exactly one
solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, and this solution belongs to
$C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$, satisfies $-\Delta u=f$ pointwise in $\Omega$
and $u=g$ on $\partial\Omega$, and obeys
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}+\|g\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\bigr)$$
with $C=C(n,\alpha,\Omega)$. This supplies the Laplace base point of the
continuity method rather than assuming it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, continuous principal coefficients on the closed ball, and $\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty\le M$. Then every $u\in W^{2,p}(B_R(x_0))$ with $Lu=f\in L^p$ satisfies the scale-invariant estimate
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2}R^{j-2}\max_{|\beta|=j}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p(B_{R/2}(x_0))}\le C\bigl(R^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}+\|f\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\bigr),$$
where $D^0u=u$ and the maximum runs over multi-indices of order $j$,
where $C$ may depend on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,R\|b\|_\infty,R^2\|c\|_\infty$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$ on the ball. A radius-independent constant requires uniform control of these dimensionless lower-order bounds and of the modulus. The theorem assumes continuity of $A$; no estimate for merely measurable principal coefficients is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

derivations.claim: First, $\log|z|^2$ is locally integrable and harmonic off zero. For a smooth compactly supported test function $\varphi$, apply [F14] on an annulus excluding $|z|\le\varepsilon$ to the one-form $\log|z|^2*d\varphi-\varphi*d\log|z|^2$. Its inner-boundary contribution is $-\varepsilon\log(\varepsilon^2)\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_r\varphi(\varepsilon,\theta)d\theta+2\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(\varepsilon,\theta)d\theta$, which tends to $4\pi\varphi(0)$; the outer contribution is zero. Thus $\Delta\log|z-z_j|^2=4\pi\delta_{z_j}$ by translation. For $z\ne z_j$, put $t_j=a/(|z-z_j|^2+a)$. Then $0<t_j<1$, $e^{u_-}=\prod_j(1-t_j)^{m_j}$, and direct radial differentiation gives $\Delta u_-=-\frac4a\sum_jm_jt_j^2+4\pi\sum_jm_j\delta_{z_j}$ distributionally. If $N>0$, let $t_*:=\max_jt_j$; then $1-e^{u_-}\ge t_*$ and $\sum_jm_jt_j^2\le Nt_*$. Hence $\Delta u_-+\kappa(1-e^{u_-})-4\pi D\ge(\kappa-4N/a)t_*\ge0$. For $N=0$, $u_-=0$ and the subsolution inequality is equality.

The denominator $R^2-\overline z_jz$ has no zeros on $\overline D_R$ because $|z_j|<R$. The logarithmic fundamental-solution identity and the boundary equality $R^2|z-z_j|^2=|R^2-\overline z_jz|^2$ for $|z|=R$ give $\Delta u_{s,R}=4\pi D$ and $u_{s,R}=0$ on $\partial D_R$. Consequently $A_R=e^{u_{s,R}}$ is smooth and nonnegative on $\overline D_R$, vanishes at the centers, and equals one on the boundary. Since $\Delta\psi_R=-\kappa$, the supersolution residual away from the Dirac masses is $\Delta\psi_R+\kappa(1-A_Re^{\psi_R})=-\kappa A_Re^{\psi_R}\le0$.

By [F10], $H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ is a real Hilbert space with the full $W^{1,2}$ inner product; [F2] gives its norm. For any $L_R>0$, [F11] and the pointwise Euclidean inequality $|
abla v\cdot
abla w|\le|
abla v||
abla w|$ give $|a(v,w)|\le(1+L_R)\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}\|w\|_{W^{1,2}}$, so the form is bounded. Also $a(v,v)\ge\min\{1,L_R\}\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, so it is coercive. For $f\in L^2(D_R)$, [F11] gives $\int|fw|\le\|f\|_2\|w\|_2$, and [F12] then gives $|\int fw|\le\|f\|_2\|w\|_2\le\|f\|_2\|w\|_{W^{1,2}}$. Thus [F3] gives a unique zero-Dirichlet weak solution of $(-\Delta+L_R)u=f$. The resolver is linear by uniqueness and positivity preserving: if $f\ge0$, then $-u$ is a weak subsolution of $(-\Delta+L_R)(-u)=-f\le0$ with zero trace, so [F4] gives $u\ge0$.

The lower and upper barriers have the same logarithmic singular part, so $w=u_--u_{s,R}-\psi_R$ extends continuously across every center. Their subsolution and supersolution inequalities imply $\Delta w-c_Rw\ge0$, where $c_R=\kappa\int_0^1\exp((1-t)(u_{s,R}+\psi_R)+tu_-)\,dt\ge0$, extended continuously at the centers. On $\partial D_R$, $w=u_-<0$ (and $w=0$ when $D$ is empty). Applying [F4] to $(-\Delta+c_R)w\le0$ with nonpositive boundary trace gives $w\le0$, hence $v_0=u_--u_{s,R}\le\psi_R$.

Set $G_R(v)=\kappa+L_Rv-\kappa A_Re^v$ and choose $L_R\ge\kappa\max_{\overline D_R}(A_Re^{\psi_R})$. For $v\le\psi_R$, $G_R'(v)=L_R-\kappa A_Re^v\ge0$, so the iteration map $T_R=(-\Delta+L_R)^{-1}G_R$ is order preserving. The subsolution inequality from step 2.1 gives $v_0\le T_Rv_0$ and the supersolution inequality from step 1.2 gives $T_R\psi_R\le\psi_R$, by positivity of the resolver in step 1.3. Thus $v_0\le v_1\le\cdots\le\psi_R$; every iterate after $v_0$ has zero Dirichlet trace. Each has a smooth representative: starting from smooth $v_0$ and $A_R$, rewrite its shifted resolvent equation as a Laplace equation, use boundedness and [F5] for $W^{2,p}$, then [F6]–[F7] and local bootstrapping; this also identifies continuous representatives up to the boundary. These representatives realize the order pointwise.

The monotone iterates have a bounded pointwise limit $v_R$ on the finite disk. If $C\ge\sup_{D_R}(\psi_R-v_0)^2$, then $0\le C-(v_R-v_k)^2\uparrow C$. Applying [F13] and subtracting the finite integral of C gives $\int_{D_R}(v_R-v_k)^2\to0$, so $v_k\to v_R$ in $L^2(D_R)$. For functions $v,w$ with $v_0\le v,w\le\psi_R$, the pointwise mean-value formula gives $|e^v-e^w|\le e^{\psi_R}|v-w|$; hence $\|G_R(v)-G_R(w)\|_2\le(L_R+\kappa\|A_R\|_\infty e^{\max\psi_R})\|v-w\|_2$. Subtract the two resolvent equations for $T_Rv,T_Rw$ and test with $u=T_Rv-T_Rw$. The form in step 1.3 satisfies $a(u,u)\ge\min\{1,L_R\}\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, while [F11] and [F12] bound the right side by $\|G_R(v)-G_R(w)\|_2\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}$; division when $u\ne0$ (and trivially when $u=0$) gives $\|T_Rv-T_Rw\|_{W^{1,2}}\le\min\{1,L_R\}^{-1}\|G_R(v)-G_R(w)\|_2$. Therefore $T_Rv_k\to T_Rv_R$ in $H^1_0$; the shifted sequence $v_{k+1}=T_Rv_k$ has the same $L^2$ limit as $v_k$, so uniqueness of an $L^2$ limit gives $v_R=T_Rv_R$. It is a weak solution of $-\Delta v_R=\kappa(1-A_Re^{v_R})$ with zero trace.

Since $v_0\le v_R\le\psi_R$ and $A_R$ is bounded on $\overline D_R$, the right-hand side in step 4.1 lies in $L^p(D_R)$ for every finite $p$. For a prescribed $0<\alpha<1$, choose $p>2/(1-\alpha)$. The disk is bounded and smooth, so [F5] gives $v_R\in W^{2,p}$; [F6] gives a $C^{1,\beta}$ representative with $\beta>\alpha$ and zero boundary values. The nonlinear right-hand side is then $C^{0,\alpha}$, and [F7] upgrades the weak solution to $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline D_R)$. Repeated local Schauder bootstrapping, using [F9], makes $v_R$ smooth in $D_R$. Setting $u_R=u_{s,R}+v_R$ proves its distributional equation and logarithmic center behavior.

If $u_R$ were positive somewhere, its boundary value is zero and it tends to $-\infty$ at each center, so it would attain a positive interior maximum away from the centers. There $\Delta u_R=\kappa(e^{u_R}-1)>0$ by its equation, contradicting the second-derivative test at a maximum. Thus $u_R\le0$; together with step 2.1 this gives $u_-\le u_R\le0$.

Fix a disk $U=B_S(0)$ containing the centers in its interior and let $s=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$. For every sufficiently large $R$, $w_R=u_R-s$ is smooth on $\overline U$. On $\partial U$, steps 1.1 and 6.1 give the uniform bounds $u_--s\le w_R\le-s$, whose endpoints are finite there. On $U$, $\Delta w_R=\kappa(e^s e^{w_R}-1)=\kappa(e^{u_R}-1)\in[-\kappa,0]$. A quadratic barrier $Q(z)=M+\kappa(S^2-|z|^2)/4$, with $M$ larger than the uniform boundary bound, satisfies $\Delta(w_R-Q)\ge0$ and $\Delta(-w_R-Q)\ge0$, and both differences are nonpositive on $\partial U$; the disk maximum principle [F4], with zero lower-order coefficient, yields $|w_R|\le Q$.

On any smaller compact disk $K\Subset U$, [F8] applied on finitely many nested balls and the uniform $L^\infty$ bound of step 7.1 yields uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for $w_R$ for every finite $p>2$, since its Laplacian is bounded. For a prescribed $0<\alpha<1$, choose $p>2/(1-\alpha)$ and then $\beta$ with $\alpha<\beta<1-2/p$; [F6] gives a uniform $C^{1,\beta}$ bound on a slightly larger compact disk. As $e^s$ is smooth and $\Delta w_R=\kappa(e^s e^{w_R}-1)$, the right-hand side has a uniform $C^{0,\alpha}$ bound there; [F9] then yields a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $K$. These bounds are independent of $R$ and are the local compactness estimates used for disk exhaustion.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 handles N=0 and step 6.1 establishes the nonpositive empty-divisor disk solution.
The Statement requires kappa>0; step 1.1 treats N=0 separately.
Step 1.1 gives the degree-one threshold a>=4/kappa.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 allow positive multiplicities and combine repeated centers through the divisor data.
Steps 1.2 and 5.1 give zero outer trace and smooth center subtraction.
Steps 1.3 and 5.1 invoke the AC-based Hilbert, resolver and elliptic suppliers.
