citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Let $\kappa>0$ and let $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$ be a finite effective divisor in $\mathbb C$, where the centers $z_j$ are distinct and $m_j\in\mathbb N$; write $N=\sum_jm_j$. For any $a>0$ with $a\ge4N/\kappa$, the function
$$u_-(z)=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\log\frac{|z-z_j|^2}{|z-z_j|^2+a}$$
is a global distributional subsolution of $\Delta u+\kappa(1-e^u)=4\pi\sum_jm_j\delta_{z_j}$. For every $R>\max_j|z_j|$ (with the empty maximum interpreted as $0$), let $D_R=\{|z|<R\}$ and define
$$u_{s,R}(z)=\sum_jm_j\log\frac{R^2|z-z_j|^2}{|R^2-\overline z_jz|^2},\qquad \psi_R(z)=\frac{\kappa}{4}(R^2-|z|^2),\qquad A_R=e^{u_{s,R}}.$$
Then $u_{s,R}$ is the zero-boundary Dirichlet Green sum with $\Delta u_{s,R}=4\pi\sum_jm_j\delta_{z_j}$; $u_{s,R}+\psi_R$ is a supersolution and $u_-\le u_{s,R}+\psi_R$ on $D_R$. Write $H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ for the closure of $C_c^\infty(D_R;\mathbb R)$ in the real Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(D_R;\mathbb R)$. For any constant $L_R\ge\kappa\max_{\overline D_R}(A_Re^{\psi_R})$, the positive zero-Dirichlet resolver $(-\Delta+L_R)^{-1}$ on $H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ defines the monotone iteration
$$v_0=u_--u_{s,R},\qquad v_{k+1}=(-\Delta+L_R)^{-1}\bigl(\kappa+L_Rv_k-\kappa A_Re^{v_k}\bigr).$$
It converges pointwise and in $H^1(D_R)$ to a solution $v_R\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline D_R)$ for every $0<\alpha<1$, with $v_0\le v_R\le\psi_R$ and zero boundary trace. Thus $u_R=u_{s,R}+v_R$ solves the distributional divisor equation, satisfies $u_-\le u_R\le0$, and has $u_R-2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$ smooth at the centers. For the fixed singular function $s(z)=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$, every compact $K\subset\mathbb C$ and every $p>2$ admit constants independent of sufficiently large $R$ such that $u_R-s$ is uniformly bounded in $W^{2,p}(K)$. For each $0<\alpha<1$, choosing $p>2/(1-\alpha)$ also gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}(K)$ bound. These are the local compactness estimates for disk exhaustion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, continuous principal coefficients on the closed ball, and $\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty\le M$. Then every $u\in W^{2,p}(B_R(x_0))$ with $Lu=f\in L^p$ satisfies the scale-invariant estimate
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2}R^{j-2}\max_{|\beta|=j}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p(B_{R/2}(x_0))}\le C\bigl(R^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}+\|f\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\bigr),$$
where $D^0u=u$ and the maximum runs over multi-indices of order $j$,
where $C$ may depend on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,R\|b\|_\infty,R^2\|c\|_\infty$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$ on the ball. A radius-independent constant requires uniform control of these dimensionless lower-order bounds and of the modulus. The theorem assumes continuity of $A$; no estimate for merely measurable principal coefficients is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice through the Poincare and Sobolev suppliers below. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, and let $L$, $a$ and the real coefficient functions $a^{ij},b^i,c$ be as in [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]], with ellipticity constant $\theta$ and bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$. Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $u\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be a real local weak subsolution of $Lu=f$. Suppose the weak sign condition
$$\int_\Omega\bigl(c\,\zeta+b^iD_i\zeta\bigr)dx\ge0\qquad\text{for every }\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega),\ \zeta\ge0,$$
holds, and assume $c\ge0$ a.e. on $\Omega$. Then:

1. **Homogeneous case.** If $f=0$ a.e., then
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^+,$$
with the boundary supremum of [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]]. If in addition $b\equiv0$, $c\equiv0$, and $u$ is a weak solution of $Lu=0$, then $\operatorname{ess\,sup}_\Omega u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u$.

2. **Forcing with signed lower order.** If $b\equiv0$, $c\ge0$ a.e. and $f\in L^q(\Omega)$ for some $q>n/2$ ($q>1$ when $n=2$), then the local inequality extends to all nonnegative $H^1_0(\Omega)$ tests and
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^++C\|f^+\|_{L^q(\Omega)},\qquad C=C(n,q,\theta,M_a,M_c,\Omega),$$
where $\Omega$ enters $C$ only through its Poincare constant and volume.

If $u$ is a weak supersolution of $Lu=f$ under either set of hypotheses, apply the corresponding bound to $-u$ for the **same** operator coefficients $(a,b,c)$ and source $-f$. This gives $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^-$ in the homogeneous case and $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^- -C\|f^-\|_{L^q(\Omega)}$ in the forcing case. The maximum-principle conclusions concern real-valued classes and real coefficients.

Assume countable choice for the mean-inequality input. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a domain, and let $u\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfy $\Delta u\ge0$. If there is $a\in\Omega$ with $u(x)\le u(a)$ for every $x\in\Omega$, then $u$ is constant.

derivations.claim: Choose radii $R_k\to\infty$ with every center in $D_{R_k}$. Let $s=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$ and $w_k=u_{R_k}-s$. For each compact disk $K$ and each $0<\alpha<1$, [F2] gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $w_k$ on a slightly larger disk. Thus $(w_k,Dw_k,D^2w_k)$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous there. Apply the Euclidean sequence statement [F6] to the finite derivative tuple on each nonempty compact disk. A countable diagonal selection under [A1] then gives locally uniform convergence of $w_k$ and all its derivatives through order two. The fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments identifies the limiting derivative tuple as the first and second derivatives of one $C^2$ function w. Thus the subsequence converges in $C^2$ on every compact disk. Set $h=s+w$.

On every compact set, $e^{u_{R_k}}=e^s e^{w_k}$ converges uniformly to $e^h$. Passing to the limit in the weak divisor equation for $u_{R_k}$ gives $\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi D$ distributionally. Since $s-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ is smooth near each center and $w$ is $C^2$ there, the prescribed logarithmic subtraction extends continuously. The equation for $w$ is $\Delta w=\kappa(e^s e^w-1)$ with smooth coefficient $e^s=|P|^2$; repeated interior Schauder regularity [F4] bootstraps $w$ to $C^\infty$, so each center subtraction is smooth. The bounds $u_-\le u_{R_k}\le0$ pass to the limit, and $u_-(z)\to0$ at infinity; hence $h\le0$ and $h\to0$.

If $h_1,h_2$ are two solutions with the same divisor and boundary condition, $v=h_1-h_2$ extends smoothly across the centers. Subtracting their equations gives $\Delta v-c(z)v=0$, where $c(z)=\kappa\int_0^1 e^{(1-t)h_2+th_1}\,dt\ge0$, extended continuously by $0$ at the centers. On $D_R$, the weak maximum principle [F7] applied to $v$ and $-v$ bounds $|v|$ by $\sup_{\partial D_R}|v|$. This boundary supremum tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$, so $v=0$ and the scalar solution is unique. When $D$ is empty, $h=0$ is a solution and the same uniqueness argument shows it is the only one.

Suppose $N>0$ and put $w=-h\ge0$. Away from the divisor, $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})\le\kappa w$. On $\Omega=(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{z_j\})\times(-\pi/(2\sqrt\kappa),\pi/(2\sqrt\kappa))$, define $U(z,t)=-w(z)\cos(\sqrt\kappa t)$. Then $U\le0$ and $\Delta_{z,t}U=\cos(\sqrt\kappa t)(\kappa w-\Delta w)\ge0$. The finite-punctured plane is path connected (polygonal paths can detour around finitely many points), hence $\Omega$ is connected. If $w$ vanished at a point, $U$ would attain its maximum $0$ in $\Omega$; [F8] would force $U\equiv0$, so $w\equiv0$ off the divisor, contradicting $w(z)\to+\infty$ at each positive-multiplicity center. Thus $h<0$ away from the divisor.

Fix $0<\alpha<\sqrt\kappa$. Since $w=-h\to0$, choose $c$ with $\alpha^2<c<\kappa$ and $R_0$ so large that $\kappa(1-e^{-w})\ge c w$ for $|z|\ge R_0$. Let $\varphi(z)=C e^{-\alpha(|z|-R_0)}$ with $C\ge\sup_{|z|=R_0}w$. For $r=|z|\ge R_0$, $\Delta\varphi=(\alpha^2-\alpha/r)\varphi<c\varphi$, so $(\Delta-c)(w-\varphi)\ge0$. The function $w-\varphi$ is nonpositive on $|z|=R_0$ and tends to $0$ at infinity. If it were positive somewhere, its positive maximum would be attained at a finite interior point, where $(\Delta-c)(w-\varphi)<0$, a contradiction. Therefore $0\le w\le\varphi$, proving the claimed scalar exponential bound.

Let $P(z)=\prod_j(z-z_j)^{m_j}$ and $s=2\log|P|$. The factor $h-s$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb C$. Define $q=\sqrt\xi e^{(h-s)/2}P$ and $A=-\frac12*d(h-s)$; both extend smoothly over the centers and $q$ has exactly the prescribed zeros. On the punctured plane write $P=|P|e^{i\chi}$; holomorphicity gives $d\chi=\frac12*ds$, hence $A=d\chi-\frac12*dh$. Writing $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}e^{i\chi}$ and using $*dh=( -\partial_2h)dx_1+(\partial_1h)dx_2$ gives $D_{A,1}q=\frac12e^{i\chi}\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}(\partial_1h-i\partial_2h)$ and $D_{A,2}q=\frac12e^{i\chi}\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}(\partial_2h+i\partial_1h)$, so $D_{A,1}q+iD_{A,2}q=0$.

To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

The curvature is $dA=-\frac12\Delta(h-s)\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$. Since $\Delta s=4\pi D$ and $h$ satisfies the divisor equation, $\Delta(h-s)=-\kappa(1-e^h)$; therefore $B=\frac\kappa2(1-e^h)=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. On the exterior of a disk, $e^{-i\chi}$ is a smooth local gauge, not asserted to extend across the zeros; it gives $q_{\mathrm{ext}}=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A_{\mathrm{ext}}=-\frac12*dh$. The phase satisfies $\chi=N\theta+O(r^{-1})$ because $P(z)=z^N\prod_j(1-z_j/z)^{m_j}$. Thus the gauge-invariant $B,D_Aq$ decay exponentially by step 4.1, while no exponential decay of the raw phase correction is claimed.

The reconstructed fields are smooth on compact sets. In the exterior gauge of step 5.1, $B$, $D_Aq$, and $|q|^2-\xi=\xi(e^h-1)$ all decay exponentially, so each squared term in the defining energy is integrable on $\mathbb R^2$; hence the energy is finite. To compute flux, write $v=h-s$, so $\Delta v=-\kappa(1-e^h)$. Since $v$ is smooth at the origin, polar coordinates and the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus give
$$\int_{D_R}\Delta v\,dx_1dx_2=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R\partial_r(r\partial_rv)\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}R\partial_rv(R,\theta)\,d\theta,$$
as $r\partial_rv\to0$ at $r=0$. By step 4.1, $\partial_rh$ decays exponentially; from $s=2N\log r+O(r^{-1})$, $\partial_rs=2N/R+O(R^{-2})$ uniformly in $\theta$. Therefore the boundary integral tends to $-4\pi N$, so $\kappa\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1-e^h)=4\pi N$. Using $B=\frac\kappa2(1-e^h)$ gives flux $2\pi N$. For the empty divisor $h=0$, the reconstruction is the flat constant vacuum and has zero flux.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $e>0$, $\xi>0$, $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, and an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$ on $\mathbb C$ with distinct centers and positive integer multiplicities; let $N=\sum_jm_j$. There is a unique real scalar function $h$, smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus\{z_j\}$, such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across each center, $h\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$, and
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j}$$
in distributions, where $\langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)$ for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$. For $N>0$, $h<0$ off the divisor; for the empty divisor, $h=0$. With $P(z)=\prod_j(z-z_j)^{m_j}$, $s=2\log|P|$, and the orientation $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$, the fields
$$q(z)=\sqrt\xi\,e^{(h(z)-s(z))/2}P(z),\qquad A=-\tfrac12 *d(h-s)$$
extend smoothly across the centers and solve $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$, where $D_A=d-iA$ and $B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2=dA$. They have finite energy
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2$$
and flux $\int_{\mathbb R^2}B\,dx_1dx_2=2\pi N$. For every $0<\alpha<\sqrt\kappa$ and every multi-index $\beta$, $|\partial^\beta h(z)|=O(e^{-\alpha|z|})$ as $|z|\to\infty$; the curvature $B$ and covariant gradient $D_Aq$ have the same exponential decay. On the exterior of a disk, the local gauge $e^{-i\arg P}$ gives $q_{\mathrm{ext}}=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A_{\mathrm{ext}}=-\tfrac12 *dh$, so the fields approach the vacuum exponentially in that exterior gauge; the raw global representative $q$ need not have an exponentially small phase correction. Negative winding $-N$ is obtained by complex conjugation and $A\mapsto-A$, with flux $-2\pi N$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim:
Define the real current one-form $j=j_1dx_1+j_2dx_2$ by $j_i=\operatorname{Im}(\overline qD_{A,i}q)$. Expanding the squares and using $[D_{A,1},D_{A,2}]q=-iBq$ gives
$$|D_Aq|^2=|(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q|^2+\partial_1j_2-\partial_2j_1+B|q|^2.$$
Also, direct expansion gives
$$\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+\frac{e^2}{2}(\xi-|q|^2)^2=\frac{(B-e^2(\xi-|q|^2))^2}{2e^2}+B(\xi-|q|^2).$$
Adding these identities yields the positive-winding disk identity with boundary term $\int_{D_R}(\partial_1j_2-\partial_2j_1)$. Repeating the expansion with $D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2}$ and $B+e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$ gives the negative-winding identity with the opposite signs.

For almost every $r$ larger than the nonzero-field radius, let $Q(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}(|q|^2-\xi)^2ds$ and $K(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}|D_{A,\tau}q|^2ds$, where $D_{A,\tau}$ is the covariant derivative in the unit tangent direction. The potential and kinetic terms of the finite energy, with polar coordinates and [F4], imply $Q,K\in L^1([R_0,\infty))$. For each integer $m\ge1$, the set $S_m=\{r\ge R_0:Q(r)>1/m\}$ has finite measure. Its complement has divergent $\int dr/r$, since removing a finite-measure set from a half-line cannot make the logarithmic integral finite. If $rK(r)\ge1/m$ for every sufficiently large $r\notin S_m$, then $\int K(r)dr\ge m^{-1}\int_{[R,\infty)\setminus S_m}dr/r=\infty$, contradiction. Thus there is an unbounded set of radii with $Q(r)\le1/m$ and $rK(r)<1/m$. By [A1] select an increasing sequence $r_m\to\infty$ from these sets. Along it, [F6] gives $\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\le2\pi\xi r_m+\sqrt{2\pi r_mQ(r_m)}=O(r_m)$, and
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}j\right|\le\left(\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\right)^{1/2}K(r_m)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$

For sufficiently large $r$, $|q|\ge\sqrt\xi/2$. On $\partial D_r$, $j=|q|^2(d(n\theta+\phi)-A)$, so $\int_{\partial D_r}A=2\pi n-\int_{\partial D_r}j/|q|^2$ because $\phi$ is single-valued and periodic. Along the sequence from step 1.2,
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}\frac{j}{|q|^2}\right|\le\frac{2}{\sqrt\xi}(2\pi r_mK(r_m))^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$
By [F3], $\int_{D_{r_m}}B\to2\pi n$.

Integrate the positive-winding disk identity from step 1.1 over $D_{r_m}$ and use [F3] on the current term. The two square integrals are nonnegative, while the boundary-current integral tends to zero by step 1.2 and the flux integral tends to $2\pi n$ by step 2.1. By [F5], the integrals of the nonnegative energy and square densities over the increasing disks converge to their plane integrals, so taking the limit gives the positive-sign exact identity and hence $E(A,q)\ge2\pi\xi n$ for $n\ge0$. For $n\le0$, apply the positive-sign identity from step 1.1 to $(\overline q,-A)$, whose winding is $-n\ge0$; its energy is unchanged and its curvature changes sign. The resulting identity is exactly the negative-sign identity for $(A,q)$ and gives $E(A,q)\ge-2\pi\xi n$. Thus the bound is $E(A,q)\ge2\pi\xi|n|$, and both identities hold when $n=0$ as well.

For each fixed divisor, [F2] supplies a smooth pair satisfying the relevant first-order equations. Its square terms in step 1.1 vanish identically; the sequence estimates of steps 1.2–2.1 apply because [F2] gives finite energy and the same boundary sector. Hence its energy is exactly $2\pi\xi|n|$. The lower bound of step 3.1 applies to every admissible same-winding configuration, so this pair is an absolute transverse energy minimum, without radial or unit-winding assumptions.

Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $e>0$, $\xi>0$, $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, and an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$ on $\mathbb C$ with distinct centers and positive integer multiplicities; let $N=\sum_jm_j$. There is a unique real scalar function $h$, smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus\{z_j\}$, such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across each center, $h\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$, and
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j}$$
in distributions, where $\langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)$ for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$. For $N>0$, $h<0$ off the divisor; for the empty divisor, $h=0$. With $P(z)=\prod_j(z-z_j)^{m_j}$, $s=2\log|P|$, and the orientation $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$, the fields
$$q(z)=\sqrt\xi\,e^{(h(z)-s(z))/2}P(z),\qquad A=-\tfrac12 *d(h-s)$$
extend smoothly across the centers and solve $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$, where $D_A=d-iA$ and $B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2=dA$. They have finite energy
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2$$
and flux $\int_{\mathbb R^2}B\,dx_1dx_2=2\pi N$. For every $0<\alpha<\sqrt\kappa$ and every multi-index $\beta$, $|\partial^\beta h(z)|=O(e^{-\alpha|z|})$ as $|z|\to\infty$; the curvature $B$ and covariant gradient $D_Aq$ have the same exponential decay. On the exterior of a disk, the local gauge $e^{-i\arg P}$ gives $q_{\mathrm{ext}}=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A_{\mathrm{ext}}=-\tfrac12 *dh$, so the fields approach the vacuum exponentially in that exterior gauge; the raw global representative $q$ need not have an exponentially small phase correction. Negative winding $-N$ is obtained by complex conjugation and $A\mapsto-A$, with flux $-2\pi N$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ and use the critical Abelian-Higgs energy and boundary-sector convention in which $D_A=d-iA$, $B=dA$, $q$ tends in modulus to $\sqrt\xi$, and its exterior phase has winding $n\in\mathbb Z$. For every smooth finite-energy field pair $(A,q)$ in that sector,
$$E(A,q)\ge 2\pi\xi|n|.$$
For $n\ge0$, the exact identity is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{(B-e^2(\xi-|q|^2))^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2+2\pi\xi n;$$
for $n\le0$, replace $D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2}$ by $D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2}$ and $B-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$ by $B+e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$, with topological term $-2\pi\xi n$. The boundary-current term in the disk identity vanishes along a radius sequence derived from the finite-energy hypotheses. The fields reconstructed for any fixed divisor by the arbitrary-divisor plane theorem attain equality, are absolute transverse energy minima in their winding sector, have zero first variation under smooth compactly supported variations, and have nonnegative second variation in those directions. This does not assert uniqueness of minimizing fields across distinct divisors of the same degree.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

derivations.claim: Decompose the integrand into the transverse density $e_\perp(x,z)$, containing $F_{12}$, $D_1q,D_2q$ and the potential, and the nonnegative longitudinal density $e_\parallel(x,z)$, containing $F_{31},F_{32},D_3q$. Since the total density is nonnegative and integrable, [F4] gives $\mathcal E_L=\int_0^L E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)\,dz+\int_{\Omega_L}e_\parallel\,dx\,dz$, where $\mathbf A_\perp=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ and $E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e_\perp(x,z)dx$ for almost every $z$. The slice hypotheses and [F3] give $E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)\ge T_n$ for each slice, while the longitudinal integral is nonnegative; hence $\mathcal E_L\ge T_nL$.

For finite $R$, apply [F5] to $D_R\times\{z\}$ to identify its magnetic flux with $\int_{\partial D_R}A_\perp(\cdot,z)$. Apply [F5] to the side $\partial D_R\times[0,L]$: its flux is the difference of the two oriented end-circle integrals. The uniform angular one-form condition makes both integrals $2\pi n+o(1)$, so the side flux tends to zero. Thus the stated angular condition enforces the required no-leakage condition and is consistent with the fixed slice flux.

For an end trace with exterior phase $n\theta+\phi$, choose a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ which is zero on a disk containing the noncanonical region and one outside a larger disk. The real function $\chi=-\eta\phi$ extends smoothly by zero to the whole plane; the allowed gauge transformation $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ therefore makes the exterior phase exactly $n\theta$. This constructs the asserted degree-zero exterior phase cleanup without attempting to extend a degree-$n$ angular map across the disk. For the planar minimizer in [F2], write $P=|P|e^{i\vartheta}$ on the exterior; $\vartheta-n\theta$ is single-valued, smooth and tends to zero because $P(z)=z^n(1+O(|z|^{-1}))$ for $n\ge0$ (use the conjugate construction for $n<0$). Applying the same cutoff extension to $-(\vartheta-n\theta)$ changes its exterior fields to $q^*=\rho_*e^{in\theta}$ and $A^*=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$; hence $A^*-n\,d\theta$ decays exponentially.

In canonical exterior gauge write $q=\rho e^{in\theta}$ and $\alpha=A-n\,d\theta$. Directly, $D_Aq=e^{in\theta}(d\rho-i\rho\alpha)$, so the real and imaginary terms are orthogonal and $|D_Aq|^2=|d\rho|^2+\rho^2|\alpha|^2$. Uniform convergence gives $\rho\ge\sqrt\xi/2$ outside a disk; thus finite kinetic energy implies $\alpha\in L^2$ there. Also $|\rho-\sqrt\xi|\le |\rho^2-\xi|/\sqrt\xi$, so finite potential energy gives $\rho-\sqrt\xi\in L^2$ there. On compact disks all fields are smooth and bounded. Consequently, for any two cleaned end traces and the cleaned minimizer, differences of connections and Higgs fields are globally in $L^2$; each Higgs field is bounded.

For any two such canonical profiles $p_a=(A^a,q^a)$ and $p_b=(A^b,q^b)$, put $A_t=(1-t)A^a+tA^b$, $q_t=(1-t)q^a+tq^b$, $0\le t\le1$, and $\delta A=A^b-A^a$, $\delta q=q^b-q^a$. The curvature is $B_t=(1-t)B_a+tB_b\in L^2$, so linearity of the flux integral gives flux $2\pi n$ for every blend because both endpoint fluxes equal $2\pi n$. On the exterior, $q_t=e^{in\theta}\rho_t$ with $\rho_t=(1-t)\rho_a+t\rho_b$; the uniform bounds and $\rho_t-\sqrt\xi\in L^2$ imply $|q_t|^2-\xi\in L^2$. Expanding the covariant derivative gives
$$D_{A_t}q_t=(1-t)D_{A^a}q^a+tD_{A^b}q^b+i\,t(1-t)\delta A\,\delta q.$$
The first two terms are in $L^2$ by finite end energy, and the last is in $L^2$ because $\delta A\in L^2$ and $\delta q$ is bounded. Thus every transverse energy term of the blend is integrable, with a bound uniform for $t\in[0,1]$. Its exterior phase, vacuum limit and angular one-form limit are preserved by convexity and linearity.

Fix $\ell>0$ and a smooth function $\sigma:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ which is zero near $0$ and one near $1$. On a collar of width $\ell$, set $t(z)=\sigma(z/\ell)$, $A_1,A_2=A_{t(z)}$, $q=q_{t(z)}$, and $A_3=0$. Then $D_3q=(\sigma'(z/\ell)/\ell)\delta q$ and $F_{3i}=(\sigma'(z/\ell)/\ell)\delta A_i$. Their squared integrals are finite by [F1] and step 1.4. Step 2.1 bounds the transverse density uniformly in $z$, so the complete collar energy is a finite constant depending only on its two profiles, $\ell$, and $\sigma$. Since $\sigma$ is constant near each end, this collar joins smoothly to constant-in-$z$ profiles. The angular limit is the convex combination of the endpoint limits; its side flux tends to zero by step 1.2.

Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. For $L\ge2\ell$, place the first collar on $[0,\ell]$, the constant planar minimizer on $[\ell,L-\ell]$, and the second collar on $[L-\ell,L]$. The profiles match smoothly because the collar cutoff is constant near its ends. The middle has no longitudinal energy and contributes exactly $T_n(L-2\ell)$ by [F2]–[F3]. At $L=2\ell$ this middle interval has zero length; the two collars meet at the constant value $p_*$, so the same upper bound holds. This admissible concatenation proves $\inf\mathcal E_L\le C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$.

Combining steps 1.1 and 4.1 gives $0\le\inf\mathcal E_L-T_nL\le C_0+C_1-2\ell T_n$ for every $L\ge2\ell$; the right side is a finite constant independent of $L$, proving the bounded-remainder conclusion. If $p_0=p_1=p_*$, the constant extension $(A_1,A_2,q)=(A^*,q^*)$, $A_3=0$, has energy $T_nL$ and satisfies the angular and no-leakage conditions. The lower bound from step 1.1 then proves it is an exact translation-invariant minimum.

For an open $V\subseteq X$, a finite integer $p\ge0$, and an $\mathcal O_X$-module morphism $\phi:\mathcal O_V^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal F|_V$, its **relation sheaf** is the kernel sheaf $\ker\phi$. The module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **coherent** if it is locally of finite type and, for every such $V$, $p$, and $\phi$, the relation sheaf $\ker\phi$ is locally of finite type. Here $\mathcal O_V^{\oplus0}$ is the zero module sheaf.

In particular, for a finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_p\in\mathcal O_X(U)$, its holomorphic relation sheaf is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_U^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal O_U$ that sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_p)$ to $\sum_{j=1}^p a_jf_j$. The structure sheaf is coherent when it is coherent as a module over itself. If $M$ is a complex manifold, an **analytic coherent module on $M$** means a coherent module sheaf over its sheaf $\mathcal O_M$ of holomorphic functions.

groups on a topological space $X$.

$$
\ker(\varphi)\subseteq \mathcal F
$$
defined objectwise by
$$
\ker(\varphi)(U):=\ker\!\bigl(\varphi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\bigr).
$$

$$
U\longmapsto \operatorname{coker}\!\bigl(\varphi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\bigr),
$$

sheafification.

corresponding module categories on each open set.

Fix $m\ge1$, write $z=(z',z_m)$ with $z'\in\mathbb C^{m-1}$, and let
$d\in\mathbb N$. A **Weierstrass polynomial of degree $d$** is a germ in
$\mathcal O_{m,0}$ represented by

$$W(z',z_m)=z_m^d+a_{d-1}(z')z_m^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0(z'),$$

where each $a_j$ is an element of $\mathcal O_{m-1,0}$, so for $m=1$ the
coefficients are complex constants, and $a_j(0)=0$.

For $d=0$ the lower-coefficient list and sum are empty, so the unique
degree-$0$ Weierstrass polynomial is $W=1$.

In particular $W(0,z_m)=z_m^d$, so every Weierstrass polynomial of degree $d$
is regular in $z_m$ of order $d$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-holomorphic-germ]].

Let $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ be regular in $z_m$ of order $d$. Then there are a
unit $u\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ and a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ of degree $d$ such
that

$$f=uW.$$

Let $W$ be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $d$ in the variable $z_m$. Then
for every $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ there exist unique germs
$q\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ and $r_0,\dots,r_{d-1}\in\mathcal O_{m-1,0}$, meaning

$$f=qW+r_0+r_1z_m+\cdots+r_{d-1}z_m^{d-1}.$$

Equivalently, every germ has a unique quotient and a unique remainder of
$z_m$-degree $<d$ upon division by $W$.

be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

derivations.claim: If $q=1$, a relation germ $g$ satisfies $gP_1=0$ by [F1]. The polynomial $P_1$ is nonzero by [F2], and [F5] makes the ring of holomorphic germs an integral domain, so $g=0$, which is already a polynomial relation of bounded degree.

Suppose $q\ge2$. If $P_q(x)\ne0$, then $P_q$ is a unit germ. For every relation $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_q)$, [F1] gives $g_q=-\sum_{j<q}g_jP_j/P_q$, hence $g=\sum_{j<q}(g_j/P_q)(P_qe_j-P_je_q)$. Each vector $P_qe_j-P_je_q$ is a relation whose component degrees are at most $d$.

Suppose $P_q(x)=0$, and set $e=\deg_wP_q\le d$. Let $r\ge1$ be its order of vanishing in $w-w_0$; this is finite and at most $e\le d$ by [F2, F6]. By [F3], after shrinking near $x$ write $P_q=u p$, where $u$ is a holomorphic unit and $p$ is a monic Weierstrass polynomial of degree $r$ in $w-w_0$. Ordinary polynomial division of $P_q$ by the monic polynomial $p$ gives a polynomial quotient and a remainder of degree below $r$. The division pair $(u,0)$ also represents $P_q$ as a holomorphic germ divided by $p$; uniqueness in [F4] makes the polynomial remainder zero and identifies the polynomial quotient with $u$. Since $P_q$ and $p$ are monic of degrees $e$ and $r$, respectively, this polynomial $u$ has degree $e-r\le d-r$ and remains a unit near $x$.

Let $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_q)$ be a relation germ at $x$. For $j<q$, divide by $p$ using [F4] to write $g_j=t_jp+r_j$, where $t_j$ is holomorphic and $r_j$ is a polynomial in $w-w_0$ of degree below $r$. Set $\alpha_j=t_j/u$ and $v_j=P_qe_j-P_je_q$. Then $\delta=g-\sum_{j<q}\alpha_jv_j$ is a relation whose first $q-1$ components are $r_j$. Its last component satisfies $p(u\delta_q)=-\sum_{j<q}r_jP_j$, whose right-hand side is a polynomial of degree at most $d+r-1$. Dividing this polynomial by $p$ and using uniqueness [F4] shows that $u\delta_q$ is a polynomial of degree at most $d-1$. Each $ur_j$ also has degree at most $d-1$, since $\deg u=e-r\le d-r$ and $\deg r_j<r$. Thus $u\delta$ is a polynomial relation with all component degrees at most $d$, and $g=\sum_{j<q}\alpha_jv_j+u^{-1}(u\delta)$ is generated by polynomial relation germs of the required bound.

Local finite type gives, after choosing a neighborhood $U$ of $x$, a finite-rank free module sheaf map $\pi:\mathcal O_U^{\oplus k}\to\mathcal F|_U$ that is surjective on every stalk. By [F1], its kernel is locally of finite type; after shrinking to $V\subseteq U$, choose finitely many sections generating that kernel on $V$ and let $\rho:\mathcal O_V^{\oplus m}\to\mathcal O_V^{\oplus k}$ be the corresponding map. The sequence $\mathcal O_V^{\oplus m}\xrightarrow{\rho}\mathcal O_V^{\oplus k}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathcal F|_V\to0$ is exact by [F2], [F3], and [F4]. Thus every coherent module has a local finite presentation.

Let $f:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ be a morphism of coherent modules and set $\mathcal K=\ker f$. Choose locally a finite-rank free epimorphism $\pi:\mathcal O^{\oplus k}\to\mathcal F$. The composite $f\pi:\mathcal O^{\oplus k}\to\mathcal G$ has a locally finite-type kernel by [F1]; its image under $\pi$ is exactly $\mathcal K$ on each stalk, since $\pi$ is stalkwise surjective. Hence $\mathcal K$ is locally of finite type by [F4]. For every finite-rank map $\eta:\mathcal O^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal K$, its composite with the inclusion $\mathcal K\hookrightarrow\mathcal F$ has the same kernel; [F1] for $\mathcal F$ makes that kernel locally of finite type. Thus $\mathcal K$ is coherent.

Let $\mathcal C=\operatorname{coker}f$. It is locally of finite type because it is a quotient of the locally finite-type module $\mathcal G$. To check its relation condition, fix a finite-rank map $\gamma:\mathcal O^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal C$ and a point $x$. Since $\mathcal G\to\mathcal C$ is a sheaf epimorphism, choose local lifts of the finitely many images of the standard basis near $x$; they define $\widetilde\gamma:\mathcal O^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal G$ lifting $\gamma$. Also choose a local finite-rank epimorphism $\delta:\mathcal O^{\oplus m}\to\mathcal F$. Define $\epsilon:\mathcal O^{\oplus(m+p)}\to\mathcal G$ by $\epsilon(a,b)=f(\delta(a))+\widetilde\gamma(b)$. By [F1], $\ker\epsilon$ is locally of finite type. Projection of $\ker\epsilon$ to the second factor has image exactly $\ker\gamma$ on every stalk: an element of $\ker\epsilon$ maps to zero in $\mathcal C$, and any stalk element $b\in\ker\gamma$ has $\widetilde\gamma(b)\in\operatorname{im}f$, so a stalk preimage under $\delta$ completes it to an element of $\ker\epsilon$. The image of a locally finite-type module is locally finite type, so $\ker\gamma$ is locally of finite type. This holds for every $\gamma$, hence $\mathcal C$ is coherent.

Consider a short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{i}\mathcal E\xrightarrow{p}\mathcal F''\to0$. If $\mathcal E$ and $\mathcal F''$ are coherent, then $\mathcal F'=\ker p$ is coherent by step 2.1. If $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal E$ are coherent, then $\mathcal F''=\operatorname{coker}i$ is coherent by step 2.2.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, so $X$ is a topological space and $\mathcal O_X$ is a sheaf of commutative rings. An $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **locally of finite type** if for every $x\in X$ there are an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, a finite integer $r\ge0$, and sections $s_1,\ldots,s_r\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that their germs generate $\mathcal F_y$ as an $\mathcal O_{X,y}$-module for every $y\in U$.

For an open $V\subseteq X$, a finite integer $p\ge0$, and an $\mathcal O_X$-module morphism $\phi:\mathcal O_V^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal F|_V$, its **relation sheaf** is the kernel sheaf $\ker\phi$. The module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **coherent** if it is locally of finite type and, for every such $V$, $p$, and $\phi$, the relation sheaf $\ker\phi$ is locally of finite type. Here $\mathcal O_V^{\oplus0}$ is the zero module sheaf.

In particular, for a finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_p\in\mathcal O_X(U)$, its holomorphic relation sheaf is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_U^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal O_U$ that sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_p)$ to $\sum_{j=1}^p a_jf_j$. The structure sheaf is coherent when it is coherent as a module over itself. If $M$ is a complex manifold, an **analytic coherent module on $M$** means a coherent module sheaf over its sheaf $\mathcal O_M$ of holomorphic functions.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$, and let $x\in X$.

The **neighbourhood category of $x$** is the full subcategory
$$\mathcal N_x\subseteq \operatorname{Open}(X)$$
whose objects are the open neighbourhoods of $x$. Its opposite category is
filtered in the sense of
[[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]]: it is nonempty because $X$
itself is a neighbourhood of $x$, and for neighbourhoods $U,V$ the
intersection $U\cap V$ is again a neighbourhood of $x$ with arrows
$$U\longrightarrow U\cap V,\qquad V\longrightarrow U\cap V$$
in the opposite category.

Because $\mathcal F$ is contravariant, its restriction to the neighbourhood
category determines a covariant diagram on that opposite category. The
**stalk** of $\mathcal F$ at $x$ is the filtered colimit
$$\mathcal F_x:=\varinjlim_{\mathcal N_x^{\operatorname{op}}}\mathcal F(U).$$

Concretely, $\mathcal F_x$ may be described as equivalence classes of pairs
$(U,s)$ with $U$ an open neighbourhood of $x$ and
$s\in\mathcal F(U)$, where $(U,s)\sim(V,t)$ when $s$ and $t$ agree on some
smaller open neighbourhood of $x$. The next lemma verifies that this is an
equivalence relation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a ringed space whose structure sheaf $\mathcal A$ is coherent in the sense that every finite tuple of its local sections has a locally finite-type relation sheaf. For all finite integers $p,q\ge0$ and every $\mathcal A$-module morphism $\Phi:\mathcal A^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal A^{\oplus q}$, the kernel sheaf $\ker\Phi$ is locally of finite type.

Let $n,q,d\ge1$ be integers, let $U'\subseteq\mathbb C^{n-1}$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb C$ be polydiscs, let $w$ denote the last coordinate, and let $P_1,\ldots,P_q\in\mathcal O(U')[w]$ be monic Weierstrass polynomials with $1\le\deg_w P_j\le d$. For every $x=(x',w_0)\in U'\times D$, each germ in the relation sheaf of $(P_1,\ldots,P_q)$ at $x$ is an $\mathcal O_{U'\times D,x}$-linear combination of relation germs whose components are polynomials in $w-w_0$ of degree at most $d$ with coefficients in $\mathcal O_{U',x'}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space and use the coherence definition on the A page. The kernel and cokernel of any morphism between coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaves are coherent. In every short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal F'\to\mathcal E\to\mathcal F''\to0$ of $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaves, if any two of $\mathcal F'$, $\mathcal E$, and $\mathcal F''$ are coherent, then the third is coherent.

For every integer $m\ge1$, the holomorphic germ ring $\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is a
Noetherian commutative ring.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $M$ be an $R$-module. The
following are equivalent.

1. $M$ is a Noetherian module ([[def-noetherian-module]]).
2. $M$ is finitely generated
   ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).
3. $M$ is finitely presented ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]).

The proof below shows exactly where the Noetherian hypothesis is used to make
conditions 2 and 3 agree.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ be nonzero. Then there is an
invertible complex-linear map $T:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^m$ and an integer
$d\ge0$ such that the pulled-back germ $f\circ T$ is regular in the last
variable of order $d$.

Fix $m\ge1$, write $z=(z',z_m)$ with
$z'=(z_1,\dots,z_{m-1})\in\mathbb C^{m-1}$, and let $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$.
For $d\in\mathbb N$, the germ $f$ is **regular in $z_m$ of order $d$** if some
representative satisfies

$$f(0,\zeta)=\zeta^d h(\zeta)$$

on a neighbourhood of $0\in\mathbb C$, where $h$ is holomorphic and
$h(0)\ne0$. Equivalently, the one-variable slice $\zeta\mapsto f(0,\zeta)$ has a
zero of exact order $d$ at the origin.

The case $d=0$ is exactly the unit case $f(0)\ne0$.

Let $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ be regular in $z_m$ of order $d$. Then there are a
unit $u\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ and a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ of degree $d$ such
that

$$f=uW.$$

Fix $m\ge1$, write $z=(z',z_m)$ with $z'\in\mathbb C^{m-1}$, and let
$d\in\mathbb N$. A **Weierstrass polynomial of degree $d$** is a germ in
$\mathcal O_{m,0}$ represented by

$$W(z',z_m)=z_m^d+a_{d-1}(z')z_m^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0(z'),$$

where each $a_j$ is an element of $\mathcal O_{m-1,0}$, so for $m=1$ the
coefficients are complex constants, and $a_j(0)=0$.

For $d=0$ the lower-coefficient list and sum are empty, so the unique
degree-$0$ Weierstrass polynomial is $W=1$.

In particular $W(0,z_m)=z_m^d$, so every Weierstrass polynomial of degree $d$
is regular in $z_m$ of order $d$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-holomorphic-germ]].

Let $W$ be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $d$ in the variable $z_m$. Then
for every $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ there exist unique germs
$q\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ and $r_0,\dots,r_{d-1}\in\mathcal O_{m-1,0}$, meaning
complex constants when $m=1$, such that

$$f=qW+r_0+r_1z_m+\cdots+r_{d-1}z_m^{d-1}.$$

Equivalently, every germ has a unique quotient and a unique remainder of
$z_m$-degree $<d$ upon division by $W$.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and let $r$ be a polyradius. Suppose
$c,c':\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ both satisfy a bound
$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$ and
$|c'_\alpha|\le M'\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$, and suppose

$$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha=\sum_\alpha c'_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha \qquad\text{for every }z\in\Delta_r(a).$$

Then $c_\alpha=c'_\alpha$ for every multi-index $\alpha$. In particular a
function has at most one such power-series representation about a given centre,
and its coefficients are $\partial^\alpha_zf(a)/\alpha!$.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

derivations.claim: Work under [A1]. In a holomorphic chart, prove the relation assertion by induction on dimension $n$, and for a fixed $n$ by induction on tuple length $q$. On $\mathbb C^0=\{0\}$ each relation space is a subspace of the finite-dimensional vector space $\mathbb C^q$, so a finite basis gives local generators. For any dimension, the empty tuple has zero relation sheaf.

If some tuple entry has zero germ at the chosen point, [F13] gives a neighborhood on which that entry vanishes identically; its coordinate in a relation is then arbitrary, and the relation sheaf is the direct sum of one copy of $\mathcal O$ with the shorter tuple's relation sheaf. The induction on $q$ gives finite local generators, and repeating this finite reduction removes every zero germ. If some remaining entry, say $f_1$, is nonzero at the point, shrink until $f_1$ is a unit; the sections $e_j-(f_j/f_1)e_1$, $2\le j\le q$, generate the relation sheaf because the relation equation uniquely determines its first coordinate.

It remains to treat a tuple of nonzero germs all vanishing at the point. By [F11], the product $G=\prod_j f_j$ is a nonzero germ. Apply [F8] to $G$; after the resulting linear coordinate change the restriction of $G$ to the last coordinate line has finite order. Since this restriction is the product of the corresponding one-variable restrictions of the $f_j$, each factor is nonzero and hence has a finite order; each $f_j$ is therefore regular in the last variable.

Apply [F9] to each of the finitely many $f_j$ and intersect the resulting neighborhoods. On one common product polydisc each $f_j=u_jP_j$, where $u_j$ is a unit and $P_j$ is a monic Weierstrass polynomial. Multiplication of the relation coefficients by the units $u_j$ is an isomorphism from the relation sheaf of $(f_j)$ to that of $(P_j)$. Set $d=\max_j\deg_w P_j$.

By [F4], whose quotient/remainder step uses the uniqueness in [F10], every relation germ of $(P_1,\ldots,P_q)$ is generated by polynomial relation germs whose components have $w$-degree at most $d$. Such vectors are identified with coefficient vectors in $\mathcal O_{\Delta'}^{\oplus q(d+1)}$, where $\Delta'$ is the base polydisc. Multiplication by the $P_j$ defines a finite matrix map $\Psi:\mathcal O_{\Delta'}^{\oplus q(d+1)}\to\mathcal O_{\Delta'}^{\oplus(2d+1)}$ by taking coefficients of $\sum_j Q_jP_j$. Its kernel is exactly the bounded-degree polynomial relation sheaf.

By dimension induction, $\mathcal O_{\Delta'}$ is coherent; [F3] therefore makes $\mathcal K=\ker\Psi$ locally of finite type. At the base point, its stalk is a submodule of $A^{\oplus q(d+1)}$, where $A=\mathcal O_{n-1,0}$ after translation. If $n>1$, [F6] makes $A$ Noetherian; if $n=1$, $A=\mathbb C$ is a field and hence Noetherian. The finite free module is finitely generated, so [F7] makes it Noetherian and its submodule $\mathcal K_0$ finitely generated.

The sheaf $\mathcal K$ is coherent: it is locally of finite type by step 6.1, and for any finite free map into $\mathcal K$, composition with its inclusion into the finite free target of $\Psi$ has the same kernel, locally of finite type by [F3]. A finite-rank free module over the coherent structure sheaf is coherent, since its standard basis gives finite type and [F3] gives the kernel condition. Choose finitely many germs generating $\mathcal K_0$ and represent them by sections on one smaller base neighborhood. Their cokernel in $\mathcal K$ is coherent by [F5]; its stalk at the base point is zero by the chosen generators and the stalk definition [F13]. Since that cokernel is locally of finite type, a finite generating family has zero germs there and vanishes after a common shrinking. Thus the selected sections generate every kernel stalk on a smaller base neighborhood.

Regard these finite coefficient sections as polynomial relation sections on the product polydisc. Together with the finitely many elementary polynomial relations $P_qe_j-P_je_q$, they generate every bounded-degree relation stalk over the smaller base neighborhood; [F4] then makes them generate every relation stalk of $(P_1,\ldots,P_q)$ throughout a smaller product neighborhood. The unit isomorphisms from step 4.1 transfer these generators back to $(f_1,\ldots,f_q)$. Equality of the generated subsheaf with the relation sheaf follows from their equal stalks by [F12]. Thus the relation sheaf is locally of finite type at the chosen point.

Since the point and tuple were arbitrary, every finite tuple of holomorphic functions on every chart has a locally finite-type relation sheaf. A holomorphic coordinate change induces an isomorphism of structure sheaves and transports the relation map and its kernel, so the chart-local property is independent of coordinates. Hence [F2] makes $\mathcal O_M$ coherent on all of $M$.
Apply [F5] to the coherent structure sheaf $\mathcal O_M$. It gives closure of coherent $\mathcal O_M$-modules under kernels, cokernels, and finite extensions, as stated.

Fix coherent $\mathcal F$, $x\in M$, and finite $\ell\ge0$. Local finite type gives a finite-rank epimorphism $\mathcal O^{\oplus p_0}\to\mathcal F$ near $x$. The finite free source is coherent by [F3] and the coherence of $\mathcal O_M$ from step 9.1; hence its kernel is coherent by [F5]. Choose a finite-rank epimorphism onto that kernel, compose with its inclusion into $\mathcal O^{\oplus p_0}$, and repeat this operation until $\ell+1$ free modules have been chosen. At each intermediate stage the kernel is coherent by [F5], so the next finite-rank epimorphism exists locally.

Only finitely many neighborhoods are used for the finite length $\ell+1$ construction; their intersection is a chart neighborhood $W$ of $x$. Each new free module maps onto the preceding kernel, so the resulting sequence is exact at $\mathcal F|_W$ and every free term before the leftmost one. No further kernel is chosen at the leftmost term, and no global choices of generators or global resolution are asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The empty tuple is explicitly assigned zero relation sheaf in step 1.1.
Zero tuple entries are removed locally in step 2.1, while zero modules are included by finite generation.
The induction covers tuple length one and all finite dimensions in steps 1.1–8.1.
Zero germs and unit germs are handled separately in step 2.1; the all-vanishing case is treated in steps 3.1–8.1.
The partial resolution includes length ell=0 and is exact at each asserted term in steps 10.2–11.1.
The adopted Axiom of Choice is stated in A1; the proof uses finite local selections and shrinkings in steps 1.1, 7.1, and 10.2.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, so $X$ is a topological space and $\mathcal O_X$ is a sheaf of commutative rings. An $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **locally of finite type** if for every $x\in X$ there are an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, a finite integer $r\ge0$, and sections $s_1,\ldots,s_r\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that their germs generate $\mathcal F_y$ as an $\mathcal O_{X,y}$-module for every $y\in U$.

For an open $V\subseteq X$, a finite integer $p\ge0$, and an $\mathcal O_X$-module morphism $\phi:\mathcal O_V^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal F|_V$, its **relation sheaf** is the kernel sheaf $\ker\phi$. The module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **coherent** if it is locally of finite type and, for every such $V$, $p$, and $\phi$, the relation sheaf $\ker\phi$ is locally of finite type. Here $\mathcal O_V^{\oplus0}$ is the zero module sheaf.

In particular, for a finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_p\in\mathcal O_X(U)$, its holomorphic relation sheaf is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_U^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal O_U$ that sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_p)$ to $\sum_{j=1}^p a_jf_j$. The structure sheaf is coherent when it is coherent as a module over itself. If $M$ is a complex manifold, an **analytic coherent module on $M$** means a coherent module sheaf over its sheaf $\mathcal O_M$ of holomorphic functions.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$, and let $x\in X$.

The **neighbourhood category of $x$** is the full subcategory
$$\mathcal N_x\subseteq \operatorname{Open}(X)$$
whose objects are the open neighbourhoods of $x$. Its opposite category is
filtered in the sense of
[[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]]: it is nonempty because $X$
itself is a neighbourhood of $x$, and for neighbourhoods $U,V$ the
intersection $U\cap V$ is again a neighbourhood of $x$ with arrows
$$U\longrightarrow U\cap V,\qquad V\longrightarrow U\cap V$$
in the opposite category.

Because $\mathcal F$ is contravariant, its restriction to the neighbourhood
category determines a covariant diagram on that opposite category. The
**stalk** of $\mathcal F$ at $x$ is the filtered colimit
$$\mathcal F_x:=\varinjlim_{\mathcal N_x^{\operatorname{op}}}\mathcal F(U).$$

Concretely, $\mathcal F_x$ may be described as equivalence classes of pairs
$(U,s)$ with $U$ an open neighbourhood of $x$ and
$s\in\mathcal F(U)$, where $(U,s)\sim(V,t)$ when $s$ and $t$ agree on some
smaller open neighbourhood of $x$. The next lemma verifies that this is an
equivalence relation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional complex manifold and let $\mathcal O_M$ be its sheaf of holomorphic functions. For every open $U\subseteq M$ and every finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_q\in\mathcal O_M(U)$, the relation sheaf
$$
\ker\!\left(\mathcal O_U^{\oplus q}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_U,\quad(a_1,\ldots,a_q)\longmapsto\sum_{j=1}^q a_jf_j\right)
$$
is locally of finite type: every point has a neighborhood on which one finite family of relation sections generates the relation stalk at every point. Consequently $\mathcal O_M$ is coherent. Coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module sheaves are closed under kernels, cokernels, and finite extensions. For every coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module $\mathcal F$, point $x\in M$, and finite integer $\ell\ge0$, there are a chart neighborhood $W$ of $x$ and finite ranks $p_0,\ldots,p_\ell$ for which
$$
\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_\ell}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_0}\longrightarrow\mathcal F|_W\longrightarrow0
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F|_W$ and at every free term except the leftmost one. No exactness at the leftmost free term and no global analytic free resolution are asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space and use the coherence definition on the A page. The kernel and cokernel of any morphism between coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaves are coherent. In every short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal F'\to\mathcal E\to\mathcal F''\to0$ of $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaves, if any two of $\mathcal F'$, $\mathcal E$, and $\mathcal F''$ are coherent, then the third is coherent.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and let $r$ be a polyradius. Suppose
