derivations.claim: Assume $r\ge1$ and fix a nonempty index set $I\subseteq\{0,\ldots,r\}$. Choose $i_0\in I$ and use $w_j=Z_j/Z_{i_0}$ for $j\ne i_0$ on $U_I$. The coordinates with $j\in I\setminus\{i_0\}$ are nonzero and all remaining coordinates range over $\mathbb C$, so $U_I\cong\mathbb C^{r+1-|I|}\times(\mathbb C^*)^{|I|-1}$; this product is open and connected. Write $b=|I|-1$.

The local Dolbeault lemma [F8], applied coefficientwise in a holomorphic frame on coordinate polydiscs in $U_I$, gives local exactness in every positive degree. In degree zero, a smooth function killed by $\bar\partial$ satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations and is holomorphic by [F9]. By [F7] the operators form a complex, so $0\to\mathcal O\to\mathcal A^{0,0}\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\cdots\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\mathcal A^{0,r}\to0$ is an exact sheaf resolution. The whole-polydisc statement [F10] also gives positive-degree exactness on each coordinate polydisc. Each $\mathcal A^{0,j}$ is a module over smooth functions, hence is $\Gamma(U_I,-)$-acyclic by [F11]. The resolution cycles lie in the supplied injective-data domain [F13], and [A1] supplies the DC required by [F12]. Applying [F12] identifies $H^q(U_I,\mathcal O)$ with the cohomology of the global Dolbeault complex on $U_I$.

For a section of $\mathcal O(k)$ on $U_I$, write its coefficient in frame $e_{i_0}^{(k)}$ as a holomorphic function $f$ on $\mathbb C^a\times(\mathbb C^*)^b$, where $a=r+1-|I|$ and $b=|I|-1$. By [F17], $f$ is continuous and separately holomorphic. Iterating the one-variable Cauchy expansions on the $\mathbb C$ factors and Laurent expansions on the $\mathbb C^*$ factors gives a mixed series indexed by $m_j\in\mathbb N$ for coordinates that may vanish and $m_j\in\mathbb Z$ for the nonzero coordinates. To prove holomorphy of each coefficient in the remaining variables, fix the Laurent contour radii and a closed parameter polydisc compactly contained in the remaining coordinates. For each fixed point $\zeta$ of the contour product, apply the iterated Cauchy formula [F15] to the remaining variables. Since $f$ is bounded on the compact product of the contours and that polydisc, the Taylor coefficient estimates are uniform in $\zeta$. On a smaller concentric polydisc, the Taylor series therefore converges absolutely and uniformly in $\zeta$. The estimate $|\int_\Gamma g|\le L_\Gamma\sup_\Gamma|g|$ allows termwise integration in the already fixed contour order, so the Laurent coefficient has a convergent power series in all remaining variables. Thus it is holomorphic. Define $m_{i_0}=k-\sum_{j\ne i_0}m_j$ and write $Z^m$ for the homogeneous Laurent monomial section whose coefficient in frame $e_{i_0}^{(k)}$ is $\prod_{j\ne i_0}(Z_j/Z_{i_0})^{m_j}$; its total degree is $\sum_i m_i=k$. Every negative exponent is among coordinates indexed by $I$.

If $b=0$, then $U_I\cong\mathbb C^r$ and $\delta_{U_I}=+\infty$ by [F5]. If $b>0$, an equal-radius polydisc of radius $s$ around $w$ is contained in $U_I$ exactly when $s\le\min_{j\in I\setminus\{i_0\}}|w_j|$: smaller radii cannot reach a forbidden coordinate hyperplane, while any larger radius includes zero in a coordinate disk attaining the minimum. Hence $\delta_{U_I}(w)=\min_j|w_j|$ and $-\log\delta_{U_I}=\max_j(-\log|w_j|)$. Each $-\log|w_j|$ is harmonic on $\mathbb C^*$ because it is locally the real part of a holomorphic logarithm. Their finite maximum is continuous and subharmonic on each complex line: at a point choose an index attaining the maximum, apply the submean inequality for that harmonic function, and bound its boundary values by the maximum. Thus $-\log\delta_{U_I}$ is plurisubharmonic by [F4], so $U_I$ is Hartogs pseudoconvex by [F5].

The domain $U_I$ has complex dimension $r$, so [F6] makes its global Dolbeault cohomology zero for $1\le q\le r$; for $q>r$ the complex has no terms in degree $q$, hence its cohomology is zero as well. The frame $e_{i_0}^{(k)}$ trivializes $\mathcal O(k)$ on $U_I$, so its restricted holomorphic-section sheaf is isomorphic to $\mathcal O$ and has the same positive-degree sheaf cohomology.

Let $K$ be a compact product with $|w_j|\le S_j$ on each $\mathbb C$ coordinate and $\rho_j\le|w_j|\le R_j$ on each $\mathbb C^*$ coordinate. Choose $S'_j>S_j$, $R'_j>R_j$ and $0<\rho'_j<\rho_j$; the corresponding Cauchy and Laurent circles stay in the domain. The iterated coefficient-integral bounds give geometric factors $(S_j/S'_j)^{m_j}$ for a Taylor coordinate, $(R_j/R'_j)^{m_j}$ for a nonnegative Laurent exponent, and $(\rho'_j/\rho_j)^{|m_j|}$ for a negative Laurent exponent. The remaining factor is bounded by the supremum of $f$ on the finite product of chosen circles, times fixed contour-length factors. There are finitely many choices of signs, and each product of geometric series converges; hence the mixed series converges absolutely and uniformly on $K$.

Define $C^p=\prod_{|I|=p+1}\mathcal O(k)(U_I)$, with the ordered Čech differential $(\delta c)_{i_0\cdots i_{p+1}}=\sum_{
u=0}^{p+1}(-1)^
u c_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_
u}\cdots i_{p+1}}|_{U_{i_0\cdots i_{p+1}}}$. For a multi-index $m$ of total degree $k$, set $N(m)=\{i:m_i<0\}$. By step 1.3, its coefficient occurs in the component indexed by $I$ exactly when $N(m)\subseteq I$. The frame transition rule in [F2] changes the local coefficient by $(Z_i/Z_j)^k$, exactly the change between the two local expressions of the same degree-$k$ monomial $Z^m$; restrictions consequently preserve $m$. Thus the differential acts on each coefficient by the finite alternating-subset complex whose degree-$p$ entries are scalars indexed by subsets $I$ of size $p+1$ containing $N(m)$.

Give the cover $U_0,\ldots,U_r$ its natural order. Step 2.2 proves that every nonempty finite intersection is acyclic for each coefficient sheaf $\mathcal O(k)$ under consideration. Therefore [F14] identifies its analytic sheaf cohomology with the fixed-cover Čech cohomology of the ordered cover.

Each mixed coefficient is given by its fixed iterated Cauchy or Laurent contour integral. Applying these same integrals in the same order to the uniformly convergent series on a compact polyannulus recovers that coefficient; the uniqueness of the one-variable Cauchy and Laurent coefficients therefore proves uniqueness of the mixed coefficients.

If $N(m)$ is nonempty and proper, choose the least $j\notin N(m)$. For an increasing output index $I$ of size $p$ containing $N(m)$, define $(h_mc)_I=0$ when $j\in I$, and otherwise define $(h_mc)_I=(-1)^{\#\{i\in I:i<j\}}c_{I\cup\{j\}}$; this maps degree $p$ to degree $p-1$. To check the identity at an input index $I$ of size $p+1$, first suppose $j\notin I$. In $h_m\delta c$, the face obtained by deleting $j$ from $I\cup\{j\}$ has sign $(-1)^{\#\{i\in I:i<j\}}$; multiplication by the same sign in $h_m$ leaves $c_I$ with coefficient $+1$. For each $i\in I$, the other term obtained by deleting $i$ occurs also in $\delta h_m c$, and its two signs differ by one because inserting $j$ and deleting $i$ reverse order; those terms cancel pairwise. If $j\in I$, then $h_m\delta c$ is zero at $I$, all terms of $\delta h_m c$ vanish except the face deleting $j$, and its two equal signs again multiply to $+1$, leaving $c_I$. Faces that delete an element of $N(m)$ have zero coefficient because the resulting index no longer contains $N(m)$. Thus $\delta h_m+h_m\delta=\mathrm{id}$ in every degree, including the minimal index $I=N(m)$.

For $k=0$, the only multi-index with $N(m)=\varnothing$ is $m=(0,\ldots,0)$; its coefficient complex is the full simplex complex. Its degree-zero kernel is the constant tuples $\mathbb C$. For positive degree define $h c_I=0$ when $0\in I$ and $h c_I=c_{I\cup\{0\}}$ when $0\notin I$; inserting the least vertex $0$ gives positive sign, and the insertion/deletion identity proved in step 3.3 gives $\delta h+h\delta=\mathrm{id}$. Every other degree-zero mode has nonempty proper $N(m)$ and is contracted by step 3.3. For $k=-1$ and $r\ge1$, no mode has empty or full negative set: all-nonnegative exponents cannot sum to $-1$, and all-negative exponents sum to at most $-(r+1)$. Thus step 3.3 contracts every mode and degree-zero cohomology is zero. For $k=-r-1$, the unique mode with full negative set is $m=(-1,\ldots,-1)$: writing each $m_i=-1-n_i$ with $n_i\ge0$, the total-degree equation gives $\sum_i n_i=0$, hence every $n_i=0$. This mode occurs only in top degree $r$, has no incoming or outgoing Čech term, and contributes one copy of $\mathbb C$. All other modes have nonempty proper negative set and contract.

The coefficient homotopy of step 3.3 defines an analytic cochain homotopy, not just a formal one. In an output component indexed by $I$, group terms by the finitely many possible selected vertices $j\notin I$. Each retained mode has $N(m)\subseteq I$ and hence $m_j\ge0$. For any compact product in $U_I$, choose outer Cauchy circles beyond its bounded coordinates and inner Laurent circles below the positive minimum of each nonzero coordinate. The estimates of step 2.3 then give absolute locally uniform convergence of each retained subseries on that compact set. Each partial sum is holomorphic there, so its limit is holomorphic by [F18]; the nonnegative $m_j$ powers extend the subseries across the coordinate hyperplane $Z_j=0$. Thus $h$ maps holomorphic Čech cochains to holomorphic Čech cochains, and the coefficient identity of step 3.3 holds for the analytic sums.

The Čech computation in step 4.1 is therefore valid for analytic sections. By the comparison of step 3.1 it gives $H^0(P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$, together with $H^0(P^r,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ and $H^r(P^r,\mathcal O(-r-1))\cong\mathbb C$ for $1\le r\le3$. For $r=0$, $P^0$ is a point, so its structure-sheaf global sections are $\mathbb C$ and its higher sheaf cohomology groups vanish.

derivations.claim: If $r=0$, then $X$ is a point, so a sheaf on $X$ is just its group of sections, global sections is exact, and every positive sheaf-cohomology group vanishes. The degree-zero Dolbeault complex is the identity on the fiber $E$, so the comparison is the identity by the derived-global-sections definition [F8]. Assume now $r\ge1$. On a coordinate polydisc with holomorphic frame $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ of $E$, write an $E$-valued form as $\sum_{a=1}^n\alpha_a\otimes s_a$ and define $\bar\partial_E(\sum_a\alpha_a\otimes s_a)=\sum_a\bar\partial\alpha_a\otimes s_a$. If the frame changes by a holomorphic matrix $G$, then $\bar\partial(G\alpha)=(\bar\partial G)\wedge\alpha+G\bar\partial\alpha=G\bar\partial\alpha$ because every entry of $G$ is holomorphic and hence satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations [F5]. Thus the local operators agree on overlaps; by [F3], their square is zero.

In a holomorphic frame, under full AC [A1], the local Dolbeault lemma [F4] applies componentwise to every closed form of positive antiholomorphic degree and gives exactness at that degree on a neighborhood of each point. At degree zero, a smooth coefficient killed by $\bar\partial$ satisfies the coordinate Cauchy–Riemann equations, so [F5] makes it holomorphic. Consequently the sheaf resolution $0\longrightarrow\mathcal O(E)\longrightarrow\mathcal A^{0,0}(E) \xrightarrow{\bar\partial_E}\cdots\xrightarrow{\bar\partial_E} \mathcal A^{0,r}(E)\longrightarrow0$ is exact: its degree-zero kernel is exactly the holomorphic-section sheaf, and every positive-degree kernel is locally the preceding image.
Each $\mathcal A^{0,j}(E)$ is a sheaf of modules over smooth functions, by pointwise scalar multiplication; hence it is $\Gamma(X,-)$-acyclic by [F6] under [A1].

Every cycle in the exact resolution of step 2.1 is an abelian sheaf on $X$, so it lies in the all-abelian-sheaves domain of the injective-resolution datum in [F8]. By [F9], full AC [A1] supplies the DC required by the acyclic-resolution theorem [F7]. Applying [F7] to that resolution and the global-sections functor gives, canonically, $H^q(X,\mathcal O(E))\cong H^q(\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,\bullet}(E)))=H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E)$ for every $q\ge0$.

For $E=\mathcal O_X$, [F10] identifies its holomorphic-section sheaf with $\mathcal O$. Then [F11] supplies $H^0(X,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(X,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$ in every stated dimension, as claimed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

For $r\ge1$, let $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ be the set of complex lines in
$\mathbb C^{r+1}$, with its quotient complex-manifold structure, and write
$[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]$ for the line through a nonzero vector
$(Z_0,\ldots,Z_r)$. For $i\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$ set
$U_i=\{[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]:Z_i\ne0\}$; its standard coordinates are the ratios
$Z_j/Z_i$ for $j\ne i$. For each integer $k$, the **projective twisting line
bundle** $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(k)$ is obtained by gluing the trivial
holomorphic line bundles $U_i\times\mathbb C$ with local frames $e_i^{(k)}$
and transition rule
$$e_j^{(k)}=\left(\frac{Z_j}{Z_i}\right)^k e_i^{(k)}\quad\text{on }U_i\cap U_j.$$
The transition factors are holomorphic and nowhere zero on the overlaps, with
$g_{ii}=1$, $g_{ij}=g_{ji}^{-1}$, and $g_{ij}g_{j\ell}=g_{i\ell}$ on every
triple overlap; hence they define a holomorphic line bundle. The sheaf
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(k)$ assigns to an open set the holomorphic sections of
this bundle, and $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}:=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(0)$ is the
structure sheaf.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For $0\le r\le3$, let $P^r$ be the complex
projective space $(\mathbb C^{r+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times$ with its
quotient complex-manifold structure; for $r=0$, $P^0$ is a point. For $r\ge1$ use the

sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is the $q$th right-derived
global-sections group of the abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$. For this ordered cover
and a sheaf $\mathcal G$, define
$$C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal G)=\prod_{|I|=p+1}\mathcal G(U_I),\qquad (\delta c)_{i_0\cdots i_{p+1}}=\sum_{\nu=0}^{p+1}(-1)^\nu c_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_\nu}\cdots i_{p+1}}|_{U_{i_0\cdots i_{p+1}}},$$
for $0\le p\le r$, with $C^p=0$ otherwise and increasing indices;
fixed-cover Čech cohomology is the cohomology of this complex. A mixed
Laurent–Taylor series is **normally convergent** when it
converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact product subset of its
domain. For $r\ge1$, every
$U_I$ is biholomorphic to
$\mathbb C^{r+1-|I|}\times(\mathbb C^*)^{|I|-1}$. For every integer $k$,
each section on $U_I$, in a standard local frame, has a unique normally
convergent mixed Laurent–Taylor expansion indexed by exponent tuples
$m=(m_0,\ldots,m_r)\in\mathbb Z^{r+1}$ with $\sum_i m_i=k$; its coefficient
occurs on $U_I$ exactly when $N(m):=\{i:m_i<0\}\subseteq I$. Restrictions
preserve each coefficient. In the ordered-cover Čech complex, every mode with
nonempty proper $N(m)$ has the cochain contraction, for $c\in C^p$ and an
output index $I$ of size $p$, given by $(h_mc)_I=0$ if $j\in I$ and
$(h_mc)_I=(-1)^{\#\{i\in I:i<j\}}c_{I\cup\{j\}}$ if $j\notin I$, where
$j$ is the least index outside $N(m)$; the resulting subseries converge
locally uniformly on the output intersections. The fixed-cover Čech cohomology
is canonically the analytic sheaf cohomology whenever that cover is acyclic for
the coefficient sheaf. For $k\in\{0,-1,-r-1\}$, the restricted sheaf
$\mathcal O(k)|_{U_I}$ has $H^q(U_I,\mathcal O(k)|_{U_I})=0$ for every integer
$q>0$, so the cover is acyclic for these three sheaves and the comparison
applies. Consequently, for $0\le r\le3$,
$$H^0(P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C,\qquad H^q(P^r,\mathcal O)=0\quad(q>0),$$
and for $1\le r\le3$,
$$H^0(P^r,\mathcal O(-1))=0,\qquad H^r(P^r,\mathcal O(-r-1))\cong\mathbb C.$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $r\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, let
$X=\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)=(\mathbb C^{r+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times$
with its standard quotient complex-manifold structure, and let $E\to X$ be a
holomorphic vector bundle of finite rank.
Write $\mathcal O(E)$ for its sheaf of holomorphic sections, and let
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ denote the $q$th right-derived global-sections group of an
abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$. For
$0\le q\le r$, let $\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)$ be the sheaf of smooth sections of
$\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$, where $\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X$ is the
$q$th exterior power of the antiholomorphic cotangent subbundle. In a

holomorphic vector bundle of finite rank.

abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$. For
$0\le q\le r$, let $\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)$ be the sheaf of smooth sections of
$\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$, where $\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X$ is the
$q$th exterior power of the antiholomorphic cotangent subbundle. In a
holomorphic local frame of $E$,

coefficient form; holomorphic transition matrices make this definition

derivations.claim: A global section of $\mathcal O(-k)$, $k=1,2$, would have an entire coefficient $f_0(t)$ with $f_0(t)=t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$. By the normally convergent expansions in [F2], the left side has only powers $t^n$ with $n\ge0$, whereas the right side has only powers $t^n$ with $n\le-k$. Uniqueness of Laurent coefficients forces every coefficient to vanish. Thus both degree-zero groups vanish.

A one-cochain on the two-chart overlap has a normally convergent Laurent expansion $g(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nt^n$. Coboundaries subtract the entire $t$-series with $n\ge0$ and the series $t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$ with $n\le-k$. These two tails converge on their respective entire charts by [F2]; the cover is acyclic for both twists because $r=1$ and $k=1,2$. For $k=1$ they exhaust every integer exponent, so the analytic first cohomology is zero. For $k=2$ the sole remaining exponent is $n=-1$; its coefficient cannot be a coboundary, and it identifies the analytic first cohomology with $\mathbb C$.

Apply [F3] to the two holomorphic line bundles on $L$. Its hypotheses hold for $r=1$ and the full AC assumption [A1]. It converts precisely the analytic sheaf groups computed in steps 1.1–2.1 to the smooth Dolbeault groups in the Statement. The transition calculation in [F1] gives $K_L\cong\mathcal O(-2)$. No scheme cohomology or unproved analytic/algebraic comparison is used.

Let $S^4={X\in\mathbb R^5:|X|=1}$ have its unit round metric and the orientation which, on the stereographic chart $S^4\setminus\{\infty\}\cong\mathbb R^4$, is $dx_0\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$. Put $z_1=x_0+ix_1$, $z_2=x_2+ix_3$, and $r^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$; in these coordinates the metric is $g=4(1+r^2)^{-2}\sum_{\mu=0}^3dx_\mu^2$. Identify $\mathbb H^2$ with $\mathbb C^4$ using a right quaternionic structure $j$ with $j^2=-1$, put $Z=\mathbb CP^3=\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb H^2)$, and define $\pi:Z\to\mathbb HP^1=S^4$ by $\pi(\ell)=\ell+j\ell$ for a complex line $\ell\subset\mathbb H^2$. Its fibres are projective lines $L_x\cong\mathbb CP^1$. In homogeneous coordinates $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]$, the fibre over finite $z=(z_1,z_2)$ is the line

$$\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2,\qquad \mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2,$$

and the fibre over infinity is $L_\infty=\{\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\}$. Give $Z$ the Fubini–Study metric induced by the standard Hermitian metric on $\mathbb C^4$ and give $\mathcal O_Z(-2)$ its induced Hermitian metric. $$H_1=\partial_{\bar z_1}-t\partial_{z_2},\qquad H_2=\partial_{\bar z_2}+t\partial_{z_1};$$

They annihilate the displayed holomorphic coordinates. Together with $\partial_{\bar t}$ they form a direct local frame of $T^{0,1}Z$. Here $H_i$ are the constant-$t$ chart lifts; their projected complex alpha-plane is intrinsic, but this chart splitting is not asserted to be the global metric splitting. Globally let $V^{0,1}=\ker(d\pi)\cap T^{0,1}Z$, and let $H^{0,1}$ be its Fubini–Study orthogonal complement. Its lifts project to the same alpha-planes and may differ from the displayed $H_i$ by vertical components. All global horizontal/vertical form decompositions use this orthogonal splitting; local computations may use the displayed constant-$t$ splitting after retaining the resulting frame and normalization factors. The second projective chart supplies the same alpha-plane at $t=\infty$. The line bundle $\mathcal O_Z(-1)$ is the tautological holomorphic line bundle and $\mathcal O_Z(-2)=\mathcal O_Z(-1)^{\otimes2}$.

The canonical bundle is $K_L\cong\mathcal O_L(-2)$; the last group is one-dimensional, and the first three vanish.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, of real dimension at least two. Its metric defines the $L^2$ pairing on forms by the Riemannian density; orientation is unnecessary. Let $d^*$ denote the formal adjoint of $d$, and $\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$ on total real forms, or on their complexification. With domain $H^2$ the operator is nonnegative and selfadjoint. Its degreewise smooth kernels $\mathcal H^k$ are finite dimensional, and there is an orthogonal smooth decomposition
$$\Omega^k(M)=\mathcal H^k\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d\Omega^{k-1}(M)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d^*\Omega^{k+1}(M).$$
The map $h\mapsto[h]$ is an isomorphism $\mathcal H^k\to H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$, over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ as appropriate.

More generally let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $m\ge1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Let $E$ be a holomorphic bundle of finite rank with a smooth Hermitian metric. The holomorphic bundle structure supplies frames with holomorphic invertible transition matrices; the Hermitian metric is separate smooth positive-definite pairing data. On $E$-valued $(p,q)$ forms, define $\bar\partial_E$ by the coefficientwise Dolbeault operator in holomorphic bundle charts and let $\bar\partial_E^*$ be its formal adjoint. For each fixed $p$, $\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}=\bar\partial_E\bar\partial_E^*+\bar\partial_E^*\bar\partial_E$ on the sum over $q$ is nonnegative and selfadjoint on $H^2$; its smooth harmonic spaces $\mathcal H_E^{p,q}$ are finite dimensional and
$$\Omega^{p,q}(X,E)=\mathcal H_E^{p,q}\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E\Omega^{p,q-1}(X,E)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E^*\Omega^{p,q+1}(X,E).$$
In particular harmonic forms represent the smooth Dolbeault quotient
$$H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X,E):=\ker\bar\partial_E/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_E$$
uniquely. Terms outside the degree range are zero. This asserts smooth Dolbeault cohomology; an identification with sheaf cohomology requires a separate Dolbeault-resolution comparison theorem.

For either complex write $D=d$ or $D=\bar\partial_E$, $P=DD^*+D^*D$, and let $\Pi,G$ be the preceding Green projection and inverse. They preserve degree, $G$ preserves smooth forms, and on smooth forms
$$DG=GD,\qquad D^*G=GD^*,\qquad D\Pi=\Pi D=D^*\Pi=\Pi D^*=0.$$
Every closed smooth $u$ satisfies $u=\Pi u+D(D^*Gu)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. derivations.claim: Write $V^{0,1}$ for the vertical tangent and use [F1]'s global orthogonal complement. Filter the smooth Dolbeault complex of $F(-2)$ by the number of horizontal covectors. Vertical restriction is the ordinary fibre Dolbeault operator. The differential has components of horizontal/vertical bidegrees $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$ and potentially $(2,-1)$; the last is the curvature of the splitting, so a bicomplex with only two differentials is not presumed. On a form annihilating vertical tangent, the mixed component is the intrinsic vertical Bott/Dolbeault operator on the horizontal coefficient bundle: it is obtained by evaluating $\bar\partial$ on one vertical and one horizontal vector. This description is independent of the lift of the horizontal vector. In the constant-$t$ local frame the vectors $\partial_{\bar t},H_1,H_2$ commute; hence that coefficient operator is ordinary $\partial_{\bar t}$.

Let $Q_x\subset\mathbb C^4$ be the quaternionic two-plane over $x$. Its Hermitian quaternionic structure gives a canonical complex alternating volume form $\delta_x$: every frame $(v,jv)$ of unit norm has determinant one for this form, and the changes are in $SU(2)$. On $L_x=\mathbb P(Q_x)$, the identity $K_{L_x}=\det(Q_x)^*\otimes\mathcal O(-2)|_{L_x}$ therefore gives an intrinsic isomorphism $\iota_x:\mathcal O(-2)|_{L_x}\to K_{L_x}$. In the finite incidence chart put $a=1+r^2$, $q=1+|t|^2$, $v_1=(1,0,z_1,z_2)$, $v_2=(0,1,-\bar z_2,\bar z_1)$ and $e=(v_1+t v_2)^{\otimes2}$. The two $v_i$ are orthogonal with squared norm $a$, so $\delta_x(v_1,v_2)=a$ and $\iota_x(e)=a\,dt$. The tautological metric is $\|e\|^2=a^2q^2$. The harmonic vertical form is $$\sigma_x=\frac{i}{2\pi}\frac{e\,d\bar t}{a q^2}.$$ Indeed its weighted coefficient $\|e\|^2/(a q^2)=a$ is holomorphic in $t$, so the local formal-adjoint equation is zero; [F2]–[F3] make the harmonic line one-dimensional. Moreover $\int_{L_x}\iota_x(\sigma_x)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb C}dt\wedge d\bar t/q^2=1$. This fixes both scale and phase. The intrinsic metric/volume construction proves agreement on projective and base-chart overlaps, including infinity, and smooth dependence on $x$. Extend this vertical form by zero on the global orthogonal horizontal complement to obtain $\sigma$. This extension need not be Dolbeault closed.

Smoothness of the needed primitive does not require a theorem about varying complex structures. Choose smooth unit quaternionic frames of $Q_x$ on a base neighborhood and a smooth unitary frame of $E$. These identify the vertical problem exactly with the fixed $SU(2)$-invariant Hermitian $\mathcal O(-2)$ problem on $\mathbb CP^1$, componentwise in $E_x$. Set $B=\bar\partial^*G$ on vertical degree one. By [F3], $\bar\partial B=I-\Pi$, and by [F2] its degree-zero kernel is zero. The estimates [F4] and the first-order nature of $\bar\partial^*$ give $B:H^m\to H^{m+1}$ bounded for each $m$. For jointly smooth $f(x,t)$, base difference quotients converge in every fibre $H^m$ uniformly on compact base sets, by the Taylor formula and compactness of the fibre. Applying the fixed bounded $B$ shows $\partial_x^\beta(Bf)=B(\partial_x^\beta f)$ at every order in every $H^{m+1}$. Sobolev embedding on the fixed two-dimensional compact fibre, with arbitrarily large $m$, gives joint smoothness in $(x,t)$. For the horizontal coefficient problem, choose also a smooth unit quaternionic frame of $Q_x^\perp$. Together the two quaternionic frames give a smooth $Sp(2)$ transformation from a fixed pair of planes to $(Q_x,Q_x^\perp)$. Its complex-linear action on $\mathbb CP^3$ is holomorphic and preserves the Fubini–Study and tautological metrics. It therefore transports the horizontal quotient, its vertical Bott operator and its induced metric to the fixed $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$ problem identified below. That inverse is likewise one fixed bounded operator componentwise, so the same derivative argument applies. Thus no moving-cokernel inverse or unproved parametric Green assertion is used.

By [A1], a sheaf class has a global smooth closed representative $\alpha$. Its vertical restriction has harmonic part $s(x)\sigma_x$, where $s(x)=\int_{L_x}\iota_x(\alpha_V)$ componentwise in $E_x$. This is smooth by integration over compact fibres. Solve $\gamma_x=B(\alpha_V-s\sigma_x)$; then $\bar\partial_V\gamma_x=\alpha_V-s\sigma_x$. Step 2.1 makes $\gamma$ smooth. A change of unit quaternionic frame acts by an $SU(2)$ fibre isometry and a change of unitary $E$ frame acts by a matrix constant on each fibre; both preserve the equation. Uniqueness from $H^{0,0}(\mathcal O(-2))=0$ makes these local solutions agree. Hence $\gamma$ is global and $\alpha_H:=\alpha-s\sigma-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ annihilates vertical tangent, proving the asserted decomposition. The harmonic/exact orthogonality and the same zero kernel prove its uniqueness.

Replacing $\alpha$ by $\alpha+\bar\partial_F\beta$ changes its vertical restriction by $\bar\partial_V\beta$; its harmonic projection and integral against the fibre trace are zero. Thus $s$ depends only on the cohomology class, and the construction is linear. It is a section of $E$, not of an unspecified conformal-weight line, because the metric quaternionic volume in step 1.2 supplies the precise canonical identification of the harmonic line with $\mathbb C$.

In the second projective chart $u=1/t$, the constant-coordinate horizontal vectors satisfy $\widetilde H_i=uH_i$. The intrinsic horizontal cotangent quotient therefore restricts to $\mathcal O(1)^{\oplus2}$; after the $\mathcal O(-2)$ twist its coefficient bundle is $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. This transition determines the vertical Bott holomorphic structure from step 1.1, rather than assuming a normal-bundle or generic Penrose theorem. If $s=0$, closedness gives $\bar\partial_F\alpha_H=0$, since $\bar\partial_F^2=0$. Its mixed component says that $\alpha_H|_{L_x}$ is holomorphic for precisely this coefficient bundle. By [F2] it is zero on each fibre. Thus $\alpha=\bar\partial_F\gamma$ globally, proving injectivity, including zero rank.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. derivations.claim: For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. On a fibre it has a unique vertical primitive by [F4]. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained.

Compute that residual in the simpler constant-$t$ local splitting, without transplanting metric-frame coefficient formulas. Let $D_j=D_{z_j}$, $D_{\bar j}=D_{\bar z_j}$ be the covariant derivatives in a local unitary frame of $E$ and set $u=s/a$. The holomorphic tautological frame $e$ is killed by the scalar $\bar\partial$. Let $\theta^1,\theta^2$ be the $(0,1)$ covectors dual to $H_1,H_2$ and vanishing on $\partial_{\bar t}$. These three vector fields commute, so scalar Dolbeault differentiation is evaluated by them without bracket terms. The form with the prescribed vertical part and zero mixed differential is
$$\psi_{\mathrm{loc}}(s)=e\left(\frac{c u}{q^2}d\bar t+h_1\theta^1+h_2\theta^2\right),\quad h_1=\frac{c}{q}(\bar tD_{\bar1}u+D_2u),\quad h_2=\frac{c}{q}(\bar tD_{\bar2}u-D_1u).$$
Indeed $\partial_{\bar t}(\bar t/q)=q^{-2}$ and $\partial_{\bar t}(1/q)=-tq^{-2}$, so $\partial_{\bar t}h_i$ equals the corresponding $D_{H_i}(c u/q^2)$ exactly. The factor $u=s/(1+r^2)$ is essential: it is the integral-normalized harmonic coefficient from [F2], not an adjustable conformal ansatz.

These local forms are regular on the complete projective fibre. For $w=1/t$, the horizontal vectors are $\widetilde H_i=wH_i$, $\widetilde\theta^i=w^{-1}\theta^i$, and $\widetilde e=w^2e$. Thus the new horizontal coefficients are $\widetilde h_i=t h_i$. They become $c(D_{\bar1}u+\bar wD_2u)/(1+|w|^2)$ and $c(D_{\bar2}u-\bar wD_1u)/(1+|w|^2)$, both smooth. The vertical coefficient changes to $-c u\,d\bar w/(1+|w|^2)^2$ in frame $\widetilde e$, also smooth. The sign is the canonical-coordinate transition, not a change of harmonic normalization. Therefore $\psi_{\mathrm{loc}}$ exists over every entire fibre above this base chart. Its difference from the intrinsic form of step 1.1 has zero vertical part and zero mixed differential. By [F4] that difference is zero. This proves that the coordinate calculation computes the actual global correction, despite using a different horizontal splitting for its displayed coefficients.

Put $S=D_{\bar1}D_1+D_{\bar2}D_2$ and $T=D_1D_{\bar1}+D_2D_{\bar2}$. Directly evaluating the remaining differential on $H_1,H_2$ gives
$$\frac{q}{c}\bar\partial_F\psi_{\mathrm{loc}}(H_1,H_2)/e=\bar tF_{\bar1\bar2}u-tF_{12}u-Su-|t|^2Tu.$$
Here, for example, $D_{H_1}h_2=cq^{-1}(\bar tD_{\bar1}D_{\bar2}-D_{\bar1}D_1-t\bar tD_2D_{\bar2}+tD_2D_1)u$, and subtracting $D_{H_2}h_1$ gives precisely the displayed expression. By [F3], $T-S=F_{1\bar1}+F_{2\bar2}=0$ and the first two terms vanish. Since $D_j=(D_{2j-2}-iD_{2j-1})/2$ and $D_{\bar j}=(D_{2j-2}+iD_{2j-1})/2$, $S+T=\tfrac12\sum_{\mu=0}^3D_\mu^2$ and hence $S=T=\tfrac14\sum_\mu D_\mu^2$. The residual is therefore exactly $-c\sum_\mu D_\mu^2(s/a)/4$ in the nonvanishing local coefficient frame $e\theta^1\wedge\theta^2$. No uncomputed curvature cancellation or generic Penrose-operator theorem is used.

For $g=\Omega^2\delta$ in four dimensions, integration against its volume $\Omega^4 dx$ and the unitary connection gives
$$\nabla_A^*\nabla_A s=-\Omega^{-4}\sum_\mu D_\mu(\Omega^2D_\mu s)=-\Omega^{-2}\sum_\mu D_\mu^2s-2\Omega^{-3}\sum_\mu(\partial_\mu\Omega)D_\mu s.$$
With $\Omega=2/a$, differentiation gives $\partial_\mu\Omega=-4x_\mu/a^2$ and $\sum_\mu\partial_\mu^2\Omega=-16/a^3=-2\Omega^3$. The product rule now proves, for this very connection,
$$\Omega^{-3}\left[-\sum_\mu D_\mu^2(\Omega s)\right]=(\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2)s.$$

$$\bar\partial_F\psi(s)=\tau(\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2)s,\qquad \tau=\frac{c\Omega^3}{8}\,e\theta^1\wedge\theta^2.$$

The local expression equals the intrinsically constructed differential by step 3.1. The same construction and calculation apply in any stereographic chart with the unit round metric. $X=\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)=(\mathbb C^{r+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times$
with its standard quotient complex-manifold structure, and let $E\to X$ be a
holomorphic vector bundle of finite rank.
Write $\mathcal O(E)$ for its sheaf of holomorphic sections, and let
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ denote the $q$th right-derived global-sections group of an
abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$. For
$0\le q\le r$, let $\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)$ be the sheaf of smooth sections of
$\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$, where $\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X$ is the
$q$th exterior power of the antiholomorphic cotangent subbundle. In a
holomorphic local frame of $E$,
define $\bar\partial_E$ by applying the scalar $\bar\partial$ to each
coefficient form; holomorphic transition matrices make this definition
independent of frame, and $\bar\partial_E^2=0$. Set
$\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)=0$ for $q>r$ and define
$$H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E):=\frac{\ker\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q+1}(E))\bigr)}{\operatorname{im}\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q-1}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\bigr)},$$
where $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ denotes the group of sections of $\mathcal F$ over
$X$ and the denominator is zero for $q=0$. For every $q\ge0$, the canonical
comparison induced by the smooth Dolbeault resolution is an isomorphism
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O(E))\cong H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E).$$
For the trivial line bundle $E=\mathcal O_X$ and $0\le r\le3$, this gives
$$H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C,\qquad H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0\quad(q>0).$$
The scalar cohomology conclusion is obtained by the direct Laurent–Čech
calculation on the standard projective cover; no GAGA theorem, Kähler Hodge
theorem in dimensions above one, or arbitrary-coherent projective vanishing is
assumed.

Let $S^4={X\in\mathbb R^5:|X|=1}$ have its unit round metric and the orientation which, on the stereographic chart $S^4\setminus\{\infty\}\cong\mathbb R^4$, is $dx_0\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$. Put $z_1=x_0+ix_1$, $z_2=x_2+ix_3$, and $r^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$; in these coordinates the metric is $g=4(1+r^2)^{-2}\sum_{\mu=0}^3dx_\mu^2$. Identify $\mathbb H^2$ with $\mathbb C^4$ using a right quaternionic structure $j$ with $j^2=-1$, put $Z=\mathbb CP^3=\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb H^2)$, and define $\pi:Z\to\mathbb HP^1=S^4$ by $\pi(\ell)=\ell+j\ell$ for a complex line $\ell\subset\mathbb H^2$. Its fibres are projective lines $L_x\cong\mathbb CP^1$. In homogeneous coordinates $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]$, the fibre over finite $z=(z_1,z_2)$ is the line

$$\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2,\qquad \mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2,$$

and the fibre over infinity is $L_\infty=\{\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\}$. Give $Z$ the Fubini–Study metric induced by the standard Hermitian metric on $\mathbb C^4$ and give $\mathcal O_Z(-2)$ its induced Hermitian metric. On the incidence chart $\lambda_1\ne0$, set $t=\lambda_2/\lambda_1$, $\mu_1/\lambda_1=z_1-\bar z_2t$, and $\mu_2/\lambda_1=z_2+\bar z_1t$. The horizontal complex directions of type $(0,1)$ are spanned by

$$H_1=\partial_{\bar z_1}-t\partial_{z_2},\qquad H_2=\partial_{\bar z_2}+t\partial_{z_1};$$

They annihilate the displayed holomorphic coordinates. Together with $\partial_{\bar t}$ they form a direct local frame of $T^{0,1}Z$. Here $H_i$ are the constant-$t$ chart lifts; their projected complex alpha-plane is intrinsic, but this chart splitting is not asserted to be the global metric splitting. Globally let $V^{0,1}=\ker(d\pi)\cap T^{0,1}Z$, and let $H^{0,1}$ be its Fubini–Study orthogonal complement. Its lifts project to the same alpha-planes and may differ from the displayed $H_i$ by vertical components. All global horizontal/vertical form decompositions use this orthogonal splitting; local computations may use the displayed constant-$t$ splitting after retaining the resulting frame and normalization factors. The second projective chart supplies the same alpha-plane at $t=\infty$. The line bundle $\mathcal O_Z(-1)$ is the tautological holomorphic line bundle and $\mathcal O_Z(-2)=\mathcal O_Z(-1)^{\otimes2}$.

At a finite point of the positively oriented stereographic chart in the definition of the incidence geometry, let $A$ be a smooth connection and $F_A$ its curvature. For $t\in\mathbb C$, evaluate $F_A$ on $H_1=\partial_{\bar z_1}-t\partial_{z_2}$ and $H_2=\partial_{\bar z_2}+t\partial_{z_1}$. Then $F_A(H_1,H_2)=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb C$ if and only if the self-dual part $F_A^+=(F_A+*_gF_A)/2$ vanishes at that point. Let $E\to S^4$ be a smooth finite-rank Hermitian bundle with smooth unitary connection $A$, and let $F$ be a holomorphic bundle on $Z=\mathbb CP^3$ smoothly identified with $\pi^*E$ so that its Dolbeault operator is the ordinary vertical Dolbeault operator and the connection-horizontal alpha-plane operator from the incidence definition. Fibrewise harmonic projection of a global Dolbeault representative defines a linear map

$$\mathcal P_A:H^1(Z,F\otimes\mathcal O_Z(-2))\longrightarrow\Gamma(S^4,E).$$

Every global closed representative $\alpha$ has a unique decomposition $\alpha=\alpha_H+s\sigma+\bar\partial_F\gamma$, where $s=\mathcal P_A[\alpha]$, $\alpha_H$ is horizontal, $\sigma$ is the normalized fibre-harmonic generator, and the vertical correction $\gamma$ is smooth and glues over the base. The map is well defined and injective. The comparison is supplied by the local analytic Dolbeault-resolution theorem; no algebraic-to-analytic comparison is assumed.

Assume the conditional analytic comparison and the hypotheses of the injective-edge lemma, with $A$ a smooth unitary anti-self-dual connection. The unique correction of $s\sigma$ that removes the horizontal-vertical component of its Dolbeault differential has remaining component $(\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2)s$ in a nonvanishing local frame. $$\mathcal P_A\bigl(H^1(Z,F\otimes\mathcal O_Z(-2))\bigr)\subseteq\ker(\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\xi\in H^1(Z,F\otimes\mathcal O_Z(-2))$ and set $s=\mathcal P_A(\xi)$. By [F2] the map is injective, and [F3] gives $(
abla_A^*
abla_A+2)s=0$. Since $S^4$ is compact without boundary and $
abla_A^*$ is the formal adjoint, integration gives $0=\int_{S^4}\langle(
abla_A^*
abla_A+2)s,sangle\,d\mathrm{vol}_g=\int_{S^4}(|
abla_As|^2+2|s|^2)\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$. Both integrands are nonnegative, so $\int_{S^4}|s|^2=0$.

On $Z=\mathbb CP^3$ use the incidence equations $\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2$, $\mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2$, with infinity fibre $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0$. Suppose $F$ is a holomorphic bundle smoothly identified with $\pi^*E$ and its Dolbeault operator is the ordinary vertical derivative and the $A$-horizontal alpha-plane operator. Then

$$H^1(Z,F\otimes\mathcal O_Z(-2))=H^1(Z,F^\vee\otimes\mathcal O_Z(-2))=0.$$

This applies to arbitrary reducible and flat summands. It assumes no algebraic-to-analytic GAGA, monad, or inverse ADHM normal form as an independent premise.

Let $S^4={X\in\mathbb R^5:|X|=1}$ have its unit round metric and the orientation which, on the stereographic chart $S^4\setminus\{\infty\}\cong\mathbb R^4$, is $dx_0\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$. Put $z_1=x_0+ix_1$, $z_2=x_2+ix_3$, and $r^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$; in these coordinates the metric is $g=4(1+r^2)^{-2}\sum_{\mu=0}^3dx_\mu^2$. Identify $\mathbb H^2$ with $\mathbb C^4$ using a right quaternionic structure $j$ with $j^2=-1$, put $Z=\mathbb CP^3=\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb H^2)$, and define $\pi:Z\to\mathbb HP^1=S^4$ by $\pi(\ell)=\ell+j\ell$ for a complex line $\ell\subset\mathbb H^2$. Its fibres are projective lines $L_x\cong\mathbb CP^1$. In homogeneous coordinates $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]$, the fibre over finite $z=(z_1,z_2)$ is the line

$$\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2,\qquad \mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2,$$

and the fibre over infinity is $L_\infty=\{\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\}$. Give $Z$ the Fubini–Study metric induced by the standard Hermitian metric on $\mathbb C^4$ and give $\mathcal O_Z(-2)$ its induced Hermitian metric. On the incidence chart $\lambda_1\ne0$, set $t=\lambda_2/\lambda_1$, $\mu_1/\lambda_1=z_1-\bar z_2t$, and $\mu_2/\lambda_1=z_2+\bar z_1t$. The horizontal complex directions of type $(0,1)$ are spanned by

$$H_1=\partial_{\bar z_1}-t\partial_{z_2},\qquad H_2=\partial_{\bar z_2}+t\partial_{z_1};$$

They annihilate the displayed holomorphic coordinates. Together with $\partial_{\bar t}$ they form a direct local frame of $T^{0,1}Z$. Here $H_i$ are the constant-$t$ chart lifts; their projected complex alpha-plane is intrinsic, but this chart splitting is not asserted to be the global metric splitting. Globally let $V^{0,1}=\ker(d\pi)\cap T^{0,1}Z$, and let $H^{0,1}$ be its Fubini–Study orthogonal complement. Its lifts project to the same alpha-planes and may differ from the displayed $H_i$ by vertical components. All global horizontal/vertical form decompositions use this orthogonal splitting; local computations may use the displayed constant-$t$ splitting after retaining the resulting frame and normalization factors. The second projective chart supplies the same alpha-plane at $t=\infty$. The line bundle $\mathcal O_Z(-1)$ is the tautological holomorphic line bundle and $\mathcal O_Z(-2)=\mathcal O_Z(-1)^{\otimes2}$.

Let $L=\mathbb CP^1$ and let $\mathcal O_L(k)$ be the degree-$k$ holomorphic line bundle. For the smooth Dolbeault complexes on $L$, the cohomology groups satisfy

$$H^{0,0}_{\bar\partial}(L,\mathcal O_L(-1))=H^{0,1}_{\bar\partial}(L,\mathcal O_L(-1))=H^{0,0}_{\bar\partial}(L,\mathcal O_L(-2))=0,\qquad H^{0,1}_{\bar\partial}(L,\mathcal O_L(-2))\cong\mathbb C.$$

The canonical bundle is $K_L\cong\mathcal O_L(-2)$; the last group is one-dimensional, and the first three vanish.

Assume full AC and the following analytic comparison: for $r\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, every finite-rank holomorphic vector bundle $G$ on $X=\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ has a canonical isomorphism $H^q(X,\mathcal O(G))\cong H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,G)$ for every $q\ge0$, and for $G=\mathcal O_X$ one has $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(X,\mathcal O_X)=0$ for $q>0$. Let $E\to S^4$ be a smooth finite-rank Hermitian bundle with smooth unitary connection $A$, and let $F$ be a holomorphic bundle on $Z=\mathbb CP^3$ smoothly identified with $\pi^*E$ so that its Dolbeault operator is the ordinary vertical Dolbeault operator and the connection-horizontal alpha-plane operator from the incidence definition. Fibrewise harmonic projection of a global Dolbeault representative defines a linear map

$$\mathcal P_A:H^1(Z,F\otimes\mathcal O_Z(-2))\longrightarrow\Gamma(S^4,E).$$

Every global closed representative $\alpha$ has a unique decomposition $\alpha=\alpha_H+s\sigma+\bar\partial_F\gamma$, where $s=\mathcal P_A[\alpha]$, $\alpha_H$ is horizontal, $\sigma$ is the normalized fibre-harmonic generator, and the vertical correction $\gamma$ is smooth and glues over the base. The map is well defined and injective. The comparison is supplied by the local analytic Dolbeault-resolution theorem; no algebraic-to-analytic comparison is assumed.

derivations.claim: For $x\in U_N\cap U_S$, both chart computations restrict the same global closed form to the same fibre $L_x$. They use the same fibre Dolbeault operator and normalized harmonic projection, so both give the same value $s(x)$. If the global representative changes by $\bar\partial_F\beta$, its vertical restriction changes by $\bar\partial_V\beta$; harmonic forms are orthogonal to exact forms, so the harmonic projection is unchanged. Hence the chart sections agree and are independent of the representative, and they glue to a global section on $S^4$.

If the glued section is zero, the decomposition in [F2] writes the global representative as a horizontal $(0,1)$-form plus a global Dolbeault-exact term. Closedness makes the horizontal form fibrewise holomorphic with coefficient bundle $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. Its holomorphic-section space is zero by the fibre calculation in [F2], so the horizontal form vanishes; the original class is exact and is therefore zero. Thus the global map is injective. A formula on one chart supplies neither the overlap equality in step 1.1 nor this zero-kernel argument.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the finite
coherent-resolution and cohomological suppliers. Let $k$ be a field and let $X$
be a smooth equidimensional $k$-scheme of finite type
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]), with Chow ring $A^*(X)$
([[thm-intersection-product-and-chow-ring-of-a-smooth-scheme]]) and
vector-bundle group $K^0(X)$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme]]).
When $X$ is additionally quasi-projective,
[[lem-k-zero-vector-bundles-versus-coherent-sheaves]] identifies this group with
coherent $K_0(X)$; that extra hypothesis is required for the coherent-group
extension. Write $A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q}:=A^*(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$. If $n=\dim X$,
$A^i(X)=A_{n-i}(X)=0$ for $i>n$, since there are no negative-dimensional
integral cycles. Every series below is evaluated only through degree $n$;
in particular positive-codimension elements are nilpotent. For the rank-zero
bundle the empty root list gives $\operatorname{ch}(0)=0$ and
$\operatorname{td}(0)=1$.

**Chern roots.** The **Chern roots** of a finite locally free
$\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ are formal symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_r$ with the property that the elementary symmetric functions in the
$x_i$ are the Chern classes: $e_i(x_1,\dots,x_r)=c_i(\mathcal E)$
([[def-chern-classes-of-a-vector-bundle]]); by the splitting principle every
symmetric polynomial expression in the $x_i$ with rational coefficients defines
a well-defined element of $A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q}$
([[lem-chern-class-naturality-additivity-and-splitting]]).

**Chern character.** Define
$$\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E):=\sum_{j=1}^{r}e^{x_j}=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{1}{m!}\,p_m(c_1,\dots,c_m)\in A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q},$$
where $p_0:=r=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal E$, while for $m\ge1$ the
power sum $p_m(c_1,\dots,c_m)=\sum_jx_j^m$ is a universal polynomial in
the Chern classes. Thus $\operatorname{ch}_0(\mathcal E)=r$; explicitly
$\operatorname{ch}=r+c_1+\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)+\tfrac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3)+\cdots$
(the denominators are why we tensor with $\mathbb Q$).

**Todd class.** Define
$$\operatorname{td}(\mathcal E):=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{x_j}{1-e^{-x_j}}\in A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q};$$
explicitly
$\operatorname{td}(\mathcal E)=1+\tfrac12c_1+\tfrac1{12}(c_1^2+c_2)+\tfrac1{24}c_1c_2+\cdots$.
For a smooth $X$ the **Todd class of $X$** is $\operatorname{td}(T_X)$ for the
tangent bundle $T_X=\operatorname{Hom}(\Omega^1_{X/k},\mathcal O_X)$
([[def-sheaf-relative-differentials]],
[[thm-differentials-smooth-locally-free]]).

**Line bundles.** For an invertible sheaf $\mathcal L$ with
$x=c_1(\mathcal L)$: $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal L)=e^{x}$ and
$\operatorname{td}(\mathcal L)=x/(1-e^{-x})=1+\tfrac12x+\tfrac1{12}x^2-\cdots$.

**Well-definedness.** After truncation at degree $n$, the positive-degree
components of the Chern character and all components of the Todd class are
symmetric polynomials with rational coefficients in the Chern roots, hence
universal polynomial expressions in their elementary symmetric functions,
the Chern classes of [[def-chern-classes-of-a-vector-bundle]]. The degree-zero
component of the Chern character is the rank $r$. Thus the Chern character
depends only on the rank and Chern classes of $\mathcal E$, whereas the Todd
class depends only on its Chern classes. For locally constant ranks these
formulas are interpreted componentwise on the finite open-and-closed rank
loci. By the splitting principle of
[[lem-chern-class-naturality-additivity-and-splitting]], these values are
independent of the choice of flag bundle or filtration: any two filtrations
have the same rank and elementary symmetric functions, and hence give the
same polynomial values. Rational coefficients are needed for
the exponential and geometric expansions, which is why the target is
$A^*(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$. The tangent bundle is finite locally free
of rank $\dim X$ by [[thm-differentials-smooth-locally-free]], so its Chern
roots and Todd class are defined; the Todd class is multiplicative in exact sequences, whereas the Chern
character is additive, and the
identification of $K^0(X)$ with $K_0(X)$ on a quasi-projective $X$ lets the
character be evaluated on coherent classes through the finite locally free
resolutions of [[lem-k-zero-vector-bundles-versus-coherent-sheaves]].

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed $R$-oriented smooth $n$-manifold, where $R=\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2$, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed $R$-oriented embedded $z$-submanifold. Put $r=n-z$ and orient $\nu_Z=TM|_Z/TZ$ in tangent-first order: $\det TM|_Z=\det TZ\otimes\det\nu_Z$. Choose a smooth metric and a tubular chart whose differential induces the identity on this normal quotient; restrict to a sufficiently small closed disk bundle. Such normalized charts exist by the construction in [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]].

The normalized Thom class $u_\nu\in H^r(D(\nu),S(\nu);R)$ corresponds to a class $\alpha\in H^r(M,M\setminus Z;R)$ by the punctured-fibre comparison and tubular excision. Write $\bar\alpha\in H^r(M;R)$ for its relative-to-absolute image. Then
$$\bar\alpha\cap[M]=(-1)^{rz}(i_Z)_*[Z]\in H_z(M;R).$$
Equivalently, $\bar\alpha=(-1)^{rz}D_M^{-1}((i_Z)_*[Z])$. The sign is the shuffle from tangent-first coordinates to normal-first cap evaluation. Over $\mathbb F_2$ all orientations are canonical and the sign disappears. A relative class capped directly with the absolute $[M]$ instead has relative homology as target; the displayed formula uses $\bar\alpha$.

ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and

$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where

([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$\rho_M:H^*(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^*(M;\mathbb R)$ be induced by
$\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Write $J_M$ for the natural de Rham
isomorphism from real de Rham cohomology to singular cohomology with real
coefficients.

For every finite-rank smooth complex bundle $E\to M$ with a Hermitian metric
and Hermitian connection $\nabla$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([c_j(\nabla)])=\rho_M(c_j(E)).$$
For every finite-rank smooth real bundle $V\to M$ with any real connection
$D$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([p_j(D)])=\rho_M(p_j(V)).$$
For every oriented Euclidean bundle $W\to M$ of even rank with a
metric-compatible connection $\nabla$, and its Thom-normalized Euler class,
$$J_M([e(\nabla)])=\rho_M(e(W)).$$
Here $c_j(\nabla)$, $p_j(D)$, and $e(\nabla)$ use the normalizations in
[[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]], while $c_j(E)$,
$p_j(V)$, and $e(W)$ are the published topological classes. In particular
$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for a complex line and
$p_j(V)=(-1)^j c_{2j}(V_{\mathbb C})$. These are equalities after passage to
real coefficients; no equality with integral torsion is asserted.

derivations.claim:
Exactness gives $0\to K\to\mathcal O^{2k+N}\to\mathcal O(1)^k\to0$ and $0\to\mathcal O(-1)^k\to K\to\mathcal F\to0$. Their classes in the Grothendieck group therefore give
$$
[\mathcal F]=(2k+N)[\mathcal O]-k[\mathcal O(-1)]-k[\mathcal O(1)].
$$
Additivity of Euler characteristic and [F4] give $\chi(\mathcal F)=(2k+N)-4k-0=N-2k$.

A fiber $L_x=\pi^{-1}(x)$ is a complex linear $\mathbb P^1\subset\mathbb P^3$. Its real codimension in $\mathbb P^3$ is $4$ and its real dimension is $2$, so the sign in [F3] is $(-1)^{4\cdot2}=+1$. Therefore $\pi^*u$ is Poincaré dual to $[L_x]$. The restriction of $\mathcal O(1)$ to this linear $\mathbb P^1$ has first Chern number $1$; [F2] then identifies its Poincaré dual as $H_{\rm top}^2$. Thus $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$.

In the algebraic Chow ring, [F1] and $H=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ give
$$
\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=(2k+N)-ke^{-H}-ke^H=N-kH^2,
$$
because $H^4=0$ on the complex threefold and the odd powers cancel. Thus $c_1^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=0$ and $c_2^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=kH^2$. In the underlying topological category the same exact sequences are exact sequences of complex vector bundles, so [F5] and the line-class identity $c_1(\mathcal O(1))=H$ give
$$
c(\mathcal F)=\frac{1}{(1-H)^k(1+H)^k}=(1-H^2)^{-k}=1+kH^2
$$
through degree six, since $H^4=0$. Hence the topological classes are $c_1(\mathcal F)=0$, $c_2(\mathcal F)=kH^2$, and $c_3(\mathcal F)=0$. The universal formulas $\operatorname{ch}_1=c_1$, $\operatorname{ch}_2=\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)$, and $\operatorname{ch}_3=\tfrac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3)$ then give the topological $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=N-kH^2$. This compares only the identical finite line-bundle resolution and its line class, not arbitrary analytic and algebraic cohomology.

Write $c_2(E)=m u$ for $m\in\mathbb Z$. Naturality of Chern classes and the pullback hypothesis give $mH^2=\pi^*c_2(E)=c_2(\mathcal F)=kH^2$ by steps 2.1 and 1.2. Since $H^2$ is a nonzero generator by [F2], $m=k$, proving both the stated Chern class and its evaluation on $[S^4]$.

citations.quote:
For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

For $r\ge1$, let $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ be the set of complex lines in
$\mathbb C^{r+1}$, with its quotient complex-manifold structure, and write
$[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]$ for the line through a nonzero vector
$(Z_0,\ldots,Z_r)$. For $i\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$ set
$U_i=\{[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]:Z_i\ne0\}$; its standard coordinates are the ratios
$Z_j/Z_i$ for $j\ne i$. For each integer $k$, the **projective twisting line
bundle** $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(k)$ is obtained by gluing the trivial
holomorphic line bundles $U_i\times\mathbb C$ with local frames $e_i^{(k)}$
and transition rule
$$e_j^{(k)}=\left(\frac{Z_j}{Z_i}\right)^k e_i^{(k)}\quad\text{on }U_i\cap U_j.$$
The transition factors are holomorphic and nowhere zero on the overlaps, with
$g_{ii}=1$, $g_{ij}=g_{ji}^{-1}$, and $g_{ij}g_{j\ell}=g_{i\ell}$ on every
triple overlap; hence they define a holomorphic line bundle. The sheaf
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(k)$ assigns to an open set the holomorphic sections of
this bundle, and $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}:=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(0)$ is the
structure sheaf.

derivations.claim:
On a chart $Z_j\ne0$ with $j\ne0$, put $w=Z_0/Z_j$. In local frames of
$\mathcal O(m-1)$ and $\mathcal O(m)$, multiplication by $Z_0$ is
multiplication by $w$ up to the invertible frame factor. The holomorphic
local ring has no zero divisors, so this map is injective on stalks. The
quotient map is restriction to $w=0$. If a holomorphic germ $f(u,w)$
restricts to zero there, then $f(u,0)=0$ and
$$
f(u,w)=w\,g(u,w),\qquad
g(u,w)=\int_0^1\frac{\partial f}{\partial w}(u,tw)\,dt.
$$
On a sufficiently small polydisc the integrand is holomorphic in $(u,w)$;
its locally uniformly convergent power series may be integrated termwise,
so $g$ is holomorphic and the germ lies in $(w)$. Thus the kernel of
restriction is precisely the image of multiplication. On a chart not
meeting $H$, the section $Z_0$ is nowhere zero, so multiplication is an
isomorphism and the quotient sheaf is zero. These stalk calculations prove
exactness of the first sequence for every $m$.

Tensor the exact $m=0$ sequence by the locally free line bundle
$\mathcal O(-1)$. Tensoring is exact because on each stalk this bundle is a
free rank-one module. By the transition rule in [F2], its restriction to
$H$ is $\mathcal O_H(-1)$; hence
$i_*\mathcal O_H\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\cong i_*\mathcal O_H(-1)$ on each
stalk. The resulting exact sequence is
$$
0\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-2)\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-1)
\to i_*\mathcal O_H(-1)\to0,
$$
as claimed.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and standard Hermitian spaces $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$ and $J:V\to W$. Define the complex and real polynomial expressions

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

derivations.claim: The adjoint of $b_z^\dagger$ is the column $b_z=(-B_2^\dagger+\bar z_2,\ B_1^\dagger-\bar z_1,\ I^\dagger)^T$. A covector $v^\dagger$ annihilates the image of $b_z^\dagger$ exactly when $B_i^\dagger v=\bar z_i v$ and $I^\dagger v=0$, equivalently $v^\dagger B_i=z_i v^\dagger$ and $v^\dagger I=0$. Such a nonzero covector annihilates every word vector $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, so stability implies surjectivity for every $z$. Conversely, if the word span $Q$ is proper, it is invariant under both $B_i$ and contains $I(W)$. The complex moment equation makes the induced pair on $V/Q$ commute, since $IJ(V)\subseteq I(W)\subseteq Q$. By [F2] its dual has a common eigenvector; pulling that covector back to $V^*$ gives $v^\dagger I=0$ and $v^\dagger B_i=z_i v^\dagger$ for some $z$, so $b_z^\dagger$ is not surjective.

A nonzero vector in $\ker a_z$ is a common eigenvector of $B_1,B_2$ contained in $\ker J$, so costability implies injectivity for every $z$. Conversely, if a nonzero common invariant subspace $Q\subseteq\ker J$ exists, then $IJ(Q)=0$ and the complex moment equation gives $[B_1,B_2]|_Q=0$. The restrictions commute and have a common eigenvector by [F2]; this vector lies in $\ker a_z$ for its eigenvalues $z_1,z_2$. Thus the two affine rank criteria are equivalent to stability and costability.

At the point $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]=[1:0:z_1:z_2]$, the displayed homogeneous maps reduce to $\alpha=a_z$ and $\beta=b_z^\dagger$. If the homogeneous maps have their monad ranks at every projective point, step 1.1 gives stability and step 1.2 gives costability.

Now suppose both moments vanish and the datum is regular. Step 1.1–1.2 give surjectivity of $b_z^\dagger$ and injectivity of $a_z$ for every finite $z$. Direct multiplication gives
$$
b_z^\dagger a_z=\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\qquad
b_z^\dagger b_z-a_z^\dagger a_z=\mu_{\mathbb R}=0.
$$
Hence $f_z=a_z^\dagger a_z=b_z^\dagger b_z$ is positive definite. On the real line over $z$, $\alpha=a_z\lambda_1+b_z\lambda_2$ and $\beta=b_z^\dagger\lambda_1-a_z^\dagger\lambda_2$; the cross Gram terms vanish by $b_z^\dagger a_z=0$, so $\alpha^\dagger\alpha=(|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2)f_z$ and $\beta\beta^\dagger=(|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2)f_z$. Therefore both maps have full rank whenever $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\ne(0,0)$.

Every projective point with $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\ne(0,0)$ lies on a unique real twistor line: after conjugating the second incidence equation, the system for $(z_1,\bar z_2)$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1&-\lambda_2\\\bar\lambda_2&\bar\lambda_1\end{pmatrix}$ and determinant $|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2>0$. On the line at infinity $(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0)$ the maps are $\alpha=(-\mu_1,-\mu_2,0)^T$ and $\beta=(\mu_2,-\mu_1,0)$, which are injective and surjective respectively whenever $(\mu_1,\mu_2)\ne(0,0)$. Direct expansion gives
$$
\beta\alpha=\lambda_1^2\mu_{\mathbb C}+\lambda_1\lambda_2\mu_{\mathbb R}-\lambda_2^2\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger.
$$
Thus the maps have the required ranks everywhere and compose to zero, so they form a bundle monad.

If $k=0$, then $V=0$, every endomorphism and map to or from $V$ is the unique zero map, and the conditions of stability and costability both hold vacuously. The affine map $a_z:0\to W$ is injective and $b_z^\dagger:W\to0$ is surjective; the homogeneous source and target are zero, so their required ranks hold at every projective point. The moments vanish and the monad is $0\to W\otimes\mathcal O\to0$. This verifies the zero-dimensional boundary case without using an eigenvector argument on the zero space.
